--- Page 11 ---
[Decorative border consisting of repeating floral and scrollwork motifs]

THE TREE OF SCIENCE
Of the VENERABLE AND DIVINELY
illuminated Father RAYMOND LULL of Majorca, whose admirable compilation and fruit will be indicated on the reverse of this (page). And in whose commendation is this extemporaneous Epigram by Josse Badius Ascensius to the pious reader.

Receive, from the scientific trees, the golden apples of Raymond, bright with heavenly light.
   Which, if you, reader, eat and store in your innermost heart:
You will call (them) Moly, or divine Ambrosia.
   Behold, in this arboreal forest you see trees endowed with four times seven members.
All (of them) filled with life-giving woods and fruits:
   Which, if you taste well, you will hunger for nothing more.
For every fruit of the mind grows in this tree,
   Which makes all things worthy of knowledge clear.
Therefore, although more excellent than Atlantean gold,
   This glory elevates citron tables.
Indeed, the trees of the Paradisiacal forest are not
   To be compared to this, even if those (trees) gave knowledge.
For those (trees) harmed Adam with forbidden fruits:
   These (trees) are able to give life to his kind.
Therefore, the Balearic (Islands) owe much to you:
   To whom these good things of yours, Llull, have been sent.

* 3

Proem.                                        1

[Woodcut illustration of a person sitting under a tree in a landscape with a city in the background]

GOD IN THY VIRTUE
the Tree of Knowledge begins.
[Small decorative ornament]

[Large decorative initial 'I'] N desolation and tears, Raymund, standing under a certain beautiful tree, was singing his desolation, so that he might somewhat alleviate the sorrow which he had, because he could not obtain the holy cause of Jesus Christ, and of all Christianity, and the public good in the Roman Curia. While he thus stood desolate in a certain beautiful valley, abounding in many springs and beautiful trees, a certain monk was coming through that valley, who heard Raymund singing. And because that song was sorrowful and pious, following the voice, he came to the place where Raymund stood. And by the habit which he saw on him, and by the great beard which Raymund had, he judged that he was some religious man of a foreign nation, and said these words to him: "Friend, what is wrong? And why do you weep? Tell me your name (if you please), and in what land you were born. For if I could help you in anything, I would gladly do my utmost. Because it seems to me that you are very desolate, and I would wish you to be in consolation, and that you would have consolation in our creator, by despising and forgetting the brief life of this world." Raymund answered him, and told him his name, and related to him a great part of his condition and life. It pleased the monk greatly, because he had found Raymund. To whom he said that he had sought him for a long time, so that he might ask him to compose a general book for all sciences, which could be easily understood, and by which his general art (which he had composed) could be more easily understood, because it seems too subtle to understand. And also because the other sciences, which ancient wise men discovered, are so difficult to understand, and require such a long time to learn, that scarcely anyone can reach the proper end. And there are also many doubts which some of the wise men have against other wise men. Therefore he asked him that he would make a general book which would help in understanding all sciences. Because a confused intellect brings great danger and the deprivation of great devotion for honoring God, knowing, loving, and serving Him, and for procuring salvation for one's neighbor. Raymund answered: "Lord monk, I have labored for a long time to investigate the truth by one method and by another. And by the grace of God I have come to the end and knowledge of the truth, which I so greatly desired to know, and which I have put in my books. And I am also desolate, because that which I so greatly desired and for which I labored for 30 years, I could not bring to completion. Also because my books are little appreciated, indeed I tell you, that many hold me for a fool because I involve myself in this business, on account of which I have no will to make or compose that book (for which you ask me) nor any other; indeed, I wish to remain desolate in my sadness. And because our Lord Jesus Christ has so few Christian lovers in this world, I propose to return to the Saracens, to protest and to show-

4 The Elemental Tree.

[Left Column]

of them, to such an extent: that the body itself is a confused substance, subject to the accidents of elemental things. By the branches we understand the four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth, which are the substances of elemental things: sustained within them. And these themselves are insensible and incorruptible, inasmuch as they are simple. By the boughs we understand the four masses, namely the four composite and sensible elements, namely fire which we perceive in flame, and moving air, which is between us and the moon, and the water of the sea, springs, and rivers, and the earth, in which we dwell and are sustained. And these are the parts of the elemental tree. By the leaves we understand the accidents of corruptible corporeal things, such as quantity, quality, etc. By the flowers we understand the instruments of things, such as the hand, which is an instrument for working: and the foot for walking. By the fruit we understand the elemental things, such as stone, apple, man, lion, fish, bird, gold, and silver.

[Decorative border of repeating floral/knot patterns]

*On the first part of the elemental tree,*
*namely the roots. And first, on Goodness.*

[Large decorative initial I] N this part we intend to
give definitions of good-
ness and the other prin-
ciples: so that the principles may be known by these definitions. Goodness is a being by reason of which good acts good, and thus good is being: and evil is non-being. Goodness is the root of the elemental tree: inasmuch as the tree is good through goodness, and by reason of goodness acts good: inasmuch as it produces pri-

[Right Column]

mary and natural things, namely branches, boughs and its other parts, and the privation of it and its operations would be evil. And its operations are primary: inasmuch as all natural elemental things are derived from it: and are essentialized from its essence. Goodness is a universal principle for all parts that are good in the tree, such as the magnitude of the tree, which is good through goodness, and the same applies to duration, power, and the other parts. And therefore goodness is the root for all parts of the tree: which derive their likeness from it, namely that they are good through it. This general goodness in itself is full of itself and of the other parts. It is full of itself in itself, inasmuch as in itself it has essential and concrete parts, which are of its essence, species, and nature: namely, that which makes good, that which can be made good, and the act of making good. Goodness is full of the other parts: inasmuch as it is great through magnitude: and durable through duration: and powerful through power. Therefore, goodness is the root of the tree with completeness: which we said above, by which there is a complete reason: by which the tree is good and acts good. Hence, since goodness is full by itself and by another: it must be a substantial root, because if it were not: it would not be full of magnitude: since substance is greater than accident, nor would the tree be substantially good. And such a privation of substantiality would be evil: and the emptiness of the tree and its parts. Therefore, goodness is a substantial part: so that nature may not have the passion of emptiness. Goodness, inasmuch as it is great through magnitude, and durable through duration, and powerful through power: and so on for the others: it is subjected to accidents, which are likenesses: which from other parts

--- Page 19 ---
Arbor Elementalis. 5

...it assumes from parts, and insofar as other parts receive similarities from it, these are those similarities which accidents receive: such as magnitude which is good through goodness, and duration similarly, and power, etc. And in this is the general source for other accidents, which proceed from the substantial parts.

*On Magnitude.*

Magnitude is that being through which goodness, duration, etc. are great: encompassing all extremities of being. Magnitude is substantially the root of the tree: so that it itself may be substantially great, and that magnitude may be what it is, for if magnitude were not a substantial principle: smallness would be in goodness, duration, power, and virtue, etc. and it would not be what it is: nor would the tree be great through it, which is impossible. Therefore, magnitude is substantial in itself: and the similarities it gives are accidental, just as we said about goodness. But since magnitude is one part of the tree: the tree is substantially great through it: just as the whole is essentially the whole through its parts. And to prove that duration, power, and the other roots of the tree, with the exception of contrariety, are substantial parts: the proof we gave for goodness, magnitude, etc., which are substantial parts, suffices. However, we do not say that contrariety is a substantial part: as we proved in the general table. Through this magnitude, knowledge is had of the magnitude of the tree, which it has according to its roots, and according to its trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

*On Duration.*

Duration is a property: through which goodness, magnitude, etc. endure. Goodness endures through duration in its existence and action, just as duration, which is good in its existence and action through goodness. Hence, just as a root assumes influence from the earth with which it participates: so duration is the root whence goodness assumes influence for enduring in itself, and also for making firm the similarities which goodness gives to the other parts of substance. And what we say about goodness: follows for power, etc. Therefore, duration is the reason through which the tree, and all its parts, endure.

*On Power.*

Power is that, through which goodness, magnitude, duration, etc. can exist and act. Goodness is: and insofar as it is: it can be, for if it could not be, it would not be. Because goodness is thus under the aspect of power, insofar as it can be, just as power is under the aspect of goodness: insofar as it is good through goodness. And since goodness can have an operation in itself through power, namely to make good: which it could not have without power: it is necessary that power itself have the ability to make possible: through which goodness can have in itself the ability to make good, which it could not have: if power did not have the ability to make possible. And therefore power is the root of the tree with making good: insofar as making good is through making possible. And the same is true for making great, enduring, and the others. Wherefore in the tree, making possible follows from possible things, according to the nature of itself and its parts. And those things which are impossible in it: are impossible, because under the aspect of

--- Page 20 ---
6 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Elemental Tree.

[Column 1]

...because under the aspect of their principles they do not exist: for just as it is impossible that fire could essentially be converted into water, and water into fire, or one species into another.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning Wisdom.*

Wisdom is that by reason of which the wise person understands. In the elemental tree there are natural instincts, such as fire, which has a natural instinct to heat the air: so that it may have concordance with it, and to heat water: so that it may have contrariety with it, so that from concordance generation may follow, and from contrariety corruption. Since it is so, that generation has concordance with being, and corruption with non-being. Hence, by reason of this, fire has a natural instinct to perform these natural operations: although it does not have discretion. Therefore, in elements which do not have discretion, and have natural inclinations towards those ends for which they exist: natural instincts stand habituated in the form of wisdom or knowledge, which is in humans. And because of this, natural instinct is the root of the elemental tree: by reason of which natural instincts are habituated and diffused in it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning Will.*

Will is that by which goodness, magnitude, etc. are lovable. In the elemental tree, according to its nature, there is no spiritual will, but in it are habituated and sown the wills of irrational animals and the appetites of plants and elements, which are natural appetites for desired natural causes under the aspect of goodness, and so for the rest. Just as fire, which has an appetite for heating

[Column 2]

the air: so that it may give its likeness to it. And just as a plant which has an appetite for rain: so that it may live and grow from it. And just as a lion, which has an appetite for a lioness for the preservation of its species: and for drinking, so that it may give humidity to its dried and heated parts: and the same is true for the other elemental things. This natural appetite is the root of the elemental tree: so that it may have particular natural appetites habituated and diffused under the universal appetite, which we have mentioned.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning Virtue.*

Virtue is the origin of union, the goodness of magnitude, etc. Virtue arises from the unity of goodness in doing good: inasmuch as doing good will be virtuous from that which makes good and that which can be made good: in which virtue will be or arises: so that doing good may be virtuous, and that which makes good and that which can be made good are similarly virtuous. And the same is true of the emanation: which virtue makes from other primary and secondary causes. And this virtue is the root of the elemental tree, by which virtue it has power in itself and in its parts: so that they may be virtuous, and that they may perform virtuous operations.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning Truth.*

Truth is that which is true concerning goodness, magnitude, etc. And to verify is that which is true concerning doing good, magnifying, etc. Fire exists: and after it exists, it is true that it exists, because if its being were not true: it itself would not exist. Therefore, fire exists thus through truth in the true: just as through heat in heating, and through light in shining. This truth which places primary things in the true: is the universal root for other truths: which consist in the elemental tree. And it itself is the genus: and those are species diffused and habituated in the tree.

But in the elemental tree there is no difference of spiritual things, but of sensible things. And through that (difference), it has species sown or diffused within itself, differing from one another: such as the species of ox and ass, of apple and horse, of leaf and flower, and so concerning other sensible things existing as elements. And because of this, this difference is the root of the elemental tree. From which difference all specific differences are derived: existing in the tree in potency through matter, and in actuality through form.

On Concordance.

Concordance is that by which goodness, magnitude, etc., agree in one and in many. Many things agree in one and in many through concordance, such as goodness, magnitude, etc., which agree: so that they are parts of one substance, like the substance of an orchard, which is good and potent and great. They agree further, so that each (quality) remains what it is in substance: so that in that substance, difference is not lost,

[Column 1]

By means of power, just as goodness, magnitude, duration, power, etc., are principles through a principle which gives them its likeness, just as it receives likeness from them. We understand a general principle in two ways: namely, substantial and accidental. Substantial, such as the efficient, form, matter, and final cause. Accidental: such as quantity, quality, relation, and other general accidents. The principle which is efficient is like fire which begins to heat, and a natural agent which begins to generate, just as a human: who generates another human. The formal principle is like form, which informs matter, just as the vegetative form, which informs the matter of a tree: insofar as it makes that matter remain vegetative. The material principle is like the matter of iron, which is a principle for many things, such as for a nail, for a sword, and for a knife. The final principle is like a human: who is the final principle of all his parts, because all

      *Concerning Greatness.*

[Large initial M] reatness is the image of magnitude,
immensity, goodness, eternity, etc.
Greatness is in three modes. For there is a greatness
which is of substantial things, such as the substance of man,
which is greater in goodness and virtue than the substance
of an ass, and moreover, since it is of more things,
because in an ass there is no rationality, but
in man. There is another greatness, which
is between substance and accident, such as
substantial goodness, which is greater
than accidental goodness. There is another
greatness, which is between accident and accident,
such as seeing, which is greater in goodness
than heating, and understanding than seeing.
Through these greatnesses in the tree there can
be many greatnesses, and some greater than others,
just as fire, which is greater in pepper for heating
than water, and a nail than a hammer in its end,
and gold than iron for buying and
selling, and so concerning other things.

      *Concerning Equality.*

[Large initial Æ] quality is the subject in which
the end of concordance, goodness, magnitude,
etc., rests. This equality in the elemental
tree is a root in three modes.
Namely, equality which is between substance
and substance, such as Raymond and Martin,
who are equal in the species of man. And equality,
which is between substance and accident, such as
quantity, which is as great in extensiveness
as the corporeal substance existing under it.
And there is another equality between accident and
accident, such as a decoction made from two
plants, one being in the fourth degree
of heat, and the other in the fourth degree of cold,
which are equal in heating and cooling the patient.
There is one other proportional equality, which is
like the members in the substance of man,
which agree according to proportion,
although one member may be greater than another.
According to these modes of equality, equality is the root
of the elemental tree, in which are disposed and
habituated many natural and particular
equalities derived from the universal equality
(which we have mentioned before).

Minority is near non-being according to the comparison

than minority. Moreover, when things
come from non-being into being, they are first
in minority rather than in greatness.

This trunk and chaos is invisible by reason of the confusion in which it is, and because its parts are continuous and each is in the other, and because visibility is only of discrete parts, just like air, which participates with the eyes by contact, and indeed, the eyes cannot see it. This trunk is a substance by reason of its substantial parts, from which it is aggregated, or composed, namely, of substantial goodness and of magnitude, and others, and it is subject to the accidents of its parts. Hence, just as substance is made or constituted from substantial parts, so in it is constituted an accident from several accidents, namely, of the quantity of goodness and magnitude, and of the others, from which one general quantity is made, and composed of simple quantities and passed into a third category, from which specific quantities existing under species pass into another category, such as the quantity of a horse, an apple, or an ox, and this transition occurs through natural agents by way of generation. Therefore, the universal trunk is aggregated from substantial and accidental parts.

About the Branches of the elemental tree.

The Branches of the elemental tree are the four simple elements. And there are four so that in them there may be difference, concordance, and contrariety. For if there were three or fewer, these would not be received in them. And if there were five, one would be superfluous, because it suffices for difference that it be in concordance and contrariety, just as the difference which is between fire and air, and is in the concordance of heat in this, that fire and air are of a hot complexion. And it suffices that it be in the contrariety of water and fire: inasmuch as fire is hot and water cold. The same is true of earth, which must stand in the concordance of dryness, which is between fire and earth, and that it be in the contrariety of earth and air through dry and humid, which are contraries. But this could not be, if the elements were not four. The same is true of the concordance of fire and air, which must agree in heat. And similarly of air and water, which must agree in humidity. And of water and earth, which must agree in coldness. And this same is true in its way of contrariety, which must be subject to the hot and cold complexion, and similarly to the humid and dry complexion. As in pepper, in which are all these complexions, and it suffices for it that it be subject to the differences and concordances and contrarieties which we have mentioned. And furthermore, because the elements are four and no less nor more, they are disposed to be figured in elementates in a quadrangular, circular, and triangular figure, which three figures are indeed necessary to be assigned in elementates. The quadrangular figure is inasmuch as it is from four elements, and a straight line is made from fire to air through the concordance of heat, and from air to water through the concordance of humidity, and from water to earth through the concordance of coldness, and from earth to fire through the concordance of dryness. And from these four lines and concordances results in elementates a natural quadrangle: through which they are extended and ample. The circular figure is, inasmuch as certain elements enter into others, just as fire, which enters into air giving it its heat, which does not abandon its own proper subject, which is fire. And the same is true of air, which enters into water giving it its humidity. And water, which enters into earth giving it its coldness. In a similar way is earth, which enters into fire giving it its dryness. And therefore in elementates consists roundness, as in an apple and in the head of a human. The triangular figure is caused by the line which goes from fire to air, and from fire to earth, and from earth to air. And this triangle is composed of two concordant lines and one contrary. And the same is true of the triangle which is of air, fire and water, and of the triangle which is of water, air and earth, and of the triangle which is of earth, water and fire, and thus there are four triangles, which complete the quadrangle, and the quadrangle completes the circle. And therefore it is necessary that there be four elements and no more nor fewer, so that in elementates there may be fullness and not emptiness, so that between one element and the rest there can be difference, and the same for concordance and contrariety, it is necessary that there be certain and proper and appropriate qualities, by which the four elements are distinguished as concordant, contrary, and differentiated, such as heat, which is a proper quality.

Concerning the Branches of the Elemental Tree.

<R>HE branches of the tree are four, namely four masses, which are general members, which are perceptible, and composed of simple elements. Such as fire which we see in flame and charcoal, and which is in stone and iron. The second mass is air, in which we breathe and in which we stand, and which we perceive in smell and wind (which is moved air). The third mass is the water of the sea, rivers and springs, rain and dew, which we perceive with coldness, color, taste, sight and smell. The fourth mass is earth, in which we stand, and which is in stones and metals, which are congealed and desiccated earths. Each of these masses is composed of four simple elements, and from them are derived individualized substances existing under species, such as the body of man, of a tree, etc. We call these four masses the four branches of the general elemental tree. And we call them branches because they have conditions that are fitting for branches, which exist according to the dispositions of the aforementioned roots, just as 'that which makes good', 'that which can be made good', and 'to make good' in goodness are branches, each looking to the other: so that it is made good and each exists in the other. Therefore, in a similar manner, the four masses are branches in this, that among themselves each element has an action upon another so that it is 'elementated', which is good and produced from simple causes or things. Just as fire, which is 'ignificative', inasmuch as it is simple, and the other elements are 'ignificable' in the masses and in the elementated things, which are from species. And this is reciprocated, just as air, which is 'aerificative', and the other elements are 'aerificable' in the elementated things, whence, just as from the branches of a plant are derived leaves, flowers and fruits, so from the four masses are derived all individualized elementated things.

In these four branches and masses, the elements are 'mortified' and released, each 'mortifying' the other, just as fire 'mortifies' air with heat, so that water, which is contrary to it, does not infuse its humidity, and also 'mortifies' it with dryness, which it receives from earth, which is contrary to the other, and this to such an extent that air cannot defend itself from fire. And conversely, air 'mortifies' fire, inasmuch as it helps itself with water against heat, and with humidity against dryness. And so in its own way for water and for earth. Whence, just as in an orchard, matter is more digested in the branches than in the boughs, and in the boughs than in the trunk, so in the four masses, matter is more digested and more disposed than in the simple elements. And therefore we compare the four masses to branches, or as branches, without which no individualized elementated thing could follow from those simple elements themselves, because an elementated thing could not sustain the simplicity of the simple elements. In these general branches are habituated and disposed all the branches of special natural trees, and in them one number passes into another, just as one matter, which passes from one species into another through generation and corruption. The simple elements, however, always remain in their being inasmuch as they are simple, for if they were to lose their being in their branches, they would have no inclination either to the generation or to the composition of elementated things, since it is so that every natural being avoids non-being, and desires its complete being, and also because neither goodness, magnitude, and the other

[P]ER natural accidents we understand leaves. For just as leaves turn themselves towards the wind, from whatever direction it may come, so accidents turn themselves and relate to the conditions of natural substances. And just as leaves serve to preserve flowers and fruits against great heat and great cold, and moreover against great wind, so accidents serve to preserve the substances in which they are sustained, just as heat, which preserves by heating with the quantity of what is capable of being heated, and through heating, fire is ultimately preserved, wherefore it exists in its goodness and magnitude, duration and power, instinct and natural appetite. And also, just as leaves serve to adorn trees, so accidents relate to substance, so that it may be adorned and beautified by them. Wherefore, for all these reasons and many others, we compare leaves to the accidents of substances, which are general accidents in the elemental tree, which is general to other natural trees derived from it, just as the quantity of simple fire is general to all elemental quantities that are of its species. The general accidents are these: quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, habit, site, time, and place. There are other accidents, such as color, taste, heating, and heat, etc., which can exist in their aforementioned genera. Therefore, first we will speak and investigate concerning quantity, whence is its principle and origin, and how it is extended through the elemental tree. And afterwards we will speak of the other accidents.

To quantity, in as much as both principles are mixed, whence follows a composite which passes into a third number, just as wine diluted in a cup. According to this continuous and discrete quantity, which are in the primary causes, namely in the roots of the elemental tree, quantity extends itself into the trunk, into the boughs and into all its parts, under one species in the trunk, and under another in the boughs, and under another in the branches, and so for the other parts of the tree: just as iron which is under one form in a nail, and under another in a hammer, and under another in a knife. Therefore continuous quantity according to its species is indivisible and in species is continuous, just as iron, which is indivisible according to its species. For although it may be under the form of a knife or a nail, it always remains iron. According to in as much as the forms are diverse, it is divisible into discrete quantities. In a similar way it is concerning quantity in the elemental tree, and in other natural trees derived from it.

De Qualitate.

**Q**ualities of each of the roots are such by quality, just as goodness by making good, and magnitude by making great, and duration by making lasting, and so for the others. And therefore quality is the reason which preserves the proper number of things, just as fire, which is such by its own proper quality, namely by its own proper heat, which properly belongs to no other element but itself. And because of this, the simple remains with its own proper quality. And in as much as it is dry by dryness, which dryness is indeed a proper quality of earth: it is composite with other elements, with which it is confused in number. Whence that fire may be able

**Column 2**
to be simple and composite, two qualities belong to it, one proper and the other appropriated; the proper one belongs to it through its own heat: the appropriated one through dryness, which it receives from earth. And since quality extends itself into the proper and the appropriated, a being is signified to be such in two ways. One way is, when the being itself is signified simply and according to its own proper quality, as if it is asked what is that which is hot by itself, and it must be answered, that it is fire, since no being is hot by itself except fire. And furthermore if it is asked, what is that which is good by itself, it must be answered, that it is that being which has its own proper goodness by itself. Another way is, when a determined being is determined by an appropriated quality, and this is determined in another and by another, as when it is asked, what is that which is hot by fire, and it must be answered that it is air. There is however another mode of determination but it is confused; in which several qualities enter, such as earth and water, which can be heated by fire, and these come and are derived in a confused trunk from their roots, just as goodness, which makes magnitude good and by power, etc. The office of quality in the elemental tree is, that there may be several qualities in potentiality. And the roots of the tree help its office, because it is good that one being is not another, so that there can be a difference between one being and another, and also a concordance of purpose and the other roots. And therefore simple fire can actually be in the elements, and it is simple in itself by its own proper quality, and it is composite in other elements by reason of appropriated qualities. goodness. And passion, which is an accident, is the
likeness of the capability of being made good, which is a
substantial and essential part of goodness.
And for this reason, accidental action proceeds
from substantial action, and accidental passion
is born in substantial passion. And according
as action and passion, which are accidents, are derived
from primary things, they are in the trunk and
branches, and in other parts of the tree in
potency, and are in act brought forth by
natural agents, so that substantial action
produces accidental action from substantial passion in a passive
quality. And for this reason, substances
move accidents towards the perfections
of substances.

De Habitu.
Primary habits are from primary
things, such as the habit of goodness,
which is a likeness of magnitude,
insofar as magnitude has in habit the power
to magnify goodness, and goodness has in
habit the power to make magnitude good. And these habits,
extended throughout the entire tree, are primary
natural habits, in which secondary habits
are in potency, by which elemental individuals
are clothed. And for this reason, species
sown in the tree are primary habits from which
the roots of the tree and all its parts
are clothed, and natural agents, from primary
habits, by way of generation, clothe elemental
individuals, just as a lion, which generates another
lion, by taking from the elemental tree,
converting what it takes into its own species,
and habituating what it takes according to its species,
places it in potency so that from that habit which
it gives to the lion it generates, another lion
can be clothed. And thus successively, one habit
existing under another and one from another,
the species of the lion is preserved, just as
many particulars, which are preserved in their
utility, and each part in another, and the whole in its parts. From these
natural habits proceed artificial habits,
which are likenesses of natural ones, such as the habit
of acquired virtue, which is a likeness of the habit
of natural virtue, just as the likeness of natural virtue,
which is extended in justice, prudence,
fortitude, temperance and other
virtuous habits, which descend from these,
such as chastity, patience, humility,
etc. There are also other artificial habits, such
as the habit of grammar, logic, and
many others, and the habit of a cloak, and a tunic,
etc.

De Situ.
In primary causes, Situation is a general
principle for the situations of secondary
causes, as in goodness, in which are situated
that which makes good, that which can be made good,
and to make good, which are of its
essence, and goodness is situated in
them. Another mode of situation is that which is intermingled,
like goodness: which is situated
in magnitude insofar as it is great by magnitude,
and magnitude, which is situated in goodness,
insofar as it is good by goodness. These are secondary
situations, which are accidental and
likenesses of the primary situations. And indeed,
simples are situated in themselves and in
others, such as goodness, which is situated in
itself and in magnitude, as has been said.
And for this reason, situation consists in two ways
throughout the entire elemental tree, from which it follows
that all parts are situated in their whole,
just as all roots in the trunk of the tree, and the whole
in its parts, just as the trunk in its roots. And
the same for one part in another, such as goodness
which is situated in magnitude, and magni

--- Page 35 ---
**Arbor Elementalis. 21**

& magnitude in goodness. And because of this, some things are contained and some are containing. There is also another situation concerning things situated in discrete quantity, such as bones in flesh and wine in a bottle, and a man lying or standing in a room, and so on for other things according to the straightness, or obliqueness, or circularity of individual entities.

**De Tempore.**
Time is an indivisible being in itself, but it is divisible in another by reason of the motion of things, which are moved in it through motion from potentiality to actuality, or from one place to another, or by increase through generation or into diminution, or by decrease through corruption, or by alteration from one thing to another. Hence, just as iron is always one in terms of its species, although it is divided into several shapes, namely in the shape of a knife, a sword, and a hammer, so time is always one in itself, although it is divided into past and future time by reason of its substantial and accidental subjects existing under motions; therefore there are moments, hours, days, years. The figures and likenesses of time appear in the motions or movements of things. The first principle in which time is divisible consists in the roots of the tree, inasmuch as the likeness of one root moves into another in that each root gives its likeness to another. And from this first motion and principle proceed secondary principles and motions from potentiality to actuality in individual elemental beings, which appear in the figures of time, as is to be said. But its form is simple, and it can neither be seen nor felt, since it is the case that no indivisible form can be seen or felt. In this time the roots of the tree and all its parts consist, just as they consist in place, virtue, and power, without which they could not exist. And it is necessary that time be in a beginning, middle, and end, without which it could not be sustained in motion. How, however, time is without end and succession, we intend to prove in the everlasting tree.

**De Loco.**
Place is considered in two ways: the first way is inasmuch as place is in itself according to its essence; the second inasmuch as place is in another. The first is like place, which is that by reason of which many things can be placed in it and in another, because just as many things can be colored by color and heated by heat, and made good by goodness, in the same way they can be placed by place. And this universal place for things placed primarily consists in the roots of the tree, and they are in it, just as it is in goodness, inasmuch as it is good, and vice versa, since without place goodness could not exist. The second way is like place which is divided in another, or extends itself, as in goodness, in which the good-making, the good-able, and the act of making good are placed, and goodness in them, and the good-making in the good-able, and vice versa, and furthermore like goodness, which is placed in magnitude, inasmuch as it is induced by its likeness and vice versa. And from this second way, which concerns its place, proceed likenesses in individual elemental beings, whose likenesses are the container and the contained, which likenesses are visible, such as wine in a bottle, in which the container and the contained appear, and which have been brought from potentiality to actuality from confused places.

22 The Elemental Tree.

And first, what are in the tree like the trunk which is placed in its parts, and branches in the trunk and boughs in the branches. Therefore, species are actually placed in the tree, in which elemental individuals are potentially placed through universal matter, and habitually through general form, and are brought into act in the similitudes of place existing under discrete quantities, just as light, which is placed in a room, and the room in the air, and so on for other similar things. And these similitudes of place are visible, but the essence of place is invisible and cannot be perceived, because place exists indivisible.

Of the Flowers of the Elemental Tree.

We compare the flowers of the tree to natural instruments. And we do this because just as a flower is closer to the fruit than the leaves of a branch or bough, or the roots, so the instrument is closer to the thing operated upon, which instrument we call "to operate," which is from the operator and the operable, just as in writing or in the act of writing, in which the pen is closer to the letter than the hand, and the hand than the arm, and because from seeing follows sight, the eyes are instruments for seeing, and seeing is the work brought about in the instruments, which are the eyes, and the fruit is sight. This natural and general instrument is the center, to which the roots relate in operating, and the same is true for the trunk, branches, boughs, and leaves. And it is general to other instruments derived from it and particularized existing under the individuals of species, just as flowers in a vegetal tree, and eyes and tongue in a sentient tree, and so on for other similar flowers. And the general and invisible instrument cannot be perceived, and its similitudes and parts appear in individualized instruments, and brought from potentiality into actuality, in which operation occurs, from which fruit results in a vegetal tree. And the fruit is of the essence of the flowers, just as fruit is of the essence of the instrument in a sentient tree. And the instrument of the vegetal tree are the eyes, which are vegetated, and the fruit, which is the sensed, is from the instrument, which is "to sense," which is a flower existing closer to it than the flower of a vegetal tree. We say, however, that the sensitive and the sensible are instruments for the sensed, one by way of action, and the other by way of passion, just as man and woman, who are instruments for procreating a son, and these are instruments in the boughs, but "to generate" is the instrument in the flower, because it is closer to the generated, as has been said, which generated thing is of the essence of "to generate" itself, and "to generate" is produced from the essence and species of the father and mother. Therefore, the generated and the sensed are individualized, and pass into another number and another essence, and remain with the father and mother in one species.

Of the Fruit of the Elemental Tree.

The fruit of the elemental tree is the elementated thing, such as a stone, gold, an apple, a fish, a bird, a beast, and the body of a human. All these are elementated and individualized, and we call them fruit, because goodness, magnitude, power, and virtue have greater rest and end in them than in the trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, and flowers, and this is because in an apple (which is fruit) the species is preserved inasmuch as another apple is contained within the apple itself, and the same is true for the other things we have mentioned. The elementated is also fruit, because in it

in it the primary intentions of the primary
causes consist: because in this, that goodness gives its
likeness to magnitude and vice versa: in the fruit,
magnitude is aggregated to goodness more
than in the other parts of the tree, with goodness and
magnitude placing themselves by primary
intention in the fruit, and by secondary
intention remaining in the
flowers, leaves, branches, trunk, and roots.
And duration, power,
instinct, and natural appetites do the same. And for
this reason, fruits are at the tops
of the tree: and in them there is more
taste and utility than in other parts
of the tree. The fruit of the general
elemental tree is invisible: and can in no way
be sensed, but its individualized
and particularized forms can be sensed and seen.
such as an apple, gold, Martin's
and his falcon, a raven, a horse, and a fish. We have
spoken of the elemental tree and its
parts: and because we propose to
investigate the primary causes and forms sown in it:
we choose some of them, namely a hundred,
which we wish to investigate: so that we may have
knowledge of them, and so that through them
we may be able to know others (which are more
numerous) and also so that
through them we may be able to know other trees
better. And first, we propose to
direct our discourse to unity,
afterwards to plurality, and so
successively to others.

Of Unity. 1.

Unity is extended in the elemental
tree: inasmuch as it is one and
united from multiple unities, just as from
one general goodness: and from one general
magnitude, and so forth for others. Hence,
by reason of its unity and the unities: from
which it is united: many unities of things
are sown and diffused in it,
just as the unity of a plant, the unity of a horse,
and so forth for others.

Of Plurality. 2.

The plurality of things is sown
and diffused in the elemental tree, and this
is because it is of many things, and
also because each of them comes to it
with plurality: just as goodness,
which comes to it with that which makes good,
that which can be made good, and to make good: and magnitude,
which comes with that which makes great, that which
can be made great, and to make great, and so forth
for the others. Hence, just as from the elemental
tree one stone, one apple,
one bird, and other unities can
follow and be derived by reason of its unity: so
from it many stones, many apples, and
many birds can follow and be derived
by reason of its plurality. And for this reason,
plurality in it is a cause for many
pluralities, just as unity, which is a cause
for many other unities.

Of Simplicity. 3.

Simplicity in the elemental tree is
from primary causes, as from the simplicity
of goodness, magnitude, and the others:
and from the simplicity of fire and
air, and the other elements. And
the same holds for its simple accidents,
such as the simple quantity of goodness
and magnitude of fire and its heat
and the others, in which simplicity is sustained
throughout the entire tree:
inasmuch as the tree is of simple
primary and general causes. Hence,
just as goodness is the reason for the good to do
good: and magnitude for the great to
make great: so simplicity, which is
a general species and reason for many
simplicities derived from it and individualized
by natural agents.

**On Composition. 4.**

Composition in the elemental tree
is a suitable species, from which many
compositions can be derived and
produced. And this is so: because the tree is composed of many
causes. Hence, just as a natural member naturally
reflects its extremities, from which its beginning
and end (are known): so that everything of the elemental tree
may reflect its composition.
Which could not be, if any composition
were not the primary cause for many
individuated elemental compositions.

**On Form. 5.**

The elemental tree is informed
by general form, as has been said in
its trunk, and therefore of all things, that form
may reflect the nature of form, the
general form itself existing as a principle
for many forms sown and diffused in it,
so that through it its elemental
individuated things may be informed, and
that they may be of its essence, so that their
informing may be with the magnitude of goodness,
duration, power of beginning, and end.
Therefore, of all things, that the forms of a goat,
an eagle, an orchard, etc., may be sown
in it and produced by natural agents.

**On Matter. 6.**

The elemental tree is of general matter,
according to what is to be said in its trunk,
from which matter many particular matters
are sown and diffused in it: and in species
sustained with the help of quality: and brought
into act by natural agents, as in a goat,
an eagle, and in other individuals.
And this exists by every reason of goodness,
magnitude, duration, power: and by reason
of greater natural appetites.

**[Column 2]**

**On Genus. 7.**

Substance is the genus, from which are
many species of the elemental tree.
Substance is so: because it is aggregated
from many substantial parts.
This substance is really the genus of all things,
and because it is composed of real and general
goodness: and of real and general magnitude,
and other things, and therefore of all things,
that it may be the primary substance for other
many special substances, just as the trunk
which is a substantial and general part,
which relates to many substantial and general parts:
from which branches and boughs (come).
Therefore, the genus is a real being
in the elemental tree, and if it were not a real
and substantial being, but merely intentional:
according to how a logician considers it:
the general principles would be lost in the elemental tree,
so that they would not be real beings of the primary cause.
And in their loss, the elemental tree would be lost,
which could not be a real being, and in its loss
no secondary cause would be from the primary:
so that each individual would be from itself,
and not from another, which is impossible:
Therefore, the genus is a real being,
in which natural species are sustained.

**On Species. 8.**

In the elemental tree, species are
sown, under which are individuated
elemental things, and because in it they are
sown really, not only are beings considered
in reason, nay, they are real beings,
for if they were not real beings,
goodness would not be the primary cause for good,
that it might act as good, and it would follow
that goodness would make it from another cause also,
and not from itself, and magnitude for the great similarly,
therefore, good would not be from goodness: nor

**On the Concrete. 12.**
IN the elemental tree are primary concrete things, which are general causes for secondary concrete things, just as in goodness [there are] the bonificative, the bonificable, and to bonify, which are its essential parts, and similarly in magnitude: in which are essential concrete things, according to the magnificative, the magnificable, and to magnify, and from these results a concrete thing which is good and great, just as the trunk of a tree, which is good and great, and its branches similarly, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits, which are concrete things, good and great. And in these are found individual concrete things, just as a stone which is good and great, and an apple similarly.

**On Generation. 13.**
GEneration is a general principle in the elemental tree, and its principle is in multiplication, which occurs from goodness and magnitude and other first causes insofar as they aggregate themselves to be one composite, which is in the 3rd number, which is the trunk, as has been said. And in this trunk are potentially the generations of particular trunks, and in the branches are the generations of particular branches. And the same is in its own way true of boughs, leaves, flowers, and D frui...

Of Emptiness. 17.

Emptiness is considered in two
ways: according to one, it is a real
being, and according to the other, intentional
and not real. It is a real being like a prin-
ciple and a middle, which relate themselves to the end
for which they exist, and cannot have it:
just as water in pepper, which has a natural
appetite, can be overcome in pepper; and the same is true of
fire in its own way, which has a natural appetite
in pepper, that it can despoil and deprive the entire essence of water, so that
it can have greater concordance with air and earth,
and that its contrary, which is water, can inflict no
difficulty upon it. Intentional emptiness
is that which the intellect con-

to be empty of water or wine or another
visible corporeal thing, and also when it con-

**28 Of a hundred forms.**

Water has contraries at its centers, just as water and earth, which are in the sphere of fire, have an appetite for being here below, and they come here below with the gravity which they have, because with it they move themselves here below. And when they ascend above, they do not ascend with gravity, because ascending and gravity are contrary to each other, but they ascend by violence and by the coercion of celestial bodies, which, together with fire and air (the latter being themselves conjoined with water and earth), attract them to the sphere of fire, so that in that water and earth they may receive the benefit of the planets, and that with that [benefit] they may descend here below. And by reason of this general gravity or ponderosity, which we have mentioned, fruits have an inclination: those which are on a tree, like an apple in an orchard, that it should descend here below onto the surface of the earth. And the same is true of rain, snow, and dew, from which they have received benefit from superior causes.

**Of Totality. 22.**

In the elemental tree there is a totality which is general to many special totalities, just as goodness, which is general to all individuated elemental goodnesses, like the goodness of iron, which is general to the goodness of a sword, a knife, a nail. And the same is true of magnitude and other things. Therefore, the totality of the tree places its likeness in the fruit of the orchard, because in the apple are potentially all the likenesses of the elemental tree, namely, the likenesses of roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits. And in this totality of the elemental tree, all species are thus sown, which relate to their individuals, just as all the likenesses of the elemental tree are sown in the apple, and therefore from one apple many apples are produced. The same follows in a fish, a bird, a human, and a lion.

**Of Parts. 23.**

In the elemental tree there are parts general to other particular parts, just as its part which is goodness, is general to another part of the whole, as for example to the part of an apple which is good, and to the part of a fish which is good, and to the part of a horse which is good, and so for others. And because of this, all parts of the elemental tree are general to the parts of individuated natural substances. And by such a nature, many parts are sown in one part, and in individuals there are certain parts within others, as in pepper, in which fire is in heat, and heat in fire, and fire in air, inasmuch as it enters into it with its heat, and air in fire, inasmuch as it is clothed with its heat and dryness. Hence, according to what has been said about totality and partiality, it is signified how in individuals there are natures and properties, and how certain parts are in others, and the whole in its parts, and the parts in its whole: and this through the natures and properties which are in the elemental tree.

**Of Interiority. 24.**

General and natural interiority is in the elemental tree: from which natural and special interiorities descend and are in trees, which are derived from it. And this general interiority is signified in its roots, like "to make good," which is within the one making good and the one capable of being made good. And from this "to make good" which is within the elemental tree, the "to make good" which is in the apple has the nature that it is within the "bonificativum" (that which makes good) and the "bonificabilem" (that which can be made good).

--- Page 43 ---
**On the Hundred Forms. 29**

...capable of being made good, which are in the apple. And in this context, properties are signified by which the contained things stand within the containing things, just as the seed which is inside the apple, and a man inside a room, and individuals within their species, and all elemental things within the elemental tree.

**On Exteriority. 25.**

General exteriority is in the elemental tree, from which particular and special exteriorities descend. And general exteriority is through difference, which makes its parts differ, just as goodness, which is different from magnitude, and the trunk from its branches, and one branch from another, and so concerning the other parts of the tree. And because of this, there are many things which differ in species, just as magnitude, which is outside the species of goodness. And because of this, in elemental things, some things are outside others, just as an apple which is outside the leaves, and outside the species of a rose, and of a horse: and just as the container, which is outside the contained thing, just as a bottle, which is outside the wine. Hence, in natural things, all these particular exteriorities are possible, by reason of the general exteriority, which we have mentioned.

**On Station. 26.**

General station consists in the elemental tree, from which particular natural stations descend, just as a tree which stands as that which is in its own number, and the same is true of its parts such as its goodness, magnitude, etc., which do not abandon their number, because their duration preserves their proper being. And from this station, as it were, descend the stations of elemental individuals, just as an apple, which stands in its own number, and Martin's horse and Martin likewise, and also the station of a stone, which stands in one place and does not move itself, and a nail fixed in a post, and eyes in a face, and so concerning other things similar to these.

**On Motion. 27.**

General motion is in the elemental tree, which is one of its parts, and is general to all motions of elemental individuals, and its principle is in the root of the tree, as was said above. And this also must be said, namely that in the goodness of the tree, it is to make good the motion from the good-making and the capable-of-being-made-good in making good magnitude, duration, etc. And that from all roots, a trunk is made good, magnified, etc., and the same concerning the motion of the trunk into branches, and so concerning the boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruit. However, this general motion does not move itself in the elemental tree from one place to another; nor does it move itself by way of alteration nor of growth, for if it did, it would not be in the whole tree. But it is a general part disposed to the motions of elemental individuals from potency into the act of movers, so that they can exist through generation; or from being into privation through corruption; or from one quality to another, just as coldness into heat, and a man who moves himself from one place to another, and who in his joints thus has a natural potency of motion through general motion, just as a body has through a general body, and quantity through general quantity. This same thing follows concerning motion, which is in the species of alteration, just as wine which has been altered into vinegar. And the same concerning growth, just as a man who is moved from a small quantity to a large one.

--- Page 44 ---
**30 Of a hundred forms.**

**Of Hardness. 28.**
Hardness is one general part, which
is in the elemental tree, from which
all hardnesses of individual elemental
things descend. And this general hardness
is of fire and earth, and water
and earth. It is of fire and earth, because fire
heats the earth, and earth dries the fire,
and therefore humidity does not have its power
in that place, and this appears in a tile
which is hard, because fire
dries it, and also in a stone which
is dried powder and congealed by water,
which restricts it, which
stone is indeed hard through water and
earth, which in it kill heat and humidity,
and this same is true of the hardness of bones and of the perfection of a shell,
and so of other elemental things, which
are hard through the aforesaid general
hardness: which is the source from which issue
particular hardnesses.

**Of Softness. 29.**
Softness is in the elemental
tree, from which descend the softnesses
which are in individual elemental things.
And it is in the elemental tree of
fire and air, and of air and water, which
fire heats the air, dissolving one
part from another, and heats water,
killing the congelation which is
in individuals through the restriction of water,
and humidity extends itself through water and
earth, killing the dryness of the earth with air,
with the help of fire, which heats the earth,
and which destroys the concordance of earth
and water, and because of this, molten
metals are soft through the humid and
the hot, and also sanguine
and phlegmatic people, and so of other similar
things to these, which are soft through the
general softness which is in the elemental
tree.

**Of Length. 30.**
Length is in the elemental tree
a universal cause for the lengths
of trees produced from it. Which
length indeed stands in the elemental
tree through the natural extensiveness
of its branches, and also

De centum formis. 31

filling air. And for this reason, plants extend their branches broadly.

*On Depth. 32.*

Depth in the elemental tree is caused by its branches, and also by its roots. And this is signified in 'to make good' and 'to magnify', which signify that depth is in the middle, inasmuch as it stands in the middle of the branches. And from this general depth descend special depths, such as the depth of an apple, and of bones, in which are the seeds of the apple, and the marrow of the bones. And this depth is more through cold and dry than through any other complexion, because earth is of spherical form, and water has a restrictive nature.

*On Potency. 33.*

Potency is in the elemental tree in two ways. One way is: inasmuch as its aptitude disposes that from it individuals can be produced from potency into act, such as an apple, which is in it primarily in potency, in that it is primarily for the apple-bearing capacity: and it stands in potency in the apple-bearing capacity, before it is brought into act. And this second potency is from the first, which first is indeed sown in the elemental tree, and thus is a real part of it, like its other parts: the second way of potency is that which is active, such as the power of heating or of seeing. And this mode is in potency in the first, whence in the good-making capacity of goodness; and the impossibility-making capacity of power, etc. And it is brought into act in the potency of the elements, which we have mentioned, such as the visual power, which was previously in potency rather than in act.

[Right Column]

*On the Object. 34.*

An object is in two ways in natural things: one is internal, and the other is external. That which is internal is like the capacity to be made good, which is of the essence of goodness, and is the object of the capacity to make good, which is of the essence of goodness. The object which is external is like magnitude, which is capable of being made good, and color which is visible. The object which is internal is general to external objects moved in internal objects, such as bread which is capable of being vegetated, and its matter is moved in vegetability, which is of the essence of the vegetating agent, which transmutes bread into flesh. This internal objectification is in the elemental tree, such as the capacity to be made good of the elemental tree, which is the object of the capacity to make good, which capacity to be made good is a general object, from which descend the objects of elemental individuals, such as in a plant, the capacity to be planted, and in a sentient being, the capacity to be sensed. And because of this, one capacity to be an object is from another.

*On Act. 35.*

Act is twofold: one is that which is brought from potency into act, such as a cluster of grapes, which a man eats, which is in act, but was in potency. There is another act, which is the work of active and passive potency, such as heating and seeing, etc. The first act is in the elemental tree a real part, not brought from potency into act, but only stands in it through creation, and through it the tree is actually so, just as a good thing, which is good through goodness, and great through greatness, and this act is general to the acts of elemental individuals, who substantially and accidentally come from potency into act: such as the act of the apple-bearing capacity, in which

--- Page 46 ---
**32 De centum formis.**

[Left Column]
...in which the apple is in actuality, and the same is true of its color. Indeed, this act of the apple tree was previously in potentiality before the apple was in potentiality or actuality in the apple tree itself.

**De Prioritate. 36.**

The elemental tree is primary by priority to the vegetative and sensible tree. And this is because priority is one of its parts, through which it is the primary tree, just as through it goodness and magnitude and other primary natures relate to secondary priorities, which are in the vegetative and sensible tree, and the subject of this priority is, insofar as goodness is primary to the goodness of magnitude, and magnitude is primary to the magnitude of goodness, and insofar as roots are primary to the trunk, and the trunk to the branches, and the branches to the boughs, and so successively up to the fruit of the apple tree, in which they place their similitudes sustained in potentials in which the apple exists potentially, and the similitudes come into act then, when the apple is generated. However, the priorities of the elemental tree do not stand successively according to time, so that first s

From these natural intentions, men take similarities and an example in having accidental and artificial intentions: just as a man who draws iron from a stone with the intention, namely, that he can make an axe, a plowshare and a hoe, a needle and a knife, and who makes houses for dwelling, and a ship for gaining, and so concerning other things similar to these. There is, however, a certain first intention and another second. The first intention is through the end and completion. And the other is in the means, by which the beginning passes to the end. The intention which is for the end, is like dwelling, and the intention which is in the means, is like a room, and like a tree, which is for fruit, and fruit, which is for man, so that he may live from it, and man, who is that he may know God, love, remember, praise, honor and serve, and so concerning other things similar to these.

**On Order. 46.**

Order is a form which is so fixed in the elemental tree, as are the non-wandering stars in the firmament. And it is thus the reason for the elemental tree that its parts are ordered, just as goodness is the reason for them to be good, and magnitude, for them to be great. And in this order, so natural and general, are habituated the orders below: just as in pepper, in which the elements are graded in order, and just as in an orchard, in which transformations from one species to another occur in order: in which there are branches before twigs, and flowers before fruits. From these natural orders, men take similarities in having ordered customs in living.

**On Operation. 47.**

In the elemental tree, operation is a natural and general form for operations existing below, sustained in elemental individuals and moved by them, whence the elemental tree thus has itself to act through its operation, which is one of its simple parts, just as fire has itself to heat, and power to its object. And because of this, the individuals below have themselves to act according to the nature of the operation existing above, which is the reason for their operations, just as in an orchard: in which there is operation from the roots into the trunk, and from the trunk into the branches, and so concerning others. From this natural operation, men take an example in having artificial operations according to mechanical arts.

**On Influence. 48.**

In the elemental tree, influence is a general form for the influences of elemental bodies. And this influence is a general reason for the influences of the roots, in which it is sustained like goodness, which influences its similarity to magnitude, duration, power, and others, and magnitude, duration, power, which influence their similarities to goodness, and so concerning the trunk, which influences its similarity to the branches, and one branch to another, and so concerning twigs, leaves, flowers and fruit. Wherefore this general influence is the cause of influence here below, just as in an orchard: in which influence is naturally made from one to another: and tasting, to which flavor is an influx. And the same is true of sight, to which color is an influx, and to smell, odor, and so concerning other natural things.

About Reflux. 49.
IN the elemental tree, the beneficent
flows into the beneficiary itself, the
beneficiary flows back to the beneficent itself,
inasmuch as it is disposed that from the
beneficent itself, to make good is produced,
which will be from the influence of both.
And from this reflux, which is general
in the elemental tree, there are refluxes
in lower things, just as in pepper, in
which fire flows its heat into the air
with dryness, and air flows back that heat
to the fire with dryness, which it does not
desire to receive. From this reflux and other
natural influences and refluxes, men
derive similarities, such as those who are
unwilling to receive certain things that
are given to them, or those who return evil
for evil, or good for good, and so concerning
other things similar to these. And in this
step, the resolution appears which returned
to the first causes and natures in the elemental
tree, not however in the number in which
they were, but in the number from which they
are, since it is so that that number is lost
in corruption.

About Production. 50.
PRoduction in the elemental tree is
a general principle, just as the production
which is in goodness and the other
roots of the tree, from which production
a third number results, just as in goodness,
to make good is produced from the beneficent
and the beneficiary, and to magnify from
the magnificent and the magnifiable, and
so concerning the others: wherefore from
these productions the trunk is produced
in a third number, and the trunk produces
branches, which produce boughs, and the
boughs produce leaves and flowers with
fruits. And from these general productions
the productions of the individualized and
specified orchard are produced, and so
concerning vegetative and sentient trees.
And in this step it appears that the vegetative,
sensual, and imaginal tree are produced
from the elemental according to the nature
of the production above.

About Origin. 51.
ORigin is a property and nature in
the elemental tree, from which arise
and are derived the origins of individualized
things below: for just as in goodness, to make
good is born from the beneficent and the
beneficiary, so individuals below are born
from primary causes, just as a child who
is born from a father and mother, by way
of generation in the species of man: and
just as to make good, which is born in the
species of goodness, and the same is true
of to see, which is born from the visive and
the visible in the species of sight, and so
concerning other things similar to these.
And in this step it is signified how particulars
are born in their universals, which must
be real entities, for if they were not, they
would not have that in which they might
be born.

and is born in goodness, and because
magnification magnifies goodness, it exits
into to magnify and into the magnifiable,
and into the magnificent and the magnifiable,
which are of the essence of magnitude and
vice versa. Wherefore in this step it is
signified that certain parts exit into others
and from others, and vice versa, and that
the trunk exits from the roots and their
operations in the trunk, and the same in
the branches, which exit from the trunk,
and the boughs, which exit from the branches,
and the leaves, flowers and fruits, which
exit from the boughs. Whence from this

**De Separabilitate. 53.**
In the elemental tree, property and nature are divided, by which in trees below certain things are divided from others, inasmuch as certain things are of others, not however that in the elemental tree certain parts are divided from others, since it is so that it itself is confused and in it every part is in another, but by reason of division, which is one of its simple parts, certain parts below are divided from others, just as an apple, which is divided from an apple tree, when a man gathers it, or when it falls to the ground, and just as a child, who is divided from his mother, and just as health from the sick, and so of other similar natural things.

**De Inseparabilitate. 54.**
In the elemental tree there is inseparability and a general form, by reason of which the parts of the tree are not separated from it, nor does any part abandon its number, just as branches, which do not abandon themselves from the trunk by reason of natural inseparability, and branches in boughs do not abandon their number. Wherefore in a similar way there is inseparability in things below, just as in pepper, in which heat does not abandon its proper subject, which is simple fire, from which it cannot be divided by reason of the nature of superior inseparability, which is its first and general cause, namely the inseparability of the heat of simple fire in pepper, and so of other similar natural things, just as in man, who at one time is fat, and at another

**[Right Column]**
time lean, in whom his radical humor is not divided from him, although it is so that his nutritive humor comes and goes. And in this passage it is signified how individuals above remain in their number, which they do not lose through accidents that come and go, and which are preserved by the inseparability existing above.

**De Possibilitate. 55.**
Possibility is a simple form of the elemental tree, and is a branch of power. Hence, just as all parts of the tree are good by goodness, so they are possible by reason of possibility. And from this general possibility are these possibilities below, such as pepper, which can be, and a horse and a falcon, and just as one pepper, which can be from another, and one horse from another, and so of other natural things. And in this passage it is signified that the vegetative, sentient, and imaginal tree can be from the elemental, and that species can be real entities, and all this by reason of possibility clothed above with positivity. And from this general possibility are possibilities below, such as pepper with magnitude of goodness, duration, etc. of natural instincts and appetites, nor can contrariety contradict, since it is so that possibility is greater through more causes than through one.

**De impossibilitate. 56.**
Impossibility is simply a part in the elemental tree, by which it is impossible that goodness should not be, this which is, and so of magnitude and the rest. And from this impossibility which is above, are impossibilities which are below, such as pepper, in which it is impossible E 3

And also contradictions, which are below, are through impossibilities, which are above, such as being a man and not being a man, and being good and not being good, which are contradictory and impossible, and so concerning other things similar to these.

          On Similitude. 57.

Similitude is a nature and property, which is a principle in the elemental tree, through which certain roots give their similitudes to others, such as goodness, which takes on magnitude from itself, and magnitude similarly. And therefore magnitude which is accidentally sustained in goodness is a similitude of substantial magnitude, and the same is true of goodness which is sustained in magnitude. And in this step, similitudes existing below can be known, such as species, which have similitude in their genera, such as man and horse who have similitude in animal. And this similitude descends from above, such as the goodness of magnitude and the magnitude of goodness, which have similitude in duration, and each stands in itself. There is also another mode of similitude, such as the bonificative, the bonificable, and to bonify, which have similitude in goodness, each existing as good under goodness, which is their species and essence. And from these similitudes are the similitudes of individuals, which have similitude in species, such as Peter and Raymond who have similitude in the species of man.

          On Dissimilitude. 58.

In the elemental tree, dissimilitude is one of its simple parts, from which dissimilitudes descend below, such as the goodness of fire, which is dissimilar to the goodness of water, and the goodness of a branch, to the goodness of a leaf. Wherefore below, the goodness of man is dissimilar to the goodness of an ass, and this is the same concerning the figure of an apple, which is dissimilar to the figure of a rose, and the figure of a nail, to the figure of a hammer.

          On Nature. 59.

Nature is the first principle in the elemental tree for the natures below, and through it, the roots of the naturalized tree and all its parts are thus, just as they are good through goodness, and great through magnitude. Wherefore these parts below are naturalized by the nature general to them above, and it is a real being, because if it were not a real being, the natures below would not have a natural nor common medium in which they could agree, which agree such as male and female, who agree in procreating a son, and gustativity and gustability in tasting, and so concerning other natural things.

          On Corporality. 60.

Corporality is a simple form, through which goodness, magnitude, and other roots of the tree are corporeal causes, through which they have the nature that from them follows the body in the trunk and in branches, boughs, flowers and fruit. And from this corporality above are bodies below, such as the body of an apple and of a man. And because in goodness above there is the bonificative, the bonificable, and to bonify: and in magnitude, the magnificative, the magnificable, and to magnify, and so concerning other roots, every body below is of corporeal parts, namely of length, breadth, and depth, which are of its essence, and those from that. And these three dimensions retain
