**Of Transmutation. 61.**
Transmutation is one of the parts of the elemental tree, through which there are transmutations below, just as the matter of bread which through vegetation is transmuted into the matter of flesh, and the heat of fire into the heat of pepper. And in this step, knowledge can be had of how transmutation occurs below from one thing into many, just as the matter of iron into the shape of a sword, and the matter of a sword into the shape of a knife, and this transmutation is from the same iron, and so concerning other things. However, these transmutations below would not exist without transmutation above, which is concerning the goodness of the trunk, concerning the goodness of the branches, and concerning the goodness of the boughs.

**Of Light. 62.**
In the elemental tree, light is one of its parts, and this is through difference, which declares the parts, and is born in the branches, just as fire and air, which have light, which is color divided into the light of fire and into the transparency of air: which is clarity, and from this light descend lights below, sustained in their colored individuals and clothed with light and clarity. And concerning this matter, we have spoken more broadly in the general table.

**Of Shadow. 63.**
Shadow is one of the parts of the elemental tree, and is concerning confusion: which appears in the shadows of water and earth, and is in water of white color and in earth of black, however shadow is primarily due to the density of the matter of water and earth, which impedes light and clarity with the restriction of water and

[Right Column]

with the blackness of earth, and not only with the whiteness of water clarified by the participation of air with the blackness of earth, which gives it its likeness. Through this shadow above, there are these shadows below, such as the shadow of an orchard, a wall, and a human, and so concerning other elemental bodies.

**Of Line. 64.**
Line is a part in the elemental tree, through which the simple parts of the tree are in lines, just as the bonificative, which is one line, and the bonificable another, and the magnificative one line, and the magnificable another: and the same is true for the branches, since simple fire stands under one line extended in simplicity, and the line of air in another, and the same is true for water and earth: wherefore these general lines above are for these lines below, sustained in the vegetal tree and in the sensual, just as the body of an orchard which is composed of many lines, and so concerning the body of a human.

**Of Punctuality. 65.**
Punctuality is a simple part in the elemental tree, which emerges from multiple lines, just as to bonify, which is one point that is in the middle of the bonificable and the bonificable², just as the center, which is in the middle of a circle, and the same concerning to magnify and the others. And from this punctuality above, points descend below into elemental individuals, which are the acts of fruits, just as to taste, which is the center of the gustative and the gustable, and since it emerges from both, which are lines, when to vegetate composes a line. And in this step, knowledge can be had of how points emerge from lines, and how lines are composed of points, and how the body is the act of conjoined points and lines.

De Fœmineitate. 70.
Femininity is a simple part in the elemental
tree, and is of the bonifiable,
magnifiable, and other passive parts.
And from this femininity descend lower
femininities, such as the femininity
of the date palm, and of the woman, and
of the hen, and so concerning other individuated
females. And because they are from passivity, they are more
digestible and consumable
than individuated males, such as the hen,
which is more digestible than the
rooster, and in the species of leek, in which the
female leek is more digestible
than the male leek, and the same
is true in the species of coctanus, and so concerning others.

Membrosity in the elemental
tree is one of its simple natural forms,
which we have compared to its branches,
just as its four masses, which we mentioned,
which are 4 major natural members,
from whose membrosity lower elemental
natural members descend, as branches

**On Insertion. 75.**

Insertion is a simple form in the elemental tree, the nature of which is that below certain substances are inserted into others, and the insertion which is above, is like air, which is inserted into fire, so that it may draw the heat of fire to its humidity, and water, which is inserted into air, so that it may draw its humidity to its frigidity, and the same is true of earth inserted into water, so that it may draw its frigidity to its dryness, and the same is true of fire inserted into earth, so that it may draw its dryness to its heat. And in this step it can be known how forms which are above are attracted below, just as forms which are below are attracted above, so that a mixture may naturally be made from the elements. Another mode of insertion is above, like the vegetative power, which is inserted into the elemental, so that it may attract the elemental to itself: and like the sensitive power, which is inserted into the elemental and vegetative power, so that it may draw the elemental and vegetative to its sensing, and similarly for the imaginative. And this insertion is necessary above by reason of the end of goodness, magnitude, duration, power of natural instincts and appetites, and similarly for other parts of the tree, which end could not exist, if the insertion of diverse powers were not one of the simple forms of the elemental tree. Therefore, insertion above is the primary and general cause for insertions which are below, as in pepper, in which one quality is inserted into another, and in the wild olive, the olive, and in the mule, the species of horse and ass, and in man, his vegetative [power] into his elemental, and his sensitive into his vegetative, and his imaginative into his sensitive, and his rational into his imaginative. Whence, just as the olive draws the matter of the wild olive to its own nature, so in anima-

[Column 2]

-ls, superior forms draw inferior forms to their species.

**On Perfection. 76.**

Perfection is a simple form which consists in the elemental tree. Perfection is that by reason of which substantial entities stand by themselves as what they are, just as in the elemental tree, goodness stands by itself as what it is. And this is the same for its essential concretions, and the same is true for the trunk and other substantial parts of the tree. And from this perfection above descend perfections which are below, as the substance of the fruit tree, which stands by itself as what it is, and the substance of the lion similarly, and similarly for other natural perfections. God, however, aids their existence as the primary cause, who makes His effect stand as what it is. And furthermore, the influences of celestial bodies aid the perfections which are below.

**On Individuality. 77.**

Individuality in the elemental tree is a simple and primary form for individuals below, by which elemental individuals are individuated. And they are thus individuated under the reason of individuality above, just as they are good under the reason of goodness above, and great by magnitude above, and similarly for the rest. Individuality above is the reason for the trunk, which becomes one individual, insofar as it is a species, and similarly for each of the branches. And each of the individuals above is its own species, like the sun, which is its own species above, insofar as no other sun exists. According to the reason of this, the individuals of the elemental tree are general to inferior individuals through individuated natural agents, just as an apple is individuated by generatio

--- Page 57 ---
**On a hundred forms. 43**

generation of the form and matter of the apple tree, and the son who is individualized by the generation of man and woman. And thus concerning other natural things similar to these.

**On Attraction. 78.**
Attraction is a simple form in the elemental tree, and it is primary to the attractions which are below. And it is above inasmuch as goodness attracts magnitude to itself, so that it may be great, and fire attracts earth, so that it may be dry. Conciliation occurs here below, just as the roots of the apple tree which draw to themselves the parts of the elemental tree, and the trunk which draws to itself that which the roots receive from there, and the branches, which attract to themselves that which the trunk receives from the roots, and thus successively from one attraction to another up to the fruit which is the apple. There is also another attraction, such as man, who draws from the apple its smell and taste. There is another attraction, such as the attraction of an apple seed sown in the earth, from which natural instincts, and the appetites of the superior tree and the inferior tree draw the tree into being, which

--- Page 58 ---
**44. On a Hundred Forms.**

**[Column 1]**

Fu, in which comes frost that burns almonds when they are in bloom, and by chance deformed men are born, and so concerning other natural contingencies, and from these natural contingencies men receive similarities which they call fortunes, just as some who are fortunate for riches and honors, and others for the contrary, and just as one horse that has a good master and another a bad one, and one man who loses a denarius, and another finds it. And so concerning these similar things, wherefore fortune is not really something in artificial forms, but only in the opinion and intention of men, like a fantastic form, which the human intellect attains and multiplies from real objects.

**On Perfection. 81.**
Perfection is in the elemental tree, by reason of which it is complete for receiving the impressions of supercelestial bodies, and it is also that by reason of which it is complete in its parts, just as in its goodness, which is complete in its parts, that is, in its essential concretes, and so concerning its other parts. The elemental tree is also complete, in that it is disposed so that from it the perfections that are below receive their complement. Which perfections indeed are from that which is above, just as an orchard and an apple, which are complete, and so concerning animals. And from these natural perfections men receive similarities in this, that they wish to be complete through riches, morals, and habits of knowledge.

**On Imperfection. 82.**
In the elemental tree there is imperfection, one of its parts, through which certain parts cannot be com-

**[Column 2]**

plete in others, just as fire which cannot be complete in heating the air, unless it receives dryness from the earth, because if it did not receive dryness from the earth, it would empty itself of its simple entity: the number of which would be lost in the composition in which it enters with the air. And so concerning the flower, which is not complete in itself, in that it is for the sake of the fruit, and not for its own sake. And from this imperfection which is above, imperfections descend below, just as an orchard, in which there is imperfection, in that it cannot have sustenance without benefits which it receives from outside, and the same concerning man who is imperfect through vices accidentally and naturally, in that he cannot sustain himself without eating, and also is not complete in the embryo according to age, and so concerning other similar things.

**On Life. 83.**
In the elemental tree there is life, one of its simple parts, from which these lives that are below and corporeal receive life, just as the vegetative, which lives by vegetating, and the sensitive by sensing, and life (which is above) is confused and sown in the elemental tree, which is disposed so that from it issues that life which is below in elemental individuals, just as iron which is disposed so that from it a nail may be made, which does not exist in it in potential without the help of a smith. And because of this, blessed be God, He draws from the elemental disposition vegetative and sensual life, just as from it He drew the first orchard, and the first lion, and the first sardine, and the first light, and the first man, and the first falcon.

De Gaudio 93.

IN the elemental tree there are natural appetites, just as goodness which has
an appetite to be great, and for greatness to be good through itself, and just as fire:
which has an appetite to heat the air: and to receive dryness from the earth, and so concerning others. And furthermore, according to natural instincts and appetites, there are natures of pleasures in plants, according to how they come to the fulfillment of their natural appetites, just like an orchard which has delight (if indeed it can be called delight: since we must speak thus: because we lack a suitable word) inasmuch as it preserves its fruit with its leaves against the great heat of the sun, or against the great coldness of the wind.

De Ira. 94.

IN the elemental tree there is a beginning, middle, and end: the beginning is like that which makes good, the end is like that which can be made good, or that which has been made good: the middle is also like making good, and so concerning others. And because in the elemental tree there is contrariety: it impedes the beginnings against concordance: lest they pass through the middle to the end which they desire, just as in fire, in which dryness impedes the fire from giving heat to the air. And from this nature which is above through contrariety, vegetative things below have an inclination to the likeness of anger. And this appears in a smaller plant which stands near another larger plant: which is not of its own species, which distances itself from its shade; as much as it can so that it can receive the heat of the sun, and because of this its trunk grows twisted: and the same is true in animals, in which there is an impression of anger naturally by reason of the impression which is above, thus a hen, which has anger, when a kite eats its chick, and the same is true of a sick person, who is angry, because they are not healthy, or because they cannot bring to an end that which they desire:
and because of this, people who are melancholic are more prone to anger than others: and this is because of dryness and coldness, in which contrariety impedes the concordance of natural appetites more than on account of humidity and dryness.

**On the Vegetal Tree.**

This tree is divided into seven parts, namely into roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits. And it is a twofold tree, inasmuch as there is a difference between it and the elemental tree into which it is inserted by creation. This is to say, that God created the vegetative power in it and from it, just as God created man from the earth and from the mud of the earth. For this reason, the lower individuals are elemental and vegetal. Therefore, since this tree is twofold, it is necessary that we lead it in a twofold manner in our intellect, so that we may have better knowledge of it.

De

--- Page 65 ---
non potest nec tangi, sua tamen figura in liquore apparet, qui est in trunco, quemadmodum apparet truncus vegetalis in trunco ficus in similitudine lactis, & in trunco leonis in figura sanguinis. Est tamen truncus vegetalis de natura corporali, quia est de partibus substantialibus corporalibus, secundùm quod est significatum in radicibus."

it cannot be touched, yet its figure appears in the liquid, which is in the trunk, just as the vegetative trunk appears in the trunk of a fig tree in the likeness of milk, and in the trunk of a lion in the figure of blood. Nevertheless, the vegetative trunk is of a corporeal nature, because it is of substantial corporeal parts, according as it is signified in the roots.

"Branchæ arboris vegetalis sunt duplices, quoniam quædam sunt ex natura elementali, & aliæ ex natura vegetali. Et branchæ huius arboris sunt quatuor, scilicet potentia appetitiua, & retentiua, digestiua, & expulsiua. Et sunt quatuor, quia sufficiunt transmutationibus, quæ fiunt per generationem & corruptionem in vegetatione, & per differentiam & concordantiam, & contrarietatem. Et minus quatuor esse non possunt, secundùm quod est significatum in branchis arboris elementalis. Et istæ quatuor branchæ generales sunt ad omnes branchas vegetatas

The branches of the vegetative tree are twofold, because some are of an elemental nature, and others of a vegetative nature. And the branches of this tree are four, namely, the appetitive power, and the retentive, digestive, and expulsive. And there are four, because they suffice for the transmutations which occur through generation and corruption in vegetation, and through difference and concordance, and contrariety. And they cannot be less than four, according as it is signified in the branches of the elemental tree. And these four general branches are general to all vegetated branches.

Arbor vegetalis. 53

by means of generation, corruption, privation, and individuation, and according to other general forms, of which mention was made at the end of the elemental tree.

Concerning the Expulsive Power.

The Expulsive Power is that faculty which expels gross matter, although the appetitive power abhors placing it in nourishment, and from which the digestive power has attracted the more subtle parts; although the appetitive power strongly desires nourishment in plants, as in an orchard: in which the expulsive power casts out the bark, which is not vegetated, and the leaves that fall from it. And this appears more clearly in the oak, which has thicker bark. And the same follows in animals, as in man, from whom the expulsive power expels the grosser and undigested matters by spitting, sweating, and urinating, and similarly concerning other excrements. These four branches, of which mention has been made above, cannot be seen or touched: because they are general to all branches of vegetal and sensitive trees, and are sustained in the elemental tree, and their individuated branches are diffused in vegetated and sentient substances. When the appetitive power desires more than the retentive power can retain, or the digestive power can digest, then the concordance is greater with corruption than with generation, and with consumption than with growth. And when the retentive power retains grosser and undigested matters against the expulsive power, then it has an inclination towards consumption and corruption. And when the digestive power does not digest as much as is suitable for the nourishment of the plant or animal, then it is against generation and growth. And when the expulsive power is too strong or too weak, then the substance is in corruption. And indeed, physicians minister to the natures of the branches for health: so that they may have concordance in the nourishment of substances, and teach how to have health with temperance, which is the subject of the concordance of the branches.

Concerning the Branches of the Vegetal Tree.

The branches of the vegetal tree are twofold, because some are from the elemental tree, and others from the vegetal tree. Those which are from the elemental tree are visible in an orchard: where renewal occurs in spring, in which flowers, leaves, and fruits are born. And the branches which are from the vegetal nature cannot be seen or touched. And they are signified more strongly by generation, corruption, privation, and renewal, than by other forms. Because through generation, the transmutation and renewals of beings occur, as was signified in the treatise on generation. And the same is true of corruption and privation in depriving certain old forms through corruption, and in generating new forms through generation. In these general branches, composed of the general elemental tree and the general vegetal tree, are in disposition all the branches of plants and animals: which are in them potentially with the help of natural agents, which lead them into actuality according to the conditions of the roots and natures of the hundred primary forms, of which mention was made in the elemental tree. In the branches of an orchard are potentially the branches of another orchard: which potentially is sustained in the disposition of the roots and the hundred forms. And when a natural agent touches these branches:

color, taste and odor, sweetness and bitter-

which are quantified, quali-

which pertain to vegetation adorn and preserve
it, just as the vegetative sub-
stance, when it makes elemental and visible leaves,
which are the coverings of vegetative things
existing from the substance of the fruit tree.
And when those fall from the fruit tree, it is signified
that the vegetative leaves have completed their course, and
their complement, in the adornment and preser-
vation of the vegetative substance, which
from then on sleeps until the time, in

which the renewal of leaves occurs in spring.
The virtue however of the vegetal leaves
placed potentially in the fruit is excited
and moved, then when the fruit
is eaten by an animal in vegetative and sentient
nourishment, in which color,
taste and odor are perceived.

Concerning the Flowers of the vegetal tree.

The flowers of the vegetal tree are
twofold, because they are composed
of elementation and vegeta-
tion, just as the flower of the fruit tree, which is visible,
insofar as it contains elemental nature:
just as it cannot be touched, nor
seen: insofar as it contains vegetative nature,
whose vegetative flowers are contained within,
and are of such subtle matter that they cannot be seen,
and they stand especially through an instrument
composed of potentiality, object, and
actuality: from which the fruit is derived,
which is closer to potentiality, object, and
actuality than other forms: just as the thing
worked, which is closer to the hand, than
to the arm, and to the hammer, than to the hand: and
so concerning other causes similar to these. In the flow-
ers which are general, there are special
flowers in potentiality: and flowers have more
of odor and taste, than leaves,
and also more of virtue: and they have
a more intense color, and this is:
because they are closer to the fruit than
leaves, which is the nobler part, which is in
the whole tree. And the flower stands through corrup-
tion and the fruit through generation: and
therefore in the completion of the flower, the fruit is gathered:
and the fruit arises in the middle place
of the flower, so that its virtue may be greater. And the flower
is lighter than the fruit: because the fruit
is more full, and because it potential-
ly contains in itself all parts of the
future tree. Flowers on the tree do not last as long
as leaves, which are for preser-

On the Fruit of the Vegetative Tree.

The fruit of the vegetative tree is twofold,
according to the twofold nature of its parts
of which it has been spoken. And the fruit,
insofar as it can be seen and touched, is
by reason of its elemental nature. And the form
of the vegetative fruit appears in taste, smell,
and color, which are its figures which
an animal perceives through sensation. And the fruit
of the vegetative [tree] stands secret and hidden from the
bodily senses, which perceive figures.
But imagination perceives it,
in which all parts are gathered in which
another fruit exists in potentiality, and therefore
it is greater in goodness, magnitude, virtue,
power, etc., than flowers and leaves: which
are by secondary intention. In
an orchard, the apple is the fruit, and because
the apple contains more of vegeta-

vegetating are directed, and it is the center in

so that the end may follow: which they desire.
The fruit is fuller and heavier
than the flower, because it relates to more things
than the flower, and because it contains more
of circle, triangle, and quadrangle,
and of a hundred forms, which are primary
natures. Some trees there are, which
do not produce fruit, such as the willow and the
ash, and this is: because in the flower
their species are preserved. And some
fruits there are in which there is no shell
outside: as in cherries, which have pits
inside, and this is because of the great
humidity, which resides in the extremities, and
dryness is sustained in the middle, namely
in the pits: there is another fruit, which has
a shell outside, which does not have a hard shell
or pit inside: such as the chestnut and
the nut: and this is, because dryness abounds
outside and humidity inside: and so for others.
Each element has four species
of plants: in which, or through which, it
dominates over the other elements: as fire,
which dominates in pepper and garlic:
which are in the fourth degree of heat: and in
the third degree of dryness: and in the second
of humidity: and in the first of coldness.
The second plant is like cinnamon, in which fire is in
the third degree of heat, and earth in the second,
and air in the first: and water is diminished.
The third plant is like fennel:
in which fire is in the second degree of
heat: earth in the first, air in three parts
of one degree: and water in two [parts of one degree].
There is another plant, in which fire is in the first
degree of heat: such as anise, in

CONCERNING THE SENSUAL TREE.

[Decorative initial A]The sensual tree is divided into seven parts, just like other trees. Namely: roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
*The roots are general principles: which are threefold inasmuch as they are of elemental, vegetal, and sensual nature.*
*The trunk is the body of the sensual [being], and likewise is threefold: inasmuch as it is constituted of the said three natures.*
*The branches are the six bodily senses: namely sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and olfaction. And likewise they are threefold: constituted of the said three natures.*
*The boughs are the bodily members, both interior and exterior, which likewise are composed of the said three natures.*
*The leaves are accidents, which likewise are threefold, etc.*
*The flowers are the acts of the sensual body, etc.*
*The fruits are sentient individuals, namely man, horse, and other animals.*

And yet we intend to speak of natural goodness, and not moral, in which goodness animals participate, and which is called a genus, in which species of particular goodnesses are sown, just as the goodness of a horse, which is one species, and the goodness of a crane similarly, from which goodness of a horse is the goodness of the horse that is Peter's, and the goodness of the horse that is Martin's. Thus, in general goodness, special goodnesses are sown, just as many seeds of diverse species in one and the same earth, which earth renders itself general to each of the seeds. And of this we have experience in a garden planted with many plants diverse in species and number. Likewise from earth, namely from stone, iron, glass, and tile are made, and the earth is the same and general to these three works. In the same way, the root, which is general goodness, is to the elemental, the vegetal, the sensible, and the imaginative, and this is because it is of four natures. Hence, when iron comes to corruption, and likewise for tile and glass, then they return to earth, their matter and nature, just as one who would make from one mass of gold a cup, a platter, and a ring, and afterwards would melt the whole together, the original mass would return to its first state and number, stripped of the figures by which

Of the Branches of the Sensual Tree.

**T**HE branches of the sensual tree
are six, namely sight, hearing,
smell, taste, touch, and speech.
Indeed, we have proven this speech to be the
sixth sense, and this in the treatise which we
made concerning it. The branches must be six
and no more nor less, because if there were
more, that which was extra would be superfluous,
which superfluity nature cannot sustain,
and if there were fewer, nature would sustain
a void, which it cannot sustain, just as if sight
were not, the visibility of things would be void,
and would not have itself towards any end.
And if speech were not [a sense], then locution,
which would not fall under the category of any
sense, would be in vain, as it would serve no
purpose: the same is true for hearing, and the
other senses. Therefore there are six senses
according to the necessity of corporeal nature,
and according to the six rectitudes of the body,
and with them all particular and corporeal
things can be attained, and all imaginable things
are impressed in them. It is necessary for the
six senses to be substantial corporeal parts, so
that the common sense may have parts which
are of its essence, in which it is sustained, which
is of corporeal nature, as has been proven. And
these six branches are in the general tree (which
we call the sensual tree) which are general to

**The Sensual Tree. 61**

...to all special branches of individual animated beings, just as sight, which is a general power for the sight of man, horse, eagle, and fish, just as general goodness, which has under itself several special goodnesses. Each of the branches has its own subjects, in which it is sustained, just as sight, which is a threefold branch, containing in itself three natures, namely, the elemental, the vegetative, and the nature of its common sense, and particularized and individualized sight, such as the eyes of Peter, which are elemental, vegetative, and sensible, and the same for hearing, and the other senses. And concerning these senses, we propose to speak in the shortest way we can, nevertheless, it is necessary for us to speak in such a way that knowledge can be had of their entities, and of their natures, and of their operations and modes.

**About Sight.**

**S**ight is a threefold branch, as has been said above, and its place is in the eyes, and that which can be seen and touched by the eyes, is of the essence of the elemental branch, and especially of the nature of fire and air, since the light of fire, and the transparency of air are instruments for seeing, and for removing shadows, which are through water and earth. And that which is vegetative in the eyes, is of the nature of the vegetative, in which are its four branches of which mention has been made, and these cannot be seen in the eyes, nor touched, since it is so, that the vegetative is invisible and intangible. And each of its branches has its own office in the eyes, just as through the appetitive power, the visual power relates itself to its proper object, namely to visibility, and retains the light of fire and the transparency of air in the line which is between the visual-
-power and visibility, and the digestive digests shadowy species, so that they may be clear and lucid, and the expulsive removes shadows, just as fire, which removes coldness from hot water. And the essence of sight cannot be seen, nor touched, and above the others, it is a form, and it is above them in magnitude of goodness, power, etc. And its essential parts are four, namely, the visual faculty, the visible object, the act of seeing, and the common visible, from which the particular visible is individualized, just as the visual faculty of Peter's eyes, which is one part of his sight, and visibility, which is of the essence of sight, and seeing, which is the act of both, which is internal, so that Peter's sight consists of these three parts, and this sight is a branch of the common sense. And visibility which is external, is like the visibility of an apple and a pear, which is a remote object inasmuch as it is not of the essence of Peter's sight, but participates in species with the visibility which is part of Peter's sight, and which is sensed, and sustained in the eyes. And the digestive digests external visibility into internal visibility, just as it digests bread into flesh, and wine into blood. And from this follows another act, which is seeing and an accidental work, so that it may be seen, which is desired, that it may be seen, and in which the visual faculty has rest. Peter's eyes are elemental, vegetative, and sensible, and his horse is visible, which Peter sees. And between Peter's eyes and the horse, there is a line extended through the air and the space which is between the eyes and the horse: and this line is composed of three natures, namely elemental, vegetative, and sensual, the line existing between two terminated points. About Smell.

Smell is the third branch, and
it is threefold: according to what has been
said about sight, and its operation, and
its mode is signified in what has been
said about sight and hearing. And its line
which is between it and the object is of a
hot and humid complexion, because through
heat there is an olfactory, attractive power,
and through the air breathing vapors, which
are outside, by breathing in which odors are
sustained, which exit from the pores of
odoriferous substances.
And in this passage it is signified that
all elemental beings consist in the trunk of the
elemental tree, and its essence goes and
comes through all things: just as odors
through the line, and through their limits.
The nose is the instrument through the
elemental tree for smelling, just as ears
are for hearing. And the odoriferous is
the subject of the elemental tree, inasmuch
as it is a simple odor that is sensed:
and the olfactory power is the form of the

instrument which is on the part of the

necessary for living by reason of the movement

digestive [power] digests those vapors into feces,
although the expulsive [power] expels them outside:
and the appetitive [power] desires other new vapors,
which the olfactory [power] places inside by breathing
to cool the heart, against great heat, and
to delight nature in good and healthy odors,
and pleasant ones to smell, which the retentive
[power] retains until they are digested, and the
expulsive [power] expels a large mass of them outside.

About Taste.

Taste is the fourth branch, and it is
threefold: according to what has been said
about the others. And its object is flavor.
And the power which relates to the object
is the gustatory [power]. And the instrument
which is on the part of the elemental, is
that which can be touched and seen in the
fruit. And that which is on the part of the
vegetative: is flavor, which is tasteable in
essence, a sense into which it is born and exits,
just as an infant which is born, and exits
into the essence of man, and iron into the
shape of a nail, and heated into the species
of heat. And that which receives this, which
is born in it and enters, is the tasteable,
which is of the essence of the gustatory.
And from the trees exits tasting, which is
of its essence. And all three are of the
essence of the common sense. And tasting
which comes from outside, is a habit, which
they receive in the throat: to which the
tongue draws the flavor of foods, which
enter by eating and drinking. And since
foods come in diverse species and complexions,

**The Sensual Tree.** 67

[Column 1]

that the horse is vegetated. And the sensitive (nature) places the sensed thing, in that the horse is sensed, and the object seen is the horse: which is the fruit of sight. And it is its fruit insofar as it is the end: that is to say, that sight exists so that there may be a seen object, just as iron exists so that there may be a nail, and a hand so that there may be an operation, and an operation so that there may be a thing operated upon, and so on for other similar things. The same follows for the fruit of hearing, whose fruit is the heard thing; and of smelling, whose fruit is the smelled thing; and of tasting, the tasted thing; and of touching, the touched thing; and of speaking, the spoken or manifested thing. And from all these fruits follows the sensed thing, which is the fruit of all parts of the tree: insofar as it is the center and end of all its parts, and all parts relate to it: because all exist for its sake.

**On the Application & Practice, Chapter**
**of Forms.**

[Large illuminated initial I]
IN this passage, doctrine is given on how man may know how to apply natural forms to individuated substances. And just as we give doctrine in this sensual tree, it can be given in others. And because application is very useful and necessary for the habits of sciences, and is the sustenance of the intellect: insofar as it sustains itself in forms and recurs to their examples: so that it may seek its object: therefore we place this treatise (which is about application) in this tree of knowledge. Unity is the reason why the sensual tree is one. And the reason by which unity is the reason that the tree is one, is by reason of the unities which the tree contains within itself: such as one unity of goodness composed of three natures, and one tree composed of three natures, and

[Column 2]

so on for other unities. And the reason by which there is plurality in the tree is, because it is composed of several things differing in essence, concerning which several things have been spoken of in the tree itself, which are several roots, several trunks, several branches, and so on for the rest. Therefore, unity and plurality are primary causes, by which the tree is one, and contains within itself several causes. Simplicity and composition are primary causes and forms, by which the tree, in one number, is simple and composed of several things. It is simple in one number, because it is composed of several simple causes: such as simple fire and the other elements, and the appetitive (power), which is a simple form, and the visual power similarly, and so on for others. And all these simple forms relate to one simple thing, like several lines to one point: which simple thing is indeed the sensual tree, insofar as it has one number. And it is composed of several causes through the composition of its parts, such as the trunk which is composed of elemental, vegetal, and sensual nature. Form and matter are the reasons by which the tree is constituted from them, just as the vegetative form which in an animal informs the elemental form, and the sensitive form informs the vegetative, and this is because of the greatness of goodness, which is greater in the end of superior forms than in the end of inferior forms, which are matter to the forms that are above, like second intentions to first ones. Nevertheless, inferior forms always remain according to their special goodness in their simple number: just as iron, which is under the form of a knife and a nail, yet always remains what it is. Genera and species are reasons, that in the tree there are several genera and several species; just as

...ria of the embryo, which is not in a perfect state, nor forms which are in potential, which are empty without a reason for their existence, and so of other causes similar to these: which forms indeed are made manifest when they are brought into actuality.

Totality and part are primary causes, by reason of which the sensual tree is a whole from its parts, and its parts are from the whole, just as a horse, which is the whole of its elemental, vegetative, and sensitive [powers], which are its parts. This could not be, if totality and part were not primary causes for totality, as the parts of a horse and of the body of a man, and so of other natural individuals.

Intensity and extensiveness are primary forms for the intensities and extensivenesses of the sensual tree: just as in a horse, which is very white, in which the color is intense, and in a brown horse the color is diffused and extensive. And this intensity and extensiveness are through the elemental nature, and when a horse has a great appetite for eating through the vegetative [power], it has an intense taste, and a diffused [taste] when it does not eat tasty things, as when it eats bitter grass. And through the sensitive [power] it has intense sight, when it has clear eyes and eyes disposed for seeing, and it has diffused and confused [sight], when it has weak eyes.

Station and motion are primary forms in the sensual tree, by reason of which it has in itself many particular motions and stations, just as a horse, which stands in one place when it does not move itself. And it stands white through the elements, and fat through vegetation, and cheerful through the sensitive [power]. And a horse is that which it is through the station of all three powers. And it is moving and movable by reason of general motion, and when it moves itself from one place to another, that motion is local through the elements. And inasmuch as it is motion it has growth, and that motion is through vegetation, and inasmuch as it moves itself to those things which it sees and desires, that motion is through the sensitive [power].

Hardness and softness are primary forms for the sensual tree, which has many particular softnesses and hardnesses, caused by general ones: just as flesh which is soft, and is soft through the elemental power, and bones which are hard through it. The vegetative, however, and sensitive [powers] simply do not have hardness, nor softness, just as they do not have lightness, nor ponderosity, nevertheless in a horse they are forms, inasmuch as they inform in it the elemental form, from which hardness and softness consist.

Order and operation are primary principles for the sensual tree, because by reason of the order which the elemental tree has in itself according to its roots, trunk, and its other parts, it is disposed that from it the vegetated and the sensed operate with the ordering of vegetation and its operation, and with the ordering of the sensitive and its operation. And this is evident in the lion, in which there is natural order and operation according to the natures of all three trees. Influence and reflux are primary causes for the sensual tree. And therefore, in the lion, influence and reflux exist according to the three trees, just as the elemental (tree), which flows into its principles the end for which it exists, and those principles flow back that end to the end of vegetation, which flows back to the principles of the sensual (tree) that which it receives from the elemental (tree), and its principles similarly, and the sensual (tree) receives that influence to the end from which its principles flow back. And therefore the lion is produced from the natural influence and reflux of all three trees. Production, origin, and emergence are primary natures for the sensual tree, just as in the elemental (tree), in which the trunk is produced from the roots, and branches from the trunk, which are born from the trunk, and emerge in themselves, because they are born in their own species. And when vegetation, through a natural agent, touches the production, origin, and emergence of the elemental (tree), it produces from it the elementated (thing), which is born and emerges in the vegetated (thing). And the sensual (tree) does the same, namely the sensitive nature, which produces in its own species a lion, vegetated and sensed, and because it emerges and is born in the sensitive (nature), it remains sensed and clothed by it. Separability, inseparability are primary forms for the sensual

(tree), just as in the lion, in which there is natural heat, which does not abandon its proper subject, which is fire, because it cannot depart from it; nor does vegetation abandon its branches, for if it were to abandon them, it would not be that which it is; nor do particular senses depart from the common sense, just as parts which cannot abandon their whole. And when in the lion these things which have been mentioned depart, namely the elementative, the vegetative, and the sensitive, then that lion comes into privation. And in this passage it is signified that simple things remain in their essence in composite things. Possibility and impossibility are primary causes for the sensual tree, just as in the elemental tree, in which it is possible that the elementated (thing) follows from it, and in the vegetative (tree), in which it is possible that the vegetated (thing) comes from it, and in the sensual (tree), in which it is possible that the sensed (thing) follows from it. And these possibilities exist because in each of the trees, each of its principles relates itself to the end for which it exists. And therefore a lion can exist from all three trees. And it is impossible for it not to exist according to the natural course. And it is impossible that a lion could exist in the elemental tree if the simple principles of the elemental tree were lost in its lion-ness, and the same is true for the vegetative (tree). Similitude and dissimilitude are primary natures for the sensual tree, just as in the lion, in which there is a likeness of air, fire, earth, and water, inasmuch as the branches of the elemental tree place their likenesses in their boughs, which the lion attains by seeing and touching, and from which it exists according to elemental nature. And the vegetative [power] in the lion establishes rectitudes, because that which it digests from the food it eats, the expulsive [power] casts downwards into feces, and the digestive [power] [sends] upwards, and into all parts, inasmuch as it gives to the brain, and to the tail, and to the right and left arms, and to the feet and to the high and low back, and in it it places the figure digested into the species of a lion, which was crude and confused in the seed. But the sensitive [power] establishes rectitudes in the six sensed senses, and the figure of the lion in their extremities on the sensed surface. Masculinity and femininity are primary causes for the sensual tree, just as the elemental tree, which in the lion establishes masculinity by reason of the nature it has from bonificativity (the power to make good), magnificativity (the power to make great), aerificativity (the power to make airy), and so forth concerning other masculine forms. And it establishes in it femininity by reason of the nature of bonificability (the capacity to be made good), magnificability (the capacity to be made great), ignificability (the capacity to be made fiery), and so forth concerning other feminine matters. And by reason of this, the lion and lioness are in the species of lionhood: and the vegetative [power] establishes in them their masculine and feminine natures, namely vegetativity (the power to vegetate), and vegetability (the capacity to be vegetated). And the same applies to the sensitive [power], which establishes in them masculine and feminine natures, such as sensitivity (the power to sense), and sensibility (the capacity to be sensed). And therefore the lion is in the lioness a natural agent in elementating through the elementary, and in vegetating through the vegetative, and in sensing through the sensitive. Memberhood and instrumentality are primary natures in the sensual tree: just as in the lion, in which the elementative power establishes members and instruments, according as it is signified in the branches and flowers of its tree by establishing its members, namely the heart, liver, head, and arms. Nourishment and impression are primary causes for the sensual tree, just as in the lion, in which the elementative power establishes nourishment according to the nature it has of nourishing: such as goodness and greatness, which nourish the good and the great to endure, and fire which nourishes its heat in the air and in the earth by heating, and it establishes impressions of its species, in that the lion is from the four elements, and has roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits, according as it is signified in the sensual tree. Touch and utterance are natural and primary forms for the sensual tree, just as a lion, which has touch through the elemental tree, in that it (the elemental tree) places in it discrete quantities under a soft form or under a hard form when touching. And the vegetative [nature] places in touch a digested taste, positioned in a state of disposition and potential, so that it can be felt and expressed; it places in potential and in disposition that which can be heard. Waking, sleeping, and dreaming are primary powers for the sensual tree according to the natures of the three trees, because the elemental nature places waking in the lion, insofar as it makes it hungry, and makes it imagine its necessities through excessive heat or cold, humidity or dryness. And in sleeping it places the nature of resting, in that the contrariety of humors ceases, which excite it to wakefulness, the contrariety of which the lion cannot endure, and therefore nature gives it rest in sleep. And the elemental nature makes it dream, insofar as it makes its imagination stand between waking and sleep— | —by reason of impressions which relate to all parts, namely to waking and sleeping, and therefore people who are of a hot and dry complexion dream of saffron colors, and dryness, and battles. And because the soul requires to recollect, understand, and love, and fire requires to heat and dry, in sleep they speak of things which are of a hot and dry nature, and similarly of battles. The vegetative [nature] places its nature in waking, insofar as it prepares for the lion the taste of food, and in it (the lion) it places its nature of sleeping, insofar as it makes it sleep, so that it can better digest food, which it cannot digest as well when waking, because the sensitive forms impede it, in that they relate to its sensible objects. And it (the vegetative nature) places its nature in dreaming, insofar as it digests fantastic images, which the imagination receives with the help of the senses. Which fantastic images are indeed between waking and sleeping. And the sensitive [nature] places its nature in waking, insofar as it makes the senses exercise feeling. And in sleeping it places the nature of resting, insofar as the tired powers of feeling have rest in sleep. And it places in dreaming confused images of feeling, which are between waking and sleeping. Joy and anger are primary forms for the sensual tree according to the natures of the three general trees, as in the lion, in which the elemental nature is the reason for pleasure, which it has through its vigorous strength, with which it has the power of conquering other beasts. And in that (lion) it places the disposition to go through cold, and through heat, and through hunger, and through thirst, and through infirmity. It also places anger in it through the opposite mode of pleasure. And the sensitive (nature) places pleasure in it through seeing, and through sensing good tastes. It also places anger in it, inasmuch as it makes it feel things contrary to living, such as hunger, thirst, and pain. Health and infirmity are primary forms for the sensual tree, just like a lion, which through health is healthy, and through infirmity is infirm. And these impressions are through the natures of the trees, just as the elemental (nature), which through temperate complexions is the reason for health, which is in the lion, and through intemperate complexions is the reason for its infirmity. And the digestive (nature) is the cause of its health then: when it digests food, as is proper. And when it errs in its operation, it provides infirmity to the lion. And the sensitive (nature) provides health by feeling pleasure in eating and drinking, because the sensed taste vivifies nature. And therefore, concerning the pleasure that the lion has in seeing those things which please it. And conversely, the sensitive (nature) provides infirmity in the lion. Industry is a general form for the industries of animals, which industry is sustained in the general powers, namely elemental, vegetative, and sensitive: just as a lion which has industry for hunting according to the elemental (nature), which is understood above in the natural instinct of fire, and in its appetite, which has a way of heating water, by heating the air which it heats: so that in the heated humidity, which the air gives to the water: fire may pass to heat and mortify the water. Likewise, fire has a way of heating air by infusing into it desiccated heat, so that with its dryness it can mortify the humidity existing in water, so that water may not receive benefit from the air. In a similar way, the vegetative (nature) is the reason for the lion, that it has industry according to its general mode, which it has in its branches: just as a lion, which has a way of being in warm places, when it is cold, and in cold places, when heat prevails. In which way the digestive (nature) can operate better according to the nature of the sensitive (nature), which provides it with cold places when it has heat, and warm places when it has cold. And furthermore, it makes itself invisible to beasts at night, because they have fear of it when they see it, and therefore it hunts more at night than by day. Substance, essence, and being are general and primary forms for the sensual tree: just as in the lion, in which the elemental and general substance places a special and individuated substance derived from four masses, whose essence is "lion-ness," which is from the elemental nature, inasmuch as that which can be seen and touched in the lion. And the same is true of its elemental entity. And the vegetative (nature) does the same, which by vegetating preserves the species of the lion. And the sensitive (nature) similarly, which by sensing or feeling preserves, and generates it with a natural agent. And "lion-ness," which is the essence of the lion, is through vegetation and through sense, because without vegetating and sensing, the essence could not stand upon the substance, which stands under the essence through vegetating and sensing, which are of the entity of substance and essence. And in this step, man can know that substance is in particulars under its essence and operation, just as good (is) under goodness. And furthermore, it can be known that

On the Trunk of the Imaginal Tree.

[Ornate initial T] HE TRUNK of the imaginal tree is common and confused in its similarities, and it is constituted from the essences and natures of its roots, and in it are potentially specific similarities, which natural and animate agents draw from it, further, things not animate. This similarity exists in two ways. One way is insofar as it is not received through imagination: such as the shadow of a plant in a mirror or in water, or on the ground, which is a similarity of real similarities, elemental, so that the plant does not imagine that similarity, nor does the mirror, water, nor earth imagine that similarity, because they are not animate substances; yet imaginability participates with them in the general trunk, which is of elemental, vegetal, sensual, and imaginal nature. And for this reason, the second mode of similarity is through an animate natural agent: such as a horse or a human, who have an imaginative power, which receives the shadow of a plant in water or on the ground by imagining that shadow. Hence, just as fire which passes to water through a medium (that is, through air), so the imaginative faculty, with one likeness, receives another likeness: namely, with its own real likeness, which is part of the imaginative animal, it receives the likeness of the fire's flame, which is a phantasmatic likeness, purified and digested in the brain, which issues from the real imaginability of the flame, which stands between the real imaginative faculty of the animal and the imaginability of the flame: just as dreaming, which is between sleeping and waking. Nevertheless, simple fire cannot be imagined in shape: but in quality, namely in heat or in lightness or in color. And in this passage it is understood how imagination multiplies forms, which are likenesses of real beings.

**On the Similitude of the Appetitive Faculty.**

The appetitive faculty is one of the branches of the vegetal tree: whose similitude is one of the branches of the imaginal tree: just as the similitude of fire, which is one of the branches of the imaginal tree. The appetitive faculty is a real being in the vegetal tree, and an animal receives its similitude in its natural appetites: just as man, who has a natural appetite for eating and drinking, and similarly for other senses. And therefore, he has a natural inclination to imagine appetible things, which he imagines with his imaginativity. And because imaginativity and imaginability are related to each other: therefore, the imaginative faculty receives its own masculine similitude with the similitude of imaginativity, and with its masculine similitude, it receives a feminine similitude from the imaginable and appetible object under the aspect of color, taste, voice, smell, or touch. And thus imagination receives similitude from the retentive, digestive, and expulsive powers. And in this step, it is understood how the imaginative faculty receives similitudes from the vegetal tree.

**On the Similitude of Sight.**

The similitude of seeing is a branch of the imaginative faculty in which visible things are impressed, just as the imaginative faculty of a man or a spider, who, because he saw a house, when he is absent from it, can imagine that house, and the spider can imagine the web it desires to make: and to imagine is a species multiplied from imaginability sustained in the visible chamber, composed of four elements, in which the general imaginative faculty is inserted with the visibility of the composite elements. And when the visual power

[Right column]

has touched the matter and the figure of the chamber, when a man is absent from the chamber, or has closed his eyes: the imaginative faculty draws from visibility a similitude, which is a fantastic species received and impressed in the imaginative faculty, and thus imaginability remains a real being signified by the visibility of the thing. And the similitude of imaginability is an operation of the imaginative faculty, which receives that similitude of imaginability by seeing in itself, and in its own imaginability, which has concordance in species with the imaginability of the chamber. And the instrument is the visibility of the chamber, with which the imaginative faculty draws a similitude from the imaginability of the chamber, and places it in its own imaginability: with which it is conjoined in man, who moves his imaginative faculty to imagine the chamber. And in this step, the nature and mode which the imaginative faculty has in multiplying species, which it draws from imaginabilities with the instrument, which is seeing, is understood: of which it has been spoken.

And therefore, the imaginative faculty, which is extended through the air and through the ears: and similarly for other parts: just as a form extended in the elemental tree when it is touched by the special imaginative faculty, (which is of its

**Concerning the Leaves of the Imaginal Tree.**

The leaves of the imaginal tree are the similitudes of the leaves of the elemental, vegetative, and sensual tree. The leaves of the elemental tree are quantity, quality, and other predicaments, which issue from elemental substance in the mode of elementation, and the imaginative [faculty] imagines these with the leaves of the vegetative and sensual tree, which are instruments for it to imagine the leaves of the elemental tree. And those instruments impress their similitudes into the imaginative [faculty], and the imaginative [faculty] receives them, and passes to the similitudes of the elemental leaves.

**Concerning the Similitude of Quantity.**

The imaginative [faculty] receives the similitude of real quantity, which similitude is fantastic, and it receives it with the help of the natures of the three trees, which are instruments for it to receive the similitude: just as the elemental tree, which makes the figure of corporeal substance, insofar as it places in it length, breadth, and depth, which are continuous quantities of substance, which cannot be seen or touched, and through sense it sees the figure. And the imaginative [faculty] considers length, breadth, and depth, from which it draws quantity in the abstract, and that which it draws is the similitude of quantity to which it passes, because it is seen in color and figure. And the similitude makes discrete quantity, of which it receives the similitude with the help of the elemental and sensual tree: just as the elemental [tree], which composes fingers, hands, and distinguishes them in number by their differences, and sight receives them as distinct in number, and the imaginative [faculty] similarly, and therefore the imaginative [faculty] multiplies number from one, two, and three, and so on for other discrete things that can be numbered. And this quantity of number is not something in itself, but is a similitude of real discrete quantities. Which similitude is an operation of the imagination that considers many things. The vegetative [faculty] still helps the operation of the imagination with its roots: just as the taste of wine, which is strong when it is pure, and not strong when it is diluted. And therefore the imaginative [faculty] considers greater and lesser strength in wine. Therefore, it considers the quantity of strength with the help of taste in tasting, which quantity it does not receive under a circular, triangular, or quadrangular figure, because taste is not visible, because it is not an object of sight, and therefore it cannot be imagined under an object of sight, but it imagines it in an object that pertains to taste. And in this step, it is recognized how the imaginative [faculty] receives one quantity according to one sense, and another quantity under another sense. And because of this, it considers one general quantity, which is the similitude of real and general quantity, which extends in trees and their parts: just as an accident, which is extended in substance in length, breadth, and depth, and roundness.

*On the Similitude of Quality.*

Sound exists through the elemental tree, and beneath sound stands the word, which is audible through the sense that is hearing. And because the word cannot be seen or tasted, but only heard, it is imaginable by reason of the sense that is hearing. And its imaginability is ordered by the elemental and sensual tree, which are instruments for imagining. With these instruments, the imaginative faculty draws a similitude from the word and places it in the act of imagining, so that the similitude holds one foot in the word insofar as it is its figure, and holds the other foot in the imagination insofar as it is its operation, and thus it stands in the middle, namely between the word and the imagination, which draws that similitude from the word with the help of hearing in listening and touch in touching: just as hearing, which is in the middle of the sense that is hearing, and touching, which is between the tongue and the air, which tongue indeed touches the air in which it forms the voice, which hearing receives in listening, and represents it to the imagination. And that which the imagination receives is a similitude: just as a seal represents its letters to the wax, and the wax assumes the similitudes of the letters, and not the letters of the seal themselves. And in this step it is understood how similitudes emerge from real beings. According to what we have said about the similitude of hearing in listening, knowledge can be had of how the imaginative faculty receives similitudes of quality in words, in which quality is extended, under which it can be asked, what kind of words did the King say to his people? And he who answers imagines the words in the similitude of those in which he retained the words themselves: just as wax retains the similitude of the letters that are in the seal. The imaginative faculty does the same with natural qualities: such as from heat, coldness, sweetness, and bitterness, and from the goodness of sweetness, and from the malice of bitterness. And because these forms are like the impressions of the letters of a seal in wax, the imaginative faculty receives a similitude from these impressions under the aspect of quality.

*On the Similitude of Relation.*

Through sight, man sees an infant born of its mother, and therefore man considers mother and son, and father and son, and because of this it is considered that if there is a father, there is a son, and if there is a son, there is a father. And the same follows concerning relation, which exists between equal causes: just as if there is equality, there must be multiple things, and the same is true of concordance. And this necessity is a real being: from which the imagination draws a similitude of relation, so that the real entity is converted with relation into one and the same number, and the imaginative faculty draws a similitude of relation, and places it within itself, from which it clothes its act of imagining: just as it clothes itself with the similitude of whiteness when it imagines white things. And in this step it is understood that relation is one cause according to reality, and its similitude is another cause according to the act of imagining: just as a letter, which is one cause in a seal, and its similitude another in wax.

previous page's text is about how the imaginative faculty forms likenesses from natural qualities (like heat, coldness, sweetness, bitterness, and their goodness/badness), similar to how wax retains the impression of a seal's letters.

The current page continues this discussion, moving to the likeness of relation, and then action/passion.

Here's the translation:

--- Page 103 ---
Arbor imaginalis. 89

On the Similitude of Time.

Sight receives day and night, namely, the likeness of both, and from this likeness which it receives, the imaginative faculty receives a likeness, insofar as it imagines one day and one night, and imagines day at one time and night at another, and thus it receives the likeness of time, and the likeness of motion, whose likeness is an instrument to the imagination, so that it may receive the likeness of the increase of time. The figure of growth does the same, which is an instrument to the imagination through which it may receive the likeness of time: just as a plant, which at one time is small and at another is large, and fruit which at one time is green and at another time is ripe. And because time cannot be touched, nor seen, tasted, nor smelled, sense shows to the imagination the likeness of time, just as taste in tasting, which shows that at one time an apple is green, and at another ripe. And therefore the imagination which receives that likeness, receives the likeness of time, and clothes its act of imagining, habituated by that likeness, and strips away from it the particular likenesses which it receives, insofar as a general habit remains, for imagining the generality of time. And from this generality it descends to imagining time, in particular things, such as the time of day and the time of night, and the past time of a dead man, and the present time of a man who is alive, and the future time of an infant who is to be born.

On the Similitude of Place.

The eyes see wine in a bottle, and see the bottle in a room, and the room in a city, and the city in the air. And therefore they represent place to the imagination, just as a mirror, which represents the figure of the thing that stands before it. And from this representation the imagination draws the likeness of place, which the eyes arrange. And because likeness exists potentially through the eyes and through the imagination: just as a nail, which exists in a mass of iron, through the iron and through the smith and the hammer, so sight, and imagination, and the instrument (which is the figure that contains and is contained, according to what was said about the bottle and wine) are the reasons with which the imagination receives the likeness of place, with which it imagines things placed, and those in which they are placed, such as wine in a bottle, and a bottle in a room. And because the eyes cannot perceive or see place, it represents its likeness to the imagination, which the imagination receives in its species and nature, as a form abstracted from a real entity, sustained in the imagination, and generalized for imagining many particular places, that is, its particular likenesses of the general likeness, which the imagination receives under the concept of place.

On the Flowers of the Imaginal Tree.

[Decorative initial F] The flowers of the imaginal tree are likenesses of the flowers of the elemental, vegetal, and sensual tree. They are likenesses of the flowers of the elemental tree, insofar as the imagination imagines its flowers as elemental, which is the flower of the elementated, and M

--- Page 104 ---
90 The Imaginal Tree.

[Left Column]
[motion,] an instrument for going, and a hand for working. And from these flowers and instruments, imagination receives a likeness, when it sees figures in which operation occurs, namely in operating, in elementating, and in going. The flowers of the vegetal tree are potency, object, and act, which act is indeed to vegetate, from which imagination receives a likeness, with sight in seeing, and with taste in tasting, inasmuch as sight sees the vegetated apple, and taste perceives the flavor. And these operations of the senses infuse their likenesses into the imagination, like a foot in sand, and the imagination receives them, like sand which receives the footprint. And the imaginative faculty imagines the operations of the vegetative faculty, and by imagining them, it moves the branches of the vegetative faculty, to have appetite for things that can be tasted. And the vegetative faculty moves the branches of the elemental tree: just as a human, who imagines some pleasant flavor, moves himself towards it by eating and drinking. The imaginative faculty receives the likenesses of the flowers of the sensual tree, such as seeing, which is a flower and an instrument, with which the visual potency receives the seen object. And the likeness which imagination receives is a habit, by which it is clothed to imagine under the aspect of seeing. Hearing does the same: as we have indicated in the accidents of imagination. The imaginative faculty receives the likenesses of the flowers of the trees, and makes one general likeness, just as a logician considers one species of many individuals. And with that general flower, it imagines special flowers according to the natures and properties of instruments and actions, forms and passions of materials, and therefore imagined things follow, which are imbued with the act of imagining them.

[Right Column]
*On the Fruit of the Imaginal Tree.*

The fruit of the imaginal tree is the likeness of the fruit of the elemental tree, which is elementated, and the fruit of the vegetal tree, which is vegetated and elementated, and the fruit of the sensual tree, which is sensed, vegetated, and elementated: like a horse, which is elementated, vegetated, and sensed. And therefore the fruit of the imaginal tree is the imagined. And this fruit is of the essence of imagination: just as a human imagined by nature, and thus elementated, vegetated, and sensed, and the imagined thing which a human receives by imagination through imagining: such as a lion and a horse imagined by a human, which are not of the essence of human imagination by reason of discrete quantity, but of continuous quantity: like the fire of Peter, and the fire of a lion, and of an apple, which are of one continuous essence, inasmuch as they are one simple element, not inasmuch as they are diverse composites. And therefore the imaginative faculty, in its fruit which is of its essence, attains the imagined, which is of the essence of a horse, which it attains in the figure of imagining, just as it attains the likeness of quantity, quality, and so on for other accidents, according as we have given doctrine in the leaves of this tree. And the fruit, which is the imagined thing that is of the essence of the imaginative faculty, is the fruit at the end of imaginable things, so that they are habits of sciences, and that animals can have industry for living in having things which are necessary for living: such as a needle and a hen's nest, a chamber and iron, with which a human draws fire from a stone, and so on for other similar things. This has been said about the tree of imagination, which is very useful.

--- Page 105 ---
Arbor imaginalis. 91

[Left Column]
...which is very useful for knowing according to mechanical and liberal arts, and he who knows it better is better disposed to acquiring habits of arts and sciences, and has more knowledge of it according to the process which we followed in its treatise, and in the treatise of the other trees. And the more a man helps himself in imagining with roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and with the hundred forms which we placed in the elemental tree, and in the application in the sensual tree, so much the better does a man multiply his imagining to receive various similitudes of real, natural, and artificial beings.

[Right Column]
The principles of this art, however, are twofold, namely, corporeal and spiritual, inasmuch as man is composed of body and soul.
   The Trunk is the human genus or the human species. And it consists of five trunks, namely, of the four aforementioned, and of this one which pertains to the rational soul.
   The Branches are human members, and powers of the soul, and thus the said branches are of two natures, namely, of corporeal nature, and of spiritual nature.
   The Boughs are properties of the said members, etc.
   The Leaves are human accidents, etc.
   The Flowers are natural acts of man, etc.
   The Fruits are individualized men, namely, Peter, John, Martin, etc. Who are called fruits in two ways, namely, fruits by reason of existence, and fruits by reason of agency, etc.

Concerning the Human Tree.

[Decorative initial A]HE Human Tree contains within itself five natures, which are the four natures of the four trees, about which it has been spoken, which pertain to the human body, which are its parts. And the fifth nature is of the nature of the rational soul joined with the human body, to such an extent that from it and from the body follows man, who is called Peter or Martin, and similarly concerning other individuals, which are under the human species. This tree is divided into seven parts, namely into roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

De Radicibus arboris
humanalis.

**R**OOTS of the human
tree are twofold, name-
ly, corporal goodness, &
spiritual goodness. And from
both goodnesses one root is formed, which is goodness composed of both, & the composition occurs in as much as each gives its likeness to the other; the same applies to magnitude, duration, power, & other roots. And therefore spiritual goodness inclines itself towards the magnitude of corporal goodness. And corporal goodness inclines itself & exalts itself towards the magnitude of spiritual goodness. And this naturally by reason of greaterness & lesser-ness, which are placed in the magnitude of goodness, because greaterness is part of spiritual goodness, since it is by the primary intention & in a nobler end, & lesser-ness is placed in the magnitude of corporal goodness, which is by the secondary intention, which is for the sake of the primary. Corporal goodness comes to the spiritual with the four natures of trees, about which it has been said, & spiritual goodness receives them in one third number which is the body, so that from these four natures one goodness of the body is formed in one natural & substantial goodness of the rational soul. And difference preserves the essence of each goodness, & it in

--- Page 108 ---
94      The Human Tree.

...and difference preserves the essence of each goodness, and it [preserves it] in the function of its roots, and similarly a special [essence/function] for each of the trunks from which it is composed, which are its gross parts, and the roots are its minute parts. Hence, when it is touched by one gross part, all parts of it respond, because its parts are mixed with each other with the parts of other trunks, all trunks responding to the touch of that touched trunk. And therefore, difference preserves the real parts in that touch. And concordance harmonizes them and brings them close to their touch, so if the substance of man is touched with too great heat, the soul and natural instinct respond by desiring water or coldness. And because of this, the soul moves the body to a spring, and the imaginative faculty imagines the spring and its surroundings: and the eyes see the paths by which man goes, and the appetitive faculty desires that man drink cold water to increase the body's coldness and to mortify the excessive heat, so that the digestive faculty may have temperate measures, which are suitable for natural heat.

*Concerning the Branches of the Human Tree.*

[Decorative initial B] RANCHES of the human tree are of two natures, namely from corporal nature and from spiritual nature, and the branches which are of corporal nature issue from the trunk, in so far as it is of corporal nature, and the branches which are of spiritual nature issue from the human trunk, in so far as it is of spiritual nature, hence first we will speak of the corporal branches, then of the spiritual ones.

*Concerning the Corporal Branches of the*
*Human Tree.*

[Decorative initial B] ORPORAL branches consist of four natures, that is, of elemental, vegetal, sensual, and imaginal nature. Of elemental nature, such as the arms and legs, which are branches of the body signified by the back of man, which signifies the elemental trunk, which is part of the human trunk. Branches, which are of vegetal nature, are the appetitive, retentive, digestive, and expulsive faculties. And the branches which are of sensual nature, are the six senses of the body. And the branches which are of imaginal nature, are 14, namely four, which are similitudes of the branches of the elemental tree, and four, which are similitudes of the branches of the vegetal tree, and six, which are similitudes of the branches of the sensual tree. And all these branches are branches of the substantial human tree, of which it has been spoken. And each branch has its own nature according to its conditions, which we have stated in the trees placed before this tree. Hence whoever wishes to investigate the secrets and natures of the corporal branches, which are such that man is constituted from them, let him inquire into them in man, according to how they are placed in the preceding trees. And this inquiry is very useful, and is arranged in the treatise which we made concerning trees, and which we propose to make concerning this tree. And because we propose to speak briefly, we do not wish to recapitulate the corporal branches in this tree, because it suffices that we have given knowledge in their own trees.
