Concerning the spiritual Branches of the human tree.

The spiritual branches of the human tree are three, namely memory, intellect, and will, which are three faculties that are of the essence of the rational soul; just as the four branches, which are of the essence of the elemental trunk, and just as the trunk, which is from its roots. Therefore, first we will speak of memory, and afterwards of intellect and will.

Concerning Memory, which is a spiritual branch of the human tree.

Memory is a branch of the human tree, and it is of goodness, magnitude, duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, difference, concordance, beginning, middle, and end, superiority, equality, and inferiority. And it is placed in the third number, because just as man is from soul and body, and transitions into a third category to the extent that it is neither soul nor body, so memory is not goodness, nor other principles, although it is from them, which principles it uses according to their nature. Memory through goodness is good, since it is the case that goodness is one of its parts, and therefore it performs good operations, which are to recall past things, by which recalling man has the habit of knowledge, which is good, and its privation would be evil. Memory is great through magnitude, and its magnitude is good through goodness, and because of this it performs good and great operations, because it is a great thing to recall past things and things absent from the senses. Because memory is of duration, therefore it has the nature that it makes things that are past endure: such as recalling those things that ancient men did, whose operations endure through memory, which recalls them. Memory is of power, by reason of which it can be what it is, and recall past things, and it can be of goodness, magnitude, wisdom. Because memory participates with wisdom, and with will, which are the other branches, it has through wisdom a natural instinct for recalling, and it has through will a natural appetite for recalling, and therefore it moves the natural instincts and appetites of the other branches, from which the body of man is constituted. Just as a man who recalls some carnal pleasure, by which recalling the elemental part moves itself to heat, and the vegetative part to grow, and the sensitive part to feel, and the imaginative part to imagine, so that that pleasure can come into act. And it is the same if a man recalls something displeasing that he had received from some man, because then he moves himself to anger through the natural instinct and appetite of memory, and moves the other branches, with which it participates, with natural instincts and appetites according to their conditions, so that vengeance can be done, and therefore men often become angry, and if they are patient, they become virtuous, and acquire merit. Because memory is of virtue, it performs virtuous works, since virtue is to recall past things according to their conditions and natures. Memory is of truth, therefore it recalls true things. And when it cannot recall true things, it is contradicted by the opposition which exists between the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative branches, with which memory itself participates. And therefore it often believes it recalls true things, and recalls the opposite. Memory is

Memory pertains to intellectual distinction, by reason of which it has in itself concrete differences which are of its essence, namely, the faculty of remembering, the memorable, and to remember, and because it itself pertains to power, it can possess. And it is good that it should possess, because it itself pertains to goodness. And it is a great thing for it, that it should possess in itself, and that they should be of its essence. And for this reason, it recalls different things, and it can recall them, and it is good for it to recall them. Memory is of quality, and therefore it is of equal parts, namely of the memorative, the memorable, and the act of remembering, which are its essential parts, and in which it is sustained. And because it is of goodness, its equality is good, and because it is of magnitude, it is great, and because it is of duration, it endures, and because it is of power, it can be, and so concerning the other forms. Memory is of minority, because it was created from nothing, and because it has in itself certain parts smaller than others, such as accidents, which are not as great as the substantial parts, which are goodness, magnitude, etc., by reason of which, memory is a substantial part of the rational soul. And smaller parts cannot be of memory, if memory were not of minority. Memory is not of contrariety, for if it were of contrariety, it would be corruptible, but it is subject to contrariety, insofar as the branches of other trees, with which it participates, are of contrariety. Therefore, man does many things against memory, in moving its parts against it, just as a man who acts against his own parts in cutting his hand, or when he labors too much, or because he does not want to eat when he is hungry, and so concerning other similar things. We have spoken of memory and its parts, and through what we have said about them, knowledge of memory and its quiddity can be had, because by knowing the parts, the whole is known. Hence, just as a sentient body responds when touched by any of its branches, or by any of its forms: so memory responds when touched by any of its forms or par-

[Right Column]
parts: as if it is touched with malice against its goodness, with the magnitude of its goodness, it responds against malice. And if it is touched with goodness, with the magnitude of its goodness, it responds by recalling good things, and so concerning other touches, by which it can be touched, because it can respond in as many ways as its parts are, and also accidentally in addition, insofar as it is of concord, through which it can respond against contrariety, and insofar as it is of truth, it can respond against falsity, and so concerning the others. This treatise on memory is very useful for knowing, and for acquiring the habit of knowledge, and also for having a method for remembering past things, because doctrine has been given on how a man may know how to move his memory to recall desired objects, so that those things may be remembered which have a likeness to its parts, namely, those from which memory consists, and according to what we have said in the branches of other trees, doctrine has been given for applying the likenesses of those branches, so that they may be recalled according to their conditions, and the conditions of the parts of memory. And this treatise which we have given concerning memory is arranged so that it may be placed in the memorative art, which can be made according to what this treatise signifies.

**Concerning the intellect, which is a spiritual branch of the human tree.**

**J**ust as it has been said that memory is of goodness, magnitude, and other principles, so we say that the intellect consists of these same principles, and passes into the third number like memory. Hence, whoever wishes to treat of the intellect, and to inquire into its natures and secrets, let him treat them according to
N

--- Page 112 ---
98 The Human Tree.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;">
  <div style="width: 48%;">
    What has been discussed concerning memory with its principles. To give a better understanding of the intellect and its natures and conditions, we wish to apply the hundred primary forms, which we mentioned in the elemental tree, to the intellect, and to investigate it with them.

    And first, with unity and plurality. The intellect is one through unity: just as something is good through goodness, and great through greatness. And it has many things within itself through plurality, namely the intellective (faculty), the intelligible (object), and the act of understanding.

    And therefore, insofar as it is one, it has the nature of considering one as one. And because it concerns many things, it has the nature of considering many as many.

    The intellect is concerned with simple principles, namely simple goodness and magnitude, etc. And therefore it has the nature that, if it is a simple part of substance and in a simple individuated number, by reason of which simplicity it apprehends simple beings; and because it is composed of many principles, in that it passes from many principles into a third number—just as man, who is composed of soul and body, passes into a third number, that is, into human being—through the nature of composition, it apprehends beings which are composed of many simple principles.

    Through the form of goodness, the intellect has a formal nature, which is good, and the same is true of magnitude; therefore, it has within itself the intellective, which is a form composed of the 'bonificative' and the 'magnificative'.

    And because it is of material goodness, insofar as it is capable of being made good, and it is of magnitude, because it is capable of being made great, it has a material nature, which is intelligibility.

    And it understands through making good, making great, etc.

    The intellect is concerned with general goodness in this, because it is of one goodness, from which is
    [N]
  </div>
  <div style="width: 48%;">
    memory and will: and the same is true of general magnitude, and therefore it has the nature of considering general beings.

    And because its goodness is special and proper to it, and distinct from the special goodness of memory and will, it has the nature of considering particulars.

    And through this nature, the logician considers the genera and species of natural beings.

    The intellect has within itself a nature, which is part of its essence: such as its own intelligibility; and outside its essence it has another intelligibility, which is not of its essence: such as the intelligibility of a lion's apple and the heat of fire; and therefore it proceeds to consider external natures with internal natures, which have a concordance in genus and species with those that are external.

    The intellect is concerned with goodness, which is an abstract form, and it is concerned with concretes, which have within them form, that is, the 'bonificative', the 'bonificable', and the act of 'bonifying'; and therefore it has the nature to consider forms which are in the abstract, and to incline itself to its concretes by understanding them, and therefore it acquires the habits of sciences.

    The intellect is not concerned with generation, for if it were, it would necessarily, according to the natural course, be concerned with corruption, through which it would have the nature of privation.

    But because it is conjoined with a corporeal substance, which is generated from the elemental, vegetal, sensual, and imaginal trees, it attains considerations of generation, corruption, and privation, and it suffers a passion through the corruption and privation of the conjoined [substance], insofar as it cannot complete its perfections, nor remove imperfections from them, which impede its organs and instruments for understanding intelligibles.

    The intellect participates with beings which are of subtle and gross matter

**100 The Human Tree.**

[Column 1]

The intellect, existing in one place according to its nature, does not pass through a medium to understand external objects, and thus it understands things that are far away as quickly as those that are near. And therefore it is signified that when it is separated from the body, it is in remote places as quickly as in nearby places. And it moves to those places, although it does not pass through a medium according to its own nature, since it is not a body, whose nature it is to move itself through a medium. Hard, soft, wide, nor deep, are not parts of the intellect, because they are forms that pertain to corporeal substance: but because the intellect is conjoined with the body subject to those forms, it accidentally consists in those parts, and through the participation it has with them, it attains their likenesses sustained in external subjects.

In the intellect consist power, object, and act, proper and appropriated. Proper, such as its own intellective [faculty], intelligible [object] and understanding: appropriated, such as the visual power, which participates with the intellect, and the object which is visible similarly, and the same is true of seeing. And therefore it understands the intelligibilities of beings, of visibles, of things seen, and of beings that are seeing, so to speak, which it attains in its appropriated intelligible [object], which is not of its essence, such as the intelligibility of color, or of sight, of a seen lion, of an apple, or of imagination. And these intelligibilities which are external, it strips bare from fantastic intelligibility abstracted from real intelligibilities, and it clothes itself with its own proper intelligibility from it, and its understanding, and thus the intellect is clothed with the habit of knowledge.

In the intellect is the first principle, and through this first [principle] it attains antecedent beings, such as are

[Column 2]

especially those which are antecedents to conclusions. And it attains secondary things, because it is of the middle, therefore it attains the minor premise, which is consequent to the major premise. And it attains the third number of individualized substance, multiplied from many parts, and placed in the third number, and it does this because it is of the end, which is one of its principles, by which it is placed in the third number, and constituted from its parts, in which number indeed is one branch of this tree.

In the intellect there is no nature of growth, or augmentation, nor of diminution, inasmuch as it is a part of spiritual substance. But it accidentally grows or diminishes in the habits it acquires according to acquired goodness, or magnitude, virtue, truth, or wisdom. And it does this by reason of the parts with which it participates, by reason of which the habits it acquires grow or diminish in their growth, or augmentation, or diminution.

Disposition, property, and proportion are forms that are in the intellect. By disposition it is disposed to understand according to its own disposition, and the disposition of its parts, with which it participates in the composite. And it has a property in itself for understanding, and has its own intellective [faculty] and intelligible [object], and because it has its own being, proper parts are appropriated to its being, just as goodness properly existing under the species of the intellect: and the same is true of magnitude, and other parts from which it is constituted. Which parts indeed proportionally consist in it, and therefore proportionally, it responds to the proportion of the parts with which it is in the composite.

In the intellect stands a nature, through which nature it has the power of understanding, and from which nature is born a likeness, which is understanding. Industry is a form with which the intellect participates, which industry comes from the sensitive part and other trees. And that industry is an instrument for it to adopt the mode of animals, which they have in living, and of plants in vegetating; just as a fox has industry in hunting, and a tendril has the industry of binding itself to the branches of trees on which it climbs, and so for other similar things. The intellect is a substantial part of the rational soul, and its essence is intelligence; and it is a being insofar as it is a full subject of essential concretes, which are the intellective, the intelligible, and understanding. It is a substantial part of the soul because it is among the substantial parts, namely, substantial goodness, magnitude, and the rest. And intelligence is its essence, insofar as its real, essential concretes equally consist under its essence. And it is a being insofar as it is composed of substantial and accidental parts: it is composed of substantial parts, as has been said, and of accidental parts, as we intend to discuss in the leaves of this tree. The hundred primary forms have been discussed, and just as they are applied to the human intellect, in that same way they can be applied to the will according to its conditions.

*Concerning the Will, which is a spiritual branch of the human tree.*

**T**he Will is composed of goodness, magnitude, and other spiritual forms, which relate to its constitution like many lines to a single point. Hence, just as man uses

[Column 2]
his parts for heating, vegetating, sensing, and imagining, so the will uses, or ought to use, goodness, magnitude, and the rest: it ought to use goodness, because it is naturally good, and magnitude similarly. And because it has the freedom to use its parts, it can acquire another goodness, which is accidental, meritorious, and moral, and is called virtue, such as justice, which is good, and so for others. The will in man is conjoined with the branches of other trees, namely with fire, which is a branch of the elemental tree, and which has a natural appetite for heating and for receiving dryness. And the will has a natural appetite for loving the appetite of fire, since it possesses these (appetites) according to the natural course; just as a man, when he is cold, has a great appetite for being warmed by fire, and the will loves that appetite because it loves the body with which it is conjoined. Therefore, a concordance occurs between the will and the appetite of fire, which is good and great, etc. But when the appetite of fire tends to excessive heat, because the will loves water with justice, it loves coldness against excessive heat; therefore, it moves man to eat cold things, to stand in cold places, and to wear few clothes. The vegetative faculty is lovable, because it is good and great, and because through it the body lives from external things, which the vegetative faculty converts into the body's natures. And because it is lovable, the will loves it. Therefore, people love flavors in which the appetitive faculty delights, avoiding bitter things, which the appetitive faculty does not require in the retentive faculty, nor in digestion. However, when the appetitive faculty seeks delight against the goodness of the will, if the will

**The Human Tree. 107**

...if the will loves that delight, to love its own is not good, indeed it is vicious, inasmuch as it loves against goodness and justice. Therefore, men who are just in the vegetative [power], love temperance, with which they restrain the appetitive [power] against undue delight, so that the will can preserve its goodness, which is more lovable than delight in the vegetative [power]. And if a man does the contrary, he loves more those things which are lesser, than those which are greater. And therefore, he remains vicious in sin and in guilt. The will loves to feel in seeing, hearing, and smelling good odors, and in tasting, touching, and in speaking. And it does this because it naturally loves the parts with which it is conjoined, therefore it moves the body to see beautiful things, because beautiful things are pleasing to see. And it moves the body to hear beautiful words, and so on for the other sensual delights, in which the body delights and finds pleasure. And because naturally the will ought to love justice more in its loving in the magnitude of goodness, than the delight of sense in feeling, if in feeling it loves greater delight than in loving to understand or to recall, it acts against the magnitude of its loving: just like men who love the beauty of women more, by reason of sense, in feeling, than the beauties of the will itself, of the intellect, and of memory in loving, understanding, and recalling. In man, the will and the imaginative [power] are conjoined, just like parts which are conjoined so that there may be a whole. Hence, when the sensitive [power] has an inclination to love, imagination is its instrument, inasmuch as the intellect imagines sensual pleasures in it, and then the imaginative [power] moves the will to love pleasures

sensual. And in this step, knowledge is gained of how certain powers move other powers: just as the will moves the intellect to imagine sensual pleasures in the imaginative [power], which is the likeness of those things, which indeed pleasures are naturally lovable. And the imaginative [power] moves the will to love those pleasures: just like a ship, which by moving itself, moves sailors from one place to another. And if the will in this movement does not move its loving with the magnitude of goodness, power, virtue, etc., it moves itself to sin, and converts the instrument, which is imagination, into evil works, which are a privation of the magnitude of good and virtuous love in loving. And in this step it can be known that evil is a privation of good, and sin a privation of virtue. And knowledge is gained of how men incline themselves to evil and sin. Which inclination, indeed, is a privation of ascent to good and virtuous works. The will is as regards equality, just as it is as regards goodness, magnitude, duration, and power, and the same is true for the intellect and memory. And therefore, the will naturally has things equally, just as good, and great, and powerful, which are its own proper object of love, lovable, and loving, which are equal in it. Hence, just as the will participates with the intellect and memory in the species of goodness, magnitude, etc., so it participates with them in the species of equality. And in this step it is known that all three powers of the soul are naturally equal: just as by goodness they are good, and by magnitude and power they are great and powerful, and so on for the others. But because men do not know how to use their equality, therefore they opine that one is greater than another. Such as to consider that the will is greater than the intellect...

[Left Column]

the intellect, insofar as it commands it (the will) to understand those objects which it (the will) desires to love, to which will the intellect is equal insofar as it commands it (the will) to love intelligible objects with the magnitude of goodness, virtue, truth, etc. And the same is true concerning the equality of memory, which is a prepared instrument, in which the will and intellect equally deposit species which they acquire and multiply, so that it can equally restore them to anyone. In the vegetative power consists the equality of natural and appetitive instincts: just as the appetitive (instinct), which is equal to the natural retentive instinct, and when it is greater, then it is against the digestive (power); the same if the natural retentive instinct is greater than the natural appetitive instinct. It is therefore necessary, according to the natural course, that in the vegetative power the natural instincts and appetites be equal in power. But because humans have a greater inclination towards sensual appetites, which give pleasure, than towards the instincts by which natural heat is produced and also preserved. Indeed, they believe that the appetitive power is greater in the vegetative power than the natural retentive instinct, on account of which they consider things against the truth of the body. They do the same when they judge the will to be greater through freedom than the intellect, which is as great through freedom as the will; for just as it is great for the will to have freedom, by which it can dispose itself to love one thing or another, so it is great for the intellect to have freedom, by which it can dispose itself to understand freely and not under compulsion, one object or another. Just as eyes, which have the freedom to see, and fire to heat, when it heats, and also just as the will has freedom to love or to hate,

[Right Column]

so the intellect has freedom to understand truth or falsehood.

Concerning the Branches of the Human Tree.

The branches of the human tree are from five natures, namely, from the elemental, vegetative, sensual, imaginal, and rational natures. Therefore, each of the branches comes with its natures and conditions into this tree: just as fire, which comes with its branches, which are the ignifying power, the ignifiable object, and the act of ignifying; in the mass which is a branch composed of the elementative power, the elementable object, and the act of elementing, with other elements. And with such a branch stands a branch clothed in the vegetative nature, whose (vegetative nature) clothes its (elemental) branch, through which clothing it is disposed to generation and corruption, privation and renovation, and it passes to the branches of the sensitive nature, by reason of which it is disposed that it may be an instrument for the seeing power, the visible object, and the act of seeing, and for the seen object, and for the hearing power, the audible object, and so for the other particulars of the common sense. Then it passes to the imaginative power, leading to it objects which it has through its own nature, and those likewise with which it is clothed through the vegetative and sensitive powers, in which (imaginative power) it is disposed that it becomes imaginable according to its conditions, which it receives and gives. And thus clothed and habituated it passes to the rational power, whose branches are in memory: the memorative power, the memorable object, and the act of remembering; and in the intellect: the intellective power, the intelligible object, and the act of understanding; and in the will: the amative power, the lovable object, and the act of loving. And therefore the soul receives in its branches the properties and qualities of the elementated branches. And it does the same concerning the vegetated, and the sensed, and the imagined. And in this step, knowledge is obtained concerning the mixture of the branches,

--- Page 123 ---
Arbor humanalis. 109

of the branches, which occurs in the human tree, through which mixture there is a continuation and participation of the branches, so that there is one continuation of humanity constituted from discrete quantities, which are discrete insofar as they are parts of the whole, which is man. For if indeed it is a whole, it is a whole composed of many through a continuous quantity. And with the branches thus mixed all together in the human tree, there is a participation of object and object, and of potency and potency, and of act and act, just as from the elemental, vegetal, sensible, imaginable, and rational. And because these objects are of the species of objectification, they are in concordance, through which they are disposed to be instruments to one another so that they may be objectified through potencies. And the same follows concerning the concordance of potencies and acts, such as the elemental, vegetal, sensitive, imaginative, and rational, which have concordance in receiving objects, insofar as they are under one species of activity. And from both concordances, the acts are in concordance, just as the element

**The Human Tree. III**

It posits similarities of other qualities. And the rational faculty produces joy, or sadness, or the habit of knowledge. And so concerning other things similar to these.

*Concerning the Relation of the Human Tree.*

Inasmuch as the human tree consists of many trees, so there are many relations, some mixed in others. And therefore in man there is a general relation of all, such as the relation of the honorer, the honorable, and to honor, or of father or of son. And the relation of the honorer, the honorable, and to honor is derived from the relations of the branches of the other primary trees, so that man Martin is an honorer, inasmuch as he is from the aforementioned primary trees, not inasmuch as he is from this tree, because no man can generate a rational soul, nor create it, and therefore the relation does not pass to all parts of the human tree. The relations of the rational tree are in its branches, namely in memory: the remembering, the memorable, and to remember; in the intellect: the understanding, the intelligible, and to understand; and in the will: the loving, the lovable, and to love; and in its trunk: namely the reasoning, the reasonable, and to reason; and in its roots: such as in goodness, in which is the relation of the one who makes good, the capable of being made good, and to make good. And so concerning the other natural relations.

*Concerning the Action and Passion of the Human Tree.*

Since the human tree is made from many trees, it is necessary that in it there are many actions and passions, just as in Martin, in whom action and passion consist through the elemental tree, because his natural heat heats the foods which

[Right Column]

he eats, and his coldness is capable of being heated, and in himself he has action through the vegetal tree, inasmuch as the digestive [faculty] digests the foods which he receives, and in himself he has passion through the corruption of the inclination to death, and of renewal into other forms, which are under other species: such as worms derived from the matter of the body. There is in man action by reason of the sensual tree: inasmuch as he perceives color with his eyes, and taste with his palate; and there is in him passion, inasmuch as he feels pain. Through the action of imagination, the flesh moves itself towards carnal delights, which flesh indeed sustains passion in the movement which it has. There are also in man action and passion, through the rational tree, just as all primary trees which have passion under the rational tree, which is the lord and informing form, guiding all lower forms towards their natural inclinations and movements. And it has passion in acquiring their necessities: just as the soul, when it considers and labors, so that the body may be able to live, and to have the necessities which it needs for living: such as a room, which it needs for dwelling, and a needle, which it needs for sewing, and a plowshare, which it needs for plowing. Furthermore, the rational soul has action and passion simply by itself, such as in the will, in which the lover is the agent, and the lovable is the patient; and also, in loving, it has the passion of both according to the impressions and passions of the habits which it receives. And so concerning other things similar to these: such as the intellect, which has passion when it cannot understand, and the will, when it cannot have that which it desires.

*Concerning Habit*

--- Page 126 ---
**112 The Human Tree.**

**On the Habits of the Human Tree.**

**T**he habits of the human tree are many and diverse. And some are natural, and others artificial; natural ones are according to the conditions of the primary trees, as has been said about them in the leaves of the elemental tree. And similarly it is concerning the habits of the vegetal, sensual, and imaginal tree, which, according to their conditions, come to the habits of the rational tree, so that they may be sustained: just as matter is sustained in its form and in its end. And from all these natural habits, the human tree is habituated and clothed. Just as through the elemental habit it is clothed with color and heat, and through the vegetal with taste, sweetness, and smell, and through the sensual it is clothed with sight and hearing, and through the imaginal it is clothed with imagination, and through the rational it is clothed with memory, intellect, and will. And from all these natural habits are derived artificial habits, which are necessary for living and for the well-being of the tree. Just as through the elemental, man acquires the habit of a tunic, so that he may not have cold, and thus in habit, he has the art of tailoring, or the art of smithing, so that he can make a knife, a needle, and a plowshare. And through the vegetal he has in habit the art of baking, and the art of medicine. And through the sensual he has in habit the art of building, and the art of beautiful figures, ornaments, and instruments. And through the imaginal he makes images. And through the rational he has the habits of virtues, which are faith, hope, and charity, justice, prudence, fortitude, etc. Concerning these moral and artificial habits, we intend to speak in the moral tree. And in this passage, in the lightest way we can, we speak of mechanical and liberal habits, and first of the art of smithing.

**On the Art of Smithing.**

**J**ust as a vegetal tree has its natural instincts for making leaves, flowers, and fruits, so the smith, considering the process of trees, has industry according to natural instinct, and a method in the art of smithing. Just as by considering the roots, in which it is signified to him through goodness, that he should make a good knife, and a large one, and durable through its size and duration, and strong through its power, and proportionate, through its proportion to the end for which he makes it. And in the trunk it is signified to him that he should make a knife from several things, just as a trunk is made from several things. And through the leaves he should consider the instruments with which he makes, and he should consider its quantity, placement, and time: and so concerning other things, according as he considers to make a knife ornate and useful, for its end. Hence, the smith following the process of trees, according to their natural instinct, disposes his imagination to imagine his art completely, and refines his intellect, so that he may know how to use his art well.

**On the Art of Carpentry.**

**T**hrough the imaginal tree, the carpenter receives the likenesses of other trees, and considers the necessities of men, which they need for living, imagining houses, chests, bowls, a plow for the farmer, and a saddle for the horse, and a spear for the soldier, and so concerning the rest that pertain to his office. And all these considerations direct and dispose him, according to the conditions of the trees, and also according to primary or secondary principles. Hence if any carpenter these...

*On the Art of Commerce.*

**On the Art of Grammar.**

Grammar is the art which teaches to
speak in an orderly manner, and to place accents
in words, as is proper, and to make
verbs, and nouns, prepositions,
substantives and adjectives agree, and so concerning
the other parts of the art. And this order and
process first begins in primary forms
sown in trees, in which they are
ordered, according to the natural
course. From which order the gram-
marian has a natural instinct, from
which he draws the order of the artificial
habit, in speaking, and in making
good Latin, and in avoiding false
accent, in which Latin he places the significations
of words, which are in the vernacular.

**On the Art of Logic.**

The Logician considers the end of Logic
by considering the false and the true.
And he considers falsity and truth,
Under the form of the noun and the verb. Under the
form of the noun he considers, so that he may have
knowledge of things, which are what
they are. Therefore he considers and
defines nouns. And so similarly he considers
and defines the verb, so that they may have
knowledge of the operations which
substances have. And in these two principles,
all things consist, namely to exist
and to act. And to investigate these
principles, the Logician has secondary
intentions, which are the significations of real
things, of which the natural philosopher treats,
and from which the Logician draws nouns,
and the similitudes of natural operations.

On the Art of Medicine.

Medicine exists so that there may be health. Therefore the physician considers the qualities of things necessary for preserving health, and for destroying illness caused by accidental factors in natural functions. Therefore he disposes and orders the nature of the patient, so that health, which used to be in him, may return in actuality. And he considers decoctions and plasters, electuaries, baths, phlebotomies, diets, and other things similar to these. He also considers the degrees of fevers and planets, and the simplicity and intermissions of fevers. He also considers the hours in which the illness begins, and in which it ceases or ends, and so concerning other things which we indicated in the principles of medicine. Whence for all these lower particulars, there are primary general causes, which are above, and which consist in the process of the trees, from which, or through which, the first physicians, by a natural habit of medicine and their art, made their considerations; and therefore those principles are very necessary for those things which concern

De Fructu arboris humanalis.

[Decorative initial F] RUIT of the human tree
is twofold; for one is
by reason of existence, and the other
by reason of agency. That which is by reason
of existence is the fruit through which man
is what he is, and the fruits that are
beneath it have this fruit, so that from
the elemental, vegetal, sensual, and ra-
tional, he is humanized. And in this
fruit stands another fruit in potentiality
with the conditions of other fruits,
which a father can give to the son he
generates, with the rational tree excepted,
which comes by creation, and therefore
humans have liberty, because if the
rational tree were to come by generation,

namely, to the flowers of seeing, hearing,
smelling, tasting, touching, and speaking
to, or speaking. To imagine is a flower
of the imaginative tree, to which the
roots, trunk, etc., relate. Therefore, it is a flower,
because through imagination, humans retain
in memory absent things which have been
heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and spoken
to, or spoken. To reason is a flower,
to which its roots relate, and likewise
for the trunk, etc. Therefore, it is a flower, so that
man may be rational, and that what
he wishes to do, he may do with reason,
because those things which are done with reason
are good and great, durable, and vir-

uses intellect and the end for which
he was created. And when he does the con-
trary, he acts like a brute animal in his
works, and he causes the flowers that
are beneath him to stand idle, through whose
idleness they cannot come to the end
for which they exist. And in this passage, it is recognized
how grave a sin it is, that so
many noble flowers deviate from the end
for which they exist.

[Left Column]

*Concerning the Moral Tree.*

[Decorative initial A] HIS tree is twofold:
one part concerns good
morals, named under the
aspect of virtues gained
or acquired, which are similitudes of the
actual human tree. The other part concerns
bad morals, called or named under the aspect
of vices, which are dissimilitudes of the
similitudes of the parts of the human
tree. Therefore, we will speak first of the
first part, afterwards of the second. The first
part is divided into seven parts, namely into
roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves,
flowers, and fruits.

*Concerning the Roots of the Moral Tree.*

[Decorative initial R] HE roots of the moral tree are
similitudes of the roots of the
human tree: just as moral goodness,
which is a similitude of real goodness, and
moral greatness, which is a similitude of
real greatness, and moral perseverance,
which is a similitude of real duration, and
moral power, of real power, and moral
understanding, which pertains to the real,
and moral virtue, which pertains to real
virtue, and moral loving, which is a
similitude of real loving. And the same is
true for moral truth, delight, difference,
concordance, contrariety, beginning,
middle, end, majority, equality, and
minority, which are similitudes of real
truth, delight, difference, and other real
things. And all these moral similitudes are
impressions of primary and natural real
forms. And just as real and substantial
forms are from five natures (according to
what has been said in the human tree) so

[Right Column]

are moral impressions similitudes of the
five real natures, such as moral goodness,
which is good under the aspect of
elementation, vegetation, sensuality,
imagination, and rationality. Moral
goodness exists under the aspect of
elementation: just as a good person who
uses elemental things in an orderly manner,
inasmuch as he applies them to the end for
which they exist: such as bread and money,
which are elemental things, and from them
he gives alms to the poor, who seek them
for the sake of God, who created them, so
that rich and poor people might live. Moral
goodness is a similitude of vegetal goodness,
inasmuch as people use vegetal things well,
just as a good person who gathers vegetal
things, so that he may perform good works,
through which God may be honored and
served, and from them he takes what is
necessary for him to live, and similarly gives
alms from them to the poor, through whose
necessity the vegetal tree itself draws from
under the earth, or from the earth, and
makes itself become fruit, and the just
person gathers them, and divides them with
justice and charity to those who need them,
and from them they receive with justice and
temperance, so that they may have a good
life, with which they can serve God. Moral
goodness exists under the aspect of
sensuality: just as a good person who uses
his senses well in seeing, hearing, and so
forth concerning the other flowers of the
sensitive faculty which are good, and uses
his sight well, when he sees sensual things
and from them receives the good

a beautiful flower, a beautiful horse, etc., in
which God ought to be praised, who created
such beautiful creatures. And the same is
true for the other flowers: just as a good
person, who when he hears instruments

And in this passage it is recognized, that blessed God permits a just person to be tempted by demons and by evil people, by poverty, dishonors, and other things contrary to prosperities, so that they may be stronger, and so that they may use the habits of virtues more often, because the more they use them, the better disposed they are, that blessed God may transmit His grace to them, which requires a great and good place, in which it can enter much.

126 The Moral Tree.

*Concerning the Trunk of the Moral Tree.*

[Decorative initial T] The Trunk of the moral tree is constituted
from the natures and essences of the
roots, from which it is constituted,
and it is a general and undifferentiated
disposition, in which particular morals are in potential,
by which well-behaved people are habituated
according to the habits they draw from the trunk
into the branches, boughs, flowers, and fruits,
from which they are born, emerge, and
exist, according as they endure through
duration, and according as they are
loved by the will, and made possible by
power, and by the goodness of the good, and
moved to an end: wherefore they exist, when the intel-
lect understands that end, and harmony
harmonizes principles and means,
so that they can come to the end against
opposition, which contradicts principles and means,
lest harmony in habits be idle and empty of its end.
The trunk of the moral tree is invisible,
and cannot be touched nor imagined
under a circular, quadrangular, nor
triangular figure, and this is: because it is not of a
corporeal nature, but is a likeness of that
nature and of a spiritual nature, which
trunk the intellect indeed apprehends in
that it has understood from the real roots
and from the real trunk, from which is
the moral trunk, whose likeness is
sustained in memory, which recalls it,
and by the will, which loves it.
Therefore, from those the intellect draws habits,
which are disposed to recalling,
understanding, and loving: such as the
habits of justice, prudence, and the other
moral virtues, which can derive
from the trunk, being so general to them according to
their likenesses: just as a mass of iron to the
shape of a knife, a sword, and a hammer.

*Concerning the Branches of the Moral Tree.*

[Decorative initial B] The Branches of the moral tree are
seven virtues. And four
are cardinal, and three theo-
logical. The cardinal virtues are justice, pru-
dence, fortitude, and temperance. The theo-
logical virtues are faith, hope, and charity. There is a dif-
ference between the four cardinal,
and the three theological virtues: inasmuch as through
the four, man is disposed to living
well in this life, and any man
can have them; inasmuch as he can na-
turally draw likenesses
from the primary natures of the moral trunk, which
are undifferentiated and disposed to being actualized.
But the three theological virtues
cannot be had without the grace
of God, and He gives them to whomever He pleases, because
they are paths to another life. He nevertheless wil-
lingly gives them to men adorned and clothed
with cardinal virtues, which are in
harmony with those, namely, the theological virtues.

*Concerning Justice.*

[Decorative initial I] Justice is that virtue, by virtue of which
men render to each what
is his own. Justice is from the roots of the
tree, and especially from equality, by
virtue of which goodness, greatness, etc.,
mutually give their likenesses to each other
equally, and in that equality of giving, justice is
born and established, for it is just
that greatness should give its likeness
to goodness, inasmuch as goodness gives
its likeness to it. And it is good
that the likenesses be given equally,
and is similarly great and endures:
because they give their likenesses to each other equally.
And therefore justice is good,
great, and durable in the equality of such
reciprocal givings. And in this passage it is known,

So that, before men begin to eat, it may move them to recall, understand & love temperance, & to hate gluttony & its circumstances. And it makes men consider the small utility of taste, & the great danger of infirmity, which comes, because great and many flavors in foods are much recalled & loved. Hence just as four brothers, or sisters, according to natural instinct have a way, & nature by which they help each other against their enemies, so the cardinal virtues have a way, & natural instinct, by which they help each other against vices.

Of Faith.

Faith is a virtue, which compels the intellect to affirm, or positively deny those things, which are true. Faith is, that it may restore lovable, & memorable, & worthy of consideration truths, so that their likenesses may be good, through which they are signified. Just as visible things absent to the eyes, whose likenesses are accepted in imagination, so that visible things may be desired, & that they can be seen as lovable. Faith is primarily for the intellect, which believes that, which it cannot understand, nevertheless memory & will assist its belief, because the will wants it to attain by positing truth, which it cannot attain by necessary reasons at that time. And the will wants this, so that it may be able to attain the desirable qualities of objects, which the intellect considers.

And memory does the same, which has a natural instinct for desirable things to remember, so that it may have concordance with the will. By reason of faith, the intellective faculty inquires into the intelligibility of truths & disposes the matter, so that it may be understood by necessary reasons, which disposition God helps. And the will's capacity for love, & memory's capacity for remembrance help. Therefore the intellect exalts & refines itself as much as it can to elevate its understanding, through necessary reasons of the truths of things, such as to understand the trinity of God, & His incarnation, & the creation of the world, & the resurrection of men, & the Sacrament of the altar, & the Papal power, which it holds through the keys, & so concerning other things similar to these. To which ascent the intellect could not come, unless it first supposed that any of the objects, which we have mentioned, is possible. Therefore faith has the office, by which the intellect may assume that it can understand truths. And it is the light of the intellect, by which it may inquire into truths, & when it has acquired those truths, or received them at a certain degree of truth, faith disposes the matter for it, so that it may ascend further with greater depth of understanding, & this from degree to degree, to the point where it can ascend no further. And faith is above the intellect, & the intellect is beneath faith like a cultivated olive, which is grafted onto a wild olive. And the more matter comes from the wild olive to the cultivated olive, the more the cultivated olive thrives, nevertheless it converts that matter which comes, into its own nature. And in this passage it is understood how faith remains,³ & the merits which man has through it, although the intellect may attain at one time truths, which are concerning God by necessary R

--- Page 144 ---

Arbor moralis.

[Left Column]
...reasons, which it previously did not reach, but supposed them to be true through the virtue of faith. If faith did not exist, simple people, and those who have to deal with mechanical arts, would not be able to participate in the truths of God and His operations, which are difficult to understand. But because faith is in these (people), they participate in those truths by loving, believing, and recalling, just as with sensations which they do not feel, they participate by imagining them, through which, having imagined, they move themselves to feel the sensations which they desire to feel by seeing, or hearing, smelling, tasting, etc.

De Spe.

[Large initial S]Hope is a virtue which makes a person hope for the end he desires, to which he believes he will come more through the power and goodness of God or another than through his own goodness or power, and the same applies to magnitude, duration, wisdom, and will. Hope is more through the end than through another principle. With it, people trust in the mercy of God that He will forgive their sins, because He has greater power to forgive sins than they have to sin, and His goodness in doing good is greater than the malice of men in doing evil; and God's will in loving good and pious things is greater than the will of men, and the same is true of God's wisdom and duration (eternity). And therefore, he who thus hopes for pardon from God attains the end he desires. People who wish to do things by which God can be served and honored, if they cannot do them by themselves, because they have little power, let them have recourse to divine power, under the hope of which they may hope for help, because the

[Right Column]
end is for the honor of that power, and such people have true hope. But people who desire to come to some end, that they may be honored, enriched, served, and, so to speak, saved, and delivered from grave dangers, and who have these desires for the sake of their own utility, and not simply for the honor of God, such people do not have true hope, because no one can have true hope while sinning, since it is so that hope and sin are contrary, and hope and the virtue of justice, and charity have concordance. Just as faith prepares matter for the intellect, so that its understanding may ascend to high intelligibilities, so hope prepares matter for the will, so that its loving may ascend to high lovabilities and memorabilities. Therefore, hope is a cause which gives great pleasure and rest to people, and the greater it is, the greater is the cause of pleasure and rest. And in this passage it is recognized that God allows some people, children of hope and cultivators of it, to be poor and in grave dangers, so that they may have confidence in God's goodness and power. For just as great cold makes a person recall the warmth of fire, or great thirst makes a person recall the coolness of water and the place where a spring is, so the labors which the friends of God suffer in this world for His love, make them recall the great power and great goodness of God. And the same applies to His great humility, piety, and will.

De Charitate.

[Large initial C]Charity is a virtue which creates fellowship and solace between a friend and a beloved, who relate to lovable things.

--- Page 145 ---
Arbor moralis. 131

lovable things. Through charity, people love God and His operations, and they love each other and themselves. And it is more through will than through any other principle. And it cannot be full without love, which relates to God and to people with greatness of goodness, justice, and lovableness. Therefore, people who have their love for God, and for themselves, are children of charity, and clothed in its habit. But those who do not have their love in God and in themselves with greatness of goodness, justice, and lovableness, their love is not clothed in charity, but is clothed in a semblance of charity, which is contrary to its form: just as hot water in which the semblance of its heat is contrary to the form of coldness. Just as money and possessions are the riches of rich people, so charity is the riches of poor people. For charity wills that the rich satisfy the poor in their necessities from their riches. Also, charity is the riches of the rich in poor people, because charity requires that poor people serve the rich in their necessities. Therefore, charity holds one foot among rich people, and the other among poor people, and love through charity tends towards God, who is loved. Charity is the likeness of the will, which desires the lovableness of the beloved. Therefore, charity makes the beloved be in the intellect and in the memory of the friend, in whom the beloved, remembered and understood, resides. Therefore, charity is a virtue which gives greater pleasure than any other virtue, and by which a friend is more bound to his beloved, so that he cannot depart from him, nor grow weary in honoring him and serving him. And because in this book we speak briefly, because people do not love prolixity, and are quickly weary in loving, we do not wish to say all that we could say about charity. We have spoken of the moral virtues, now it must be said how one virtue has concordance with another. And this is, so that instruction may be gained on how some virtues can be possessed with others, and how vices (which are contrary to them) can be opposed.

On Justice and Prudence.

Prudence disposes its objects for justice, inasmuch as it inquires into what is lawful and unlawful, because it is an operation of the intellect, which understands those things. Therefore, inasmuch as it prepares its objects for justice, it is reason disposed to judge, by reason of which disposition it is helped by prudence in making judgment. The same is true of justice, which helps prudence, because inasmuch as prudence attains that it is better to love God than creation, justice disposes prudence, how it may have both skill and industry, how it may move the wills of people to love God more than anything else, since it is just to love greater lovableness more than lesser, and more noble things than less noble. And at this point, one can recognize that when wise people are tempted against prudence, how they help themselves with justice, and when they are tempted against justice, how they help themselves with prudence.

On Justice and Fortitude.

Fortitude strengthens justice against injustice then, when people use fortitude. Just as a judge when tempted by money to give a false judgment, and he considers fortitude—

As a judge, when tempted by money to give a false judgment, and he considers fortitude multiplied from goodness, greatness, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, and glory, which are better than money, then he contradicts injustice, and is strong in his judgment, through which fortitude justice has material for judging, and conversely, in that justice justifies fortitude, because it is just that fortitude use the natures from which it is constituted, and that it be against the contrarieties of its parts. And in this passage, knowledge is had of how fortitude makes one consider what is lawful or unlawful before the will moves itself to love, or justice to judge.

*On Justice and Temperance.*
Temperance disposes justice so that a good and true judgment may be made, in that temperance makes men wise and have a subtle intellect. And justice disposes to temperance equal measures, according to which it ought to move men to eat and drink temperately, and to speak and work temperately, and so concerning other things which justice measures with equal or proportionate parts. And when men wish to eat too much, or drink, or speak, or spend, or go, justice represents what is lawful and unlawful to the natural instinct of temperance, which it has through the greatness of goodness. And through the end for which man was created, it has concordance with the natural instinct of justice, which is through greatness, goodness, and through the end for which man was created. And thus, with concordance existing between the two natural instincts, which relate to one end, that concordance overcomes the concordance of gluttony and injustice,
which is against the end of justice and temperance.

*On Justice and Faith.*
Justice is the reason that faith exists for men who are occupied with temporal matters and mechanical arts, who cannot have a high intellect for investigating subtle things, which faith attains, because it would be unjust that men occupied with their necessities should not participate with God and His truths. Therefore, justice wills that the intellect captivate itself in believing true and high things, which indeed it does not understand, because it is occupied in understanding the lowest things. And faith helps justice in that it captivates the intellect to believe high things, because in this, faith prepares the material for justice: that the credulity which the intellect has may be clothed with the habit of justice, because by reason of that habit it is disposed to making good and true judgment.

*On Justice and Hope.*
Justice prepares its objects for hope: in that it is just that men should have greater hope in the power of God and in His goodness, greatness, and will, than in created power, therefore, because justice justifies and requires this, it participates with hope, by which participation hope justly uses itself in hoping from God for help, mercy, and forgiveness. Which hope indeed is the cause of justice, that it may have in it a good and true judgment. And in this passage, it is known that justice and hope have concordance against injustice and despair.

**On Justice & Charity.**

It is just to love lovable things, and to hate hateful things, and inasmuch as this is just, justice disposes to charity its lovabilities. And inasmuch as charity relates itself to God and to neighbor, justice disposes to it its objects, namely, its justifiabilities, because it is just that man love God, and his neighbor, and also himself. And at this point it is recognized that men have fault, who wish to love neither God nor their neighbor: because they do not prepare for justice its objects in a way that they have concordance with it, and because they have fault, it is fitting that they be punished by justice.

**On Fortitude & Hope.**

Fortitude is the strength of hope, and hope is the instrument and habit of fortitude, with which its nature can be used and also its operation. Just as a person who has hope in the mercy of God in their necessities, to such an extent that they are not overcome by despair—which (despair) seeks to conquer hope by making one consider the great sins of men, even those who place their hope in the great justice of God. Therefore, fortitude and hope are feet: with which the poor walk, and seek alms from the rich, and sinners seek the mercy of God.

**On Fortitude & Charity.**

Fortitude is the power of charity, with which charity strengthens itself against cruelty and enmity, and stands strong against its enemies. And therefore charity is a difficult habit, so that it may be a great strength, just as for an injured person, to whom it is necessary to have great strength of charity in loving their neighbor who has injured them, and it is also difficult to serve God and honor Him because of the great impediments, which God allows to be great, so that charity may use greater power in handling the honor of God. And therefore, when people who love God have great weariness in serving Him: fortitude is called upon so that it may be a great strength for charity, so that charity can be great, which greatness it achieves in the greatness of vigor, which is fortitude, with which it strengthens its love with which it loves God and His honor. And the same is true of a poor person who gives alms to another poor person, which alms are very difficult: because they need what they give to another.

**On Temperance & Faith.**

Temperance and faith have a concordance in the concordance they have with fortitude, like two sisters who have concordance with fortitude in loving their brother: because by reason of fortitude (which is the strength of temperance and faith) faith and temperance have concordance: Therefore faith strengthens temperance, and temperance strengthens faith, because through temperate food the intellect is disposed to believing against incredulity, just as intoxicated people, who easily believe or disbelieve. And people who have faith love temperance, so that they may better use faith.

**On Temperance & Hope.**

Temperance brings forth merit, which merit indeed disposes the habit of hope, which hopes for reward. And when people have sinned against temperance, when they repent and love temperance: temperance disposes the habit of hope, through which habit sinful people had confidence in the mercy of God, who remits the defects which they committed against temperance. And hope causes the habit of temperance, inasmuch as it makes people consider the mercy of God, supposing that they hate gluttony, and that they love temperance.

For charity to be a virtue, temperance is necessary for people, because without temperance charity could not be a virtue, because in gluttony it cannot be sustained

**Of Faith & Hope.**

Faith is the light and testimony of God's great power, humility, and mercy, because great power is that which makes two natures (namely, the divine and human nature) exist as one person, who is called Jesus Christ. And great humility it is that the divine nature (which is the Son of God) willed to be clothed in human nature, which is Christ, man. And great mercy it was that God, without the human race having asked forgiveness from Him, willed to remit [sins] through the Incarnation, which Mercy (who is God) received. Therefore faith causes great hope, which man had in the great power of God, and in His great mercy and piety, or humility. Indeed, this hope could not be caused if man did not believe in the Incarnation of God. And in this passage it is recognized that unbelievers are not disposed to having such great hope as Christians, since it is so that unbelievers do not believe in the Incarnation of God.

**Of Faith & Charity.**

Faith and charity have concordance, because in this, that through faith we believe in the divine production

**[Column 2]**

through generation and spiration: whence follows the Trinity of persons, namely, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and because we believe in the Incarnation, and in the passion of Christ, man of God, faith causes charity in the magnitude of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, truth, and virtue, since the Trinity and Incarnation are objects very lovable to a will disposed to loving great lovabilities through the light of faith. For the greater faith is, the more the will is disposed to having great charity. Therefore there is concordance between charity and faith through the magnitude of goodness and other forms, which are instruments for their concordance. And in this passage it is recognized that those have little charity who are not cultivators of faith with the magnitude of goodness, virtue, truth, wisdom, and power.

**Of Hope & Charity.**

In the magnitude of charity, the magnitude of hope is multiplied, because the more men have greater charity towards God, themselves, and their neighbors, the more they cause magnitude in hope, and vice versa, because the more man has greater hope in God and in his friends, the more he causes magnitude in charity. Therefore charity and hope, inasmuch as they are great, each cause in the other a magnitude of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, truth, and virtue of purpose and concordance. Therefore men can have as much charity and hope as they wish to have. And in this passage it is recognized that those who are negligent in having a magnitude of charity and hope have great fault. On Holiness.

Holiness is that virtue by which the holy are innocent and clean from sins. For holiness to be a virtue, the other virtues lend their aid, wherefore it is a common virtue derived from many: just as justice, which makes men holy, insofar as there exists in them the opportunity to be just. And prudence makes them wise, insofar as it signifies to them those things by which they can become wise. And fortitude strengthens them against vices, and temperance makes them sound and have a subtle intellect and utter appropriate words, and faith makes them believe truths which they cannot understand, and hope makes them hope for those things which they attain through that great faith. And charity makes them participate in society and love and brotherhood, and in loving God and serving Him. And all these virtues and also others which descend from them, are aids and instruments for men to be holy and to have an exalted life, and to be clean from sin.

On Patience.

Patience is that virtue by which a person acquires passive virtues: such as strong men, who have patience against those who do unlawful things to them. Therefore, patience disposes the matter in passions, by which men are humble, and have charity according to natural appetite and instinct and the concordance which exists between forms and matters. For according as the matter is disposed, the form takes pleasure in operating within it and producing from it that which it desires. Therefore a certain wise woman said that patience is a virtue which conquers, and which cannot be conquered. And it is a virtue by which the demon is more often overcome than by any other virtue.

On Abstinence.

Abstinence is that virtue which then restrains the will when it wishes to desire hateful things. Abstinence begins by reason of the end of charity, and prudence illuminates it, fortitude strengthens it, and justice justifies it, and hope makes it hope for those things which it desires. And while abstinence makes men abstain, prudence has deliberation, and justice likewise, and the same for temperance, for making good and true judgment, and for choosing those things by which man comes to happiness, and avoiding those things which cause harm. Therefore abstinence is that virtue which more strongly opposes anger in its beginning than any other virtue.

On Humility.

Humility is that virtue which, with justice, subordinates lesser virtues to greater ones, and with itself, subordinates greater virtues to lesser ones; therefore it is greater through those things which are greater, than through those which are lesser, and through itself than through justice. Whose goodness is multiplied in lesser and greater beings. Therefore S says

**De Constantia.**
Constancy is that virtue which makes a person persevere in their good purpose. Constancy strengthens people with fortitude and hope towards greatness, goodness, perseverance, justice, and truth. Therefore, people who are constant in their good purpose are strong against vices, and have hope in the help of God, and in their merits which they acquire in long perseverance of goodness and truth. Therefore, a wise man says that people, sons of constancy, are strong, and have more friends, through whom they are constant against their enemies.

**De Diligentia.**
Diligence is a virtue with which charity and prudence conquer laziness. Through diligence, people are quickly agile, and consider those things which can happen, and prefer to watch more than to sleep, and do not wish to be fat so that they may be able to go more quickly to the end they desire: and when they are hindered, they languish from excessive desire, and when they are tired, their fortitude strengthens their desire with prudence and hope to such an extent that charity makes them bold, and does not permit them to sleep much.

**De Suauitate.**
Gentleness is a virtue, daughter of charity, born or arisen in prudence and humility. Gentleness makes strong people gentle, because it binds them with charity in patience and humility. And therefore, they allow themselves to be led by proud, cruel, and impatient people, to their will to such an extent that with their humility they conquer their pride, and with their patience they conquer

their anger, and with their charity they conquer their cruelty to such an extent that with their likeness they tame them. And for this, the lion gives an example, who is tame and gentle towards other small animals, which use gentleness with him against pride and against anger, and which have a likeness with him in will.

**De Conscientia.**
Conscience is that virtue which advises with fear to do good and avoid evil. Conscience makes people have fear of the Lord, who renders good for good, and punishment for evil. And therefore, conscience threatens with the power and justice of the Lord, and those who fear the threats show reverence to the Lord, through which they acquire merits and multiply virtues. And when they do not fear the threats, they sin against the Lord to whom they show no reverence. Therefore, conscience binds them with justice to punishment, and does not permit them to have hope in the Lord. And this conscience is according to natural instinct.

**De Timore..**
Fear is that virtue by which people fear to offend charity, and have fear of justice. Fear is the handmaid of love, which moves prudence to consider those things which are dangerous, and which makes one imagine many harmful things that do not happen. And therefore, fear makes people exist between justice and charity, because through justice they fear to err against the Lord, and through charity they fear that they might offend the goodness of the Lord. And this kind of fear brings hope, which with charity has con-

The leaves of virtues are the accidents of vir-

Concerning the Quantity of Virtue.

The justice of Martin, and so for his pru-
dence, fortitude, and other virtues,
is quantitative: by whose quantity
it can grow or diminish:
because without quantity, it can neither grow
nor diminish. And that quantity can-
not be touched or seen: nor is it of
real essence, but it is multiplied in
an imaginary species which is the habit of vir-
tue which is called justice: just as a habit
is multiplied, so that it is the habit of justice.
Therefore, quantity does not have length,
breadth, or depth, nor does it consist
under a bodily, circular, quadrangular,
or triangular figure: but only
under a spiritual figure, which represents the quantity
of the habit of justice, which
is a continuous quantity: inasmuch as it is
the essence of a unified habit, and it is discrete,
inasmuch as the distinction of the potency
of the object and the act are the three branches of justice.

Concerning the Quality of Virtue.

The prudence of Martin is qualitative accord-
ing to goodness, by reason of which a man
says that it is good. And it is qualitative
by greatness, by reason of which a man
says that it is great. And so for du-
ration, power, and other accidental forms,
whose quality in its
species represents particular qualities:
just as the heat of fire, which represents the heat
of pepper and garlic. Hence, just as
heat is the proper quality of fire, and is
appropriated to pepper and garlic, remaining
one in its species: so the quality of pru-
dence is its proper quality. And the quality
that justice has in the habit of pru-
dence is a quality appropriated to pru-
dence so that it may use the habit of justice. And in
this passage, there is much of moral
philosophy.

Concerning the Relation of Virtue.

Relation is in virtue, just as in forti-
tude and in others, according as re-
lation is to be considered in several ways.
As in a form which is in the abstract and
in the subject: just as if there is fortitude, it is strong,
which is clothed with the habit of fortitude—

[Left Column]

of fortitude: and if it is a subject, it must be habituated. Just as magnanimity which is strong in war, or in judgment, or in patience, or in the prosperities of this world or in poverty. There is another mode of relation, according to what is signified in the branches of prudence, which is by reason of the power of the object and the act, because if it is fortifying, it must be fortifiable and to fortify, and vice versa. And the same is true of the relation which is through equality and concordance.

*On the Action & Passion of virtue.*

IN temperance, there is an active virtue through form, and a passive virtue through matter. And passion is felt before action, because passion is felt in the need of the appetitive faculty, which requires much food, and afterwards comes the form, which disposes the matter to the habit of virtue. Therefore, in having temperance, humans have a passion which is a passive virtue, concerning which the active virtue operates or acts. Nevertheless, those who have great temperance so much love the operation of virtue, that the passive virtue does not compel them to passion according to the rational form that their will possesses from sensible and passible quality. Just as fire, which moves according to its natural instinct, even if water does not cause it great passion.

*On the Habit of virtue.*

FAITH is a virtue, and is a habit under which the intellect is habituated and led to believe the truths of God and His works, which it does not understand argumentatively, but positively: whose propositions are resemblances of necessary reasons, which are by force of argument. And this habit of faith is virtu-

[Right Column]

ous, because under it virtuous and marvelous works are done, because it is a great marvel to attain the truths of things without necessary reasons. Therefore it is said that faith is not a natural habit, but is a gift of grace and an infusion of God, who gives it, because it is necessary for humans, which necessity human nature cannot give, because if it could give it: it would follow that faith would be a natural habit, and that necessary proofs would naturally be superfluous.

*On the Situation of virtue.*

HOPE is a virtue, and is situated in the goodness, greatness, and other similar things of real and primary beings: because just as a body is really situated according to the elemental, vegetative, and sensitive tree, so hope is a situated similitude in many similitudes, because just as a body has one situation by a circular figure, and another by a triangular one, and yet another by those things which are lowest, and another it has by higher things, and so concerning other rectitudes: so hope is situated in one way according to goodness, and in another way according to greatness, and so concerning other similar things. And the same is true of the situation which hope has in other virtues, since it is so that certain virtues are situated in others: just as hope which is in justice, since great justice is in humans, who have greater hope in God than in money, possessions, and friends. And the same is true of prudence, since wisdom is to have hope in God. And so concerning other situations of virtues from which a human can have knowledge by what has been said about the situation of hope.

Arbor moralis. 143

On the Time of Virtue.

Charity is a virtue, and it is in time inasmuch as it is begun in time: it can exist at one time and not at another, and inasmuch as it can be greater at one time than at another. The existence that charity has in time is appropriate to it according to the nature of real time, and not according to the nature of charity, since charity is not from real things, but is a likeness of them, inasmuch as they are lovable or loving. And time, which is a real form, is of a corporeal nature: just as an accident which is of the nature of substance, not that it is of the essence of substance, but is a nature through which substance can exist: just as charity, which can be begun, or multiplied, or deprived in time, without which time it could not be begun, multiplied, nor deprived: just as substance, which without quantity could not be quantitative, nor without quality qualitative, nor without color colored.
