According to what has been said about the flowers in the primary virtues, knowledge can be had about the consequent flowers, descending from the primary ones: as from the flower of sanctity, which is a merit sanctifying the other flowers, and purifying them from sin.

*Concerning the Fruit of the Moral Tree.*

[Decorative initial F] The Fruit of the moral tree consists in two ways. One way is concerning the reward of the flowers. The second way is that God be honored virtuously, and served. The first way is like the reward of justice, which is through judging, and the reward of prudence, which is from discretion, and the reward of fortitude, which is from strengthening, and the reward of temperance, which is from tempering, and the reward of faith, which is through believing, and the reward of hope, which is through hoping, and the reward of charity, which is from loving, or through loving. And in these ways the rewards of the roots enter, such as the rewards of justice through doing good, magnifying, and other things which clothe and adorn their flower. The second way, the fruit consists more above, and is higher and nobler than the first, and is the cause of the first, namely, moralities are that God be served virtuously, as with virtuous justice and the others, and also with virtuous goodness, greatness, and the others. And the same concerning virtuous remembering, understanding, and loving. Therefore, no one can reach God who wishes to serve Him viciously, nor does God Himself, the blessed, wish to accept service from him. And in this passage is known the reason why God has so few servants, and that there are more of those who bring great dishonor upon Him, inasmuch as they serve Him viciously, and believe they serve Him virtuously in this world; therefore, when they are dead, they have no retribution from what they believed they would have, but rather they have punishment, inasmuch as they wished to serve God viciously.

*Concerning the Second part of the moral tree.*

[Decorative initial I] This part is concerning vices, and it has as many parts as the first. Which parts indeed are roots, trunk, branches, and others. And by what has been said about the first part, knowledge can be had from this one, just as one contrary is known by another contrary. Nevertheless, because we wish to declare this tree, we intend to speak of vices.

*Concerning the Roots of Vices.*

[Decorative initial R] The roots of vices are four, namely malice, foolishness, falsehood, and privation of end. And to these four relate magnitude, duration, power, will, delight, difference, concordance, contrariety, beginning, middle, majority, equality, and minority. Magnitude relates to malice, inasmuch as malice is great, and relates to foolishness, which is contrary to wisdom, inasmuch as foolishness is great, and relates to falsehood, inasmuch as falsehood is great, and relates to privation of end, inasmuch as privation is great; therefore, magnitude in vice is perverse, contrary to what it used to be in virtue, wherefore the definition of magnitude existing in vice is this, namely, magnitude is that by which malice, foolishness, falsehood, and privation of end are great. And in this point, the principles of sin can be known, and where they originate, and from what, and by what means they originate, and why man has freedom to do good and evil, which freedom, indeed, that man has to sin is not a creature, but is from the nature of nothingness, inasmuch as men incline themselves through it to the general principle from which they are, namely, to non-being, or nothingness. And inasmuch as they have being, and are created for good, they have a nature from created freedom to do good, and through that they initiate good, against evil. And this point is very useful for knowing, and difficult for understanding, namely for those who know little, and especially for those who are vicious, and against good principles. The vicious mean is the privation of the virtuous mean, and is the subject in which the privation of the end flows its likeness to the principle, and the principle flows back its evil likeness to the privation of the end. Therefore, in this inflow and outflow are the first perverse forms in vices, and in evil likenesses, whence great durable and possible evils follow, which are against the natural instincts and appetites of good forms. The privation of the end is the emptiness and emptying of the good mean, and of the good principle. Therefore, the privation of the end is evil, and under its malice and habit, good forms are perverted into sins and evils, and they are empty of their good natural principles and means. Therefore, in hell, good natural forms are empty of their good natural ends, to which good natural principles and means are habituated by accidental vicious principles and means, and they will never attain the end to which they would tend, according to

Concerning which punishment we intend to speak at greater length in the eternal tree. Vicious greatness is that greater imperfection which relates to non-being, and which makes its contrary (which is smallness) agree with being. Which smallness, indeed, naturally has concordance with non-being. And in this point, knowledge can be had under the aspect of the likeness of non-being, and the likeness of being, which are forms that are contrary likenesses of being and non-being. Therefore, evil men, the greater they are in malice, the greater concordance they have with non-being, than men who are not so evil, who, by comparison, have a concordance with being by reason of their malice. And in this point, knowledge can be had that greatness is evil in the privation of the end, and in foolishness, and in falsehood, in which greatness, indeed, evil people are unfaithful under the habit of foolishness, and also avaricious rich Christians, who allow common goods to be idle, and in privation of the end against the poor. The equality of one evil and another is the privation of the equality of one good and another. Therefore, avaricious men are worthy of great punishment. And the more avaricious they are, the greater punishment they are worthy of, because they multiply the equality of one evil and another, and deprive the end for which their riches were created. Which privation of the end is very evil, in which many great evils agree, against the end of goodness, and against the end of its greatness, duration, its power, its instinct, and its natural appetite. and in this passage the manner can be known, by reason of which knowledge can be had of the quiddity of virtue, and of the quiddity of vice. It has been said about vicious roots, and about their definitions, through which knowledge of them can be had, and how they stand under four vicious habits, namely under the habit of malice, foolishness, falsity, and privation of the end, under which four habits, there are other habits, of other roots, which relate to their species, just as the material of a wild olive tree, which relates and converts itself into the material of an olive tree grafted onto it. And from these four forms, which are above, which live from inferior forms, the trunk of the vicious tree is composed.

*Concerning the Trunk of the Vicious Tree.*

[Decorative initial T] HE TRUNK of this tree is from the similarities which we have mentioned, which are its roots, and which is a common general confusion which is the source, in which particular vices are disposed in potentiality, which vices indeed a natural agent draws from disposition, and brings them into act and into habit, just as vicious Martin, who draws his malice and the magnitude of that malice from it. And the same concerning his foolishness and the power he has, by which he can become foolish, and the duration he has in persevering in evil, and in foolishness, and also in falsity, and in the privation of the end of virtue, which is a trunk contrary to the trunk of vice. This trunk is invisible, nor can it be seen, since it is from similarities, which similarities are sin, which is this trunk. And because in it stands a multitude of malice, any person can multiply and augment their sin, since it is so that from general forms, special forms can be multiplied. And since in the trunk there is a minority as one of its parts, sinners can lessen their sins, and increase them, since majority is one part of the trunk, and also because privation of the end is one part of the trunk, sinners can deprive their sins, and they can do this with power, which is one part of the trunk. Nevertheless, they can with the help of God, against the power of the trunk, and they can with contrariety, which is one part of the trunk, in which there is a concordance of virtues, thus in disposition and potentiality morally, just as coldness naturally in heated water. And this passage declares how the sinner has power in beginning virtue by reason of contrariety, which is against vice, yet with the help of God, without whom the sinner could not escape from sin, since he is imprisoned in the prison of justice. And this passage is very useful for knowing.

*Concerning the Branches of the Vicious Tree.*

[Decorative initial B] RANCHES of this tree principally are gluttony, avarice, lust, pride, sloth, envy, and wrath. And these seven branches are habits, under which are forms, from which the trunk consists. Concerning which we propose to give definitions, so that from them we may give better knowledge.

| ...and against natural instincts and appetites. And when they have erred, they do not recall their transgressions or errors, nor the manner they held when they erred: wherefore men who are angry ought to be bound, until they lose their anger or fury, and have the light of the paths of intellect and memory, and until the darkness is removed, through which angry men wander by chance without discretion, who are worse than beasts, which do what they do with imagination, and with natural instincts and appetites. No sin is as dangerous as anger: because it so binds the arms and feet to contrition, conscience, patience, abstinence, and other virtues, that they cannot come or perform any work. Wherefore anger is against being and has concordance with non-being, inasmuch as it inclines good things worthy of being towards non-being, and produces evil things unworthy of being into being. Wherefore an angry man makes no difference between the destruction of himself, his father, son, and sister, and brother, and kinsman, private person, and stranger, for he spares no one, nor forgives, nor listens to reason. | Gluttony and avarice have concordance against temperance and generosity. And therefore gluttony disposes the matter of avarice so that it is against generosity. Just as gluttonous men, who gather temporal goods in greater quantity than they need, for the foods they desire. Therefore avarice is against generosity, which retains those things that ought to be given, after there is a sufficiency of food in those things which they desire to eat. Lust does the same, which disposes the matter of gluttony: so that through it, it can be against chastity and temperance. And in this passage it can be known that certain vices are in concordance with others against virtues, and how the concordance of vices is understood in the trunk according to the nature of the roots, which are the primary dissimilarities of virtues. |

--- Page 167 ---
**Arbor moralis. 153**

[Left Column]

One must ascend against pride and avarice. Therefore, a certain rich man was hindered who did not know if he should raise his son for avarice or for generosity.

*Of Avarice, & Sloth.*

Avarice and sloth have a concordance against generosity and diligence, because avarice is against generosity, with sloth, which is against diligence. Therefore, avarice is against itself. For this reason, avaricious merchants cannot ascend to such great riches as generous ones, who have a concordance with diligence, and the avaricious with laziness, and sloth is against generosity with avarice, inasmuch as it has a concordance with it.

*Of Avarice, & Envy.*

Avarice and envy have a concordance against generosity and charity, because envy is against charity, through which generosity exists. And avarice is against charity, inasmuch as it is against generosity, which is an instrument of charity.

*Of Avarice, & Wrath.*

Avarice and wrath are against generosity and abstinence, because avarice, inasmuch as it is against generosity, prepares material for avaricious people, so that they are angry when it happens that they lose their riches, or when someone advises them to be generous, and reproaches them for avarice. Which wrath indeed is against generosity, inasmuch as avarice is its instrument.

*Of Lust, & Pride.*

Lust and pride have a concordance against chastity, and

[Right Column]

humility, because inasmuch as lust is against chastity, it is against humility, which humbles people to subject themselves to chastity. And inasmuch as pride is against humility, it is against chastity, under which it does not wish to be subjected, but rather loves to be free in the pleasures of lust.

*Of Lust, & Sloth.*

Lust and sloth have a concordance against chastity and diligence, because inasmuch as lust is against chastity, it prepares material for sloth, so that people are lazy in acquiring chastity, and in resisting diligence. And inasmuch as sloth is against diligence, it prepares material for lust, so that people are lazy in acquiring chastity.

*Of Lust, & Envy.*

Lust and envy have a concordance against chastity and charity, because envy makes one covet beautiful women, therefore it prepares material for lust, against chastity. And it makes one desire riches, through which it prepares material for lust, inasmuch as through riches people can have beautiful women. And inasmuch as lust is against chastity, it prepares material for envy, so that it is against the charity of the husband and his beautiful wife, whom lust makes one desire and envy. This is the same: concerning lust, which makes one desire the riches of a husband, so that Peter, who is envious, can revel with them.

*Of Lust, & Wrath.*

Lust and wrath have a concordance against chastity, and absti-

--- Page 168 ---
154 The Moral Tree.

[Column 1]
stinence, because lust, insofar as it is against chastity, moves the will of the lustful Peter to wrath when he cannot have the woman with whom he wishes to lust. And wrath, insofar as it is against abstinence, is the cause of lust against chastity, which chastity the lustful Peter cannot have in the deliberation of his will by reason of a sudden impulse, which is against chastity.

*On Pride, & Sloth.*

Pride and sloth have a concordance against humility and diligence. Because in this, that pride is against humility, it is against diligence, which is acquired with humility; and insofar as sloth is against diligence, it is against humility, which is acquired with diligence.

*On Pride, & Envy.*

Pride and envy have a concordance against humility and charity. Because insofar as pride is against humility, it is against charity, which has a concordance with humility. And insofar as envy is against charity, it is against humility, which has a concordance with charity.

*On Pride, & Wrath.*

Pride and wrath have a concordance against humility and abstinence. Because insofar as pride is against humility, it is against the deliberation of abstinence, which has deliberation in a humble and patient will. And the same is true in a humble intellect and memory. And insofar as wrath is against abstinence,

[Column 2]
it is against humility, which is acquired with abstinence against wrath.

*On Sloth, & Envy.*

Sloth and envy have a concordance against diligence and charity. Because in this, that sloth is against diligence, it prepares the material for envy, in that the lazy Peter desires idleness to gain Martin's riches, through which idleness he covets those riches which he is unwilling to gain with labor. And insofar as envy is against charity, it is against the diligence of gaining riches.

*On Sloth, & Wrath.*

Sloth and wrath have a concordance against diligence and abstinence. Because insofar as sloth is against diligence, it has a concordance against wrath, against abstinence, which cannot be had without diligence of will, memory, and intellect. And insofar as wrath is against abstinence, it has a concordance with sloth, insofar as it prepares material for idleness, which has a concordance with the deprivation of diligence.

*On Envy & Wrath.*

Envy and wrath have a concordance against charity and abstinence. And insofar as envy is against charity, it is against abstinence. And insofar as wrath is against abstinence, it is against charity, which is gained with abstinence. We have spoken of the principal vices, and we have mixed some with others, so that they may be known through certain others. Now we propose to speak of some vices which are consequences of the former.

**The Moral Tree. 155**

Of morals. And first, we must speak of injury.

**Concerning the Consequent Vices. And first, concerning Injury.**

[Large initial I] njury is a vice which is against justice in itself. And it is against justice inasmuch as it has concordance with vices that are against justice, such as with pride, because it is proud to contradict justice, which is so exalted by goodness, greatness, fortitude, and wisdom; and especially with pride, which has no goodness in itself; indeed, it makes all who are clothed in its habit to be the lowest. Indiscretion is a vice which is against prudence, inasmuch as it is its privation. And it is against prudence with the aid of laziness and anger, because through laziness people are indiscreet, inasmuch as they are unwilling to inquire into the truth of things. And through anger their intellect is obscured, existing in darkness; therefore, people are ignorant.

156 Arbor moralis.

[Column 1]
And it has concordance with mercy. Cruelty is that which is against charity, with avarice and pride, to such an extent that charity cannot defend itself against its contrary, unless it helps itself with the contraries of the contraries, with which cruelty helps itself, which are humility, which is against pride, and generosity, which is against avarice. And because charity, humility, and generosity have concordance with being, and pride, cruelty, and avarice have concordance with non-being, cruelty, pride, and avarice cannot be against charity, generosity, and humility. Treachery is that which is against fidelity, which men have in many ways, because one way is that which men have against fidelity with lust, and another way is that which they have against fidelity with avarice. Therefore, wise legal men help legality according to the diverse ways. Just as against lust they help with chastity, and against avarice with generosity. And when they ignore the ways, fidelity cannot stand against treachery. Such as one who would wish to help fidelity against treachery, which is through avarice, with chastity. Homicide is that vice which has more ways than any other, because it can be through envy, through pride, anger, lust, and through many other vices. Therefore, discreet men, when tempted to commit homicide, consider the ways by reason of which they have such a temptation, and help themselves with the contraries. Therefore, a certain man was once deceived, who wished to mortify the temptation to homicide with the fear of justice, and not with the charity of his neighbor, which is stronger against avarice than fear

[Column 2]
against death, and he committed homicide, which he would not have done if he had helped himself with charity. Robbery is a vice which is more through gluttony than through any other vice. Therefore, temperance is more contrary to it than any other virtue. And therefore a certain man was deceived, who did not know how to help himself in temptation against robbery, against which vice he wished to help himself with fidelity, and not with temperance, and he committed robbery. Lying is that vice whose contraries are especially truth and shame. Therefore, a certain man was deceived, who wished to mortify lying more with justice than with truth and shame. And therefore he lied, inasmuch as he spoke false words, and when he lied, truth and shame excited his conscience more than justice. Therefore he recognized that truth and shame are more contrary to lying than justice alone. And because of this he adopted the method that when he wished to lie, he looked to truth and shame rather than to justice or any other virtue. Cursing is that vice whose contraries are especially goodness and charity. And therefore a certain discreet man, when he wished to curse, looked to goodness and charity, by which regard goodness deprived its contrary from the will, and charity similarly, and they turned the will to blessing against cursing, which is especially through malice and cruelty. Impatience is a vice which is with pride and anger against patience. And conversely, patience is with humility and abstinence, against impatience. Therefore there was a battle in the will, between patience and impatience, in which will patience indeed conquered impatience,

[Column 1]

with the help of God, who helped humility and abstinence against pride and anger. Since it is so that God always helps virtues, and not vices. Therefore it is not true, what some men say, that it is easier to use vices than virtues. Nevertheless they speak truly according to the natures which men have through their lesser state, and through the roots from which they proceeded, namely from non-being and from the infection which they have by reason of original sin. And they speak falsely, inasmuch as those things which God helps are easier to do than those which do not have help from God. And because of this, men have blame, who do not do good, but do evil. Inconstancy is a vice, which is against constancy, with indiscretion and weakness of spirit. And constancy is against inconstancy with prudence and fortitude. And because of this it happened once that there was a battle between constancy and inconstancy, in the conscience of a certain man, and constancy was defeated, because sloth helped indiscretion and weakness of spirit, and because diligence was too slow. Impurity is a vice, which is against sanctity with malice, and with the great injury of indiscretion, weakness, intemperance, incredulity, despair, and cruelty. And conversely, sanctity is against impurity with goodness, and with the greatness of justice, prudence, fortitude, temperance, faith, hope, and charity. And therefore it happened that sanctity and impurity fought in the freedom of one man. But sanctity was defeated in this, that gluttony, avarice, lust, pride, sloth, envy, and anger came to help the battle. Falsity is a vice, which is against fidelity with hypocrisy

[Column 2]

and simony. And conversely, fidelity is against falsity with truth. And because of this a battle took place in the free will of a certain man. And falsity was defeated by fidelity, because fidelity with truth can do more than falsity with hypocrisy and simony. And therefore a certain prelate was reproached for hypocrisy and simony, who was overcome by falsity, and excused himself by the temptation of hypocrisy and simony. Laziness is against diligence with usury. And conversely, diligence is against laziness with trade. And because of this a certain usurer was reproached for the usury he practiced, and it was written that usury was a sin, so that laziness would not exist among men, through which men have an impediment to earning goods which are necessary for living, which are earned with diligence and trade. Discourtesy is the opposite of courtesy with gluttony, avarice, and pride. And courtesy conversely is against discourtesy with modesty. And because of this a battle took place between courtesy and discourtesy, and courtesy won, which is stronger with modesty than discourtesy with gluttony, avarice, lust, and pride. However, it was necessary that modesty be great, because one small virtue cannot stand against many vices. Therefore a certain sinner was reproached, who excused himself because he had erred with the temptation of many vices, and had no help except from one virtue, which was defeated because it was small, and would have had victory if it had been great. Disobedience is the opposite of obedience, and in a certain religious man they fought against each other. But obedience was fortified by patience, abstinence, and

humility. And disobedience was fortified by impatience, anger, and pride. And obedience was defeated, because anger deprived the habit of prudence, by the deprivation of which obedience was defeated, because if prudence had been in that battle, obedience would have had deliberation to consider patience, abstinence, and humility.

          On the Branches of Vices.

[Decorative initial R]HE branches of gluttony are from active appetitiveness, and passive appetibility, and from the middle of both which is to desire. And these are its three principal members, in which occurs the generation of its habit, and the deprivation of the habit of temperance, which is corrupted in the branches, in which occurs the renewal of many sins existing under the habit of gluttony sustained in the habits of its branches and members. Man can consider the branches of avarice and other vices according to what has been said about the branches of gluttony, and according to what we have said about the branches of other trees. And because we avoid prolixity, we commend to the intellect, which is exercised in this science, the knowledge that can be had concerning the branches of other vices.

          On the Leaves of Vices.

[Decorative initial F]HE leaves of vices are resemblances of real accidents, which resemblances are against the resemblances of real accidents, which are clothed with virtues. And because these leaves are difficult to understand, so that we may give clear knowledge about them, we propose to treat of each one.

          On the Quantity of Vice.

[Decorative initial V]ICE is limited by quantity, because if it were not limited by quantity, all vices would be equal, and would be as great in the beginning as in the middle and at the end, nor would there be a difference between venial and mortal sin, which is impossible.

Therefore, vice is limited by quantity, and quantity is an extended and continuous resemblance through the nature of the elemental, vegetative, sensual, imaginative, and rational tree. And it is discrete, in terms of the distinction of trees: just as a lustful Peter, when he imagines the pleasures of lust, the flesh, which is an instrument, grows. And in that growth, fire places heat and extension of length, breadth, and depth. And the vegetative power places delight, the greater the imagination. And the sensitive power places feeling in it. And the imaginative power, imagining; and the will, desiring; and memory, recalling; and the intellect, understanding. And each of these powers multiplies its act and operation in that movement and growth. Therefore, it is necessarily required that the habit of lust be the measure of operations with quantity. Which quantity cannot be seen or touched, because it is a resemblance of carnal movement, and is not of its essence, but is its accidental figure. Just as a quadrangular figure is a resemblance of a man's form. And this resemblance of quantity, which is through the habit of lust, comes from potentiality into actuality through an agent, who draws it from the disposition of matter (in which it stands in potentiality) through a natural agent and through its own nature. Just as a nail which is in potentiality in a mass of iron through the disposition of the iron and through the power of the smith,

--- Page 173 ---
Arbor moralis. 159

smith, who draws from the mass the figure of a nail, which has quantity. However, there is such a difference, because the figure of the nail is a created thing insofar as it is placed in the disposition of iron, and it is not a created thing insofar as it is formed by an artificial agent. The quantity of lust is not a created thing originating solely from the power of the lustful man, and the carnal movement extended and clothed in the habit of lust. Through the imaginative, sensitive, vegetative, and elemental power, it is natural, and its quantity is a created thing. And at this point, it can be understood that the quantity of lust is on the part of the rational faculty, and not on the part of the corporeal subject. And therefore, brute animals do not have lust, because they lack reason.

**De Qualitate vitij.**
Peter's avarice is qualitative by malice, and is qualitative by magnitude, and so for other forms. And quality is the likeness and impression of the habit of avarice, with which habit his will is clothed, which multiplies it. Just as inwardly one who multiplies a fantastic species, under the aspect of quality insofar as he understands a qualitative object, and memory does the same. And thus the habit of avarice is sustained by the quality of the acts of all three powers which move the imaginative faculty to imagine things moved to be subjects of avarice.

**De Relatione vitij.**
The relation of vice is: just as if there is gluttony, it is necessary that there be a glutton, without whom gluttony could not exist, and vice versa. And there is also a relation in the branches of this tree, as is signified in the boughs. As the will which desires to eat against temperance, in which desire there is a relation between the power that desires, and the desired thing. And this relation is a habit clothed in gluttony, which strips the will of the habit of temperance, insofar as it draws away the relation with which temperance is clothed.

**De Actione, & Passione vitij.**
In vice there are action and passion: as in anger, because the will is an active power, which moves the elemental faculty to heat, so that it heats, along with the imaginative, the vegetative and sensitive faculties, to such an extent that the angry man feels passion through the sensitive faculty, and the will has sadness through passion. And at this point it is known that the will has its own proper and natural matter, substantial to its essential form, which moves it to sadness and passion with the vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and elemental faculties, which are its instruments for that movement of action and passion, because they are conjoined with it. Therefore it can be known that the angry and sad will, insofar as it formally possesses the potentiality, draws from its matter disposed to sin the habit of anger, which clothes the act of anger, which proceeds from the matter of the will, in which the act was disposed, before it proceeded from it.

**De Habitu vitij.**
The habit of vice is: such as pride, and sloth, and other vices. Which habit indeed is an accidental form and a dissimilitude of the habit of virtue. As pride, which is a dissimilitude of the habit of the virtue of humility, and infidelity,

-lity, which is a dissimilarity of the habit of faith. And the habit of pride manifests in action through the form of the will, which wills to exalt the base above the noble against justice and charity, and through matter, inasmuch as that exaltation is lovable against justice and charity. And in this step it is understood that the proud habit comes from an unjust tendency to love and lovableness, which are born in the habit of pride from a real tendency to love and lovableness. Just as the likenesses of the eyes, nose, mouth, and other parts of the face in a mirror disposed to receive those likenesses, which the real parts of the face impress upon it: just as a seal which impresses its letters in wax, which are likenesses in the wax of the letters that are in the seal. And in this step it is understood how real entities multiply their likenesses in other substances, which are not of their essence: just as in wax, which is not of the essence of the seal. Therefore, unjust tendency to love and lovableness (which are real parts of the will) multiply their likenesses into dissimilarities of justice, which are aroused and exist in the injury hardened by pride. By which will it wills that noble entities be subjected to the base, or less noble ones.

        **On the Situation of Vice.**

Just as situation is the principle by which one likeness is situated in another under the habit of virtue, so is it the principle by which one likeness is situated in another under the habit of vice. As in the habit of sloth, in which the will is sluggish to do good, and desires evil things, for which desire it is solicitous. And thus its operation is situated from sluggishness against goodness, and from diligence in handling evil. And the same

[Right Column]

is true of the intellect and memory, which in the habit of sloth have their operations situated from the likenesses of goodness, greatness, and other things. And in this step it is understood how the habit of vice is situated by a vicious situation, which from the vicious habit is hardened, one vice proceeding into another, namely, the vicious habit into the vicious situation, and the vicious situation into the vicious habit. And in this step knowledge can be had of great moral philosophy.

        **On the Time of Vice.**

Time, inasmuch as it is a real entity, is not under a vicious habit, but inasmuch as vicious habits are in it, they signify the likenesses of time. Just as at one time envious Peter can desire his neighbor's wife, and at another time his vineyard, and at another time his horse, and thus time is the general object of the habit of envy for many particulars, existing at different times, not that time is a universal in itself, but it is a subject disposed to diverse works, which Peter cannot perform at one time. Just as the vegetative faculty which at one and the same time cannot form the species of a grape or a cluster in a hot and dry complexion, and a cold and dry complexion. And in this step knowledge is had that envy, and so concerning the other habits of sin, are not proper to time, but time is their instrument inasmuch as they can be sustained in another, because many things can exist at different times.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning the Fruit of Vices.*

[Decorative initial F] HE fruit of sin is in two
ways. One is the consequence of
guilt, namely punishment, which the
justice of God inflicts, who punishes sinful
men by giving them an evil punishment contrary
to goodness, and a great one contrary to real
greatness, and a lasting one contrary to
real duration, and so concerning other
real forms, of which man is constituted,
against which He gives punishments in the
contrariety of real and accidental forms,
according as sins are great, or small, and diverse:
just as for a corporal sin, He gives
a corporal punishment, and for a spiritual
sin, He gives a spiritual punishment.
As for the sin of lust, He gives the heat
of fire, and the deprivation of the will's end:
and for the sin of gluttony, which loves
savory and flavorful things, He gives tasteless
things in the vegetative and sensitive aspects of the being,
and in the imagination, which imagines
a great quantity of punishment, and in the
rational faculty, which understands that punishment
to be eternal, and understands that it has
eternally lost the end for which it was
created, which end, indeed, is devoid of its
principle and of the means which naturally
relate to that end, which the intellect has lost,
and the same concerning

[Column 2]

memory and will. And in this passage,
knowledge is given how spiritual punishment
is great, and greater than corporal.
The second mode of fruit is more primary
than the first. And it is good that punishment
follows from sin, which is an instrument,
with which God punishes sinners and
their sins: and the punishments which they
have are instruments, through which the merits
of the just may be better known, and the glory
which God bestows upon them corporally
and spiritually. Wherefore, just as venial
sin is a certain preparation by which
the just man moves himself to practice virtue
through the excitation that venial sin causes,
which excites virtue from its contrary:
just as water in a furnace, which excites coals
to greater heat, so the punishment of sinners
and their guilt is a certain disposition and
example to excite the intellect of the just
to better know the grace of God, mercy,
justice, and their glory, which they receive
from God. Nevertheless, we do not say
that God is the occasion of sin: just as
the injury of an injurious man is not the
occasion of the good justice of the Prince;
for if it were, it would follow that one
contrary would be the occasion of its contrary,
which is impossible. We have spoken of
the moral tree, and to know it is very useful;
and for those who preach, it is very good
to follow its process; and it is good for those
who hear their sermons, because according
to the disposition of the tree, knowledge is
given concerning moralities, namely, what
they are, and whence they come, and in what
they consist, and how virtues can be acquired
and multiplied, and how vices can be destroyed.

Concerning the Imperial Tree.
SUMMARY.

[Decorative initial A]N Imperial Tree per-
tains to the governance of the common-
wealth. And it is divided
into seven parts like other
trees, namely into roots, trunk,
branches, boughs, leaves, flowers,
and fruits.

The roots are the general principles
of this art.
The trunk is the common rule or
the emperor.
The branches are the barons and offi-
cials, etc.
The boughs are the virtues, which ought
to be in the prince.
The leaves are the circumstances, etc.
The flowers are the judgments of the prince and
of his officials.
The fruit is the peace of nations.

[An illustration of a stylized tree with circular fruits. On the left, a figure in a robe and hat holds a scroll. On the right, another figure in similar attire also holds a scroll. The roots of the tree are visible at the bottom.]

[Woodcut illustration of a tree with various figures. At the top center, a figure holds a sword and a balance. Labels within the woodcut: "Gloria" (Glory) at top left, "Pœna" (Punishment) at top right, "Monachus." (Monk) by the figure on the left, and "Raymundus." by the figure on the right.]

*Concerning the Imperial Tree.*

T HIS tree is divided into seven
parts, namely into roots, trunk,
branches, boughs, leaves,
flowers & fruit. It is also
divided into two parts. The first part
corresponds with the first part of the
Moral Tree, & is a likeness & impression
of that part, just as letters that are in
wax are likenesses of the letters that
are in a seal. Therefore, in this part, the
roots of the first part of the Moral Tree
ought to correspond to the first roots of this
tree, & the trunk to the trunk, & so
on in order up to the fruit. And we
intend to speak about this first part of
this tree, & to give examples, & through
it the second part can be understood, which
is [the situation] where, with the first part of this tree,
an Emperor or Prince is contrary to the
second part of this Moral Tree. &

                                                                      concerning

--- Page 179 ---
Arbor Imperialis. 165

concerning this second part of this tree, it is not necessary to give examples, because through what we will say about the first part, and through what we have said about the second part of the moral tree, knowledge of it can be had, and a way to rule in peace both the people and the kingdom.

De Radicibus arboris Imperialis.

**R**oots of the Imperial Tree are goodnesses, magnitudes, durations, powers, wisdoms, wills, virtues, truths, delights, concordances, beginnings, middles, ends, majorities, equalities, and minorities, which agree in one community of one goodness, one magnitude, one duration, one power, and so in order, down to minority. If indeed this goodness belongs to one common person, and the same for magnitude and the others, that person is called by this name, which is Emperor, or Prince. The goodness of Peter, and the goodness of Martin, of the general root, and so of others, transfer themselves to the habit of goodness of the Prince or Emperor, so that he may rule them in such a way.

166 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Imperial Tree.

[Column 1]

emptiness and smallness have such great
concordance, that in all ways it
agrees with privation and non-
being, and is above so many great
and real good qualities, and above so many
good, great, and real durations, and makes
the duration of vice exist, and power
over so many, and such great powers. Likewise,
it makes foolishness, or the ignorance of that
(person/thing) exist, above so many, and such great
wisdoms, and the hatefulness of that (person/thing), above so many,
and such great lovabilities. And so concerning vice,
that it is above virtue, and concerning falsehood,
which is above truth, and so
concerning emptiness, which is above ends, and
so concerning others. And this is as if
poison were inserted into theriac, and
darkness into light, and pain into rest. And so
concerning other forms inserted into those contrary
good qualities, from which evil forms
attract and pervert the nature
of those good qualities into evil customs.
Hence, since this is so, it is a great
wonder that any man would wish to be
a Prince, since he can fall into such a grave
situation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning the Trunk of the Imperial Tree.*

[Decorative initial T] he Trunk of the imperial tree
is mixed, that is, the common
rule which signifies the common
person of the Prince, in which common
rule, indeed, are disposed, and in potential, the
particular rules of men existing
in castles and villages, cities, which
rules come into actuality through the Prince,
if he uses his general goodness, his general
greatness, and so concerning other common
forms multiplied from the roots of the
tree; which, just as a general smith is
with his general hammer, to draw from a mass
of iron, which is general for many particular shapes:

[Column 2]

namely, to the shape of a knife, a sword, and
a nail: so a prince who is good, draws
into actuality with his general forms,
that which is disposed for the rule
of the general trunk and the matter of all
those particular rules. And
when the Prince is bad, his common
trunk is for leading into actuality the
emptinesses of good ends, which are above
him: just as he who makes them empty,
inasmuch as he deviates them from the end
for which they exist: as one who would empty
from the power of making good, and the capacity
for being made good, to make good; and from the power
of making great, and the capacity for being made great, to make great,
so that it is not made good, and not made
great, and that he would fill them with making evil,
and making small, so that it becomes made evil,
and made small. A good Prince,
who is a common trunk to many
particular trunks, when he fulfills the ends
of the forms that are beneath him: he fulfills
his end from the ends of the forms
that are beneath him, just as one who would fill
one goodness with many goodnesses,
and one greatness with many greatnesses.
Therefore, to a Prince so full, many
honors and loves are fitting.
And if a Prince empties with one malice
many good qualities, and with one smallness
many greatnesses, no one could
conceive or speak of the vanity of that Prince.
And in this passage, knowledge is given:
how a good Prince is an object for many
affections, so that he may be loved, honored,
and praised by many. And how a bad
Prince is an object of many
hatreds: and how by his
people he is hated, cursed, dishonored,
and disobeyed.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *Concerning the Branches of the Imperial Tree.*

[Decorative initial B] ranches of the Imperial Tree are
ten. The first is Barons, as they are

Arbor Imperialis. 167

[Column 1]

Counts, Dukes, Marquesses, & Viscounts.
The second is, as are Knights of one
shield. The third is, as are Burgesses.
The fourth is, as are Counselors or the
Council. The fifth is, as are Procurators.
The sixth is, as are Judges. The seventh
is, as are Advocates. The eighth is, as
are Sergeants & Messengers. The ninth

is, as are Inquisitors. All these branches
ought to be habituated & imbued with
the first branches of the moral tree.

Concerning Barons.

[Decorative initial B] Arons are fitting for the Prince,
that they may help him to reign
& possess his nobility; for in the
nobility of the Barons is preserved the
nobility of the Prince: just as many
particulars preserve their universal.
Therefore, those Princes do ill who are
against the nobilities of their Barons,
because by destroying their nobilities,
they destroy their own nobilities. For
it is more noble for a Prince to have
Barons under him than not to have
them: just as substance, which is a
genus, is more superior than body,
which substance indeed would not be
so superior: if body were a species, &
could not be a genus. Moreover, Barons
are necessary for the Prince in war, so
that he may have many banners with
many men arrayed, under each banner,
& each banner arrayed under the greater
banner of the Prince. For if there were
no Barons, it would not be necessary
that there be more than one banner in
war, and the Prince would have to satisfy
the ordering & governance of his knights
& his people, which governance indeed
would necessarily be confused, because
his wisdom would not suffice

[Column 2]

to govern so many particular governments,
and he could lose his utility & honor in
war. Just as Barons are necessary for the
Prince, so the Prince is necessary for the
Barons, so that the Prince may help &
defend them in their necessities. For
every Baron is stronger through his
Prince against another Baron who wishes
to injure him. Therefore, those Barons
do ill who are against their Prince, &
who seek from him privileges & liberties,
by which they may have power & honor
against the power & honor of the Prince.
And in this passage it is recognized that
according to the ordering of unity &
plurality, it would be necessary that
there be only one Emperor in the world,
thus above many Kings & Princes, just
as there is one Pope above many prelates.
But because the Emperor is not of that
power which he used to be, namely when
the Roman Emperors reigned, it has
come to an equality, which exists between
Prince & Prince, and one city & another,
and the empire is divided into many
parts, & into many communities of cities.
And therefore there are wars & troubles
in the world, & there is no useful power
in the world which helps to put an end
to those troubles, which are caused by
wars & evil men. And this is because
private interests are loved more than
public ones.

Concerning Knights.

[Decorative initial M] Knights are necessary for the
governance of the Prince, because
through horses men have the prerogative
that they are stronger than others who
do not have horses, & through horses
greater honors are due to them, & also
on account of the honor anciently
imposed upon knighthood. Therefore,
the more knights have-

--- Page 182 ---
**168 The Imperial Tree.**

have of power and honor, so much
the more are they suitable, or opportune
for the rule of the Prince, and slowly would they do
blame and unlawful things. Because
honor naturally makes men to be
above, and vileness below according to
morality, and therefore honor is graded
such that it better suits knights
than burghers, and burghers
than merchants, and merchants
than the common people, among whom there is no rank
superior, nor inferior, inasmuch as
common people in mechanical arts are
necessary for the castle, town, and city. Therefore,
that Prince acts badly who does not observe
the ancient honor of knighthood,
inasmuch as he makes some knights who
are not worthy, and those likewise who
are made bring disgrace to knighthood.

**About Burghers.**

Burghers are men who ought to govern
cities, and hold or preserve
their privileges. Therefore burghers
have an excuse for not having other
offices, namely that
they are not knights, nor merchants,
nor that they practice mechanical arts,
who are necessary to the Prince, so that they may be
guardians of the city's customs, and
that through them the artisans may be organized.
And therefore some honor is due to burghers,
which is not due to merchants,
because they have a general office, through
which honors they ought to have horses,
and they ought to be rich in such a way, that
they can live from their incomes, and sustain
their office.

**About the Council.**

A good council of good persons
is fitting for the Prince, and in
his council there ought to be Barons, knights,
burghers, merchants, and some
men who are from the common people, and also
it is necessary that he who is his confessor
be there. Barons ought to be there, because
they are parts of the government, and the same for knights,
burghers, and men of the common
people, who know the state of the people and the
city. And the same is true for the Prince's Confessor,
so that the Prince may fear him in council,
and that the Confessor may rebuke him,
if he acts against his good counsel.
Just as the goodness of the people commits itself
to the goodness of the Prince, and the power of the people
to the power of the Prince, and the same for wisdom,
will, and other forms, about which
it has been said in the roots of this tree,
so the Prince commits himself to his council,
and entrusts to it the general goodness, and
other forms, which have been entrusted
to him by his people. And therefore it is very
necessary for the Prince to have a good council
by goodness, and a great one by greatness,
and a durable one by duration,
and a powerful one by power,
and a wise one by wisdom, and a charitable one
by charity, and a virtuous one by virtue,
and a true one by truth, and a complete one
by purpose. And a council of this kind
makes a good Prince, through good
governance. And the opposite makes
bad Princes, and bad governments. And
therefore the Prince often loses his
principality, and his people stand in anger and sadness,
and in danger of losing another
eternal principality. Wherefore those Princes
act badly who cast out noble, wise,
powerful, and virtuous men from their council,
and submit themselves to a vile, wicked council,
empty of the forms of which it has been spoken.
For indeed, such a vile council is the infirmity of the kingdom, and its
darkness, and the bad reputation of the Prince, and
the toil of the people thus afflicted: like sheep
that are troubled by wolves, when they have
no shepherd.

--- Page 183 ---
Arbor Imperialis. 169

**Concerning Procurators.**

Procurators are necessary to the Prince, just as are Bailiffs, Vicars, and Castellans, who gather his revenues, and other procurators similar to these, whom the Prince is said to have as procurators, who should be clothed in the habits of virtues against vices. Because through bad procurators Princes lose their lands and their money, and their office is brought into disrepute by them. And therefore those men do wrong who wish to be procurators more for their own benefit than for the benefit of the Prince, because they are against the public good. And the Prince does wrong, because he makes those men procurators who seek the office from him: just as the Pope would do wrong if he consented that someone be elected as a prelate or a public official: if he sought that, or such an office, or committed simony: so that he might have such an office.

**Concerning Judges.**

Judges are necessary to the Prince for rendering judgments. These judges indeed ought to be wise, and ought to receive a salary from the Prince, so that they may have greater liberty for giving true judgment through truth, and good through goodness, and virtuous through virtue, and so concerning other forms. Which liberty they cannot have so well if they accept a salary from others. And therefore Princes do wrong who allow judges to accept any salary from others, but rather that they themselves bestow upon them so much that the judges themselves can live honorably, according to what is fitting for the office. Because just as the Prince signifies God on earth by keeping men in peace: so the judge in his judgment signifies the Prince, because the honor of the judge is the honor of the Prince, and the baseness of the judge is the disgrace and bad reputation of the Prince.

**Concerning Advocates.**

Advocates are necessary to the Prince, who should be good, faithful, and wise, and that he should have advocates in every city, and hired by the Prince, and that it be forbidden to them that they accept a salary from clients, so that they may be more faithful, and that they do not prolong lawsuits, nor that they cause litigants to spend (money), and such advocates are very necessary to the Prince: therefore Princes do wrong who do not have such advocates. But to this the monk replied, and said, that those advocates would cost the Prince too much. To whom Raymond replied that the Prince is bound to have such (advocates), because all things that pertain to good judgment are instruments of the Prince, who is the general judge: just as a hammer, shears, and an anvil pertain to a smith, so that he may make a nail well, and that he may make a nail quickly, or that the end may follow in that time which is fitting for him.

**Concerning Sergeants or Messengers:**

Sergeants are necessary to the Prince, so that through them those who are accused may be captured, and those who are guilty may be punished, and that they may be messengers of the procurators and judges. These sergeants, or messengers, indeed should receive a salary only from the Prince so that they may be more truthful and better in their office. And in this respect the Prince can consider that it is not fitting that he be proud, because every sergeant, or messenger, represents his person, since it is so,

that the Prince exists to punish those who do evil, and he appoints bailiffs, whose office is not concerned with noble matters.

**Concerning Inquisitors.**

**I**nquisitors are necessary to the Prince, who inquire if judges and prosecutors, advocates, and bailiffs have done anything against the Prince, or against his people. And those inquisitors ought to be good, and wise, and rich, and that they should be of three kinds, namely that they should be from the greater class, the middle class, and from the common people, so that they can better know the truth, and that the greater ones should conduct the inquiry themselves concerning all matters, and the same applies to the middle ones, and the lesser ones. And this method is necessary, so that judges may have greater fear, and other officials of the Prince. Indeed, the Prince ought to punish his officials, if he finds them in fault, or in crime. Because a Prince who spares one official, does more injuries to more men, which injuries are against his office, concerning which he must render an account to God, who does not always spare, and indulge.

rali. And love is fitting for a Prince, that he should love his people, and that he should be loved by his people, because love and the beloved have concord. Therefore, the Prince is said to nourish his people more strongly towards loving than towards fearing, since it is so that to love is nobler than to fear, because a person endures more through love than they would endure through fear. Therefore, those Princes do wrong who do not care whether they are loved or not loved, but wish that men fear them. Indeed, such fear cannot be good without love, nor can it last long, since it is so that fear without love gives great suffering to the souls of men. Indeed, this suffering causes many things to be considered against the Prince, from which hatred is nourished against love, and injustice against justice, and betrayal against loyalty, and so concerning other things which come through fear without love. And the nourishment of love occurs with the loveliness of lovable things: such as with justice, which is naturally lovable, with humility, honesty, and other forms, concerning which it was spoken in the first part of the moral tree. And the nourishment of hatred occurs through the contrary, which is from hateful forms, concerning which it was spoken in the second part of the moral tree. Therefore, the Prince, inasmuch as he wishes to be just, chaste, and humble, and so concerning other virtues, nourishes his people to love lovable things in himself, and from that nourishment he nourishes his people to love lovable things in himself, and from both these nourishments of love, hatred is nourished to hate hateful things, which are injustice, pride, lust, and other vices.

**[Right Column]**
**Concerning the Fear of the Prince.**

Fear is a branch that is fitting for a Prince in two ways: one way is more principal, namely that he should fear God, and the other way is that he should fear his people. He is said to fear God, so that he may not cause offense to his people, whom God has entrusted to him like sheep, which are entrusted to a shepherd. He is said to fear his people, so that he may not cause offense to the love which his people have for him, because the Prince does great injustice to his people when he commits injustice and deception against them. In a similar way, the people are said to fear God, so that they may not cause offense to Him in the Prince, whom God has given to them as Lord, and also they are said to fear the Prince, so that they may not cause offense to his love, and that they may not destroy the harmony of love and fear. There is also another mode of love which the people are said to have for their Lord, considering the power of the Prince, and the wisdom of him and his judges, procurators, and counselors, and the justice of the Prince. And therefore that Prince does badly who diminishes his power, and who does not have discreet counsel and discreet officials, because he nourishes his people to little fear, from which nourishment follows lesser love, and in time, hatred and contempt, which the people have for their Lord.

It pertains to the Prince that he be wise and discreet so that he may know how to have knowledge of the purpose for which he is Prince, and so that he may know how to rule his people, so that the people

And the same is true of other good created beings. And because man has the liberty to do good and to avoid evil, if he does good and avoids evil, he has merit, by reason of which he obtains a greater good than the good he did. And if he does evil and avoids good, he has fault: by reason of which he incurs a greater evil, and loses a greater good than the good he was unwilling to do. And in this passage, another life is signified, with the greatness of God's justice. God did not give man liberty to do evil, since it is so that He gave him liberty to do good and to avoid evil. And if God had given man liberty so that he could do evil, He would have created liberty against liberty, and would have created two powers, one good and the other evil, and two liberties, one good and the other evil, which is impossible, that God should be the creator of evil, and that one liberty in one subject should be against another, whose liberties are intellectual parts, for then they would be necessary forms according to the natural course. Just as fire is freely against water, and water against fire, nevertheless in the subject in which fire and water are conjoined, one is master, and the other is subject: as it is in the choleric, in which fire is master, and water in the gourd is mistress. And the reason why man has liberty for evil is this: because he holds or has from the nature from which he is, namely from non-being, and because original sin exists. Hence he thus has liberty to do evil by reason of the nature appropriated to him,

And in this passage, knowledge is given, with which the principles of the liberty that men have to do evil can be known, which liberty is a privation of the liberty which men wish to use in doing good and avoiding evil. And this passage is very useful and subtle for understanding. According to what has been said about liberty, the Prince must consider liberty for the sake of knowledge, so that he may love it for doing good and avoiding evil, and that he may hate liberty for doing evil. Therefore, the people are not said to be against the liberty that the Prince has to do good and to avoid evil, for if they thus incline the Prince to use bad liberty in doing evil, then that people acts against itself, which desires that in the city there be some ancient customs which are against justice, and against the liberty of doing good and avoiding evil. What has been said about the branches of the Imperial Tree, and according to the seven modes of which it has been spoken, the Prince can consider other branches that are suitable for him: such as steadfastness. For it is noble for a Prince to be firm and constant, and it is of great utility to him that he not be of double words. And the same is true of patience, fidelity, and generosity, and of other primary forms that are suitable for the Prince.

On the Leaves of the Imperial Tree.

[Decorative initial F] The leaves of the imperial tree have been
signified in other primary trees,
nevertheless we wish to treat
briefly of them in this tree. And when Raymond
first wished to treat of quantity, he considered
that customs, laws, and ancient
ordinances pertain to the Prince,
which signify the leaves for the preservation
of his kingdom, and its ordering.
And in this consideration he dwelled
for a long time. And sighing, he spoke these
words: "Oh, what a great loss it is
that I do not have assistants who
would help me in treating of the public good.
For if I had assistants, I see a way
by which the science of law (which is confused)
could come to clarification, and in a short time
could be known." "Raymond," (said the monk)
"it is good that in this book you set forth
the method you speak of, for it is possible
that what you desire may yet be accomplished."
And therefore Raymond said that he could not
set forth the method in brief words, nor
would he wish to set it forth in many words,
and therefore he would not treat of that matter. But
the monk spoke so many words to him that
he made him feel a sense of duty if
he did not treat of that matter, since
God had given him knowledge, given that
God gives nothing in vain. Therefore
those to whom He gives are at fault if

selling.

**De Qualitate arboris Imperialis.**

IN the sale of a horse, the quality of
goodness is placed, in that the knight
promises that the horse is good, and the
quality of gold is placed, inasmuch as the
merchant promises to give good gold, and
also because the merchant promises to give
a number of a specific quality, and the knight
a specific quality of horse, namely white, or
black, or this one, or that one. And in this
quality are aggregated several qualities,
namely several similarities of real qualities:
such as the quality of words through the
sense of the listeners, and in the sound, which
is of the elemental tree of sustained things,
and so concerning other imagined and sensed
qualities, by which qualities the buying and
selling of the horse is conditioned under the
habit of quality.

**De Relatione arboris Imperialis.**

IN the buying of a horse, a relation
stands, inasmuch as one sells, and another
buys, and the subject of that relation stands
in the horse and in the gold, or in its value,
and in the knight, and in the merchant, so
that in that relation there are four terms,
without which the relation could not exist,
nor without the relation would buying and
selling be nothing: nor if one or more of the
terms were missing. Therefore, buying and
selling are conditioned according to the
natures of the primary forms of relation. To
which relation the trees behave in diverse
ways, according to their natures, in which
natures the relation is sustained.

**De Actione & Passione arboris**
**Imperialis.**

IN buying and selling there are
action and passion, just as the knight who
has action in the money, and the merchant
in the horse, because there is an exchange
of action and passion, so that the knight will
have action in the money by reason of the
action he had in the horse, and the merchant
will have action in the horse because of the
action he had in the money. And so passion
is a consequence of action, and this
according to the conditions of the trees,
for if the knight promises to sell a whole
and good horse, he will have action in good
gold, and in the due number named by word,
and in the heard sound, that word
remembered by the merchant, understood
and loved. And if the knight does not
promise to sell a good and whole horse, he
will not spiritually have action in the price,
if it is the merchant's intention to buy a good
and whole horse for one hundred florins.
Nevertheless, the law according to the
reason of the sensual tree wills that the
merchant be punished, because he does not
seek what should be said about the horse,
heard and seen, because he ought to ask the
knight if the horse is good and whole, and
also that he should test it according to the
action that the merchant's sense has in
reaching the truth of the horse, nevertheless
that action which the knight wishes to have
in the one hundred florins is not according
to spiritual law, because it is against the
branches of the first part of the moral tree.

**De Habitu arboris Imperialis.**

THE buying and selling of a horse
under a general habit, under which many
things can be bought and sold. And there-

Arbor Imperialis. 177

[Column 1]

...this, it would be necessary that one habit be formed concerning buying and selling in the science of law, namely, a statute ordered and regulated, natural principles in sown trees. Just as a knight who is said to sell a horse under the habit of justice, prudence, fortitude, and charity, and therefore ought to state the conditions and manner of the horse, namely, whether it has good or bad conditions, because for good ones he has charity for himself, and through bad ones, for his neighbor. And if there is any defect in the horse, and the knight does not reveal it to the merchant, he sells the horse against justice, prudence, fortitude, and charity, by reason of which sale, justice punishes him in spiritual goods, which come through that prudence, fortitude, and charity. And this punishment belongs to God, not to the Prince, so that the merchant may be so diligent in buying under the habit of prudence, knowing the conditions of the horse before he pays the money, just as the knight sells under the habit, namely, of prudence, inasmuch as he wants to know whether the florins are of good gold and weight.

*On the Situation of the Imperial Tree.*

IN the buying and selling of a horse, there are words situated under certain terms, because the knight situates them according to his voice, which signifies the sale and the goodness and conditions of the horse, and the merchant receives those situations in memory, intellect, and will, in which the words of the knight are so situated under the form of sale, just as the letters of a seal, by placing their likenesses in wax. And the same is true for the words which the merchant says, for giving one hundred florins to the knight for the horse, which words the knight receives in his memory, intellect, and will. And the passage of impressions

[Column 2]

consist of the instruments of the sensual and imaginal tree. And therefore, according to the likenesses which are in the first part of the moral tree, those situations are said to be, so that they may have a complete figure, namely, circular, triangular, and quadrangular, which are measures and conditions, from which the figures are complete, which signify natural forms that are suitable for buying and selling. And the circular figure is in the continuation of justice, prudence, fortitude, and charity. And it is quadrangular inasmuch as buying and selling are of four terms, namely, concerning the action of the knight and the merchant, of which it has been spoken, and concerning the subject which is the horse and the gold. And the triangle is concerning the intention which the merchant has to buy the horse, and in selling or delivering the gold, and concerning the respect in which are the situation and the promise of the horse and the gold. And the same is true for the intention of the knight. And this treatise on situation applied to buying and selling is very useful for knowing, and is a species of the art of commerce.

*On the Time of the Imperial Tree.*

IN the buying and selling of a horse, there is the time of present words, by which the knight and the merchant agree. Which agreement indeed is that the knight delivers the horse at that same time in which he receives the florins from the merchant, and that the merchant at that same time in which he promises to deliver the florins to the knight, receives the horse from the knight. Therefore, time only relates according to its presence to the money as to the horse. And if the merchant pays the money, although he has not yet had the horse, he ought to retain the condi-

### On the Fruit of the Imperial Tree.

[Large decorative initial F] RUIT of the Imperial Tree is the peace of nations, so that in peace they may be able to remember God, understand, and love, honor, and serve Him. For nations that are at war and mutually in struggles, are not in a disposition that they can greatly love, honor, and serve God, nor have charity for themselves or even for others, being so occupied in the labors and wars of the lands. Hence, just as plants, according to their need, require the warmth of the sun and the dew of night, so the people require justice and peace from the Prince. Wherefore Princes do evil who suffer wars in their lands, or have wars among themselves against justice and peace, and [against] the flowers of other trees, for which Princes exist. For a bad Prince places all the fruits and flowers that are under him in labor and war, and therefore he is worthy of a great punishment when he does not hold or guard his kingdom in peace and justice. And in this passage it is held that the merits of a good Prince are great, and great are the rewards he expects to receive, and if he is bad, great are the punishments he expects by reason of the great faults he has. The fruit of the Imperial Tree is general to those fruits that are under it: just as the heat of fire, which is general to the heat of pepper, man, lion, crane, and fish, without which general heat, the heat of these individual things, of which it has been spoken, could not be an instrument by which individual entities would be warmed.

[Right Column]

Therefore, the fruit of the prince who must respond to such fruits is weak when he inclines himself to special interests against general and public ones: just like a bad Prince, who loves his own utility more than the utility of his people. For because of the weakness of the Prince's fruit, the fruits of the people are weak. Just as pepper, man, lion, crane, and fish, who would be weak, if fire were to draw its heat to itself and not give it to them. In no fruit is there so much bad taste and odor as in the fruit of a bad Prince, for if a general fruit is bad in taste and odor, it is bad for those who are special and small, but the fruit of a bad prince, which is general: gives a bad taste and odor to all. And because of this, it is wonderful how a bad Prince believes he has worth, when in him there is a fruit of such bad odor and taste, from which so many evils and such great infirmities issue forth and are derived against so many and such great nations, and against so many and such great healths, which are things of great worth. And the bad odor and taste of the Prince's fruit are perceived in his evil works, which he believes he can hide and conceal from the people under the guise of good taste and odor, and because the bad odor and taste of the fruit is general, it cannot be hidden and concealed from the people: just as fire cannot conceal its heat from a man who eats pepper, nor can a Prince conceal his vice from the people, inasmuch as he inflicts injuries and deceptions upon his people. Indeed, these people have eyes with which they see, and ears with which they hear, because they have neither peace nor governance nor even a good example from their Lord. And in

In this passage, knowledge is given that there is no tree that produces such bad fruit, so dangerous, so harmful, nor from which so much evil comes: as from the tree of a bad Prince.

      On the Apostolic Tree.

      SUMMARY.

[Decorative initial A]HE Apostolic Tree concerns persons and ecclesiastical and spiritual matters.
And likewise it is divided into seven parts, namely into roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
The Roots are the Cardinal and Theological virtues,
The Trunk is the general person, who is called Apostolic or Pope.
The Branches are the Cardinals and other Prelates.
The Boughs are the ten precepts, etc.
The Leaves are the Sacraments and Canons.
The Flowers are the fourteen articles.
The Fruit is the salvation of the nations.

Concerning the Apostolic Tree.

[Large initial A]THE Apostolic Tree is divided into seven
parts, which are roots, trunk, branches, boughs,
leaves, flowers, and fruits. And it is a general tree
for spiritual matters and orders, in
which are the vicarious impressions of Saint Peter,
the subject of which is a white rock, pure,
clean, and inscribed with holiness, in which
are the impressions of the letters of the seal
of our Lord Jesus Christ. Indeed, these
letters are His operations and
His good examples, which He gave to the nations
in loving and honoring God and
their neighbor. And because those letters
are impressed upon rock, they are stronger
than if they were impressed upon wax. And
because the rock is white, they are more apparent
than if they were impressed upon sand.
And also the letters are beautiful and
clean, because the rock is white.

182 The Apostolic Tree.

**Concerning the roots of the Apostolic Tree.**

[Decorative initial R] The roots of the Apostolic Tree are the Cardinal and Theological virtues, about which we have treated above in the moral tree. Therefore, the Pope ought to be just through justice, and prudent through prudence, and strong through fortitude, and temperate through temperance, and a nurturer of Christians through faith, and ought to give them hope of another life through hope, and ought to have love for his people through charity. And if the Pope does the contrary of this kind, he acts against the roots of his principles. The Pope's justice ought to be good through goodness, and great through greatness, and durable through durability, and powerful through power, and illuminated through wisdom, and loved through love, and virtuous through virtue, and true through truth, and it ought to be a tranquil haven, in which the particular acts of justice of his people may find rest. And the same is true for prudence, and for the other virtues and roots of the tree. The Pope's justice ought to be characterized by differentiation, such that he ought to be just in one way, according to moral virtues, and in another according to Theological virtues. Likewise, in the Pope's justice there ought to be concordance, namely between one virtue and another. For it is just that several virtues should have concordance with the end for which they exist. Furthermore, the Pope's justice ought to be against injury through the contrariety that exists between virtues and vices. And the Pope's justice ought to be a principle for the justices of his people, through an efficient and formal principle. And the Pope's justice ought to be a medium between God and his people through a general medium, which people, indeed, God entrusted to him like sheep, which are committed to a shepherd. Likewise, the Pope's justice ought to relate to its end through completion, for it is just that the Pope should do this, for which he was created a universal prelate and general to all prelates. And furthermore, the Pope's justice ought to be greater, by the preeminence of his office, than any other justice that exists among his people, for it is just that it should be so: since he is a prelate and general vicar. And the Pope's justice ought to relate to charity through equality, for it is just to render to each what is his own. And the Pope's justice ought to incline itself to the humble members of his people, by acknowledging their lesser status and his own greater status, for it is just that the greater Lord should humble himself and incline himself to the humble members of his people, or to the sheep, so that he may guard them from rapacious wolves. The Pope ought to have that faith which blessed Peter had, since he is his Vicar. And it is necessary that he should have that faith under the guise of goodness, such that the Pope is good, because faith is good. It is necessary that the Pope should have great faith, because the faith of Saint Peter was great. And it is necessary that the Pope should have such great faith that it corresponds to the faith of his people. Likewise, it is necessary that his faith be durable, since it is general, for when the general cause is absent, particular durations are also lost. Furthermore, the Pope's faith ought to be strong, so that its strength may fortify the faith of every person. And therefore, it was God's ordinance that the Roman Empire was given to the Pope, so that with the secular arm the Pope might be strong to resist the enemies of the faith. Moreover, the Pope's faith ought to be clear to men through wisdom, and through good example, because that cla
