**Apostolic Tree. 183**

[Column 1]
its clarity illuminates each person's faith, just as the sun, which illuminates many stars, illuminates many small lights with its great light. And the Pope's faith ought to be charitable and amiable, so that he may admonish his subjects to charity, and to the warmth of love through great fervor. And the Pope's faith ought to be virtuous, so that it may be against vices. Likewise, the Pope's faith ought to be true, so that it may be against falsehood and error, and therefore the Lord Jesus Christ said to blessed Peter: "Peter, if you love me, feed my sheep." And he said it to him three times to signify that the sheep belong to God the Father, and God the Holy Spirit, and God the Son and man, who are one God, one Christ, who chose one shepherd for his sheep, so that he might give them the truth of faith to eat, with which truth they might revive. And in the person of blessed Peter, the sheep are entrusted to the faith of each person of the Pope. And for this reason, that Pope does wrong who does not increase faith in many sheep, so that it may be very universal, and that many sheep may live in it, because the grace of spiritual life is much greater than that of corporal life. The Pope's faith also ought to be the peace of each person's faith, just as particular goods find peace in general ones. And in the Pope's faith there ought to be no difference, namely between his faith and the faith of his people, because there ought to be one faith in himself and in his people. Likewise, the Pope with his faith ought to bring the faith of each person into agreement. And with his faith, the Pope ought to be against those who are against the faith, by reason of which opposition he ought to strive to destroy the errors that are sown among Saracens, Tartars, and among Jews, with which errors they are against the Christian Faith. He ought also to destroy schisms, which are so-

[Column 2]
wn among Christians, or schismatics deviated from the true Christian faith. The Pope's faith also ought to be a beginning and a light, by going before all his sheep with a good example, so that they may see the place where there are pastures and eternal living waters. The Pope's faith also ought to be a medium, in which light is received from God, and which gives that light to his people: just as the moon receives power from the sun and infuses it into lower plants and sentient substances. The Pope's faith also ought to relate to the end for which he is Pope, which end indeed is that he may illuminate the paths with his faith, and show by which the saints go to a holy and contemplative life, and to penance. The Pope's faith also ought to be greater, just as the shepherd is greater than his sheep. The Pope's faith also ought to be equal to the faith of his sheep, in believing those things which are true of God. And also because the Pope is a shepherd and is in one faith with his sheep, he ought to incline himself to their lesser states, so that he may cause them to ascend above to receive benefit from his greater state: just as fire inclines itself to the air, which is not of such great power as it is, and causes it to ascend above, inasmuch as it magnifies it in power. And the sun does the same with fire, because it causes it to ascend, inasmuch as it multiplies its heat. Just as we applied the first principles to justice and faith, which are among the roots of the Apostolic tree, so they can be applied to the other roots of the tree, from which the trunk comes. And so the first principles pass to the roots: they pass to the trunk, according to what suits its disposition, they also pass to the branches. And so concerning the other parts of the tree-

Concerning the Trunk of the Apostolic Tree.

The Trunk of the Apostolic tree is a general person, who is called the Apostolic one. And in this trunk, the elemental trunk places the parts that pertain to the body, and the vegetative, sensual, imaginal, and human tree [places its parts] in its own way, just like the elemental one. And the rational tree places in that general person the parts that pertain to the soul. And the apostolic office places the generality of the person, with the first part of the moral tree. Therefore, the apostolic trunk is greater and fuller in the magnitude of goodness and other virtues than any other trunk of its people, because in it stand the other trunks of its people, ordered and disposed to the end for which they were created. Nevertheless, if the Pope is bad, no trunk is as damaging as his trunk, nor one in which so much is perverted from good to evil, nor one who is worthy of such great punishment: just as if he is good, he is worthy of having greater glory than anyone. The Sun is greater than the Moon: therefore the Moon receives benefit from the Sun, and it would not be fitting for the Sun to receive benefit from the Moon, because it stands higher and is greater than the Moon. Nevertheless, there is a natural opinion that the light of the Sun is a point, which is the center of many lines that come from the light of the fixed stars in the firmament, which gather their power in the Sun, so that in it influence may be made below from the stars, which are above in many parts, according as these lower bodies have need of superior influences. In a similar way, the apostolic trunk is high in virtue through the influence which is from above through Jesus Christ and through the Saints, and it is a gathering in which the influence of its office and its virtue is divided and transmitted to the lower particular trunks, who need it, so that they may be enlightened and taught by it, and also disposed to receive influences from above. Therefore, the apostolic trunk is similar to the Sun in splendor and in office. And therefore the trunks which are lower, and their particular ones, and committed to it, ought to show it reverence and honor, like parts to their whole. Therefore, such a beautiful and noble positioning of splendor exists, which is in the midst of influences existing from above, and reverberations from below. And if it happens that some dark cloud, which is from the second part of the moral tree, resides in the general apostolic trunk, the figure of that cloud is very intense in shadow against light, and in evil against goodness, and in vice against virtue. And because it is in a high place, it is seen by many people. And because it is a great shadow, it greatly impedes the clarity which cannot descend from the superior trunk to the lower and particular trunks. Whence follows a great privation of good, and as great as the shadow is. And that shadow multiplies as much evil as there is privation of good. And in this passage it is known that just as the apostolic trunk, through virtue and splendor, is a cause for great good, so through vice and through darkness it can be a cause for great evil. And because of this it is wonderful how much men love to be in the apostolic office, since it is so perilous. The trunk is in the middle of the roots and branches, because it exists through the roots, and the branches exist through the trunk. And when the roots fail, the trunk fails, and when the trunk fails, the branches fail, and in the failure of the branches, they have a failure...

*On the Branches of the Apostolic Tree.*

[Large decorative initial B]
The Branches of the Apostolic Tree
are Cardinals, Patriarchs,
Archbishops, Bishops,
Abbots, Priors, and Ministers, and other
common persons. And these branches are
its officials, so that it can rule its people
according to the nature of the end, wherefore
the trunk is a general and common person
according to the roots, which pertain to the trunk,
just as many parts pertain to their whole. From a good
trunk, a good branch, and the better
and greater the branches are, the better
and greater is the trunk, and vice versa,
because in the goodness and magnitude
of the trunk stand the goodness and magnitude
of the branches, therefore there must be great
harmony between the trunk and the bran-

[Column 2]

-ches, and between one branch and another,
so that in the trunk and in the branches there may be a magnitude
of goodness, and of the other roots
of the trunk, which are general to the roots
of the particular branches. And when
it happens that there is opposition between
the trunk and the branches, and between
branch and branch, the magnitude of goodness
is perverted into a magnitude of malice,
which wounds the trunk and the branches,
by whose wounds the boughs are weakened,
and the leaves, likewise the flowers,
and fruits of the tree. Therefore, opposition
is a great privation of good, if it exists in the
Apostolic Tree. Just as the trunk is a point
aggregated from many terms,
which are the terms of its roots, so
it is one point and one center,
to which many branches relate. And
thus the trunk is a double point,
because one point is through the lower
nature, and the other is through the higher
nature. And if these two natures are
in discrete quantity and not in continuous,
then they are weakened, wherefore the
health of both natures lies in continuous
quantity, so that one nature is in
the other, so that the trunk is full in all its parts,
and the branches likewise, and that there is
an influx and reflux from discrete quantities
into one continuous quantity. And through
such an influx and reflux the trunk grows
through the roots, and the branches grow through the trunk.
And the trunk gives the branches its
likeness, which it receives from below.
And the branches give the trunk their
likenesses, which they receive from it. And therefore,
when there is harmony of
discrete quantities in continuous quantity,
such things are possible in the magnitude
of goodness, in the branches, which are
not possible when discrete quantities
are not aggregated in continuous quantity.

Concerning the Branches of the Apostolic Tree.

The branches of the Apostolic tree are
ten among others, and we call seven other
branches, which are placed in the Imperial
tree, which also pertain to the Apostolic
office. But the ten branches are the ten
commandments, which are

[Column 2]
to worship one God, and to keep the Sab-
bath day, not to take the name of God in
vain, to honor father and mother, not to
bear false witness, not to steal, not to kill,
not to commit adultery, not to covet another's
wife, not to covet a neighbor's goods.
Nevertheless, many other precepts are
understood under these ten. And these ten
precepts can be applied to the two precepts
which the Lord Jesus Christ spoke when he
was asked, of which the first is: Love the
Lord your God with all your heart, and with
all your mind, and with all your strength.
The second is: Love your neighbor as yourself.
And concerning these two precepts we intend
to treat. And first concerning the first.

Concerning the First precept of the
Apostolic Tree.

The first precept is divided into
four parts. One is, inasmuch as it says:
Love the Lord your God with all your heart.
This precept is made for the will, because
the heart is the place in which the will
chooses the object it desires or hates, and
inasmuch as it says "with all your mind,"
the precept is made for the intellect and
memory, which precede the will, when the
mind is formed to choose an object for itself.
And this second precept is twofold, one is
for memory, and the other for the intellect,
and so there are three commands. And
inasmuch as it says "with all your strength,"
the precepts are multiplied in the multipli-
cation of souls, which are powers, namely
the vegetative soul, and the sensitive soul,
and we can also understand the imaginative
power, and the elemental power, inasmuch
as the soul has power over elemental things,

powers, from which there are six precepts: from the part of the rational soul there are three, and from the part of the vegetative [soul] there is one, and from the part of the sensitive [soul] another, and from the part of the imaginative [soul] the remainder. And thus the four precepts, which are contained in the first part, are multiplied into seven parts. The second precept, inasmuch as it says: Love your neighbor as yourself, is multiplied into the aforesaid seven parts, since it is so that man is lovable, inasmuch as his will, his intellect, his memory, his imaginative power, sensitive, and his vegetative power are lovable, and also inasmuch as the elementative (which is one part of man) is lovable through itself: just as a part which is lovable through its whole. And therefore we wish to lead the process of these branches with two precepts multiplied into seven, so that the first part is the command of the will, the second of the intellect, the third of the memory, the fourth is the command of the imaginative [power], the fifth of the sensitive, the sixth of the vegetative, and the seventh part is the command of the elementative power. Whence all these precepts are made for the Lord Pope and all his subjects, and so much more for him than for anyone else, as much as he can serve God more than anyone else. And so concerning the Cardinals and other ranks, according to how they are in higher ranks: just as fire, which according to its natural course wills that pepper, which is in the fourth degree of heat, should use more heat than cinnamon, which is in the third degree of heat, and cinnamon more than fennel, which is only in the second degree of heat, and fennel more than anise, which is only in the first degree of heat. And in this passage it is recognized that public or common persons, the higher their rank, the more they are obligated to ob-

serve the precepts of God, and are more disobedient if they do not obey Him, than persons who are not common.

*Concerning the First precept of the Apostolic*
*Tree, which is made for the will.*

To the Holy Apostolic Father is given the command that he love God with all his heart. And because God is a great Lord, He makes a great command, and He makes it to a great person, because the Apostolic [Father] is great, inasmuch as he is a public person, and the command is made to his will, under which there are many wills to obey the superior will. And because the will is great, which is superior, and God says that he should love Him with his whole self, in this He makes a command to the whole power of the will and to the whole greatness which the will has in loving, and similarly to its whole goodness, duration, virtue, truth, concordance, beginning, middle, and end, superiority, and equality. And therefore the command is made concerning many and great things, and it is made for loving great things, namely the goodness of God, and His greatness, and so concerning other forms essential to Him. And it is great that the will of the Apostolic [Father], which is so high (because it is general and is mistress over so many and so great wills) should love God with its whole self, namely with all its goodness, greatness, duration, power, and the rest. Therefore he ought to love every good that he can love, and he ought to love a good as great as his loving can be great, and he ought to love as much as his loving can endure. And in this passage it is recognized that the will of the Apostolic [Father] is obligated to love, as much as it can, the honor of God and the utility of his people.

188 Apostolic Tree.

*Concerning the Second precept of the Apostolic Tree, which pertains to the intellect.*

God commands the Apostolic intellect that it understand Him, and that it cause Him to be understood in all His goodness, magnitude, power, duration, virtue, and truth, and likewise concerning other forms. And this precept signifies the conversion of the Gentiles, they being cast out from error and led to understand the truth of God and His operations, so that they may be able to rest in the glory of God without end. It is therefore a great precept, because it is of a great Lord, and it is for a great Lord, who has a general intellect for many intellects, and it is made concerning great things, and things which are good and durable, which can be great, because God does not make any precept concerning impossible things; wherefore the Apostolic can obey the command that is given to him, and is obligated to obey the supreme Lord as much as the command is great, and as much as things are possible, that they may be understood for the honor of God and the utility of His people. And God gives him this command, inasmuch as He tells him to love God with his whole mind.

*Concerning the Third precept of the Apostolic Tree, which pertains to memory.*

The memory of the Apostolic was created for recalling God, and also it was created so that it might cause God to be recalled by his people. And a command is given to him, that with all his power which he has in the magnitude of goodness, duration, virtue, truth, and likewise concerning other forms, he should recall God, and cause Him to be recalled by his people, who have been entrusted to him for recalling God and His operations. And God gives him this command inasmuch as He tells him to love Him with his whole mind. It is therefore a great command, and it is concerning great things, and for a great Lord, under whom are so many and such great men obligated to follow His will. And this, which his intellect understands, and which his memory can justly recall, according to what is commanded to him: Wherefore, just as the command is great, so obedience ought to be great, and if obedience is not great, disobedience is great, and thus magnitude is perverted from obedience into disobedience. Whence follows a great evil, powerful, durable, false, and vicious, from which many evils follow. And by this step it is recognized that God makes a great command and to a great Lord, and concerning great things, that He Himself wishes to be recalled with the magnitude of goodness, duration, power, virtue, and truth. Which magnitude indeed is lovable, intelligible, and possible through power, and good through goodness, and virtuous through virtue, and true through truth, and durable through duration. It is also recognized that God does not wish to be recalled with a smallness of recalling, since recalling can be with the magnitude of goodness, duration, and the rest.

**Apostolic Tree. 191**

**On Baptism.**

**B**aptism is a sacrament necessary by reason of original sin, which has been proven in the commentary of the general table. Baptism is a likeness through the figure of holiness. Indeed, this holiness is an impression in the sacrament, which converts itself to the end for which man was created, just as an olive branch grafted onto a wild olive tree converts the material and the influence flowing from the wild olive tree to its own nature. For the form of the sacrament, placed in the recipient who receives baptism, purifies and cleanses, and transmutes impurity into purity, and darkness into light. And this it does with divine power given to man, like an instrument to use it in the place of God, who wishes to recover what He lost in His subject. For just as a hammer is an instrument to a smith, with which he makes a nail and a knife, so divine power is an instrument to the priest, with which he sanctifies and cleanses the subject made impure by original sin. And this is a great marvel, that man can use the power of God, as God (does). And this marvel excites man's intellect to understand the great power of God, and his will to love it, and his memory to recall the greatness of faith, hope, and charity. And the elemental tree places water in that Sacrament, and the vegetal, sensual, imaginal, and moral trees place their properties and natures in it, inasmuch as they are passive forms in the subject of the Sacrament. In which forms an impression is made by the superior forms which are in the rational tree, which move the instrument with the order of words, which are from the sensual tree, in which the instrument makes impressions that the inferior forms receive, so that they may be sanctified, and returned to the end for which they were created, and participate with God: like letters in wax, which participate in likeness with the letters of a seal.

**On Confirmation.**

**C**onfirmation is, so that a child who was not disposed to understanding when he was baptized, may receive the impression of the first Sacrament in his understanding, and the same applies to his memory and will. Therefore, this Sacrament of Confirmation is an instrument of the first Sacrament, which, inasmuch as it was itself disposed to make an impression on the powers of the soul of the subject, yet could not make it in the acts of those powers, namely in recalling, understanding, and loving, but only makes impressions on the powers themselves. And through the Sacrament of Confirmation, the characters of the Sacrament are made in the acts of the powers, inasmuch as the baptized person consents that he is cleansed from original sin, by recalling, understanding, and loving.

**On Matrimony.**

**M**atrimony is a Sacrament which orders the union of man and woman to the end for which masculinity and femininity exist, namely, to multiply the human species, so that God may be honored and loved by more people. And this Sacrament specifies such a man and such a woman with an order of words, and an order of interior conception, which move the words of him who acts...

entering with natural contrariety, which contrariety superior forms convert into harmony above the natural course, which is represented in the harmony that fire and water have in air, when it properly happens that fire in it has great heat, and water great passion: thus in the Sacrament, in which superior forms have great action, and inferior forms great passion. And such great action and passion, that greater cannot exist between Christ and the priest. And it is very delightful to understand and consider this so great action and passion of God and creature. The end for which the world was created is known in the Sacrament of the Altar, which end indeed is, that the magnitude of divine goodness, duration, power, and other forms of God may be known, and also that the magnitude of human goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, and other forms of Christ's humanity may be known. And this end is known in the Sacrament, in which is the great end of superior and inferior goodness, and so of other forms. And therefore the Sacrament is a state in which the end of the world's creation is known. And therefore that state is a more beautiful mirror, which can exist in this life, between God and man, namely, by seeing in that mirror so many and so great magnitudes of ends, and of the perfections of superior forms, which perfect inferior forms. In the Sacrament of the Altar, God and man participate with greater fullness, because God can no more pour forth of His goodness, magnitude, duration, power, wisdom, will, and so of other forms. Nor can man in his goodness, magnitude, duration, power, and so

[Right Column]
of other forms, receive more of the superior influence. Therefore God and man participate with a greater fullness of influence, and this participation of greater fullness, which is between God and man in this life, could not exist without the Sacrament. And therefore those men who are priests do evil, who could celebrate the Sacrament more often, and do the contrary. In the Sacrament of the Altar, God participates with man, with great humility of His goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, and truth, because it is great that He who is God and man would wish to participate below, and so greatly humble Himself, with all His heights, which are so high that they could not be higher, that He allows Himself to be moved from one place to another, and to be given to men. And therefore those priests do evil, and those men who receive the Sacrament, when they are proud, since it is so that pride and humility are contrary. And in this point it is recognized that priests ought to be more humble than other men, in speaking, dressing, eating, riding, and dwelling: and so of other things which are fitting for great humility, just as Jesus Christ, who in this world was humble in all things.

*About Order.*

Order is a Sacrament necessary for other Sacraments, because it is the instrument with which other Sacraments are performed. And Order is so great, as it pertains to the magnitude of other Sacraments: like a hammer, which ought to be proportioned to the size of the nail. Whence, since the Sacrament of the Altar, and of Penance is so great,

**Apostolic Tree. 197**

loves that the Sacraments are great.
It has been said of the seven Sacraments
of the Holy Church, which are its ornaments,
and just as the Sun, which is the ornament
of the earth, in that it gives it light, and
it is the same with light, which removes
darkness from a room at night, and which
shows those things that are in the room, so
the seven Sacraments with light, and
the participation of superior and inferior forms
show the nobility of the creator and creatures.

*On the Second part of the leaves of the Apostolic tree.*

The leaves of the Apostolic tree are
canons, which are accidents that
the Pope needs for his governance. These
canons are sown in the
decretals and decrees, and many others are
in a state of being known:
and those that are known can be
applied to a certain number of other
more general known things: so that
artificially many particulars could be applied
to a few universals, and from them a practice
was given according to the method
which we gave in the leaves of the Imperial
tree. This method we wish to repeat
in only one leaf,
and this by discussing general
accidents. And the method we will give
in discussing is a doctrine on how
a person may know how to discuss through the leaves
artificially, through general accidents.
And through this doctrine a person could
deduce to the necessary knowledge in
brief a long positive rhetoric
called canon law.

*On the Most Holy Trinity: and first on*
*Quantity.*

We firmly believe in the Most Holy Trinity,
and simply confess it,
without continuous and discrete quantity.
For inasmuch as we believe in one Father,
one Son, one Holy Spirit,
and all three, one God, and
not three Gods, we believe and confess
that in the Trinity there is no
quantity: for in it there cannot be,
since all three remain one
essence, one God, one nature, one
goodness: and so concerning other essential
forms, or reasons. For discrete
quantity cannot exist without a diversity
of essences, or without a diversity
of essence and hypostasis, or of the concrete:
just as in created goodness, in which the
benefactor, the recipient of goodness, and the act of bestowing goodness
are distinct, inasmuch as one is not
the other. And although it is so that each
is of one essence of goodness, none of
them is goodness, and therefore each is
reached by quantity, and determined in the
quantity of goodness. But this
is not the case in the blessed Trinity of God: for
the Father is the whole divine essence, and the Son
is the whole divine essence, and the Holy Spirit
is the whole divine essence: and the Father from his
whole self produces the Son, and the Father and the
Son from their whole selves produce
the Holy Spirit. And because the Father is infinite,
and the Son is infinite, and each from
his whole essence produces, the product
from them cannot be quantified in extension, nor in
eternity: because the product
is from an infinite and eternal essence,
wherefore in that blessed production
quantity can in no way have a place.
Therefore, we firmly and simply believe
that in the blessed Trinity of God there is no quantity,
nor can there be.

body, nor any nature of a body: because an infinite being in extension cannot be a body, since it is so that a body cannot exist without length, breadth, and depth, nor without a circular, or quadrangular, or triangular figure: but none of these can fall into infinity. And therefore those ancient Philosophers, and still some modern Saracens, who are their followers, did wrong, who denied that God is essentially outside the firmament, nor inside, but potentially and virtuously: and so concerning other forms. And they denied this, because they feared to affirm that God would be a body if He were essentially inside and outside: just as fire, which is a body, supposing it is inside and outside a room: because just as God is infinite through eternity, in which is the time of the world, and the motion of the firmament, and that [eternity] is outside inasmuch as the world is not eternal, but has a beginning, and eternity is inside the world, because it is not a divisible being, so the infinite extension of God is inside the world and outside, although it is so that He is not a body. And this divine and spiritual extension is the essence, which is the Father, who from Himself produces the Son, and from the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit. Wherefore position, which is a creature, is a mirror and likeness, in which the human intellect grasps the mode, according to which the divine persons are in the essence, as if in the likeness of situation: just as the Father who is in the essence as generating and spirating, and the Son as generated and spirating, and the Holy Spirit as spirated. And the same is true of the essence, which is in one way the Father, and in another the Son, and in another the Holy Spirit, and it remains indistinct in itself, although persons are in it. And this mirror of situation, and figure is

[Column 2]
a creature so disposed and ordered, that the human intellect can see through it the mode of the divine essence and persons: and so concerning other divine forms. As in divine goodness, in which is the Father bestowing goodness, and the Son made good and capable of being made good, and the Holy Spirit similarly: and to bestow goodness, which is between the Father and the Son, is by way of generating, and between the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit by way of spirating. But the human intellect could not understand this, if position did not exist, which is an instrument so necessary for understanding the mode of the persons: just as color is necessary for imagining something colored.

On Time.

IN the Trinity of God there is no time, since it is so that time cannot exist without a beginning, and the motion of things moved and originated, in which time is sustained. And also because the Father generates the Son from eternity, inasmuch as He generates Him from Himself (who is eternity): and the same is true of the Father and the Son, who from themselves, who are eternity, spirate the Holy Spirit. Wherefore just as a smith who makes a nail from iron cannot make it from wood, after he makes it from iron, so and much better, that which is produced from eternity essentially and naturally, and substantially, cannot be from time, nor from any nature of time, since it is produced from eternity, and in eternity. And therefore Saracens and Jews do wrong, who deny the Trinity in God: because if they affirmed the Trinity in God, they would believe they were affirming time in Him, and denying eternity. And in this passage man can recognize, how human,

Concerning Place.

IN the Trinity of God there is no place, since place cannot exist except in finite beings. Just as a flask, which is the place of wine, and a room which is the place of a man who stands in it, and so concerning place according to what has been said in the elemental tree. Therefore, place cannot exist in an infinitely extended subject, such as God the Father, who is infinite in extensiveness without length, breadth, and depth, and without any nature of place. And from his whole self he produces the Son, because He Himself cannot be in one place, nor the Son in another, for they would be finite suppositions if the Father were in one place and the Son in another; nor would the Son be produced from the essence of the Father, who is an infinite being in extensiveness, nor from the whole Father. And the same is true of the Holy Spirit, who infinitely, without quantity (without which place cannot exist), proceeds from the Father and the Son, and proceeds in the Father and the Son, so that He may proceed in infinity, and proceeds in Himself so that He may be infinite. And so in no way can place exist in the divine Trinity. Therefore, Saracens and Jews do wrong, who hold the opinion that Christians believe that the Father is in one place and the Son in another, and the Holy Spirit in another, because they believe that all things that are distinct require distinct places: such as a man, a tree, Martin and his son. And in this that we say, that the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and so concerning the Holy Spirit, it does not follow that we say that one part is in another, since it is so that the persons

[Right Column]

divine are not parts, because a part does not fall into infinity, as has been said, but the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father, and so concerning the Holy Spirit, so essentially and naturally, that they are one by essence and nature. It has been said concerning accidents in which doctrine is given, how man may know to deny those accidents in the supreme Trinity, and itself

that the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified and dead, descended into hell, on the third day rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and that He will come to judge the living and the dead. And these fourteen articles we call flowers; because they are higher things which we can believe about God and His works, and the belief which man has about them is a flower, from which is born fruit, which is the holy mother Church sustained in just, holy, and Catholic men, who are the sheep of the Lord Pope, Vicar or successor of Blessed Peter who was crucified and died in Rome. Indeed, Rome is the seat of his Vicar, whose seat is called Petra (Rock), whose conditions are that it be strong, living, and white. And therefore those do evil who do not guard that Rock from death, fragility, and impurity, since it has been entrusted to them according to its conditions, which require men who are living, strong, and clean from sins. Before we come to prove one God, first we will prove that eternity exists, afterwards infinite goodness, and infinite magnitude, and other forms, since the nature of God is signified by these forms, and according to their nature we intend to draw proofs and conclusions. Then we will prove that God exists, and afterwards the articles. And we wish to prove each article by five reasons, and by the primary forms, and by their definitions. Indeed, these primary forms are goodness, magnitude, and others. Nevertheless, if in anything we speak against the holy faith of the Roman Church, we will not speak knowingly, but ignorantly. And therefore what we say, we humbly submit and entrust to the most holy Roman Church, because

[Right Column]

what she does, we will believe.

*Concerning the Forms or Attributes of God.*

IF eternity does not exist, everything that exists began from itself, which is impossible, because it would have existed before it existed, which is impossible. Therefore eternity exists, which we call supreme duration. If supreme goodness does not exist, neither does lowest goodness, which is impossible, since they are relative to each other. Therefore supreme goodness exists, which is infinite: because if it were not infinite, it would follow that a greater good which is less distant from infinity, would be more distant from infinity, because it would be more about non-being than a lesser good, and thus a lesser good would be greater than a greater good, which is impossible. Therefore supreme goodness exists, which is infinite. If infinite magnitude does not exist, everything that exists is limited in extension, and thus eternity is infinite in duration, and goodness in supremacy, as has been proven: but they are limited in magnitude, which is impossible, since infinite and finite have no proportion in the same substance. Therefore infinite magnitude exists: just as eternity and supreme goodness exist. If infinite power does not exist, all power is finite, which is impossible: because eternity is in infinite duration, and since it is in infinite duration, it can be in infinite duration by power, because without power it could not be infinite. Therefore infinite power exists, by which eternity can be in infinite duration. Eternity exists, as has been proven, and because it exists, it is knowable, and thus its knowability is infinite: just as eternity itself is infinite, and can be infinite through infinite power. And it is good,

concordance is finite, they do not agree, therefore

That God exists.

That God exists, we wish to prove by five
reasons in this manner. If God exists,
His being is good, and great, and eternal: since
it is so, that we consider God to be
perfect in goodness, greatness, and
duration. And if God does not exist, His privation
is evil, and eternal greatness is evil,
because God never was nor will be:
whence it follows, that the magnitude
of evil is eternal, if God is not so: just as
it follows by the contrary, namely that
God exists, is the magnitude of eternal good,
therefore it is necessary that God exists by necessity,
because greatness has greater concordance
with goodness in duration:
than with evil, because privation and duration
are contrary: and duration and being
have concordance, and greatness and
goodness have concordance with being, and
smallness, which is contrary to greatness:
and evil, contrary to goodness, have
concordance with non-being: therefore
it is proven that God exists. If God exists:
there is more of possibility than of im-
possibility in the eternity of magnitude
and goodness. And if God does not exist,
the contrary is true: because supposing
that God does not exist, eternity must
necessarily exist, because if

[Right Column]
eternity did not exist, that which is originated by
itself would exist, which is im-
possible, that any substance could originate
itself: because if it could originate
itself and produce itself,
its power would be in some subject
that had already existed before, and thus
the contradiction would be multiplied, that something
would exist, and not exist: which contradiction
is impossible. Therefore eternity exists by
necessity, in which eternity there is greater
possibility of magnitude, of goodness,
if God exists: because if God is eternity,
it can be infinite in the magnitude
of goodness, God existing as that eternity:
and if God does not exist, it cannot
be infinite in the magnitude of goodness,
and thus magnitude and eternity have
greater concordance with the im-
possibility of good, than with possibility,
that possibility existing in pure act,
which indeed greater concordance
is impossible, so that magnitude and eternity
do not have concordance with
evil and impossibility, and that they
have concordance with goodness,
and with good posited, and possible, so to
speak, therefore God exists by necessity.
If God exists, truth is in a greater reality
of goodness, magnitude, and eternity:
and if God does not exist, it is in a minority,
and falsity in a majority of opinion
and fantastic species, in which the
being of God is considered, which is infinite
goodness, magnitude, eternity. And this
consideration is false, and is greater
than the reality of magnitude and good-
ness, which are infinite in eternity.
And thus eternity has greater con-
cordance with the magnitude of good-
ness, with falsity in fantasy, which
the human intellect accepts, and which
is not of the essence of eternity, nor is
substantial, than with the magnitude
of real goodness, which is truth and sub-
stance.

206	Apostolic Tree.

[Left Column]

to receive glory from Him, God existing through man recollected, understood & loved, which are the three forms, ends, & complements of all created beings. And so it follows, if God is, that the principles & means of beings relate to an end, & attain that end, & in it have rest. And if God is not, the aforesaid inconveniences follow, which cannot be according to the natural course, nor even according to the supernatural course: since it is so, that if God is not, no being is above the course of nature, which if it were, non-being would be the cause of being, or of that thing which is, & thus something would be, & something would not be, which is impossible.

On the Unity of God.

Just as blessed God is good through goodness, & great through greatness, eternal through eternity, & powerful through power, etc. so it is necessary that He be one through unity: for if He were not one through unity, there would be other forms greater in God than unity, & unity would be in God in a state of minority, which is a being close to non-being. And thus the unity of God would not be God, nor His nature, which if God were thus lesser through unity, that minority would be evil against goodness, & small against greatness, & privation against eternity, & fragility against power, & so for others, which is impossible, namely that in God there be contrariety, or defect, since He Himself is pure

208 Apostolic Tree.

Son. The fourth article is to believe and affirm the Holy Spirit. And these three articles we wish to prove by proving the Trinity, which we intend to prove in three ways, according to what we proved in the fifth book of wise men. The first way to prove the Trinity is to prove in God a plurality of many things. The second way is to prove that those many things are persons, which are properties, so that one is the paternal property, another the filial, and another the passive spiration. The third way is to prove that in God there are three persons, so that there are not more, nor fewer.

Concerning the Plurality of God.

God is one, and is good, great, eternal, powerful, etc. Hence, just as God relates to understanding through wisdom, and to loving through will, so He relates to uniting through unity, and to making good through goodness, and to magnifying through greatness, and to eternalizing through eternity, and to empowering through power. And this must be so, that wisdom and will do not relate more to an end than unity, goodness, greatness, eternity, and power. God, therefore, relates to uniting through unity in such a way that He produces one, who is so uniquely one that he is not another, so that unity is the principle for one to produce one: just as goodness is the principle for good to produce good, and will is the principle for the lover to produce the beloved, and wisdom is the principle for the intelligent one to produce the understood. God, insofar as He is one, cannot produce Himself, namely His unity: because no being can produce itself. And because it is necessary that He produce

one, so that unity may be the reason for its own end: it is necessary that there be one God, who produces one God, so that one is the producer, and the other is the produced, and that one proceeds from one, and that from both there is a unity: so that under the aspect of unity there are three concrete realities of His essence and nature, and all three are one essence and one nature, and not multiple essences nor natures, so that unity may be great: and the other three are the uniter, the unifiable, and the act of uniting. Therefore, it is necessary that there be a distinction between them, insofar as one is not the other, without which distinction unity could not be the principle for one to produce one, and it would be useless, and through it nothing would follow in its essence, nor from its essence and nature, and it would be small in itself, and great in creatures, in which it serves as the principle for one creature to produce another creature by way of generation and according to the natural course: just as Martin, who is one, for whom the unity of God is the principle that he produces Peter, who is his one son: therefore it is necessary that the unity of God, which cannot be a greater principle for another than it is a principle in its own essence for one God: that it produces one God. It is therefore proven that in God plurality exists of necessity according to the magnitude of unity and His goodness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, and glory. Every unity is greater in magnitude of goodness and power by existing and acting, than by existing only, or by acting only. Just as fire, which is greater by its being and by its heating, than by its being only, or by its heating only: and that it would not be what it is. Therefore, the unity of God is greater in magnitude of goodness, eternity, and power by existing and acting, than it would not be by one [mode only].

On the Divine, Eternal Number.
It has been proven that in God there is a plu-
rality of persons, namely of the Father,
and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; now we
wish to prove that the persons cannot
be fewer, nor more than three,
according to the magnitude of goodness,
eternity, power, and other things. The mag-
nitude of goodness is that it has in
itself and from itself that which makes good, that which
can be made good, and the act of making good: and the mag-
nitude of eternity is that it has in
itself and from itself that which makes eternal, that which
can be made eternal, and the act of making eternal, and the same
applies to other forms. And therefore it is signified
that the divine persons are
three, and neither more nor fewer: because
if there were more, it would be necessary that in
the forms that 'more' would be superfluous.
As in goodness, in which it would be necessary
that it have two or more 'bonificatives',
and two or more 'bonificables',
and two or more 'bonificares'.
And one 'bonificative',
one 'bonificable', and one 'bonificare'
would not suffice, and thus the magnitude of each
would be deficient, which defect would be evil, and the small-
ness of each. And if in goodness there
were only one 'bonificative', and that not

...[if in goodness there were only one that makes good, and that not] that which can be made good, who would be of its essence, and to make good that which would be of the essence of both, there could not be a relation in the magnitude of goodness, and magnitude would be lacking to it, and this would be evil. Therefore, in goodness there are three, and no more, nor less, and this same in eternity, and in other forms. And there is the bonificativus (that which makes good), magnificativus (that which magnifies), æternificativus (that which makes eternal), possificativus (that which empowers), and intellectivus (that which understands), and in love, the amativus (that which loves), who is the Father. And the bonificabilis (that which can be made good), magnificabilis (that which can be magnified), æternificabilis (that which can be made eternal), and intelligibilis (that which can be understood): and in love, the amabilis (that which can be loved), who is the Son, in which love, to love is the Holy Spirit, who is to make good, to magnify, to make eternal, to empower, and to understand. [Left Column]
necessary for those who desire to have knowledge of the Holy Trinity. The greatest concordance that can exist in any number, consists in the ternary number, thus in goodness, the concordance of the Giver of Goodness, the Receivable of Goodness, and the Act of Making Good; and in greatness, the concordance of the Magnifier, the Magnifiable, and the Act of Magnifying; and so concerning other things. And because it is necessary that the greatest numerical concordance possible be in God, and not a lesser one, therefore it must consist of three only, and not of more, nor fewer. It cannot be from fewer: because the concordance would be lesser; because the greater concordance is from three, than from two. It cannot be from four, because a fourth would be superfluous in the concordance, as in goodness, in which the concordance of three suffices, namely the concordance of the Giver of Goodness, the Receivable of Goodness, and the Act of Making Good. Therefore, the greater concordance is from three, and it is greater from three than from any other number: because one is born from another one, and one proceeds from two, and all three remain, one essence, one nature, one God in number, so that a fourth number does not follow, which follows in creatures: as man who is composed of body and soul, and from the conjunction of both, passes into a third entity which is not any of its parts, nor is any of its parts man; but in God, the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and all three are one God, and that God is the Father, and who is the Son, and who is the Holy Spirit. And thus the number remains in three persons, and in one God, and the one is nothing other than three persons, nor are the persons anything other than that one. And thus it must necessarily be, that in God there are no parts, nor composition, and that great-

[Right Column]
-ness concerning itself, and concerning goodness, eternity, power, and other things, suffices in the ternary number, about which it has been said above. The greatest equality that can exist among several things, can exist in the ternary number: as one, which can be equally between two, and more equally than between three or four, or among more: because the second would be further, or more remote from the fourth, than from the first, or from the third, and the first would be nearer to the second than to the third and fourth, and the third would be nearer to the fourth than to the first. Even if equality is made from six, so that two are in the middle, and two are first, and two at the end, great equality cannot exist from six: as from three only, because one of the two that are in the middle, is nearer to the two that are at the beginning, than the other which is its companion, which is nearer to those two that are at the end. Therefore, it is necessary to consider the ternary number in God, so that there can be in the number of divine persons the greatest equality and nearness that can exist, as the Holy Spirit who is in the middle of the Father and the Son, inasmuch as he proceeds from both: as love which is in the middle of the lover and the beloved, inasmuch as it is from both; and the Son who is in the middle of the Father and the Holy Spirit; and in this, that the Holy Spirit proceeds as much from the Son as from the Father, the Father being in the middle of the Son and the Holy Spirit: because the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit as much as he generates the Son. Every perfection can exist in a beginning, middle, and end, and outside of these it cannot exist, nor can it exist without these three. And it follows according to the natural course, that lesser goods are more lovable than greater ones, and greater evils less to be feared than lesser ones, and this is unfitting. Therefore the world is created from nothing, so that the aforementioned unfitting consequences do not exist, and that magnitude may have greater concordance with goodness than with malice, and inasmuch as the world will be better according to eternal life, which we will prove in its tree. We have proved the blessed Trinity of God, in which the Father eternally produces the Son, and the Father and the Son eternally breathe forth the Holy Spirit. And if the world is eternal, the production of divine eternity is equal to the eternity of the world according to duration, so that in eternity there are two equal productions, namely the divine production, and the production of the world. And so it follows that the inner operation does not in all ways comprehend the operation which is outside, which exterior operation is the world, which is equal to the interior operation in duration, which equality is impossible in duration, just as in goodness, magnitude, and other things, so that the eternity of God is equally before the created world in time: just as the goodness of God is before the goodness of the world, and before its other forms existing by quantity in the quantity and goodness of God, existing without quantity. Therefore the world is created and new. If the world is eternal in its parts, there is no general principle that is of its essence, because its eternity is not principiate, nor its power, nor any of its general forms which are of its essence, is

principiate, and therefore they cannot be a general principle for particular principles which are of its essence. Nor can there be a universal end in the world, because a universal [end] cannot exist without a universal beginning, with beginning and end existing from the essence of the substance. Nor can there be a general middle in the substance of the world, because a general middle cannot exist without a general beginning and a general end. Therefore, beginning, middle, and end are not general forms that are of the essence of the world. Wherefore it necessarily follows that in the world there are no particular forms existing under general beginning, middle, and end, which is impossible and contrary to the experience we perceive. Just as Peter, who has a beginning, middle, and end, and his horse, and a falcon similarly, and the same is true of an apple and a fish, and of all things existing in generation and corruption. Therefore, it is necessary that there are natural general forms, under which stand inferior particulars, existing from a superior essence and nature, just as parts existing under a whole, which are governed by their whole. It is therefore proven that the world is created by reason of the experience we have of particular beginnings, middles, and ends, which are of the essence of the world and its parts, which could not exist if the world were eternal. We have proven that the world is new, and that God is the creator and the world is created. And therefore the Lord Pope, and his brothers the Lord Cardinals, would do well if they strove to destroy the opinion held by Saracens, Tartars, and many Schismatic Christians, that the world is eternal, in which opinion they die, and go to perpetual infernal punishments, which will have no end. to His eternity in the opinion of those who deny that God is Creator. Prejudice is also done to God, and to His eternity, by those who could destroy that opinion, and are negligent in destroying it. Moreover, that opinion is very dangerous, because it is strongly multiplied in the world, because its multiplication diminishes faith and the hope of another life, since if the world is eternal, whatever we believe about the Old Testament and the New Testament, we believe against the truth. It is therefore good, indeed excellent, to prove that the world was created by God.

**On Recreation.**

Recreation is the sixth article. And we divide this into four parts. The first part is that the first man sinned. The second part is that his sin was general sensually. The third part is that that general sin was spiritual. The fourth part is that recreation was accomplished.

**That the first Man sinned.**

God created the world, as we have proved; man is a part of the world, therefore God created man. And He created him with greatness of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, concordance, beginning, middle, and end. Since it is so, that all these forms are in God, and were in the creation of man. It is therefore necessary that man was created in greatness of goodness, duration, and the others, so that between active and passive forms there might be a concordance of greatness and greatness, goodness and goodness, and so on for the others. Just as the sun, which is great in quantity, and in light, in virtue, and in motion: it was therefore created with greatness of goodness, duration, power, and the others. Similarly, man is great, and greater than the sun in greatness of goodness, power, and virtue according to the natural course, because naturally more good things participate with man than with the sun, because man feels and imagines, and can remember, understand, and love God, and the sun does not do this. And because man, when he is first born, begins to feel evil rather than good, and to do vanities and wicked things, and sins, before virtues, he begins contrary to the end for which he was created; the sun does not have such a beginning, because it is always in the state for which it was created. And the same is true of the elements, plants, and brute animals. It is therefore necessary that man had in the beginning a perversion from good to evil, and from greatness to smallness, and from duration to privation, and from power to weakness, and from virtue to vice in the first created general man, through whom man fell into perversion, which is through mortal sin. Therefore, the first man sinned. An olive tree that is grafted into a wild olive tree draws matter to itself from the wild olive tree, and from it receives growth, and produces fruit of its own species, and not of that which is the species of the wild olive tree; nor does the wild olive tree have wherewith to produce fruit of its own species, because the olive tree converts the species of the wild olive tree into itself. Similarly, the rational tree is grafted into the sensual, and according to the nature of greatness, goodness, and virtue, it ought to draw the sensual to good and not to evil, and to virtue and not to vice. And according to how man begins in his youth, it is the opposite: as if the wild olive tree were to draw to itself the nature of the olive tree, which is superior, and that the wild olive tree produces fruit

--- Page 233 ---
# The Apostolic Tree. 219

it would produce fruit of its own kind, and not the olive's. So the body draws the rational soul downwards to love vanities and sin more than virtues and the end for which man was created. But this could not be, unless the first man had sinned, because this general tendency is in all men in the beginning, when they begin to come into this world, nor can it originate from a man who is not general nor first: just as neither pepper nor garlic would be of a hot and dry complexion, if fire in the beginning were not hot and dry, and one general hot and dry fire from which all hot and dry things would descend, which could not descend from fire that comes from stone and iron, which is not general for the generation of pepper or garlic. Therefore the first man sinned, by reason of which sin the body inclines the soul more easily to vices than the soul inclines the body to virtues. According to what was said in the elemental tree, goodness is the reason for good, that it may do good, and magnitude is that, by reason of which goodness is great, and duration is that, by reason of which goodness endures great, and magnitude good, and so for others, but this is not in the state of man, because after the world was created until now, there is more of evil than of good, and greater evil than good, and the magnitude of evil has always endured. And of this we have successive experience, namely that one man has from another, therefore it does not follow that goodness is the reason for good, that it may do great good, because the magnitude of goodness is lacking, and goodness to magnitude, and duration is lacking to both, and magnitude agrees that malice is the reason for evil, that it may do great evil, and duration agrees with the magnitude of evil, and good-

ness remains a small reason for good, that it may do good, and this according to the state of the world, but this could not be, unless the first man had sinned, because a second man, or a third, or a fourth, and so from one to another would not suffice for this perverse generality from good to evil, and from great goodness to great malice, and from great duration of goodness and magnitude to the duration of malice and smallness. Therefore the first man sinned, by reason of which sin follows this generality of the magnitude of evil, and which has endured so much, and still endures. Contrariety is an accidental form, and concordance is substantial in one way, and accidental in another, according to what was said in the elemental tree. Therefore concordance is closer to magnitude than contrariety, and therefore concordance can naturally do more in good than contrariety in evil, since it is so, that a power which is greater, can do more than a power which is lesser. Just as the power of pepper, which can heat more than the power of anise, and one pound of ice cools more than one ounce. And because contrariety has deviated the world in man from the end for which he was created, in a greater quantity of deviation than of retention, which concordance retained in man, so that the world might remain in the end for which it was created: in this it is signified that the first man sinned, whence it follows that contrariety, which is naturally a lesser form than concordance, has overcome concordance. For if the first man had not sinned, contrariety would not have been able to overcome concordance so generally, and also because concordance is good according to the natural course, and according to what it is as a creature. But we speak-

we speak of contrariety, which is a privation of concordance, just as malice, which is sin, is a privation of goodness. Being and privation are contraries, and virtues and vices, good and evil, great and small, truth and falsehood, and so with other contrarieties. And therefore evil, which is sin, does not agree with being, since it is the case that good, which is virtue, agrees with being, just as falsehood does not agree with being, after truth has concordance with being: and the same is true of the magnitude of evil and of falsehood, which do not concord with being, after the magnitude of good and of truth has concordance with being. And this is according to the natural course, which is perverted into the unnatural: just as the natural heat of man is perverted into the unnatural, by some occasion of excessive eating, or drinking, or some excess or injury to the complexions. Just as a man who, because of excessive choler, has a fever, or through the corruption of some humor, or has a headache when he has eaten or drunk too much, since without some occasion the perversion of natural heat into unnatural, nor of health into infirmity, could not occur. It is therefore necessary that this infirmity in which men are, inasmuch as they are more ready to do evil than to do good, and to great evil than to great good, and there are more men who do evil and are in falsehood without faith, than those who do good and have faith, and more evils have been done than goods, and more men are in error than in truth among men: thus through the first man, who sinned, from whose sin is our infirmity, which could not be general without the sin of the first man, gener-

-al to all men, inasmuch as all are derived from him, therefore the first man sinned. We have therefore proved that the first man sinned; however, some men might say that every man sins when he sins through his own liberty and actuality, and not through the first man, and in this we do not contradict according to the manner of particular actual sin: just as Peter, who is a sinner, and Martin likewise, and it could be that William and James are just men: wherefore actual sin is not extended to all, but is only particular. Furthermore, man does not sin through the liberty he has: just as a smith who does not sin by making a knife, which he does not make well because of the hammer, but because he does not know how to make it well, or because he does not want to make it good. And the reason we have adduced to prove that the first man sinned, is from general principles, namely from the greater readiness, or promptness, that we have to do evil than to do good, and we do it more willingly, and we do more evil than good, and we do evil before good, and we feel the evil of punishment before the good of rest. And by this such generality, which cannot exist without an occasion, and the occasion cannot be originated in a particular man, we have proved that sin originated from the general man, who is called Adam, from whom we all proceeded.

Arbor apoſtolicalis.                                 223

riety. Therefore, the reason still remains true, namely that in the body there is more concord than contrariety according to the natural course.

That original sin is in the soul.

According to the process which we have maintained concerning natural trees, we respond that the vegetative tree is inserted into the elemental tree, and the sensual into the vegetative, and the rational into the sensual. And we call the rational tree the soul of man, inserted into the body and conjoined with it. Wherefore, just as fire, which is inserted into air, inasmuch as it stands above it by way of action, and air inserted into water, inasmuch as it gives it heat which it receives from fire, so elemental power descends through vegetative power in a plant for elementing, and vegetative power in a horse draws the sensitive power downwards for vegetating, and in man the sensitive power draws the rational power downwards for sensing. And thus superior forms act upon inferior forms, and inferior forms, by reason of the appetite they passively have within themselves, attract superior forms, just as matter attracts form. And therefore the vegetative moves the elemental in a plant, and the sensitive moves the vegetative in a horse, and the rational moves the sensitive in man.

And in this step it is signified that original sin extends to the rational soul of every man according to the inclination which we have mentioned, because the body of man is infected and corrupted, and being so corrupted as it is, the rational soul moves it to element, vegetate, and sense, and moves it to its necessities, namely to eating, drinking, dwelling, and clothing, and so concerning other things which are external, which are creatures of God, which the body is not worthy to use inasmuch as Adam was against his creator: and in this way the rational soul of Peter and Martin is an instrument for sinning because of original sin, through which instrumentality it has general guilt. There are two ways of sinning, namely original sin, and actual sin. Actual sin is divided into mortal sin and venial sin, just as a Saracen, or a Jew, or anyone else who is not a Christian, in whom original sin extends corporally, as we have proven. And the same is true in Christians according to the nature of mortality and punishment, but not according to the redemption which was made through the passion of Christ, by reason of which passion and recreation the soul of a Christian is cleansed from guilt, and the body from original sin, and the soul of a Saracen remains infected, although it is not of the essence of Adam's soul, and that infection and guilt is for him a venial sin, but by reason of the body it is for him a mortal sin. Just as crystal, which is white in itself, and when placed on a black subject takes on a black color, in which color it is judged accidentally black. Just as a man existing in injury is injurious, and in luxury is luxurious. And in this step a man can know that the soul of a Saracen or a Jew, who believes to be in truth, and who does not sin mortally in actual sin, will not have spiritual punishment, but will have punishment through the body, inasmuch as through it he will have lost spiritual glory. There is therefore original sin in the souls of infidels, and it is in them morally through the body because of the likeness which it takes: just as a man who is unjust in injury, clothed

--- Page 238 ---
224 Apostolic Tree.

[Column 1]
was clothed in that condition. In Adam, the entire human species was exalted above all other corporeal species, all of which were created to serve man. And Adam sinned, as we have proven, wherefore, according to the great justice of God, it is necessary that just as through grace the entire human species in Adam was exalted in the magnitude of goodness, so afterwards it was entirely broken in the magnitude of malice by reason of justice, to such an extent that it was in a worse condition than any other creature, by reason of sin and guilt, and subjected to greater punishment. But this could not be, if the soul of every human being had not been infected by original sin, and if God could give more to man through grace without any merit of his, than the justice of God could punish man for guilt. And because the grace of God and His justice are one and the same goodness and magnitude in number, it is necessary that God can punish for guilt as much as He can give through grace. Therefore, the human species is in a worse condition because of original sin than the species of fruit tree, horse, fish, and crane, because these individuals do not suffer punishment after their death, and thus are not of such a vile condition as are men who die in original sin. And it would be an injury to God's justice, which could not punish as much as God's grace could give. If there were no original sin in the unrecreated man, his body after resurrection would not be tormented, because it would not have that with which to feel torment; or it would be necessary that his soul would have glory, and that the body itself would have punishment, and the body would be in hell, and the soul in paradise, and this is impossible. Therefore, it is necessary that the soul be subject to original

[Column 2]
sin, so that it may be the instrument with which the body of an infidel, dead in original sin, can be tormented and punished for that sin after resurrection. Adam sinned, as has been proven, and original sin remained corporally in all men, as we have proven, and the persistence of sin could not remain general without a subject, and the body of an unrecreated man could not be by itself alone the subject of the persistence of sin, which requires a subject, which is man, who cannot exist without soul and body. Therefore, it was necessary that the soul entered into the subjection of the persistence of sin, so that man might be subject to that persistence. And therefore, indirectly and obliquely, original sin falls upon the souls of infidel men, and directly and without medium upon their bodies. Wherefore, just as one man would be damaged by another and not by himself, so the soul is infected by original sin and not by itself, and this is by reason of the great conjunction and participation that exists between it and the body. And at this point it is recognized how great a thing holiness is, and how grave sin is. The fourth mode of proof is concerning recreation, the proof of which does not fall in this place, since we have to prove that the Son of God was incarnate, and insofar as man, crucified. Wherefore, once it is proven that He was incarnate, and crucified to recreate man, this article concerning recreation is proven in the proof of those two articles.

That God is the Glorifier.

This article, which is the seventh, bears witness that God is the Glorifier, namely, that He gives glory:

be a resurrection, since creation

**The Apostolic Tree. 227**

whiteness, and just as a hot substance, which is contrary through heat to a cold substance. Blessed God created the soul to remember, understand, and love Himself, indeed He created it so well that it might so strongly remember, understand, and love God with the magnitude of duration: just as with the magnitude of goodness, power, wisdom, will, virtue, and truth, since it is so that God is so much to be remembered, understood, and loved through His eternity: just as through the magnitude of His goodness, power, and other [qualities]. Therefore the soul is immortal and everlasting, since God is eternally to be remembered, understood, and loved: it is also immortal so that the magnitude of God may satisfy the magnitude of God's memorability, intelligibility, and lovability in eternity. If the soul were mortal, since it is not of an elemental nature nor even corporeal (as has been proven), after its death there would be no subject in which it would be sustained. And the same is true of its parts, which are the roots of its tree, and there would be nothing, and thus God would be unjust if He did not punish the wicked soul and did not reward the just soul, and if He were to create it another time, He could not recreate it in that first number, because its parts would be new and different: since it is so that in two creations there must be two numbers so distinct in plurality as two creations. And this passage is subtle to understand. Therefore the soul is not created another time, therefore it remains immortal, so that its number may remain subject to God's justice and glory, if it is good, and to punishment if it is evil. The just soul is not rewarded in this world, because in this world it has no rest, because the whole

[Column 2]

world cannot satisfy or complete it: because when a person desires one thing, they immediately desire another, and because God is just, it is necessary that the rational soul be immortal, so that it may have rest in which it may attain merit from the good things it has done by remembering, understanding, and loving God. And the same is true of the soul of an unjust person, who cannot be punished in this world among those people who have prosperity and few labors in this world, therefore it is necessary that it be punished in another life with the magnitude of justice, namely in eternity, which we wish to prove.

*That God will give glory to the Saints*
*in glory.*

God created the world with the magnitude of goodness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, glory, and truth. And therefore His magnitude is such a reason that God created the world by reason of glory just as by reason of goodness. Therefore the end of the world is as great through glory as through goodness. Therefore truth suffices to glorify humans in glory: so that magnitude may suffice for the end of glory, just as for the end of goodness. Therefore it is proven that God, who created the world, will give glory to good people. And this passage is pleasing to understand: because the intellect rejoices in attaining the truth of glory: which it expects, it also rejoices in the new mode of proof: which we give according to the general table. In God is glory, and He is His own glory, and if He did not give glory to those who love His glory, He would do injustice to the lovability of His glory, and to the love of those who love His glory. And thus He would be unjust and avaricious towards His own lovability and love.

[Column 1]

concerning the concordance which goodness and greatness, power, wisdom, will, glory, virtue and truth have in eternity against privation. And the same applies to the end and other forms. And this passage is very pleasing to understand, and signifies great glory because of the concordance of all divine forms, which they have for glorifying the saints in heaven. It has been said concerning the seven articles which pertain to the Godhead. Now it is necessary to speak concerning the seven articles which relate to humanity.

That the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

This article requires three proofs. The first is, that there is an incarnation. The second is, that the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and not by man. The third is, that He Himself is incarnate, and not for the purpose of being incarnated.

That God is Incarnate.

When God created the world, His goodness, His greatness, His wisdom, and His will were present in that creation. Wisdom understood the greatness of the end, by reason of which He Himself created the world. And that great end it understood by reason of God's greatness, which was in the creation, and as good by reason of goodness, and as lovable by reason of will. Therefore the world was created for a great, good, intelligible, and lovable end. It follows therefore that if God is incarnate, the end for which the world was created is in such great capacity for goodness, capacity for greatness, intelligibility, and lovability, that it cannot be in

[Column 2]

a greater [state], for if it could be in a greater [state], the divine capacity for goodness, capacity for greatness, intellectiveness, and capacity for love would be lacking for a greater end, which is impossible: therefore God is incarnate, since there is a greater end for which the world could be created, namely, that in one part of the world God is incarnate, that is, in man, in whom more natures participate than in any other creature, which man is indeed personified in God, and joined with Him, and that from the divine and human nature there is one person, one hypostasis, one God, one man, not two gods, nor two men, but one deified man, and the Son of God made man. God willed to assume human flesh, so that just as His dignities have rest within themselves in an operation which is so great that it cannot be greater, so they might have rest in external operations, namely in creatures, but man could not be, if He had not been incarnate, and had not deified the creature, for just as His goodness cannot be a greater reason for good to perform good: just as if it were a reason for a good God to produce God (and the same applies to greatness and other [attributes]), so divine goodness cannot be a greater reason for a good creator to produce a good creature: as is the

--- Page 244 ---
