| Left Column | Right Column |
| :---------- | :----------- |
| magnitude, which cannot magnify it more. Therefore, God is incarnated, so that His dignities may have rest in external works. And if God were not incarnated, nor would goodness be a reason for the good creator to incarnate, that He would create a great good with magnitude, and God would not create something so great, as goodness and magnitude would be reasons for creation, and wisdom would know this, inasmuch as it would know a greater creatability of magnitude and goodness, and thus goodness and magnitude would not have rest, nor wisdom, nor other forms in creation, and God would create good and great creatures infinitely, and at no time would they come to an end, nor to completion, which is impossible. Between the cause and its effect there is a concordance, through which concordance every efficient cause naturally loves its operation. God is the first cause, and the world is His effect, namely His operation. Therefore, there is a concordance between Him and the world, the subject of which concordance is the participation of God and creatures, which participation the will desires to be so great that it cannot be greater: it cannot be greater if God is incarnated, because in that incarnation He participates with all creatures, inasmuch as man contains within himself the nature of all creatures. But if He is not incarnated, the divine will does not love great participation nor concordance between God and creature, but rather has concordance with smallness and contrariety against magnitude and concordance, through which concordance, which it has with smallness and with contrariety, it is against the operation of magnitude, goodness, eternity, and power, and so forth for others, which contrariety is impossible, | therefore God is incarnated. God created the world by reason of goodness, and therefore created it good, and created it by reason of magnitude, and therefore created it great. God is deity: just as He is goodness and magnitude, therefore it is necessary that He should have created the world by reason of deity, therefore it was necessary that the world should have been deified after it was made good and great. For if it had not been deified, goodness and magnitude would have been in creation, but not deity, which would be idle in creation, which is impossible, since it is so that that goodness and magnitude are one and the same in number, and likewise with God, who created the world. Therefore, the world is deified in one man, who is God: because the whole world is not entirely good, in the unity of goodness, nor entirely great, in the unity of magnitude, which unities are in the deified man, who is part of the world, in whom deity was the reason for God to deify man, in whom He would be incarnated and humanized. Because God is incarnated, there can be an end and completion of all corporeal things in eternity, but this could not be if God were not incarnated: for if God were not united to a body, no elemental, vegetal, or sensual nature could reach Him, nor participate with Him, and thus they would be empty of an end, to which end their beginning and middle would naturally tend in eternity, and at no time would they reach it, which emptiness would be evil against goodness, and small against magnitude. Therefore God is incarnated, so that that glorious body which He assumed might be visible and His word audible. In which glorious body are the natures of the elemental, vegetal, sensual tree, and thus it is a full beginning and middle, |

**Apostolic Tree. 231**

...and middle, and the end of corporeal creatures in that glorious body, which is the end of all corporeal things, because all corporeal things rest in it according to the nature of corporeality, for whose rest no creature would suffice, which was not deified.

*That the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit.*

**P**otency and object have concordance in operation, just as the visual faculty and the visible, which have concordance in seeing, and the intellective and the intelligible in understanding, and the bonificative and the bonifiable in bonifying, and so concerning others. And the greater the concordance, the more simple is the act, and the more proximate to the potency and the object. Therefore, it is necessary that Christ be conceived of the Holy Spirit in our Lady, Saint Mary, the Glorious Virgin: because if he had been conceived by a man, the act would not have been so pure, nor so simple between God and our Lady Saint Mary, and Christ would have had two fathers, namely one God and another man, and our Lady would not then have had such a pure conception in conceiving God, as she had without the coupling of a man, and the conception would be lesser, and likewise the potency, by reason of which lesser degree, the incarnation could not occur, for the incarnation requires the greatest possible concordance that can exist between potency and object. Therefore, Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit without the coupling of a man. If Jesus Christ had been conceived by the carnal coupling of a man, the Son of God would have had two fathers and one mother, namely God the Father and a human father, which human father would be his father just as his mother is his mother by nature. But this is not fitting according to the greatness of the Son of God, because since one God the Father suffices, it is not necessary that he have a human father; also, the filiation of one father and one mother is more natural than that of two fathers and one mother. And because a greater concordance of father and mother and son must exist in the incarnation, it is necessary that Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit and not by a man. If Christ had been conceived of a man, he would have been, in the conception of a human father and a female mother, a man just like any other man, and there could not be the incarnation, which must necessarily be, so that man would be made human in the Godhead, and not in himself, so that one person could exist from both natures, namely from the divine nature and the human, which person indeed could not be one, if Christ as man had been man in himself, and not made human in the Godhead, because he would then have been conceived from a human father and a woman. Therefore, Christ is man by the Holy Spirit, and not generated by a man, but produced from a mother in the Godhead. If Christ had been conceived by a man, our Lady Saint Mary could not have been a Virgin in conception, but would have been corrupted by a man, through whose corruption holiness and intention would have been diminished in purity, goodness, greatness, will, power, in the Incarnation, and so concerning other forms, and thus the conception would not have been worthy to unite the divine and human nature in one person, and in the person of the God-man. Therefore, it is necessary that our Lady was a Virgin, so that in conception she might exalt her dignity and power to a greater degree of greatness, goodness...

--- Page 246 ---
232 Arbor apostolicalis.

...goodness, virtue, etc. God made man from the earth, and made woman from man according to order. It was therefore necessary that He make man from woman, and if Christ had been the Son of man and woman, the third mode would have been lacking, namely in producing man from woman, without man. Which defect indeed would have been an emptiness of order and magnitude, goodness, and other things, which emptiness is impossible, since it is against the goodness of magnitude and other things.

*That God is already Incarnate.*

It is necessary that the incarnation be with a magnitude of truth, so that in it there can be a magnitude of goodness, which could not be in it, if it were with a smallness of truth, to which smallness of truth the magnitude of falsehood and malice would resist, and thus the incarnation could not be. And because it has been proven that the incarnation exists, it is therefore with a magnitude of truth, if God is already incarnate. For if it were to incarnate all men who believe, or have believed, that He is already incarnate, they are in falsehood, and against the truth, believing one and the same incarnation, and thus they are in malice, and in sin, and they go to infernal fire, and a smallness of truth follows, and a privation of the magnitude of goodness, in divine will, power, and wisdom, which is impossible. Therefore God is already incarnate, so that He may restore the magnitude of goodness and truth in men, who have believed and believe, and will believe: that He is already incarnate. If God is not incarnate, He is to be incarnated, and when He would be incarnated in His incarnation, men would not have a place to believe it: for their opinion would be that that incarnation was false: just like that which is past, which men believed to be true, and thus they would not have the freedom to believe, and belief would be impossible according to the magnitude of goodness, wisdom, will, truth, and virtue, by reason of which impossibility the incarnation would be impossible. Therefore God is already incarnate, so that the aforementioned impossibility may not follow. If God is already incarnate, it is just that reverence and honor be paid to the Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Apostles, Martyrs, and Confessors: who are authenticated, and who are held to be saints. And if God is not already incarnate, Christ born in Bethlehem, and crucified in Jerusalem, was a false man, and all believing in Him are falsified by Him. And thus God is against justice, and against the mode of incarnation, and a lesser degree of mercy and piety follows in God: because all Christians, Jews, Saracens, and Pagans go to Hell, inasmuch as God has no mercy or piety for them. Therefore He is already incarnate, so that God may have great mercy and piety, and that the saints who believe in the incarnation may be rewarded for the sufferings they endured through faith. It is necessary that the incarnation be with a magnitude of end in duration, just as it is with a magnitude of end in goodness, wisdom, power, and will. And if God is not already incarnate, the end of the incarnation is against a greater magnitude of duration subject to the magnitude of goodness, power, wisdom, and will, inasmuch as the time that has passed, up to the time when He will be incarnate, was not subject to the magnitude of goodness...

--- Page 247 ---
Arbor apoftolicalis. 233

of goodness in the duration of power, wisdom, and will. Therefore duration fails forms, and conversely forms fail duration, which is impossible. Therefore God is now incarnated, to whom it may please, that we may be able to see God himself as man in his glory, through his great piety. If God is incarnated, an order is placed between the first intention and the second. We call the first intention the New Testament, and the second intention the Old Testament, which has concordance with the New successively, and in a continuous quantity of time. And if God is not incarnated, the contrary follows, and there is a concordance of continuous quantity in privation, and it is in discrete quantity, and this belief that Christians have is a false medium, if God is not now incarnated. Which discrete quantity indeed builds contrariety between the first intention and the second, against the greater concordance, which is in continuous quantity and in discrete. Therefore God is now incarnated, so that there may be a greater concordance of quantity, between the first intention and the second.

That the Lord Jesus Christ was born.

It has been proven that God is incarnated, and the consequence of the incarnation according to the means and the end follows the principle of incarnation, which is continuous, namely that he was born. For if he had not been born, and yet had been incarnated, the principle of incarnation, the means, and the end would not follow, and the magnitude would be lacking for the truth of incarnation and humanity, which defect would be evil against goodness, and a vice against virtue, and so on for others. Therefore Jesus

Christ was born man-God, after man-God, after man-God was incarnated. Jesus Christ was born naturally, so that his nativity might be the manner of a natural course, which pertains to the birth of man. And he was born in human form, because he was man and Son of God: insofar as he was man, he was born man, and

234 Apostolic Tree.

[Left Column]

in the beginning, middle, and end of the Incarnation and Nativity of His Son, which sufficiency of goodness would not have existed, if Christ had not been born of a Virgin, from which Virgin He was born, so that the magnitude of goodness might remain, in the intention of virginity. If Jesus Christ was born of a Virgin, and conceived of a Virgin, His virginity, purity, and sanctity were in greater concordance of goodness, magnitude, duration, power, wisdom, will, glory, virtue, and truth. And if the Lord Jesus Christ had not been born of a Virgin, there would be concordance in a lesser degree of magnitude, goodness, and other things, which concordance of a lesser degree is impossible. Therefore, Jesus Christ was born in greater concordance of Virginity.

That Jesus Christ died.

The Godhead honored, as much as it could, the humanity of Jesus Christ, because it could not honor it more, than by creating it in the Godhead, in which it was conjoined with the Son of God. It was therefore necessary that humanity should honor the Godhead as much as it could, since it could not honor it with temporal prosperities and delights, because the Godhead does not require honors of prosperities, nor of delights, but requires that man be poor in this world, and that he endure labors and death to honor it. It was therefore necessary that Christ, inasmuch as he was man, should die, so that humanity might honor the Godhead, and that he might be an example to others in honoring it. Jesus Christ died to give an example that He was a mortal man because of original sin, yet He was immortal, inasmuch as

[Right Column]

He was sustained in the Godhead. And He was mortal, so that with His special mortality, general death might die. Indeed, this general death was vanquished because He through whom the whole world was created, endured suffering, so that the world might be recreated. Indeed, this special suffering suffices to remove general guilt, just as the end suffices for the generality of the world, which was created for Christ's end and because of Him. And in this step it is proven that the world was recreated by the death of Christ, which had to be, so that the world might be recreated by it, and that it might return to the end for which it was created. For if the world had been eternally deviated from the end for which it was created, the magnitude, goodness, and other divine forms would fail the end of creation, which is impossible. It is proven that the world exists deviated from its end because of original sin, therefore Jesus Christ willed to die, so that His death might be a reason for His people, for whom He died, to love Him, which reason indeed could not be of such great magnitude of lovability as it was through death, because a shepherd cannot love his sheep more than when he dies for their good. And because Jesus Christ loved His people with a great magnitude of love, He willed to die for the sake of the magnitude of love. And in this step man can know that Jesus Christ permits that there be Saracens and Pagans in the world, so that Christians may have great material for lovability, and also that in it they may use great love, so that they themselves may endure labors and death, so that they may convert infidels to God, and recover the Holy Land. And therefore the Lord Pope and his brothers the Lord Cardinals moisten,

He redeemed with His own blood. And it signified that in the underworld He had no affliction from the pains of those who were in the underworld, and this signification was a sign and manifestation to the Prophets and Saints that the guilt of original sin had been consumed, after the soul (which was like theirs) had no suffering in the place where they were. So that the damned might have greater punishment, the soul of Christ descended to the underworld, because in it was manifested the victory He had in saving those who believed in Jesus Christ, while those who had denied His coming remained perpetually in the underworld. Therefore, just as His representation was greater glory to the just, so it was necessary that it should be greater punishment to the unjust. Just as [small cross-like mark] Jesus willed to descend from life to death on the cross, so He willed to descend from the life acquired on the cross through His death to the state of death of the Saints, who existed in darkness because of original sin. And it was necessary for this to be so, that His descent might be in the greatness of goodness, charity, and humility. But this could not have been, if Jesus Christ had not descended to the underworld.

That Jesus Christ rose from the dead.

A greater end of goodness, greatness, and other things consists in man as a whole, than in any of his parts alone, therefore it was necessary that our Lord Jesus Christ should rise again, so that a greater end might come. For if He had not risen, it would have been necessary that there be some fault in Him that would impede a greater end. Indeed, such a fault could not be in Christ, because man is united and personified in the Godhead and sustained in it. Jesus

[Right Column]
Christ rose again, so that He might be man of soul and body, just as He was before He died. And when He died, He was man, inasmuch as the Son of God was man, but He was not man, inasmuch as the soul was not in the body. And because the Son of God willed to be man constituted of soul and body, Jesus Christ rose again, so that the divine will might have achieved what it willed, which it would not have achieved if Jesus Christ had not risen from death to life. Because Jesus rose from the dead, it was signified that He had completed on the cross the victory against original sin. And if Jesus Christ had not risen, it would have been signified that the victory was not complete. Therefore it was necessary that the Lord Jesus Christ should rise from the dead, not by another but by Himself: for just as the Son of God was incarnated by Himself, so by Himself the soul of Christ returned to His body from which it had departed. Jesus Christ rose again, so that He might be an example and sign of the general resurrection of men, which is to come. Therefore He placed men in greater hope of resurrection through His own resurrection. For if He had not risen, it would have been contrary to this greater hope; and in opposition to this greater hope, Jesus Christ could not have been according to the magnitude of goodness, justice, and charity. If Jesus Christ had not risen from the dead, His body would have been in the earth, and His soul in heaven, and His body would not have had a privilege in the magnitude of goodness, glory, and will above the bodies of other men. Indeed, this privilege is necessary for Jesus Christ to have by reason of the union of the divine and human natures, in which union the human nature of our Lord Jesus Christ is exalted in a greater magnitude of goodness, glory, and end.

--- Page 251 ---
**The Apostolic Tree. 237**

...of purpose and will, than that of any other creatures. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead.

**That Jesus Christ ascended to the heavens.**

IN the Empyrean heaven are the souls of the Saints; there they contemplate God and see Him face to face, and with a spiritual eye to eye; and in this mortal life, no soul can contemplate or see God without a mediator, namely, without an imaginative species. Therefore that higher place is nobler than the place of this mortal life. It was therefore necessary that Jesus Christ should ascend with His body to those heights or altitudes, in which is the nobler place. But this could not be, if Jesus Christ had not ascended to the heavens. Jesus Christ ascended to the heavens, that He might give glory to the Saints, because through His vision they have greater glory; and if He had not ascended to the heavens, they would have had less, and thus our Lord Jesus Christ would have been against greater glory, and would have had great concordance with lesser glory, which is impossible, since it is so that glory and greatness have concordance in the magnitude of goodness and other things; because the Lord Jesus ascended to the heavens, He placed the souls of the Saints in a greater aspect of resurrection. For in this, that they saw the Lord Jesus Christ who rose from the dead, the general resurrection was better revealed and signified to them, by which greater revelation and signification the Saints had greater glory and greater hope of resurrection. Our Lord Jesus Christ recreated the human race, and drew the souls of the Saints from hell, which went into Paradise. Since it is so, that Paradise is the place where the end is attained, for which the world was created. Therefore this life in which we are, is in the beginning and in the middle, and the other life is in the end. Hence, if the souls of the Saints went to Paradise, it was well necessary that the soul of Jesus Christ should have gone, and His body should have ascended, since it is so that He Himself is the end and complement of the restoration of those souls. The Lord Jesus is nobler by reason of His divine nature than by reason of His human nature, and therefore if He had not ascended to the heavens, the divine nature would have been injured in the human. And the same is true of the soul and the body, since it is so that the soul is nobler than the body. Just as if an olive tree which is grafted onto a wild olive tree, were to send its nature downwards, and the nature of the wild olive tree were to ascend upwards, so that the olive would produce olives of the species of the wild olive tree and not of the olive tree. Jesus Christ therefore ascended to the heavens, so that the inconveniences mentioned above would not have existed in Him. God is good, and His goodness is His reason for doing good; and God is great, therefore His goodness is God's reason for doing great good: His goodness therefore is not His reason for doing a small good and not a great one, since He is great Divinity, He could not have acted fittingly towards the humanity He assumed, if He had kept it in places where great things are not attained, but only small ones. Therefore, the glorious humanity of Jesus Christ ascended to places where great goods are attained.

**That Jesus Christ is Judge on the day of judgment.**

IT is necessary that the day of judgment be concerning good and evil people, so that the end of beings which were created may follow.

Gg 3 That

--- Page 252 ---
238 Apostolic Tree.

[Left Column]
Indeed, that judgment must be understood, seen, and heard, because without understanding, seeing, and hearing, there would be no full realization in the magnitude of goodness, truth, and other things: therefore it is necessary that the judge be God and man. It is necessary that he be God, so that the judgment may be understood in the magnitude of truth; it is necessary that he be man, so that the judge may be seen, and that his judgment may be heard. Therefore it is necessary that the nations be gathered in one place, so that they may be able to see and hear the judge, but this could not be, if Jesus Christ were not the judge. Therefore the Lord Jesus will judge the good and the evil on the day of judgment. It is necessary that the judgment be in the continuous quantity of beginning, middle, and end. And because quantity remains in diverse distinct quantities, sustained by the difference which is between the beginning, the middle, and the end, it is necessary that there be judgment, according to what pertains to the beginning, the middle, and the end. Hence, if our Lord Jesus Christ is judge, his judgment is concerning principles, namely, concerning that which pertains to honoring the Godhead and the humanity joined with it. And the same is true concerning the middle, since it is so that Jesus Christ, in as much as he is man, is the mediator between God and his people. And the same is true concerning the end, since it is so that all created beings are for honoring God and the humanity of Christ. Therefore Jesus Christ will be judge on the day of judgment. The Lord Jesus Christ will be judge, so that there may be greater glory for the good, and greater punishment for the evil. For it is great glory for the good, that they see that he who will be like them, will give judgment and call them to perpetual glory. And great punishment will be for the evil, who will see such great power of man, which will judge them to perpetual punishment, and because judgment

[Right Column]
must be in the magnitude of truth, it will be greater, in as much as it will give greater glory to the good, and greater punishment to the evil. Therefore it is necessary that the Lord Jesus Christ be judge. One and the same heat is great in one subject, and small in another: just as the heat of fire which is great in pepper, and small in anise, is great in pepper because it can receive great heat, it is small in anise because it is not among its conditions that it can be subject to great heat. In a similar way it will be concerning the greater judgment, which will be at the end of the world. Indeed, that judgment could not be great, if there were not some great subject in which it would be sustained. A great subject could not exist: if he who will give judgment were not the first and greatest judge who can exist, hence since God is not a body: if he were to give judgment by voice, and the voice were not from him, and the voice were not part of him, he who would speak would not be the first judge, but rather a medium, and thus the judgment could not be great, because it would not have a subject in which it could be great. Therefore it is necessary that that judge who will judge the good and the evil: be that same one who will speak, in as much as he will give judgment, but this could not be, if God were not man. Therefore Jesus Christ will judge, who in as much as he is man will be that same one who will speak, and in as much as he is God will be the first judge, and thus the judgment will be great. Concerning the magnitude of judgment is, that he who judges, be the end of the judgment, and that he who is judged, relates himself to that end according to the magnitude of goodness, and the concordance of the judge and the judged. And the same follows according to the magnitude of evil, and the contrariety of those who have sinned against the judge. Therefore it is necessary

...fore that our Lord Jesus Christ be judge, since he himself is the end, inasmuch as he is God and man of all created beings, to which end the just relate themselves with greatness of goodness and concord, and the wicked who manifest it with greatness of malice and contrariety.

*On the Fruit of the Apostolic Tree.*

THE FRUIT of the Apostolic Tree is that (one), in which are gathered all the fruits of other trees, of which it has been spoken. Because all things whatsoever that are in this present life according to divine ordination, which God has placed in the creatures of this life, in which we are, direct themselves thus to the Apostolic and general tree: just as many lines (direct themselves) to one point constituted from them and a center, in which they meet each other, and have their completion.

to proportion the cultivator to the fruit, and the elected Pope to preserve himself in that proportion.

    Concerning the Celestial Tree.

    SUMMARY.

[Decorative Initial A]THE Celestial Tree is similarly divided into seven parts, namely into roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

The roots are the general principles, excluding contrariety.
The trunk is the heavens.
The branches are the twelve signs.
The boughs are the planets.
The leaves are the celestial accidents.
The flowers are the celestial acts.
The fruits are the inferior created things.

*Concerning the Branches of the Celestial Tree.*

<span style="font-size: 3em; line-height: 0.8em; float: left; margin-right: 0.1em;">B</span>RANCHES of the celestial trunk are the twelve signs, which indeed ought to correspond to the branches of the elemental tree, according to the ordering of inferior bodies, & superior bodies. Nevertheless, according to the position set forth by philosophers, we see some contradictions according to the necessary order: such as Aries, which is judged to be of the fiery complexion; & Taurus of the earthy complexion, & Gemini of the airy complexion: because according to natural reason, & the arrangement to which the situation of the branches of the elemental tree ought to correspond, three signs should be of the airy complexion in spring, & three of the fiery complexion in summer, & three of the earthy complexion in autumn, & three of the watery complexion in winter. The three signs that are of spring are Aries, Taurus, & Gemini, and the three that are of summer are Cancer, Leo, & Virgo, and the three that are of autumn are Libra, Scorpio, & Sagittarius, and the three that are of winter are Capricorn, Aquarius, & Pisces. Nevertheless, just as the four seasons of the year go in a circuit around the earth, so the signs go in a circuit around the earth according to the arrangement of spring, summer, autumn, & winter. And if philosophers have erred in this course, it is not to be wondered at if their followers fail in their experiments & judgments, which they give in the art of Astronomy. If Aries is good, & Taurus good, & Gemini good, the entire quadrant of spring is good. And just as they agree in goodness, they ought to agree in mobility, & in masculinity.

And by reason of the concordance they have, they ought to agree in Mars, which is given to Aries, & in Venus, which is given to Taurus, & Mercury, which is given to Gemini. And to this contradicts the femininity, which they attributed to Taurus, & the mediocrity, which they attributed to Gemini: & so concerning other things similar to these, which lead to many inconveniences according to ancient positions. Such as Saturn, to whom they attribute the earthy complexion, which is the lowest element, & has a slower motion & a smaller circle, and Saturn, who is the highest planet, & who makes a greater course than all other planets. And therefore the Lord Pope & his brothers the Lord Cardinals would do well, that according to the necessary order of superior & inferior impressions, they would cause the science of Astronomy to be ordered in its proper situations by inquiring into the experiences that would follow from that ordering. And this investigation could be done according to the process of this book with the aid of the process of the inventive art & the general table. The branches of the celestial tree ought to correspond to the branches of the vegetal tree: such as Aries, Taurus, Gemini, which ought to move the appetitive faculty towards objects of a humid & warm complexion by reason of spring: & Cancer, Leo, Virgo towards objects of a warm & dry complexion in summer: Libra, Scorpio, & Sagittarius towards objects of a dry & cold complexion in autumn: Capricorn, Aquarius, & Pisces ought to move the appetitive faculty towards objects of a cold & humid complexion in winter. Nevertheless, if Leo in summer moves the appetitive faculty towards a cold & humid object, it does this so that they may have more material for heating & drying, & because matter that is excessively heated & dried has an appetite, which

Therefore, each sign ascends according to the Earth's straightness. Let us suppose that A is east, and C is west, and B is south, and D is north.

[Column 2]
Therefore, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini ascend from A to B. And Cancer, Leo, and Virgo from B to C. And Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius from C to D. And Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces from D to A. And because of this, we have the experience that the sun is hotter when it descends from B to C than when it ascends from A to B, because it receives more virtue from Cancer, Leo, and Virgo than from Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. When Aries ascends from A to B, its ascent is its head, and its descent is from B to C, which is its tail, and B is its middle. Therefore, it influences the branches of the elemental tree in one way according to the head, and in another according to the middle, and in another way according to the tail. Therefore, the astrologer makes one judgment in the head, another in the middle, and another in the tail. And the same applies to other signs. They also make a judgment about Cancer, Aries, Libra, and Capricorn, which are mobile: namely, that things which occur under their dominion do not last, and that those things last which occur under the dominion of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, which are not mobile, and that those things last, but not for long, which occur under the dominion of Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces, which are mobile in part and not in whole. Aries descends from B to C according to the arrangement of the upper circle, which is from A to C. And Gemini descends before it, and Taurus similarly. Therefore, the astrologer first makes a judgment about Gemini in the quadrant from B and C, rather than about Taurus or Aries, and so for other signs. Therefore, there are twenty-four hours in a natural day, so that the astrologer may know how to judge a sign according to its hour. And the same applies to the twelve months and four seasons:

Masculinity is attributed to one sign by reason of form, and femininity is attributed to another sign by reason of matter, and this so that one sign may have action, and another passion, and so that from that which has action, male and day may follow, and from that which has passion, female and night may follow. Nevertheless, in one and the same region and hour, male and female are generated, and this is by reason of the conception of inferior bodies, which receive impressions from superior bodies, according to how they are disposed to receive. Just as fire, which always has the nature of heating that substance which it touches, nevertheless does not heat the skin of the salamander, which lives in fire, and this is because it is born and nourished in fire, and is more of it than of any other element. In a similar way, although one sign may be masculine, its masculinity is not the reason that its region produces a male in that matter which is more disposed to a female according to the disposition of the branches of the elemental tree. And in this step it is recognized that the judgments of astronomy are difficult to understand. The reason why mobility is attributed to one sign, and stillness to another, is because it is necessary that things which are produced by generation, be produced by motion, which is augmentative and from alterable causes, by which motion instruments are fatigued: just as a horse which is fatigued by running, and the heart by thinking, and the mouth by speaking, and the hands by working. Therefore nature requires rest, according to what we experience in sleeping, and in plants, which do not yield fruit in winter, and a horse which is fatigued by running, and a ballista which is tired from drawing, which does not make a great

It is also said that some signs are not mobile but moderate: like Virgo, and the reason for this is that motivity, mobility, and stability oppose each other. And all these things happen according to inferior impressions, since it is so that the signs continuously stand fixed in the firmament, and in its parts, according to the judgment that is made concerning mobility in one, and immobility in another, and mediocrity in another, it happens with regard to the lower world. Just as the sun with one and the same power dries a tile and melts wax. And in this, Astronomers take judgment, that Aries is good, because from it follows good, and Leo is evil, because from it follow wars and battles. It is also said that good signs make men fortunate for good prosperity, and long life, and health, and pleasures, and evil signs do the contrary. And they intend to say this according to natural impressions, to which the soul, by reason of its liberty, does not always consent, also because God, according to His goodness or justice, uses His effect according to His will at all times and in all places. *On the Branches of the Celestial Tree.*

[Decorative initial R] The branches of the Celestial Tree are the seven planets. And the ancient philosophers say that Saturn is superior, and Jupiter afterwards, and so in order for the others down to the moon. And they say that Saturn is evil, and that it causes lead, and Saturday. And they say it is of the complexion of earth. They also say that Jupiter is good, and that it causes tin, and Thursday, and that it is of the complexion of air. They also say that Mars is evil, and that it causes iron and Tuesday, and that it is of the complexion of fire. Likewise they say that the Sun is good, and that it causes gold and Sunday, and that it is of the complexion of fire. Furthermore they say that Venus is good, and that it causes copper and Friday, and that it is of the complexion of water. They also say that Mercury is neutral, and that it causes quicksilver and Wednesday. They say that the moon is good for the good, and evil for the evil, and that it causes silver and Monday, and that it is of the complexion of water. According to the arrangement of the elements, it is necessary that the planets be arranged so that the ordered arrangements correspond to each other. The spheres of the elements are ordered in this way: the sphere of fire is superior, and the sphere of air is contiguous with the sphere of fire, so that fire has an inclination towards air; and air is su-

[Column 2]

perior to the sphere of water so that it has an inclination towards it, and water is above the sphere of earth so that it has an inclination towards it. And thus by reason of the inclination which occurs from superior to inferior, influence comes downwards; but this is not ordered according to the arrangements which the philosophers ordered in the planets, because they placed Saturn above, which is dry, and air below, which is humid. And they placed Mars and the Sun, which are hot, below air, and thus with one participating with another, an excessive similarity of heat follows, and the order of arrangement, which pertains to that which is in the spheres of the elements, is destroyed. They also placed the complexion of water below Mercury, which is dry. Our art also teaches many inconveniences in the arrangement of the planets according to the opinion of the ancients: nevertheless, it maintains that through a contrary arrangement, Saturn would be superior by dryness, and Jupiter afterwards by humidity, so that one line of contraries follows, thus from dryness above to humidity below: just as it happens in the spheres of the elements, whence follows a concordance between heat, which is above, and humidity, which is below, namely between the heat of fire and the humidity of air. Our art also maintains that the heat of air, which Jupiter has, descends to the heat of fire, which is from Mars. Our art also maintains: that the dryness of Mars descends to the dryness of the Sun, and the humidity of Venus descends to the dryness of Mercury, and thus the dryness of Mercury to the humidity of the moon. And our art maintains this so that a mixture of the influences of the planets and the impressions of the elements may occur. The planets move from west to east, contrary to the motion of the signs which move from east to west. And therefore there is an encounter

*Of the Leaves of the Celestial Tree.*

[Decorative initial F] We compare the leaves of the celestial tree to the general accidents of the tree, which are the reasons for the lower accidents. Thus, namely, that the quantity of the region of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini is the reason and cause of the quantity from the east to the south. And so of other accidents, about which we wish to treat briefly.

*Of the Quantity of the Celestial Tree.*

[Decorative initial Q] The quantity of the celestial tree is considered in two ways, namely continuous and discrete: and we consider these two ways in three figures, namely in circular, quadrangular, and triangular figures. Continuous quantity is considered, as from Aries and Taurus, and so of others up to Pisces: and from Saturn and Jupiter, up to the Moon, and from Aries and Taurus, and so of others: and from Saturn up to the Moon. This continuous quantity is extended throughout the entire firmament, and is one of many, namely of the primary quantities of the roots: and because the roots are different, the continuous quantity is from discrete quantities: just as the common quantity of substance, which is from discrete quantities, namely of form and of matter, which are quantitative. And this discrete quantity of the roots appears in diverse

There is another mode of continuous quantity, which is from Aries to Libra, and from Cancer to Scorpio, and from Saturn to the Moon. And this comprehends all places that are within the eighth sphere, and is sustained in the general forms of the fifth essence, and also the four substances of the world. And discrete quantity consists in goodness, which is one in the fifth essence, and is another in the four substances of the world. Just as iron, which is under one form in a knife, and under another form in a hammer: and the same applies to magnitude and other forms: wherefore, just as in the flesh of a finger there consists one continuous quantity, so the entire universal substance of the world is extended in one continuous quantity of goodness, and continuous quantity thus has parts that are of its nature, just as the continuous quantity of a finger has discrete parts, which are bones.
And in this passage it is recognized how the discrete quantities of the fifth essence and the four substances correspond, which thus receive influence from the superior continuous quantity: just as the quantity of the bones of a finger receives from the quantity of the flesh. And just as the quantity of flesh places nothing positive that is of its essence, but only of its nature, into the discrete quantity of the bones, so the quantity of the fifth essence places nothing of itself into the inferior quantities insofar as it is its essence: but insofar as it is its nature, with which it participates, according to continuity with the inferior quantities. And in this passage it is recognized how the Sun multiplies quantity in the growth that a plant makes, and in the heat of pepper, although its quantity does not descend here below nor recede from itself, even though inferior quantities receive in-

-fluence and impressions from it. And this philosophy is delightful to understand, and is a way to know more principles and natural secrets. The quantity of the fifth essence consists in a circular figure according to its arrangement, which is from Aries to Pisces, and from Saturn to the Moon, and from Aries to the Moon, and it is in a quadrangular figure, inasmuch as it is in four regions: one is of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini: and another is of Cancer, Leo, and Virgo: and another is of Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius: and another is of Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. And the triangular figure consists in the planets. And the same applies to the quadrangular, according to how they form a triangle and a quadrangle. And concerning this matter, it has been said in the branches of this tree. And in this passage it is recognized how the superior quantity is arranged, and the cause of the arrangement of the inferior quantity according to the circle, quadrangle, and triangle.

**On the Quality of the Celestial Tree.**

THE SUN is qualitative by the difference it has with other planets, and it is qualitative because it is good and shining. And this quality is proper to it, although the moon is good: just as fire is good and air is good: but because fire and air are distinguished by hot and humid, the goodness of fire is under one quality, and the goodness of air under another. The same applies to the goodness of the sun and moon, since it is in the sun under one species and property, and in the moon under another species and property. There is another mode of quality, which is appropriate: such as the heat of the sun, which is its appropriate quality, and similarly the coldness of the moon, and this is by reason of the operation they have in diverse ways: for
the sun is the cause of fire by multiplying
li 2

--- Page 266 ---
252 Celestial Tree.

heat by reason of its light, which agrees
with the light of fire, which is properly hot.
And the same is true of the moon, which in
water multiplies coldness by reason of
its shadowiness, which agrees with the
shadowiness of water. And from two shadows
night follows, which is the source of coldness
and shadow. And the same is true of the clarity
of the moon, which is a quality appropriated
to it by the Sun. And the same is true of the other
qualities of the other planets, which impress
their similarities in the proper and appropriated
qualities existing here below. Therefore it is said
that Saturn is evil and of the complexion
of earth, and so of the others: because it is the
cause below for multiplying dryness, coldness,
and melancholy in humans, by reason of which
they have many evil thoughts: and so of
the others.

On the Relation of the Celestial Tree.

THE SUN is of magnitude, goodness,
and the rest: and in goodness there is
that which makes good, that which can be made good,
and to make good, in which stands relation,
which is a part of the sun, and through which
the sun has the nature of making good in
inferior relations, which are in the species
of goodness. Therefore, just as the light of the sun
is the reason for multiplying the heat of fire,
because with it it has concordance in light,
so is the reason of its relation for multiplying
the relation of fire in that which heats,
that which can be heated, and to heat, and in
that which makes good, that which can be made good,
and to make good. And in this step the manner
is known, according to which superior accidents
impress their similarities in inferior accidents.
The instrument for this intention is the motion
of the firmament and its parts, which is greater
above than here below, by reason of which greatness are made

impressions in inferiors by superiors.

On the Action and Passion of the Celestial Tree.

THE SUN is of goodness, magnitude, and
the other roots, and its great goodness
would not exist, if it were not a reason for good,
which would produce good: but because good
cannot be done without action and passion:
therefore the Sun has action, inasmuch as it is
that which makes good, and its essential
'that which can be made good' is passive,
like matter under form, and to make good
is from both. And the same regarding action
and passion in the Sun under the reason of goodness:
and the subject of operation is magnitude,
which is 'that which can be made good', and duration
likewise, and power, and the other parts
of the Sun receive similarities from its goodness,
inasmuch as they are good parts and essences
under the reason of goodness. And from this action
and passion which are within the substance
of the Sun, one passion follows externally:
just as the Sun, which has action upon Venus,
inasmuch as it gives its similarity to it,
and Venus is passive, inasmuch as it receives
that similarity. And Venus, which is an active
planet, inasmuch as it has action upon Mercury,
and Mercury is passive, inasmuch as it receives
it. And the same is true of Mercury, which
has action upon the Moon, and the Moon,
which is passive, inasmuch as it receives it.
Therefore it is said that the Moon has more
matter than any of the other planets, so that
its matter may be disposed to receive more
and great passions, which come to it from
the superior planets. Therefore the Moon
signifies its properties more strongly in
inferiors than any other planet.
Hence sailors look to the Moon: and hu-

& men when they wish to let blood, to plant, & to cut down trees: & women when they wish to conceive children, & so concerning other similar things: just as the crab of the sea, which under one Moon is fuller than under another. And in this passage it is recognized that superior actions & passions are reasons for inferior actions & passions according to the natural course. And from this is taken the opinion that men have concerning good fortune, & bad fortune: who are ignorant of the liberties, which are in inferiors in rational souls, over which superior bodies have no action, which souls indeed have greater action over the bodies, with which they are conjoined, than superior bodies. And those wise ones who know this say that good fortune, & bad fortune are not anything according to the reality of spiritual things.

*De Habitu arboris cælestialis.*

The Sun has in its habit the drying of clay tiles, & the softening of wax: & just as fire has in its habit the drying of clay tiles by reason of the dryness which it receives

They have no shadow, from which follows the time of days and nights upon the surface of the sphere of fire. Time therefore above does not multiply day, nor night, but here below by reason of the earth's shadow. Because all that which is above is illuminated, or brightened by the sun, and by the stars without the shadow of night. Nevertheless, time is multiplied in another, not in itself: just as Saturn, which has one motion, and Jupiter which has another, and so on down to the Moon. Wherefore in those [bodies] time stands in discrete quantities, and in itself it stands as one: just as one day, which stands in several moments without shadow and multiplication of several days. And in this passage, time is revealed to the intellect, according as it is in itself and in another. Time therefore stands thus in itself without motion, like a circle without beginning and end. Just as a sinful man needs God's mercy, and a man wronged in his justice, so lower substances have a necessity that time be varied in higher substances, just as Saturn, which at one time is in one place, and at another time in another, and at one time is in the rectitude of Aries, and at another time of Taurus, and therefore requires lower time according to its natural position, order, and the position of higher time, so that higher time here below transmits its likeness to the time which is here below, which it receives in elemental substances, which at one time are in one place, and at another time in another place, also that at the same time, one and the same substance operates diversely: just as fire which heats, illuminates, dries, and softens: and so concerning other things similar to these, which it would be long to narrate.

De Loco arboris cæleſtialis.

[L]ace is one part of the celestial tree, because just as the firmament stands in time by itself, so it stands placed in itself, and within itself it contains all things which participate with place. And outside itself according to the natural course, place has no subject: because the eighth sphere contains all things placed. Therefore some say that outside the firmament naturally no body can exist, so that there is no infinite place, nor that the nature of place is infinite, also that place has no appetite beyond the limit, in which a corporeal substance is terminated and placed. Because just as if a stone were to move from below up to Aries, it would be ascending for it, which motion indeed would be unnatural for it: so it would be an unnatural appetite for Saturn, if it wished to be above Aries or Aries above Taurus, or Taurus above Aries. Place is therefore terminated according to the natural course within the eighth sphere. Nevertheless, according to faith we hold that there is a crystalline heaven, and the empyrean above the eighth sphere. We intend to speak of the empyrean heaven in the eternal tree.

De Floribus arboris Cæleſtialis.

Just as the flower of Aries, which is in Mars, and the flower of Taurus in Venus, and the flower of Gemini in Mercury, and of Cancer in the Moon, and of Leo in the Sun, and of Virgo in Mercury, and the flower of Libra in Venus, and of Scorpio in Mars, and of Sagittarius in Jupiter, and of Capricorn in Saturn, and of Aquarius in Saturn, and of Pisces in Jupiter, and these flowers are thus considered accor-

**On the Fruit of the Celestial Tree.**

**F**RUIT of the Celestial Tree
consists in two ways, one
is of its nature, and the other is a-
bove its nature, which is gathered in
the empyrean heaven. The fruit which is of the na-
ture of the celestial tree, is from moved
causes, to which motive forms move them-
selves in moving movable things, so that they may produce
moved substances from potentiality into actuality,
and the same concerning accidents: like gold,
an apple, a horse, and the body of Martin, and
his castle, and a knife, and his book:
and so concerning other things moved by
natural or artificial agents with the help
of superior forms. The fruit which
is superior, is by reason of the end: just as man
who is a fruit, in whom are gathered
the fruits of the elemental tree of plants,
and of irrational beings, if however that man
serves God in this life. And in such a man
are gathered the fruits of Aries, and
Taurus, Saturn, and Jupiter, and so concerning others. And
if man is a sinner, those fruits are
lost in him: just as gold which is
lost in the destruction of a ship, which is lost
in the deep sea. And therefore
sin is against all corporeal fruits
which God created and acquired
virtues have concordance with all those
fruits. Therefore the superior fruit is man
moved in his substance, and above man there is
another superior fruit, to which all
fruits relate by reason of the end,
namely to know, remember, and love God, to honor,
and to serve Him. May it please
Him that His people may be
able to gather
this fruit.

On the Angelic Tree.

S U M M A R Y.

[Decorative initial A] HIS Angelic Tree
is concerned with the
Angelic nature. And
similarly to other trees,
it is divided into seven parts, namely
into roots, trunk, branches,
boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

The roots are goodness, greatness,
and other general principles, with the
exception of contrariety.
The trunk is spiritual substance.
The branches are three virtues,
namely memory, intellect, and will.
The boughs are the correlatives of the said
virtues.
The leaves are spiritual accidents.
The flowers are Angelic acts.
The fruit is to love and praise
God, and to serve Him.

On the Angelic Tree.

[Illuminated initial A]HE Angelic Tree is divided
into seven parts, namely
into roots, trunk,
branches, boughs, leaves,
flowers, and fruits. And it is a spiritual
tree, which cannot be seen or touched,
and which has no corporeal form,
nor is it produced from something else, but
from nothing. And it has many other conditions
which trees that are of a corporeal nature
do not have.

On the Roots of the Angelic Tree.

[Illuminated initial B]OODNESS, magnitude, duration, and other
forms, with the exception of contrariety, are
the roots of the Angelic Tree, from which
the Angelic Tree is constituted, just as
a human being is constituted from soul and
body. And thus the tree passes into a third
number above the roots, which re-

258        The Angelic Tree.

remain its parts; just as man, who is
in the third number, as has been said. The good-
ness of the Angel is produced from nothing, and
is produced in particularity, and not from
generality, namely from general good-
ness. Therefore the Angel is its own
species, since it is of one goodness, which
is not from another goodness. The same is true of
its magnitude, and its other parts,
which thus multiply and constitute one spe-
cies, just as one substance, one essence, and one
individual subject, which are the Angel. There-
fore the Angel is a simpler creature than
another. The goodness of the Angel is produced in
magnitude, therefore it is great: and in
duration, therefore it endures, and in po-
wer, therefore it has power: and in
wisdom, and therefore it is the reason that wis-
dom is good: and in will, therefore
it is lovable: and in virtue, and therefore it is
virtuous: and in truth, therefore it is tru-
e, and in glory; and therefore the Angel has rest
in goodness: and in concordance without
contrariety, therefore it is good and incorruptible:
and in the beginning, therefore it is originated
in time: and in the middle, therefore its act of making good is
in the middle, which is between the good-making
principle and the good-receivable principle, which are of its essen-
ce: and because it is produced in difference,
the good-making principle, the good-receivable principle,
and the act of making good remain distinct: and because good-
ness is produced in the end, it is the reason for making
good: and because it is produced in
superiority, it is produced substantially,
since it is so that a substance is greater,
and has more of entity than an accident,
and because it is produced in equality,
its concrete elements are equal by
essence: and because it is produced in inferi-
ority, it contains within itself accidents, which
are its instruments and garments.
And what we have said about goodness, can be
said about magnitude, duration, and
others. The Angel is produced from these
roots, which we have mentioned, and they themselves
are produced from nothing, and because some
are produced in others, the Angel is constituted
from them. Therefore the Angel is
naturally occasioned to perform
operations similar to its roots, name-
ly, good operations by reason of good-
ness, and great operations by reason of magni-
tude, and durable operations by reason of duration: and
so forth for the others. And that the operations are
more numerous, because the angel is constitu-
ted from many things, which are for it rea-
sons for the many operations which
the good Angel performs. And the malignant
angel acts by the contrary, so that
it perverts its natural goodness,
so that it is accidentally a reason for evil, and its
magnitude [is a reason] for great evil. Just as an
injurious and wicked King, who perverts his great
power in doing great evils, great
injustices, great vanities, and many other vices.
And this kind of contrariety of interior forms,
and exterior operations is the bond,
with which the evil angel is obstinate,
captured and bound, so that it cannot do
good, and is licensed to do evil.

Concerning the Trunk of the Angelic Tree.

[Illuminated initial S]PIRITUAL substance which has no
inclination towards a body,
is the trunk of the angelic
tree. For the trunk is called an ag-
gregation of roots which multiply the third,
with each root extended into another:
just as goodness, which is extended
in magnitude and in duration, inasmuch
as magnitude is entirely good,
and duration likewise. And the same [is true] of mag-
nitude extended in goodness, and in
duration, inasmuch as they are
great by magnitude. And the same is true of

duration, inasmuch as magnitude and goodness are durable through duration. And through these extensions and mixtures, a multiplication occurs, which is the trunk, which is good through goodness, great through magnitude, lasting through duration, and so on for the rest. Because goodness comes to the trunk as bonifying and bonifiable, and magnitude as magnifying and magnifiable: and so for the other roots, the trunk is a substance composed of spiritual forms and spiritual matters, and under one general form and general matter, because the general form is constituted of bonifying capacity, magnifying capacity, and other forms: and the general matter is constituted of bonifiable capacity, magnifiable capacity, and the others. And the conjunction of the general form and general matter is constituted by the real and essential acts of making good, making great, and the other acts which are parts of the substance. The trunk is a substance, because it underlies each of its parts, which subsist in it. Just as the body of Martin, which is called a substance because it stands under accidents. And according as the angel's trunk is touched, so it responds with its parts, which are its principles for responding. Just as if the will loves some lovableness, goodness responds with making good, so that loving may be good, and magnitude responds with making great, so that it may be great, and duration with enduring, so that loving may be lasting: and so for the others. Such touches touch divine dignities, so that the Angel may touch itself and its parts, and so that it may respond to what touches it from outside according to the magnitude of goodness, duration, and so on for the others in loving divine dignities. And a good Angel does this, and a malignant Angel does the contrary. The Angel's trunk does not have

length, breadth, nor depth, because it is not of a corporeal nature, nor does it have a circular, quadrangular, or triangular figure: for just as it is separated from a corporeal surface, so it is separated from length, breadth, and depth, and from natural contrariety, and from hardness, softness, color, heat, humidity, coldness, and dryness, it is also separated from heaviness and lightness, and also separated from vegetation, sense, and imagination. And the extension of its parts extends itself without place, really, with some parts existing within others, just as imagination extends itself fantastically in imagining one small figure, and in imagining another large one: just as Martin who imagines a horse, and afterwards imagines a great mountain. And the same is true of loving, which spiritually extends itself in loving one person more than another, or one woman more than another: and so for other things similar to these.

& by minority, lesser than innate species, which by majority are greater, about which it has been said. And in this passage it is recognized how Angels acquire merit in receiving objects, and become just, charitable, holy, and virtuous. And malignant Angels become the contrary, because they receive objects against the natures of their first principles. A benevolent Angel does not have an investigative intellect with doubt, but with affirmation or negation. Just as Saint Michael, who does not doubt whether Martin is just or unjust: because in Martin's conditions he attains the truth of his goodness and malice as quickly as wax impressions attain the likenesses of the letters of a seal: but demons do not do this, because their intellect is weak and deviated from its end, therefore it first begins to doubt before affirming or denying whether Martin is good or bad.

De Ramis arboris Angelicalis.

<span style="font-size: 2em; float: left; margin-right: 0.2em;">M</span>emorative, memorable, and to remember are one branch of memory: intellective, intelligible, and to understand are another branch, which is of the intellect: and volitive, volible, and to will are another branch, which is of the will. And thus there are three branches: just as there are three powers: and thus the branches mix themselves in receiving objects: just as the branches mix themselves in those objectifications: just as the memory, intellect, and will of Saint Michael, which mix themselves in receiving some object, recalled, understood, and loved, by reason of which mixing, the memorative, intellective, and volitive, the memorable, intelligible, and lovable, to recall, to understand, and to love, mix themselves. Just as memorative, memorable, and to remember are one branch of memory: so bonificative, bonifiable, and to bonify are another branch of goodness, which is contained in the branch of memory. And the same for magnificative, magnifiable, and to magnify, which are one branch of magnitude, which is contained in memory. And the same is true for the branch of duration, power, virtue, etc. Also, bonificative, bonifiable, and to bonify are a branch of goodness, which is contained in the intellect, whose branch contains within itself a branch of goodness, so that its branch may be good. And the same branch of goodness consists in the branch of will, so that there is one branch of goodness in itself, and it is distinct in the branches by distinct properties, namely by memory, intellect, and will. And in this passage it is recognized how one branch is by essence, and multiple by operations distinct from each other. The branch of memory is of the essence of memory, and the memorable, which pertains to the essence of the branch of intellect, is different from the memorable, which pertains to the branch of memory. And both memorabilities are different, insofar as the difference of the branches participates in the unity of essence, insofar as they are of one and the same goodness, one and the same magnitude. And the same is true for the lovability of the branch of will, and for the lovability of the branch of memory, and intellect, and the same for intelligibility. And in this passage it is recognized that the Angel is created in the likeness of the supreme Trinity, and unity of essence. A good Angel understands itself, and understands itself in its intelligibility, which is called the possible intellect. And it understands with its intellectivity, which is called the agent intellect, and to understand is from.

[Column 1]

duration, which duration is quantifiable inasmuch as it has a beginning, but is not quantifiable inasmuch as the Angelic substance will endure eternally. Therefore, the quantity at its beginning is a measure of time, because it was originated in time. And by this measure are measured the parts of the Angel and its substance, without a corporeal subject and not extended in length, breadth, and depth, just like the duration of the substance, which does not extend corporally into eternity. And in this passage, the extension of spiritual quantity is recognized: just as goodness extends itself eternally in magnitude, so it extends itself in eternal duration. According to numerical quantity, there are more Angels, and it is signified that there are more of them than humans, inasmuch as their substance is more similar to God than the substance of humans, since God is a spiritual substance, and an Angel is similar, and man is composed of corporeal and spiritual substance. Hence, since there is magnitude in God, and similarly in an Angel and in man: it is necessary that the magnitude of God has greater concordance with the magnitude of an Angel than with the magnitude of man: since there is greater concordance between one spiritual substance and another, than between one spiritual substance and another corporeal one. Therefore, by reason of the greater concordance (as has been said), it is signified that Angels are in greater number than humans, and also that their number is odd: so that it may be more similar to the Most Blessed Trinity of God. It is necessary that the quantity of Angels be in a ternary number, namely in greaterness, equality, and lesser-ness, without which their numerical quantity would not be perfect. Therefore, there are some Angels who are greater in the magnitude of goodness,

[Column 2]

power, wisdom, and will, than other Angels. And these are closer to God, nor do they have an office, but only contemplate God. And there are other Angels, who are lesser in the magnitude of goodness, power, wisdom, and will, who have the office of administering to humans below, so that they may guard them from demons, and lead them to virtues, and keep them away from vices. There is another mode of orders of Angels, who are in the middle: who equally have the office of administering to inferior Angels through the influence they receive from superior Angels. And these are those who perform embassies, and revelations, and prophecies. And from these three hierarchies of Angels, nine orders are multiplied to signify the seven planets and the eighth sphere, and the trunk of the elemental tree. For if God placed corporeal substances in order, it is certainly necessary that He placed spiritual substances in order, and in that number in which corporeal and spiritual substances have greater concordance. Also, the subjects of order are nine, namely God, Angels, heaven, soul, imaginative, sensitive, vegetative, elemental, and the creative power.

**Of the Quality of the Angelic Tree.**

Saint Michael is good by goodness, and is great by greatness, and thus is such by his special forms, by reason of which he is individuated in himself, and not from another: just as a knife and a nail, which are individuated in themselves, nevertheless are individuated from others, namely from a mass of iron: but this is not the case with Angels, because

--- Page 279 ---
Arbor angelicalis. 265

niam each one is such by its own proper individuality, not individuated from another substance. Also, it has two qualities from goodness: one is innate, and the other acquired. That which is innate is its part, from which it is constituted. The acquired is its goodness acquired by reason of which it has merit, and this is the quality appropriated to it, which God confirmed in it, because it serves Him freely. Fire has its heat in diverse substances, namely in the substance of pepper, garlic, and fennel, and heat is one quality in itself, and is several qualities in others: just as one is the quality of pepper, another of garlic, and another of fennel. Therefore, it is one and the same quality distinguished by something else and not by itself, namely by the distinction of substances, which are different. According to this manner, the quality of Saint Michael, and likewise of any other Angel, is not distinguished, but in another way, namely that Saint Michael is good, inasmuch as he loves God, and inasmuch as he understands Him, and inasmuch as he remembers Him, and likewise inasmuch as he remembers, understands, and loves Saint Gabriel or himself: and so of others, and according to how his remembering, understanding, and loving have nobler objects, goodness extends itself to remember, understand, and love: just as the heat of fire which extends itself more in heating air than water. Fire which heats pepper more than fennel, in that greater heating puts more heat than in the lesser: because pepper can receive more than fennel. And the same is true of remembering, understanding, and loving, which Angels have in the objects they receive, in which they place more or less, according as certain objects are more disposed to be remembered, understood, and loved than others. And in

this passage it is known how Angels do not use their qualities in the way that humans use their qualities in this life: like a greedy man who remembers more and more often the magnitude of treasure, than the magnitude of understanding good, loving good, and remembering good, which are made good by charity, justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance, hope, and faith. Saint Michael the Archangel does not use his qualities in vain, as humans use them in vain in this life. For Saint Michael understands that Saint Gabriel is, nor does he say that Saint Gabriel is not Saint Raphael, nor does he say that Martin's horse is not Peter's horse, because he accepts an object only according to what it is, but after he understands that Saint Gabriel is, and Saint Raphael likewise, it would be superfluous for him if he were to say that Saint Gabriel is not Saint Raphael, which indeed would be a vice against virtue for him, and a smallness against the magnitude of goodness, intellect, memory, will, truth, and glory. And in this passage it is known how Angels have rest in the truths they attain. The sun does not shine more in one time than in another in itself: but its light multiplies its likeness more in one time than in another: just as a day is clearer in the third hour than in the morning, and at midday than in the third hour: in a similar way, an Angel is not better nor wiser in one time than in another, but his knowing and his goodness are in a greater magnitude of goodness by receiving one object than another, and this happens through the greater magnitude of goodness which is in some objects, and through the lesser magnitude of
Ll

--- Page 280 ---
266 The Angelic Tree.

of magnitude and goodness, which is in other objects. And in this step it is understood how an Angel, with one and the same quality, can be greater or lesser in goodness through another, its goodness always remaining under a certain determined quantity. And this step is a way to know more natural secrets of proper qualities, and appropriated qualities, which insofar as they are proper qualities, do not put more or less of themselves in apprehending objects: but insofar as they are appropriated qualities. Therefore, there is a difference between innate and generated species, which indeed, being generated, are attracted from objects, and multiplied from them.

Concerning the Relation of Angels.

IN Angels there is an interior and an exterior relation, and from interior and exterior things. The relation which is interior, is as in goodness, in which are the relatives: that which makes good, that which can be made good, and to make good; and in its magnitude: that which magnifies, that which can be magnified, and to magnify. And that which magnifies, magnifies its magnifiable aspect, by magnifying its own goodness, which is magnifiable: just as magnitude, which is capable of being made good. And the same concerning duration and other things, which relatively give their similarities to one another. This relation is within the substance of the Angel, and is one of its parts. There is also another relation, which is internal and external, according to which Angels apprehend objects. As Saint Michael who is intelligent, and Saint Gabriel intelligible. Therefore, it is necessary that if something is intelligent, it must be intelligible, and to understand, and vice versa. And this relation is necessary in Angels, so that it may be in the magnitude of goodness, duration, power, etc. And in this step is known the privilege, and excellent virtue, and nobility which Angels have above men, because many things are intelligible to Martin, which he himself does not understand. It is also known how Angels apprehend the truths of corporeal substances, although they do not have eyes, nor any of the other senses, but they apprehend those truths through intellect, because they are intelligible, and because benign Angels are intelligent with a magnitude of goodness, duration, etc.

Concerning the Action and Passion of Angels.

Action and Passion are in Angels in two ways: one way is internal, and the other external. That which is internal is substantial in one way, and accidental in another: it is substantial on the part of form and matter, from which the substance of the Angel is constituted, as was said in the main body [of the work]. It is accidental, insofar as one form gives its similarity to another form: as the goodness of Saint Michael, which gives its similarity to his magnitude. And insofar as it gives it, it is an active form, and insofar as magnitude receives it, it is a passive form. Action and passion which are internal and external, are, insofar as Saint Gabriel is understood, loved and recollected by Saint Michael, and insofar as Saint Michael receives pleasure in recollecting, understanding and loving Saint Gabriel. And the same is true for malignant Angels, who have action in tormenting men, and in tempting them, according as it is permitted to them by divine justice; they also have passion in tormenting and tempting them.

--- Page 281 ---
**The Angelic Tree. 267**

**On the Habits of Angels.**

In every Angel there are three general habits, which are its branches. Therefore, just as if in Martin there were the habit of grammar, logic, and rhetoric: so every Angel has the habit of recollecting, understanding, and loving: but an Angel has nobler habits than Martin, because it continually uses its particulars, which are under the habit, to the end that the habits may be in magnitude of goodness, duration, power, etc. And if Martin uses grammar, he does not use logic, nor rhetoric, nor does he at one time use all the particulars that stand under the habit of grammar. And in this passage it is recognized that the habits of Angels are great, and each habit and its parts correspond to one another at the same time. Therefore it is recognized that good Angels have great glory, and consequently the punishment that evil Angels have, whose habit corresponds with their particulars in such a way in contrariety of nature, just as the habits of good Angels do with their particulars in natural concordance. There are also other acquired meritorious habits: such as the habit of justice and charity in Saint Michael, which justice is indeed habituated by goodness, inasmuch as it is good, and concerning charity, inasmuch as it is lovable: And the same is true of the habits of evil Angels: just as Lucifer is habituated by injury and cruelty, and just as his injury is from malice. And so concerning other habits acquired through faults and sins.

**On the Arrangement of Angels.**

The substance of an Angel is arranged according to the arrangement of a tree, namely according to the arrangement of roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits. And the roots are arranged some in others, just as goodness clothed in magnitude, which inasmuch as it is great through magnitude, consists in magnitude, and conversely inasmuch as magnitude is in goodness, because it is good through goodness, And the same is true of the arrangement of the trunk, which is arranged in its parts. And branches similarly, and so concerning the other natural arrangements of the tree. In the Empyrean heaven, Angels are arranged, as was said in the chapter on quantity. And in a similar manner they are arranged concerning the arrangement of object and act, one Angel being an object to another Angel with magnitude of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, and others. And in this passage it is recognized that great is the glory of good Angels, and the punishment of evil ones, whose arrangement in hell is in the greater magnitude of malice, wrath, vices, and natural instincts. And the same is true in equality and minority.

**On the Time of Angels.**

An Angel is originated, inasmuch as it is created, and inasmuch as it is originated outside eternity: it is originated in time, since it is so that everything that exists must be in eternity or in time, and the time in which the Angel is originated, which time indeed requires corporeal motion, is not a part of the Angel, which is a spiritual substance, but in time it is so originated, just as it is placed in Ll 2

any place without occupying the place. Therefore,
an Angel does not require successive
motion in time according to its

its nature, the motion of an Angel, which would be
