**On the Places of Angels.**

[Large initial L] We consider place in Angels in two ways:
there is one place which is within, and another without.
That which is within is like Saint Michael, who is
spiritually placed within himself, just as
the whole in its parts, and the parts in its
whole, and one part in another: just as the goodness
of Saint Michael in his magnitude,
and magnitude in goodness, and roots
in the trunk, and the trunk in the roots. And
this kind of placement which is within
does not require an external surface, which might be
among the conditions of a place that
contains corporeal substances within itself. Therefore, the sub-
stance of an Angel is in a place above the
nature of place, inasmuch as it does not occupy that
place in which it is. Just as the substance of an
Angel moved from one place to another, which
does not exhibit in its motion the succession
of the first nor the last, nor of future
and past time, which are distinct from the present,

[Column 2]

therefore several Angelic substances
can be in the same place without
occupying the place: just as they can be in
time and in motion without the succession of
first and last parts, which are
in the motion of a heavy body, in which its head is
first in motion, and its feet are
last. And in this passage it is recognized
that Angels are in a place above the nature of
place, which place indeed is outside their
essence, and which is not a part of them.
There is another place of Angels which is ex-
ternal, just as the Empyrean heaven, in which
some Angels are in one place, others indeed
in another according as they are nearer
to Our Lord Jesus Christ. And the same
in hell, according as some malignant Angels are in
a greater abyss than others. There is also an-
other mode of place, which is external and internal
objectively, just as an object which Saint
Michael receives, in which he has to
recall, understand, and love, and that
place is external, inasmuch as it is not
of the essence of Saint Michael, but of
the essence of Saint Gabriel or another
Angel, and Saint Michael has his
presence within himself. And in this
passage it is recognized, that just as in poten-
tiality, nor in an object, does the occupation
of place occur: so spiritual substances do not mutually
occupy other spiritual substances by being in
one and the same place, nor by receiving
one and the same object, nor by recalling,
understanding, and loving the same object.

are of two kinds: some
are particular, and others universal.

to make good what has been acquired, to magnify, to endure,

[Column 1]
to enable, to understand, to love, to verify, to glorify, to differentiate, to harmonize, to originate, to mediate, to complete, to magnify, and to equalize, all these infinitives are acquired flowers: just as a righteous man who acquires righteousness, and a chaste man chastity. And the subjects of these flowers are the natural and essential infinitives of the branches, namely, natural remembering, understanding, and loving, adorned and clothed with those flowers, which are instruments for acquiring general flowers, which are the acquired and produced remembering, understanding, and loving in goodness, magnitude, duration, power, etc. This is to say that the infinitives of the branches are implicated and clothed in the acquired and produced flowers, so that Angels may be worthy of remembering, understanding, and loving God and His operations, and also that they may be worthy of being remembered, understood, and loved by our Lord God, and glorified by Him. And in this passage it is known how benign Angels attain God face to face fixedly and without mediation, remembering, understanding, and loving Him, praising and blessing Him, and receiving glory from Him, the Blessed One. The Seraphim understands God, and flowers aid its understanding; and inasmuch as it understands God as good, the flower makes its understanding good; and inasmuch as it understands Him as great, the flower of magnitude makes its understanding great; and because understanding endures, the flower of duration aids the perseverance of understanding; and so that it can understand God without mediation, the power given to aid understanding helps; and the will loves that aid, which is the understanding of the Seraphim, with the acquired power to make good, to magnify, to make endure, to enable; and the same applies to other flowers, therefore the will rests in understanding.

[Column 2]
For as much as understanding ascends above through the aid of flowers, so much does the loving of the will ascend, and it stands fixed in the beloved. And just as understanding is aided in ascending through flowers, so loving is aided in ascending through flowers. And in the ascent of loving itself, understanding has rest, because they ascend equally to the object, and are equally clothed and adorned with flowers. And the same follows for remembering, which ascends to the remembered with the aid of flowers, to such an extent that God is remembered, understood, and loved with all flowers through the branches of the Angel. And just as the Sun draws up the warmth of the dew, which ascends above with the aid of the sun, so the goodness of God draws up and causes to ascend higher the goodness of the memory, intellect, and will of the Seraphim, namely, in remembering, understanding, and loving. And the same is true for the magnitude of God, and for His dignities, and thus the higher dignities and lower flowers correspond to each other in the ascensions of the acts of the branches. And this kind of correspondence and ascension is very pleasing to understand, and if he who understands it well commits any offense against God, he is worthy of great punishment. The Seraphim understanding God, so highly are the dignities of God an exemplar for the understanding itself of the Seraphim. And the same is true for the remembering and loving of the Seraphim and its other flowers. And thus it attains God in two ways, namely, naturally, and supernaturally. Naturally, according to its primary principles, of which are its trunk, its branches, and its boughs: just as fire naturally heats the air, and the sun naturally illuminates the moon, and this kind of nature is licensed by the merit of the flowers. And it attains above its nature, inasmuch as God causes the acts of the branches and flowers to ascend.

Concerning the Aeternal Tree.

S U M M A R Y.

THE Aeternal Tree is divided into seven parts,
namely into roots, trunk,

branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and
fruits.

The roots are merits concerning general principles.

The trunk is duration.

The branches are Paradise, and
Hell.

The boughs are retributions.
The leaves are accidents.
The flowers are the acts of the glorified,
or of the condemned.
The fruits are the fulfillments of
ends.

Concerning the Eternal Tree.

[Large decorative initial P] Y another life we con-
sider the eternal tree,
which is divided into
roots, trunk,
branches, boughs, leaves,
flowers, and fruits. By roots we under-
stand merits, which come through second-
ary intentions, which are made by means of
artificial works under the aspect of first
principles, which are roots: just as
merits acquired through goodness, great-
ness, perseverance, power,
etc. also through the branches of the tree
of humanity, and of Angels, and through the
moral tree: because concerning all
these it is necessary to give judgment and rea-
sons, so that the end may be in the first
principles. Blessed Peter who is just,
and the same concerning the Seraphim, is good through
his own

his justice, which is good under the aspect of goodness. Therefore, it is necessary that he be rewarded with good; and because his justice is great, it is necessary that he be rewarded with great good; and because his justice was durable in this life, it is necessary that it be durable in the next: and similarly for other forms, namely that through good power he be rewarded with good made possible, and through good understanding he be rewarded with good understood, and for good loving with good loved, and through virtuous loving with virtuous loved, and for good truth with true good, and for glorious loving with glorious loved; and the same for concordance, difference, beginning, middle, and end, greaterness and equality. And these acquired forms are the roots of the tree, and are meritorious forms, namely the merit of good with good, and the merit of great with great, and so on for the rest. Muhammad, and likewise Lucifer, was unjust and a false Saracen, and because his injury, luxury, and sect were evil, it is necessary that he be rewarded with evil for evil; and because he did great evil in that he led many men into error, it is necessary that his reward be great in punishment; and because their evil endured and endures, it is necessary that the remuneration in punishment endure; and the same applies to the other forms. And these acquired faults are roots and bad merits. The same follows for the mechanic who does bad work, with which he deceives people. And the same applies to the bad judge who gives false judgment, and to the avaricious rich man who obstructs the purpose of his wealth, which he takes from the poor who are in need of that wealth; and so for others similar to these. Just as the substance of an orchard and a horse, and the same applies to other natural substances, are full of real forms, and nature does not

[Column 2]

tolerate them being empty: so the justice of God does not tolerate that any works done by men and by angels, in acting, in thinking, and in other ways in which works can be done, be forgotten at the end of judgment: because the justice of God is great, by reason of which it is necessary that the subject of judgment be great. And in this passage it is recognized that sinful men who have long persevered in sin, or sins, from which many evils have followed among their followers, will have to give account for many things on the day of judgment. And to consider this passage is very terrifying for sinful men.

*On the Trunk of the Eternal Tree.*

By the Eternal Trunk we understand the duration of good merits, and of evil ones, and of great ones, and of small ones, and of those which have been acquired through great power of goodness, or great evil, or small understanding, great lovingness, or small, and great hatred, or small, and great virtue, or small, great vice, or small: and so for the rest. Wherefore all forms of the trunk, which are its roots, constitute one duration of merits and faults, which will have no end, which duration we call the eternal trunk, which will always endure, so that the justice of God may have a subject in which it can judge. In this life are the works of men: first in the beginning, afterwards in the middle, and finally at the end, when they die; and after the end they cannot cease to be, because then the end would not be what it is: just as Martin would not be what he is without a head; therefore, works remain eternal at the end in such a way:

*Concerning the Branches of the Eternal Tree.*

[Decorative initial D] N TWO ways we consider
the branches of the eternal tree,
in one way we understand para-
dise, in another way we understand hell.
And we understand paradise to be in
the Empyrean heaven which is above the firma-
ment, which is full of light, with
which light glorified bodies will be
clothed, which will shine as much as
that light and even more than the light
of the sun, which shines more in the sun than
in the moon, and thus there will be light from light.
And that light will eternally endure and
will be greater in some bodies,

[Right Column]

than in others, according as the me-
rits will be greater or lesser in
just men: wherefore just as there will eternally
be light from light, so will paradise
eternally belong to the saints according to
their merits, and it will be for the glory of God
by remembering, understanding, loving
and praising Him, He being blessed, giving Himself
objectively to eternal glorification
through goodness well, and through greatness
magnificently, and through duration
eternally, and through power power-
fully, through understanding intelligibly, through
love amiably, through virtue virtu-
ously, and through truth truly, and through
glory gloriously, and through the end
completely. Hell will be the second branch
of the eternal tree, and it will be in the abyss of the
earth, and in the greatest contrary of light and good-
ness, truth, the end of glory and amiability.
And according as the faults will be
greater, greater will be the punishments, magnifi-
cently, badly, eternally, intelligibly,
hatefully and despairingly, and in the emptiness
of all completeness. And it will be as
eternal in hell as the branch of paradise in the Empyrean heaven.

*Concerning the Boughs of the Eternal Tree.*

[Decorative initial D] HERE are two boughs of the eternal
tree, one is of the branch of para-
dise, the other is the branch of hell.
The bough of paradise is multiplied into
three boughs. One bough is of justice,
another indeed of grace, another is of passions.
The bough which is of justice is that
which renders good for good, and great for
great, and durable for durable, and so
for others. And the bough which is by grace
is that which gives more good than the me-
rit obtained for good, and more of great
good, and gives eternal duration through duration, and
so forth.

and likewise for other forms which multiply gifts, without which the Saints could not acquire everlasting glory. The third branch is of passions, namely, of retributions received in glory. In glory justly through justice, and everlastingly through grace, which remunerations the Saints receive from the supreme liberal judge without any deficiency. The infernal branch is multiplied into two branches, one is of justice and the other is of passions. The branch of justice gives evil for evil, and great evil of punishment for great evil of guilt, and gives everlasting evil, so that it can everlastingly punish sinners who have erred against eternity, which is infinite in duration, and which produces its likeness in everlastingness with the greatness of goodness in the good, and with the greatness of evil in the evil, and with the greatness of duration in the good, and with the greatness of duration in the evil, which greatness of duration is everlastingness, which is some likeness in the duration of eternity, inasmuch as it is without end. Which everlastingness must exist by necessity, so that eternity can produce so much of its likeness, just as divine goodness in goodness and divine greatness in greatness, and likewise for others,

Concerning the Leaves of the Everlasting Tree. And first concerning quantity.

EVERLASTINGNESS is thus in quantity: like a line which would be terminated at the beginning and not at the end: as in the form of fire, which has a multiplicative power, according as combustible and heatable matter can suffice, for fire would always grow and endure in burning, if wood were always multiplied. Therefore, the quantity of everlastingness is in time

[Column 2]

begun by reason of merits and faults, which had a beginning in time, and is not terminated at the end, because the reward of the just endures, and the punishment of the unjust, and the justificatory power of the superior judge; fire does not have this power, because it cannot make wood endure by its power, because it is against the wood which it burns, but the superior justificatory power makes the justifiability of the just endure by its power in a continuous everlasting quantity, because with them it has concordance in the greatness of goodness and eternity, and makes the punishability of the unjust endure, because its judging has concordance with the greatness of goodness, eternity, etc. Just as the continuous quantity of goodness is sustained in discrete quantities, which are of the essence of the continuous, namely, the bonifying, the bonifiable, and to bonify, which are of the essence of goodness, so the continuous quantity of everlastingness has discrete quantities, in which it is sustained, namely, the quantities of men and Angels, in which is sustained the everlasting continuous quantity of glorifiability in the glorious, and of tormentability in the damned, by reason of which sustenance it is necessary that there be discrete everlasting quantities, so that the continuous everlasting quantity can have everlasting subjects, in which it can be sustained: just as the greatness of goodness, whose continuous quantity has the necessity that it should have discrete quantities in which it can be sustained, so that the essence of goodness may be durable.

Concerning the Qualities of the Everlasting Tree.

THE QUALITIES of the everlasting tree are acquired likenesses, and likenesses of real forms in the good,

*On the Relation of the Eternal Tree.*

According to the natural course, as long as substance endures, the relation of form and matter always endures, such that form is the agent and matter the patient. In a similar way it is with eternal relations, since as long as blessed Peter endures as good through justice, the remunerative, the remunerable, and the act of remunerating in doing good endure, in which they are related by reason of the good subject, which is blessed Peter. And if the relation were to fail, it would be injurious to the subject, and in that subject would endure the relation of contraries, namely the injurious, and through goodness the remunerable, the capable of being made good, and the capable of being glorified. And this is impossible, that such a duration would exist in eternity, nor outside eternity, since the justifying (principle) above is in the magnitude of goodness, eternity, etc. Therefore there is a superior eternal relation between the justifying (principle), the justifiable, and in good the remunerative, the remunerable. Judas Iscariot was evil through malice, in which malice began the relation of the maleficative and the maleficable, in doing evil, which was the sin of Judas, and the subject of the relation; whence, Judas having died in malice, the subject of the relation remained, namely sin converted into doing evil. Therefore it was necessary that after the death of Judas, the subject of the relation of the punitive and the punible, sustained in punishing, should remain in eternity. Whatever God created, was created for a supreme end, so that it might be created with the magnitude of goodness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, and end. Therefore the whole world was created by reason of supreme recollectability, intelligibility, and amiability. Therefore it is necessary that created things which are the memorative, the intellective, and the amative, respond in eternity to supreme objectabilities, so that they relate in remembering, understanding, and loving in eternity, being sustained, without which the objectabilities would fail the superior magnitude of goodness of created objectivities, by which the magnitude of the end, for the sake of which they were created, would fail, and thus there would be a contradiction in the relation of active and passive forms, which contradiction is impossible. Therefore it is necessary that there be concordance in the eternity of the relations which are aforesaid. And the same follows concerning contrary relations: such as Lucifer, contrary to supreme objectabilities with evil recollective, intellective, and amative (powers).

*On the Actions, & Passions*
*of the Eternal Tree.*

In the glorified body of blessed Peter, actions and passions will stand in concordance without contradiction: just as fire which will heat air, water, and earth, so in natural concordance: just as there is concordance of form and matter, which relate to constitute substance, in which they rest. Therefore the action and passion which will be in the body of blessed Peter will be without corruption and generation, and will be as eternal as a circle, which is without discrete quantity. And the same will be true of spiritual actions and passions in the just: such as the will of blessed Peter, which will be eternally rewarded in its amativity and amiability with the magnitude of goodness and love. The body of Judas Iscariot will be eternally infernated and subject to many a-
Mm 3

--- Page 292 ---
278 The Eternal Tree.

[Column 1]

...actions and passions with a contrariety of qualities without any concordance: just as fire heats the air, from which heating the air will have a passion, because the concordance which they used to have in this life will be removed. Likewise, fire will heat water, and water will cool fire, with the contrariety of both, heat enduring in the fire and in the water; and in the fire and water, coldness will endure by reason of judgment and its subject. And the same applies to the contrariety of other elements, and thus in them, concordance cannot endure, so that the punishment may be simple, and contrariety will endure in eternity, so that judgment may have a subject in which it can endure. And this subject, which has eternal actions and passions, is neither generable nor corruptible. For just as a stone ascends artificially against its weight, so above the natural course, eternal contrarieties of actions and passions will endure in the bodies of the damned. And the same will be true in spiritual actions and passions: just as the will of Judas Iscariot, which will have a passion in loving and in hating by reason of the action which his intellect will have in understanding, that the will will never have what it desires, and eternally will have what it does not want. And the same follows concerning the passion which the intellect will have in that which the will desires, and it will hate the rest which its intellect does not want, and it will love the deprivation of that end. And these actions and passions are so great that no one could think or narrate them,

*On the Habits of the Eternal Tree.*

[Large initial H] Eternal habits are two according to the branches of the tree, namely

[Column 2]

that some are habits which the saints have and will have of glory: and others are those which the damned have and will have of sorrow. The saints have habits of joy, and the damned have habits of sorrow, just as blessed Peter has in habit such joy, as justice and holiness: and just as Judas Iscariot who has in habit eternally such sorrow, as injury and punishment. The understanding of blessed Peter is habituated in eternity, which he understands in such a way as he understands his intellectivity, which understands the intelligibility of eternity, and he understands it under the habit of the goodness of glory and charity. And the same is true of Judas's understanding, which is habituated in the contrary in his eternity, his intellectivity understanding the intelligibility of eternity under the reason of malice, punishment, and hatefulness, and the same follows concerning the habit of memory. And these habits are instruments by which the Saints have glory eternally, and the damned punishment. Judas has the habit of conscience and despair with the habit of sorrow, and with the habit of eternal understanding, and of memory likewise, to such an extent that all habits will be so appropriated to eternity, as the light of the sun without corruption of light and substance. And this passage is very horrible for sinners to consider, and on the contrary, it is very pleasing and delightful for the Saints under the reason of holy consideration habituated by charity, glory, justice, and goodness.

*On the Arrangement of the Eternal Tree.*

[Large initial I] In the Empyrean heaven are Angels before the Lord Jesus Christ, arranged and ordered according to the magnitude of goodness, justice, and charity, and the same is true of holy men. And of this kind

--- Page 293 ---
**Arbor æuiternalis. 279**

And this kind of arrangement will be eternal. And in hell, demons are eternally arranged, and the same will be true for damned humans, who will stand thus arranged in fire, some above others, just as on high mountains some stones are above others. And the same will be true for those who will stand arranged in boiling water, like fish in the sea. And this kind of arrangement will be real, inasmuch as the substances subject to it, which will be eternally understood, will be as necessary as the real arrangement itself. And this passage is very horrible and fearsome, which men should consider more often, so that they might have fear, and resist sins.

**On the Time of the Eternal Tree.**

When God created the world, He created it with a great measure of goodness, wisdom, and will, and His wisdom comprehended a certain number of creatable humans. And His will loved that comprehension of the number, and goodness made that number good. Therefore, humans were created under a certain foreseen number, before they were created by the wisdom of God. It is necessary, therefore, that the motion of the firmament, which exists for generation and corruption in the lower regions to generate and produce human bodies, should have an end and a stop, beyond which end there will be no motion of the elements nor of the firmament. Therefore, the production of the number of humans will be complete, to such an extent that there will be no natural bodily motion in the firmament nor in the elements. Therefore, time will not have a subject, in which there can be a multiplication of years and months, days, and hours, and moments. Therefore, there will be no time in the succession of moved substances from one time to another. Therefore, there will be eternal time without motion. A fish moving in water moves from one place to another: but not from one water to another, since water is one in itself by essence, so that the fish makes no difference to the essence of the water. Similarly, glorified bodies in glory will move in time from one place to another, each body moving according to its will under the aspect of goodness and pleasure, so that in time there will be no differentiation in itself through any succession of motion: because neither the hour nor motion will multiply themselves from one time to another. Therefore, their motion will be in eternal time without succession of time: although there will be succession according to the motion of place, the body of the Saint moving from east to west, and from west to the Empyrean Heaven, and so to other places. Just as the motion of a glorified body will not multiply the hour, nor the moment, the day, nor the year in time, so the activity of the powers which will relate to glorification in remembering, understanding, and loving, hearing, and seeing will not multiply the hour, moment, day, nor year in time, and there will be succession from one object to another according to the magnitude of goodness, glory, and truth: just as there will be succession of motion of which it has been said. And this passage is pleasing to consider, and in it divine glory is signified to be eternal.

**On the Place of the Eternal Tree.**

The Saints of glory will move at will from one place to another, and in whatever place they are, they will have glory, so that the difference of one place and another may not consume eternal glory: which

*Concerning the Flowers of the Eternal Tree.*

**F**LOWERS of the eternal tree
are eternal glorifications: such
as glorification, doing good, enduring,
being able, understanding, loving, making virtuous,
to be glorified and clothed with all these ornaments.

*Concerning the Glorification of doing good.*

**G**LORIFICATION which is of doing good
in eternizing will be in the Saints under
the aspect of goodness, with goodness
existing as the reason for doing good, and glory to glorify

that doing good, so namely that the good-
making, the capable of being made good, and the act of doing
good will be full of glory, and the essence of good-
ness likewise, since it is so that its
complement are the good-making, the
capable of being made good, and the act of doing good, which com-

To glorify, which is of doing good, will help
to magnify, so that it may be great, which
indeed to magnify will be extended
through the whole good-making, the capable of being made good,
and the act of doing good, which indeed to
magnify could not be extended with-

for if eternizing and glorifying were lacking,
in that there would be diminishing, and
it could not be magnificently, which has
concordance with making greater.
To glorify, which is of doing good, helps
to endure, which extends itself into the good-

glorifying, so that they may be in eternity: for
inasmuch as the good-making endures,
it is necessary that the capable of being made good,
and the act of doing good endure, and vice versa. And through
this duration, glorifying endures: for
it is a great glory of the good-making,
that in eternizing and glorifying it can
have its capable of being made good, and its act of doing

in the capable of being made good, and the act of doing good. To glorify,

and from both possibilities, doing good can be,
and from doing good, and making possible,
which are in eternizing, eternal glorifying
follows; therefore there remain in eternity
the good-made product, the capable of being made good,
the glorified, and the capable of being glorified.

To understand helps to glorify,

To love will help glory, which is about making good: because the will of the blessed will desire that in its goodness there be eternally the one making good, the one capable of being made good, and the act of making good, and so it will be as it desires. And because in goodness that which the will desires will follow, glory will follow in its loving, from which glory there will be light for the intellect in making good. And thus there will be two lights eternally in glory, one light received from another light. And this step is very pleasing to consider. To make virtuous will help glory, which is about making good: because the goodness of virtue will eternally stand in the essential concretes of goodness: whence eternal glory will follow in making good, because it will be a great glory of goodness that it eternally has within itself the virtuous one making good, the virtuous one capable of being made good, and the virtuous act of making good. To verify will help glory, which will be about making good: because the truth of God will eternally place in the true the one making good, the one capable of being made good, and the act of making good of goodness. And from this, glory will follow in making good, because it will be a great glory to goodness that its concretes are eternally and truly in verifying the one making good, the one capable of being made good, and the act of making good. According to what has been shown, how other flowers help the flower of goodness, doctrine has been given, how one flower helps to have glory in eternizing: just as glory which will be about magnifying, which the flower helps

And just as we have given examples concerning goodness, so examples can be given concerning others. In the eternal tree there are flowers, which are contrary to those flowers of which it has been spoken. Indeed, these contrary flowers are eternal torments sustained in the damned, such as real torment, of goodness, of magnitude, of power, of intellect, of will, of virtue, and of truth, which are real and natural parts of the substance of the damned. And these flowers help each other to torment, so that the torment may be great.

**Concerning the Torment which is of loving itself.**

THE TORMENT which is of loving, will help to make evil, so that loving may be evil. Inasmuch as malice will extend itself into the loving subject, the lovable object, and the act of loving of the will, so that the loving subject, the lovable object, and the act of loving may be evil. The loving subject will be evil, inasmuch as it will love evil, and it will love that which it cannot have, and it will hate that which it will eternally have. And its lovable object will be evil, because the lovable object which it will love will by its nature be hateful. Therefore, loving will be an evil produced from the lover and the lovable object in eternizing and tormenting, because there will be great torment from the lover, the lovable object, and the act of loving existing eternally in making evil. Magnitude will help to torment, which will be about loving, because the loving subject will be great in loving injurious and great things, and in hating great things worthy of being loved. Therefore, the torment of loving itself will be great in eternizing, in which it will hate God, who is the most lovable object, and greater in the lovability of goodness, of eternity.

On the Fruit of the Eternal Tree.

The fruits of the eternal tree are the fulfillments of the ends of the real parts, from which are the substances of the Saints. Such as the fruit of goodness, and the fruit of greatness, duration, power, wisdom, will, glory, and truth. And the fruits of the damned are the privations of the fruits of the saved: such as the privation of the end of goodness, and the end of greatness, and the end of duration, and so forth for other privations. And all these fruits, and the fruits of the saved, are eternal, so constituted in eternity, just like the fruits of trees which are gathered in summer. And these eternal fruits are thus sown in this life, just like the fruits of plants which are sown in winter, so that in summer another fruit may be gathered and multiplied from them, which gathering and multiplication signify the gathering and multiplication of eternal fruits.

On the Fruit of Goodness.

The fruit of goodness consists in the fulfillment of the bonificative (that which makes good), the bonificable (that which can be made good), and the act of making good, which indeed fulfillment could not exist without eternity: for if the act of goodness were to fall into privation, there could not be the fulfillment of the bonificative, bonificable, and the act of making good: therefore, the fruit is gathered in eternity, in which there is no cessation nor idleness of the bonificative, bonificable, and the act of making good.
The fruit of greatness is the fulfillment of the magnificative (that which makes great), the magnificable (that which can be made great), and the act of making great, namely, that the magnificative may always be great in making great things great. And the same for the magnificable, made great in the great act of making great, which indeed act of making great may be so great that it contains no shadow of smallness, for if it contained it, it could not be the fulfillment of the magnificative, magnificable, and the act of making great. Therefore, it is necessary that their fulfillment be in eternity, and that it be gathered in it, to such an extent that at no time in the act of making great is there a shadow of diminishing, nor of smallness.
The fruit of duration cannot be gathered in the privation of itself, nor of its durificative (that which makes endure), durificable (that which can endure), nor its act of making endure: therefore, it is necessary that it be gathered in the end of all three of its concretes and of itself. This gathering cannot be of the partial duration of the glorified substance, except in eternity, in which the end of the glorified substance is gathered and sustained: just as color in substance, and heat in fire, and light in the sun.
The fruit of power is that it can eternally have in itself real concretes, and that it itself is the reason that goodness can exist, and greatness similarly: and so for the other parts of the glorified substance. Also, that through it each of the primary parts can have essential concretes in itself: just as goodness, which through the reason of power can have in itself the essential bonificative, bonificable, and the act of making good. Therefore, the fruit of power is gathered.

286      The Maternal Tree.

About the Maternal Tree.

S U M M A R Y.

[Decorative initial A] THE maternal tree concerns our Lady,
the Virgin Mary. And it is divided,
like other trees, into seven parts:
namely, into roots, trunk, branches,
boughs, leaves, flowers, & fruits.
The roots are the ultimate purposes of
regenerated humanity.
The trunk is the disposition of multiple
states.
The branches are two, namely, the divine
nature, & the human nature.
The boughs are hope, piety, advocacy,
&c.
The leaves are the nine general
accidents.
The flowers are the acts of our Lady's
dignities.
The fruit is the Lord Jesus
Christ.

                                                                    About the Tree

--- Page 301 ---
Arbor maternalis. 287

[Woodcut illustration of a tree with various circular fruits. At the top center is a figure of Christ. To the left is a figure labeled "Monachus." holding a scroll. To the right is a figure labeled "Raymundus." holding a scroll. In the top corners are labels "Gloria" and "Pœna."]

**Concerning the Maternal Tree.**

WE attribute this tree to
Our Lady Saint Ma-
ry, mother of the just and of sin-
ners; therefore we call it the maternal tree. And we divide it
into seven parts, like other
trees.

**Concerning the Roots of the Maternal Tree.**

THE roots of the maternal tree are
many, among which are the ends of
recreated men, who had been lost
by reason of original sin, who were to be re-
stored through the death of Jesus Christ, through
whom original sin was brought to an
end, as was said above in the
apostolical tree. Adam and his
                                        followers

--- Page 302 ---
288 The Maternal Tree.

[Column 1]
followers were created for glory, and because of original sin they were deviated from that glory: but it pleased the Son of God to assume human flesh, and the Son of God became man for our Lady, so that He might restore Adam and his descendants to the end for which He created them. Therefore, our Lady is the Mother of their end. She is Mother inasmuch as she is matter, because the Son of God assumed human flesh from her, so that He might restore the ends of the first humans to their original state. Therefore, our Lady is the mother of the end of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, blessed Peter and Paul, and also of all those cleansed from original sin, through our Lord Jesus Christ, her Son. The end of man is to remember, understand, and love, to honor, praise, bless, and serve God, and to have eternal glory in Him. Therefore, the end of man is very great in goodness, in magnitude, and in other primary forms. And because many men are recreated, our Lady is the Mother of many ends, which are the roots of her maternity. And in every root of man, our Lady is the Mother of many ends: just as in the root of Adam, in whom there are many partial ends: such as the end of his goodness and the end of his magnitude, and so concerning other corporal and spiritual ends. Therefore, the maternity of our Lady is great, since the ends are so many and so great in so many and so great men, wherefore such a mother, so great and so worthy to us, should be loved, remembered, praised, understood, honored, and served. According to what has been said in many places, man is the end of all corporal things, whose end was lost through original sin, and its loss was in the deviation of the end of men. And because the end of men to the pri-

[Column 2]
mary state returned through the recreation made by the Son of our Lady, the ends of celestial bodies, and of all elements, and of things made from elements, returned through that recreation to the end for which they were created. Therefore, our Lady is the Mother of all those ends: for if she were not, none of those ends would have returned, nor would they return to their primary state, and the Sun and Moon, stars, and fire, and other elements, orchards, and other plants, iron, and other metals, horses, and other animals would serve man in vain, inasmuch as man would be a sinner and disobedient to his Creator. Therefore, their ends had been lost, which are, that they might serve a just man, a friend, and a servant of God. But because our Lady is the Mother of recreation materially, she is the Mother of all those ends which are for serving man. Therefore, our Lady is the mother of a great maternity, inasmuch as the ends are many and of great necessity, utility, and virtue.

Of the Trunk of the Maternal Tree.

The TRUNK of the maternal tree is the maternity of the roots, as has been said. And the trunk is constituted from many things, inasmuch as it is a general habit, by reason of which all corporal ends can return to their pristine state. Therefore, when our Lady is touched by some particular end, the trunk, which is universal, responds to that particular touch, just as a whole responds to its parts. Therefore, the trunk is a habit of many touches and responses, which are natural according to the nature of the touches: just as Martin, who as a son of hope touches our Lady, our Lady responds to him as a mother of hope. And if he touches her with piety, she respon-

--- Page 303 ---
Arbor æuiternalis. 289

[Column 1]

responds to him Our Lady, as a mother
of piety, and so concerning other forms. Therefore,
by reason of the nature of touches and responses,
sinners find in Our Lady, in their necessities,
help and restorations. For such a
trunk, which is so general for so many
and such touches, and which immediately
responds to all with completeness,
ought to be held very dear, by loving it, remembering it,
understanding it, honoring it, and serving
it. It is also more general in the
magnitude of goodness, power, and
virtues, than the splendor of the sun, or the
heat of fire: because neither the sun nor
fire responds to the touch of hope, and piety,
charity, mercy, and forgiveness, to which
the maternity of Our Lady responds.
And because of this, Christians do wrong
who do not show the nobility of such a trunk
to infidels, who have no hope in Our
Lady nor knowledge of her goodness; indeed,
they deny and disparage and disbelieve
the excellent virtue and nobility,
in which God placed her as the mother
of all corporal creatures, inasmuch as
her son, with her, recreated all
corporal creatures (as has been said)
by his benignity.

About the Branches of the Maternal Tree.

[Large illuminated initial B] RANCHES of the maternal
tree are two, namely the
divine nature of Jesus Christ, and
the human nature. And Our Lady
is the mother of those branches inasmuch
as they came forth in the filiation which
was made in her from both aforementioned natures,
which filiation is indeed the Son, God-
man, who is Son of God by Divinity,
and Son of man by humanity:
and because both filiations are joined

[Column 2]

in one Son, the maternity of Our Lady
reaches both branches born
from her, in this, that one Son, God-
man, was born from her. From Our
Lady came forth the human branch with
the divine branch, which generated it
from the flesh and blood of Our Lady,
and generated it with the conception
of Our Lady, who consented to the generation.
Therefore, Our Lady is mother
in the incarnation materially as
regards the body of Our Lord Jesus
Christ, which was corporal matter, and
formally she was mother, inasmuch as she
loved and believed the conception, and thus
she was mother corporally and specially, and
materially, and formally. She was also
mother through a superior divine
form, which moved her spiritual
conception and corporal matter
to filiation. Therefore, the branches came
forth from Our Lady in a great
filiation of great maternity, and thus
great in the magnitude of goodness,
duration, power, wisdom, will,
virtue, and truth, which cannot
nor could be greater through Divinity
in humanity, nor through humanity
in Divinity, nor through the creator
in the creature. Therefore, the magnitude of the
branches corresponds to the magnitude of
maternity, and the magnitude of maternity
corresponds to them to such an extent that a
greater response cannot exist. Great
trees have great branches, and
according as the branches are great,
the shadows they make are great: in
which men shade themselves when
there is great heat. Therefore, all
men who have been born and
will be born, who are in a state of salvation,
shade themselves under the branches of maternity,
inasmuch as they are defended from the punishment
which fell upon the human species by reason
of original sin. Therefore, let the trunk be praised,
Oo &

--- Page 304 ---
290 Maternal Tree.

and blessed, from whom such great branches
emerge, under whose shadow so many and
so great men rest.

On the Branches of the Maternal Tree.

**M**ercy, hope, piety, advo-
cacy, humility, and virginity,
are the branches of the maternal tree.
Mercy is a branch of the maternal
tree, inasmuch as sinners find mer-
cy through Our Lady in her son who remits
sins: because Our Lady is the mother of
mercy, inasmuch as her Son, God-man,
is mercy. Whence,
inasmuch as there is great mercy
of the son, and maternity of mercy, mercy satis-
fies for great pardon, grace,
and gift to those who seek mercy.
Our Lady is the refuge
of sinners, and of those who need
to have virtues and temporal goods, and
who are in tribulations, and dan-
gers, and she is the refuge of those, inas-
much as they have hope in her, that she may
help them in their necessities: just as a
sinful man who is in the sin of lust
or avarice, or in another sin, who
has hope in Our Lady, that
she may help him to have chastity,
charity, or another virtue, which
he desires. Therefore the hope that Our
Lady has in her son, that he may give to sin-
ners what they ask of him, corresponds to the hope
of sinners, and so both hopes respond
to each other with a concordance of
magnitude, goodness, virtue,
and charity, by reason of which re-
sponse no one ought to weary themselves of
Our Lady, since hope is in her:
for if one were to weary themselves, Our
Lady would weary herself in her son with the mag-
nitude of hope, which is impossible:
and the same applies to others, who are poor in
temporal goods, who have hope
in Our Lady, that she may help them to live,
so that they may serve her son and herself.
Also a good woman, who has her son
sick, has hope in Our
Lady, that she may cure him. Likewise
a sailor, who is at sea in danger
of death, has hope in Our Lady,
that he may be able to come to a good port.
The piety that Our Lady has for
sinners, is one branch of the tree,
and it is a great branch: it is great, in-
asmuch as she has great piety.
Since it is so, that all the works of Our
Lady are great in magnitude
of goodness, wisdom, will,
virtue, and truth. It is also a great
branch because of the great necessi-
ty of men, for whom Our Lady
has piety, and who seek
help from Our Lady through piety,
and who have piety because of her love,
and thus both pieties correspond to each
other, namely the piety
of Our Lady, and the piety of men,
by reason of which response sinners
attain through Our Lady what
they desire. Likewise Angels
count the tears that men shed
then, when they ask Our Lady
to have pity on them.
Advocacy is a branch of this tree,
namely the advocacy that Our Lady
makes for sinners, when the justice
of her son wishes to punish them, and Our Lady
advocates with mercy, hope,
and piety, and with the love, which she has
for her son, and which she has for sin-
ners, and with the love, which they have
for her, and for her son, also with
the contrition, which they have for their
sins, and with the confession, which they
make, also with the satisfaction, which
they promise, and with several other
forms Our Lady forms her advo-
cacy

292 **Maternal Tree.**

which is as great as the goodness of the tree, and which is extended through all the qualities of the tree. And God has appropriated each of these qualities of the tree to maternity with such a magnitude of virtue and goodness, that He makes them mothers through recreation for all the good things and virtuous qualities of recreated and saved humans: just as the goodness of Saint Peter and his virtue, which are acquired qualities, and given by the grace of God, which are leaves through the recreation of acquired and given qualities from the maternal tree. And therefore the qualities of the maternal tree correspond to the qualities of saved humans: just as general qualities correspond to special qualities: such as the goodness of Our Lady which is general to the good things of saved humans. And in this passage it is recognized that Our Lady is worthy of all praise, and that she should be greatly praised and served by her people, since she is so good, so great, and so complete with all perfections that it belongs to her to complete all perfections which the qualities of recreated saved humans require.

**On the Relations of the maternal tree.**

Mother and son are related in creatures: for if there is a mother, there must be a son, and if there is a created son, there must be a mother, but outside of creatures there can be a son even if there is no mother, just as the Son of God has no mother insofar as He is God, and He places Himself in relation with a mother insofar as He is the Son of Man, which sonship and maternity indeed correspond to each other so well, magnificently, and univocally, as they correspond to each other relatively. Therefore, the response of this relation is in such a high degree that no other degree of relation can be so great in goodness, power, glory, virtue, love, and truth, existing as a degree of both created and uncreated relation: There is another degree of relation, which is between creature and creature, in a greater magnitude of goodness than any other created degree: such as the relation which is between Our Lady and her Son, a man, who is greater in goodness than all creatures: for all creatures exist on account of Him, who is the end and perfection of all. Therefore, the relation between Him and Our Lady is above all created relations: just as the Son is better than any other created son, even than all created sons. Hence it follows that the mother is greater, since she has a greater son than all other mothers. And just as her son is the end and perfection of all created sons, so his mother is the end and perfection of all created mothers.

**On the Action and Passion of the maternal tree.**

Our Lady has power over demons, because none of them can harm her sons, who are her sons through the hope they have in her: and they are her sons through charity, insofar as they love her: they are also her sons through guardianship, because she guards and defends them, like a good and strong shepherd who guards and defends his sheep. Hence, since the power of demons is great, which they have in doing evil, therefore great is the power that Our Lady has over demons.

the greater Mother.

**On the Habit of the Maternal Tree.**

Our Lady has memory,
intellect, and will: through
memory, in habit, she has to recall,
and through intellect, to understand, and through
will, to love. In habit, she has to re-
call, so that she may recall sinners who
recall her in their necessities, tri-
bulations, and fears, and who
cry out to her that she may help them: because
if she does not help them, they are dead and
lost, and placed in many shames.
Wherefore, just as the sun has in habit
that it illuminates the earth, which it circles
according to the disposition of its motion,
so also, and much better, since it is so
that Our Lady is greater in goodness
than the sun, and has more virtue,

she has in habit to recall, when
she is touched by the recollection of a sinful
man, who recalls her in his necessities,
and who seeks help from her:
just like fire which has in habit to warm
a man who approaches it,
because he is cold. And if fire, which does not
have as great a habit in warming
as Our Lady has in
recalling, since memory
is a nobler and higher habit than
heat, so strongly warms the object
that approaches it, how much more
then does Our Lady have in habit
to recall the sinner who approaches
her with penitence, hope, and recollection.
And what has been said about the
habit of memory, must be said in its own
way about intellect and will.

**On the Situation of the Maternal**
**Tree.**

Our Lady is in the Empyrean
heaven before her Son, the Lord
Jesus Christ, and she is nearer to her
Son than any other creature, and beneath
her are Angels and men standing
in order, each next to the other, who
singing praise and bless her,
and show her reverence and honor,
whose glorious body is situated in
greater splendor than the Sun,
whose head also is crowned with virginity and
greater sanctity than
any other head, except the head of her Son.
Therefore, the situation of the glorious
body of Our Lady is very
beautiful and comely for living and very
lovely to be seen. There is also
another situation of Our Lady, which is
spiritual, just as her memory is
situated in good recollection, and her intellect
in good understanding, and her will in
good loving. And according to what ob-

294 **The Maternal Tree.**

the objects which Our Lady receives by recollecting, understanding, and loving, are situated in the greatness of goodness; her recollection, understanding, and love are situated in the greatness of goodness. Therefore, there is a great arrangement which Our Lady has in recollecting her Son, God and man, and the sinners who call upon her, and those who place their goodness, nobility, and charity in their recollection, understanding, and love.

**Of the Time of the Maternal Tree.**

[Decorative initial A] From the beginning of the world until the Son of God was incarnated and crucified, no man entered paradise. Therefore, the Prophets and Saints, who were in hell (the Limbo of the Fathers), awaited the time in which Our Lady was to be born, and also the time in which her Son would be incarnated, so that the fruits of the blessed might be gathered in that time, just as the fruits of plants are gathered in summer. Wherefore that time was very noble, and thus the center and end of all others: like a point in the middle of a circle, to which the union and aggregation of many lines relate. Furthermore, to that time related all other times of celestial and terrestrial bodies, and their movements, so that they might be recreated, because all things served men disobedient to God, in whose service they did not attain the end of service, nor the end for which they were created, which end they lost because of original sin. Therefore, the time in which Our Lady was born was in very great exaltation, and in the greatness of goodness, and in great desirability of the saints and their utility, and in great amiability of celestial and terrestrial bodies.

**Of the Place of the Maternal Tree.**

[Decorative initial D] Our Lady is in paradise and a mother in her Son, God-man, in whom God-man is the Son, so that the mother is mother through the Son, and the Son is Son through the mother. And likewise, in their own way, concerning sinners who have hope in Our Lady, who are sons of hope, insofar as they are sons of Our Lady in the hope in which they are. And this is a great wonder, that they are sons of hope, and that they are in hope, and that through hope they are sons of Our Lady, in whom they are with hope: nevertheless, according to the great locality of motherhood, it is not a great wonder: for just as the firmament contains many things within itself by reason of its great quantity and locality, so Our Lady contains within herself many hopes of sinners, with which sinners are placed and overshadowed in her: just as chicks warmed by the heat under the wings of their mother hen, signifying the warming of sinful men, which they have in loving Our Lady. Indeed, these sinners are warmed by the love of Our Lady, who clothes them with hope and invites them to the blessed place where she stands, in which they may be eternally placed.

**Of the Flowers of the Maternal Tree.**

[Decorative initial F] The FLOWERS of the maternal tree are the acts of Our Lady's dignities, with which fruit is gathered, such as to do good, which is an act of Our Lady's goodness, and to magnify, which is an act of her greatness, and to persevere, to do good, and to magnify, which is an act of her duration, inasmuch as she causes her good and great recollection, understanding, and love to endure.

[Left Column]

to love, to do good, and to magnify. And the same is true of the act of power, which is to make possible, with which it is made possible to remember, understand, and love the good and the great. And the same is true of the act of virtue, by reason of which Our Lady's remembering, understanding, and loving are virtuous. And the same is true of the act of truth, which is to verify, by which other flowers are in truth. And the same is true of the act of glory, through which other acts are in glory. Just as several voices according to the art of music or the sounds of celestial bodies produce one third common and pleasing sound to hear: so the acts of goodness, greatness, duration, power, virtue, truth, and glory produce three flowers, which are general, which are Our Lady's remembering, understanding, and loving, so that with them a great and very excellent fruit in goodness, duration, power, glory, virtue, and truth may be gathered, without which excellence and greatness of the flowers, excellent acts could not be gathered. Our Lady's remembering, understanding, and loving are sublime and lofty flowers, so much better than the lily flower, which stands high in whiteness and fragrance, and like the rose in redness and fragrance, and the flower of the vine, which ascends above the flower of any other tree with which it shares, and the flower of aloe, which is superior in usefulness than the plum flower. And so lofty are Our Lady's flowers: that all the flowers of sinful men who have hope in her are overshadowed beneath the shadows of the superior flowers, and these (the flowers of sinful men) receive from them (the superior flowers) taste, usefulness, color, and fragrance. May we be able to come to that shadow because of her love.

[Right Column]

**About the Fruit of the Maternal Tree.**

**J**esus Christ is the fruit of Our Lady, the glorious virgin and mother. And just as an apple is a fruit that is gathered in the time of warmth, so Our Lady gathers her fruit with love, and she gathers it in the time of mercy, namely when her Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, remits the sin of the sinner because of her love. And just as an apple is gathered to give taste and fragrance, and a rose to give a pleasing color, so Our Lady gathers her fruit with the pleasure of remembering, understanding, and loving, which she has in her son and in her works. Our Lady's fruit is gathered to give life to men who were dead because of original sin, and in Him who is the fruit, the unity of divine and human nature, Our Lady gathers the fruits of sinners who have hope in her, which fruits are indeed the ends, about which it was said in the roots of this tree, and sinners gather hopes, contritions, tears, sighs, lamentations, and loves, so that they may gather Our Lady's fruit and come to her glory. Our Lady gathered her fruit at the nativity with virginity: because as a virgin she conceived Him, and she gathered Him with poverty: because with humility she conceived Him, and she gathered Him without any suffering: because she conceived Him without any corruption, and she gathered in her Son, man, the Son God, who is her Father and Son, He is her Father by creation, and her Son by incarnation, Our Lady gathered such a Son, thus gathered, with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and with

      SUMMARY.

De Arbore Christianali.

This tree is divided into se-
ven parts, which are roots,
trunk, branches, boughs,
leaves, flowers, and fruits: and it is a twofold tree, one part is concerning the creature, the other truly concerning the creator. And it is a tree in which the creator participates with all creatures insofar as both natures are united in the unity of one person.

De Radicibus arboris Iesu Christi.

Two natures are from the roots in
this tree: some roots are
from the part of human nature, the others truly
from the part of Divine nature. The roots which
are from the part of human nature, are
like human goodness: real, elemen-
tal, vegetal, sensual, imaginal, and
rational, as has been said in the natural
and primary trees. And this goodness

The trunk, according to how it is touched by Martin, responds: because the great love of the Lord Jesus Christ does not respond with a great love to Martin's little love, after it is touched with little love, nor does it respond to the great love that Martin bears for his son: because it is touched injuriously, in that Martin touches a greater goodness with lesser love, and a lesser goodness with greater love. And in this passage, the manner is understood, by reason of which men who pray to the Lord Jesus Christ inordinately are not heard, and are punished in their petitions, in which it is fitting that they be thus punished by justice: just as they would be heard, if they had had a good manner in praying to the Lord Jesus Christ. In an apple there are four elements in one way according to concordance, and in another according to contrariety: according to concordance: just as fire and air, which have concordance in heat, and in that fire gives its likeness to air, and air has an appetite for receiving its likeness, namely the heat of fire. According to contrariety, just as fire and water, which are contrary through heat and coldness: because water does not wish to receive the likeness of fire, but resists it with its coldness as much as it can. This kind of mode of contrariety which is in the apple, is not in the trunk: because divine and human nature have concordance, divine nature giving itself to human nature, so that God might become man, and man might become God, divine nature receiving the human, the divine nature itself remaining that which it is without any change or alteration. And in this passage, it is understood that divine nature does not receive any alteration or mu-

-tation of itself in the conjunction which it makes with the human: just as fire which receives no alteration in the constitution which it makes with air through heat, and exalts the air to a nobler state, in that it clothes it with its heat with concordance; just as human nature, which receives exaltation, in that divine nature is clothed with concordance. Therefore Saracens and Jews do evil, who deny the incarnation of the Son of God, saying that God would receive alteration in the conjunction and union which he would make with man, in whom there are many natural defects, a man who desires to be God, so that it may be known that His goodness and perfection can receive no infirmity or alteration through any union or conjunction which He makes with man: because His eternity makes Him endure immutable, and without increase and decrease. In the trunk, divine nature is the principle, and human nature is that which is originated: because God originated man from Our Lady, and originated him in Himself, namely in His Godhead, therefore man cannot originate anything in God, after he has been wholly originated, and originated from a material principle into a formal principle: wherefore man, neither by his nature nor by anything pertaining to him substantially or accidentally, can debase divine nature, nor diminish it, nor magnify it: in which divine nature, indeed, nothing can originate, multiply nor alter, although it is conjoined with it. And in this passage, it is understood that when God created the world, He received no change in Himself, because He originated the whole of it, wherefore the world stood wholly originated from nothing, and was from nothing ori-

originated, so that it might be entirely originated: for if it were eternal, it would not be entirely originated, and since the whole world was originated, nothing can originate in God: because if something could originate in Him, He would not be entirely originated, nor would God be the whole formal principle, and in some part He would be a material principle, which is impossible.

Concerning the Branches of the Tree of Jesus Christ.

**T**here are two branches of the tree of Jesus Christ, namely the divine and human nature. And the human branch is elemental, vegetal, sensual, imaginal, and rational: since it is so that He is from these five natures, and contains them in Himself, and through these natures, which are His parts, Jesus Christ perceived sensible objects in this present life. He perceived through the elemental nature, heat, and cold: and through the vegetal nature He had an appetite for eating and drinking: and through the sensual nature He apprehended heat, voice, taste, and smell: through the imaginal nature He multiplied species by imagining the figures of corporeal substances: and through the rational nature He recollected, understood, and loved, and used reason. Therefore He was a true man, and used natural conditions naturally and virtuously.

The Divine branch is filial, eternal and infinite, and is goodness, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, and glory. And therefore in this present life in which the Lord Jesus Christ was, the divine branch used miracles beyond the natural course, nor did it have hunger, thirst, heat, or cold, and it apprehended corporeal objects without the multiplication of species, and without sensual powers.

Insofar as one branch was in the other, one branch apprehended objects according to the nature of that [other] branch: just as the divine branch, which by reason of its conjunction with the human, apprehended hunger, thirst, heat, and cold, and with its eyes saw color, and with imagination multiplied species and likenesses of corporeal substances, and recollected, understood, and loved like a man. And it did this, because the divine branch was, and is, man through the human [branch]: just as a white substance which is white through heat, and a substance which is a body through length, breadth, and depth, and the human branch, by reason of the conjunction it had and has with the divine, apprehended corporeal objects really without species being multiplied, so that it did not need a medium or likenesses, nor did it have hunger, nor thirst, heat nor cold, nor ignorance of anything, and it was and is immortal. And in this passage is known the manner in which the Lord Jesus Christ in this life acted in His works according to the natures of the branches and their conjunction.

The branches of this tree are great in goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, glory, virtue, and truth: each branch is great by itself, and the human branch is greater in the divine than in itself, and the divine branch is greater in the human through the human than all created branches, since it is so that the human branch is greater through the divine than all other created branches. Therefore both branches are great, whence since the branches are so great, who could think, say or write the magnitude of the trunk, of which the aforesaid two branches are? There is a difference between the two branches, because Fp 3.

One is the divine nature, and the other is the human nature. And the greater the branches are, the greater is the difference: and the greater the difference, the greater is their concord, which both branches have in being one person, one trunk, one Jesus Christ. Therefore the branches are great in difference and in concord, and so great, that just as the concord is greater than any other concord which is between creator and creature, so it is necessary that the difference between branch and branch be greater than any other difference which is between creator and creature. Which greater difference signifies a greater distinction, which is between one divine person and another, and the same is true of the concord. Therefore those speak wrongly who say that between the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit there is not as great a distinction as between God and a horse: since it is so that among the divine persons there is a greater concord than between God and a horse, which greater concord could not exist without a greater distinction of persons. Both branches are great in their purpose with greatness: in their purpose they are great with greatness, because the purpose of the divine branch, so to speak, cannot be greater, since it is so that it itself is infinite and eternal, and the end, and the complement of all creatures. And the purpose of the human branch is so great that a greater creature cannot exist: because all other creatures were created for its sake, and it itself is joined with the purpose of the divine branch.

the divine will and the human will, which relate to each other in loving; and the divine and human intellect, which relate to each other in understanding; and the eternity of God and the memory of the Lord Jesus Christ, which relate to each other in remembering. **Christ.** Therefore it is necessary that prayers be heard by reason of the great union of both natures. And this aspect is very pleasing and delightful for sinners to consider, who look upon the heights of the Lord Jesus Christ from the weak places in which they fell into sin, and from which they rise by looking upon the heights of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the branches, recollecting, understanding, and loving those very branches more than anything else. In this respect, to understand, recollect, and love is such a great concord that no contrariety can exist there, which contrariety would be in that respect if the divine nature did not hear the human nature concerning the prayers it makes to it for sinners, that it might forgive them and give them salvation. But because both natures are in one person, there is one judgment, which judgment indeed is loved by the human nature, which loves all that the divine nature loves; even the human will loves the divine will more than itself or the salvation of sinful men. Therefore, it makes prayers with justice, with which follows the mercy of the divine nature, which is a sister to justice, which justice cannot fail its sister. And this aspect is an object of fear and hope for sinful men.

**Concerning the Leaves of the tree of Jesus Christ.**
**And first concerning Quantities.**

**J**ESUS Christ, insofar as he is man, is adorned and clothed with accidents, without which he would not be man: such as concerning quantity, which he has according to the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational tree. And because the divine nature assumed the human, it assumed in that [human nature] continuous and discrete quantity, and in itself [the divine nature] it remains without quantity: just as water which takes color and flavor from diluted wine, and water in fire takes heat, and man takes virtue in justice and prudence, and so concerning other similar things. And thus infinity and quantity participate: infinity, inasmuch as the divine nature, which is infinite, and in that there is one suppositum, which is the trunk, possesses in human nature the continuous quantity throughout all the trees, which represent the conditions of human nature. And because they are distinct, that continuous quantity is sustained in discrete quantities. And just as infinity has quantity in another nature and not in itself, so quantity in another nature is infinite, and in itself remains terminated, but this could not be without the conjunction of both natures in the unity of the person.

**Concerning the Qualities of Jesus Christ.**

**Q**uality is considered in two ways. For there is proper quality, and appropriated quality. Proper is like Martin who is naturally good, insofar as he is a creature. Appropriated is like Martin who is good because he is just, and wise, charitable, and temperate, and so concerning other acquired habits of virtues: the divine nature appropriates these appropriated qualities to itself, insofar as it assumed human nature: just as fire appropriates to itself the dryness of the earth, insofar as it clothes itself with earth, which earth indeed appropriates its dryness to fire: so human nature appropriates its conditions to the divine, and it does this because substantial and divine qualities meet substantial and accidental qualities of man in the unity of the trunk.

304      The Christian Tree.

in the unity of the person. And in this passage, this is known, why the Lord Jesus Christ in this world loved acquired virtues, so that the divine nature could have them in the human nature.

**On the Relations of the Tree of Jesus Christ.**

The divine nature and the human nature of the Lord Jesus Christ are really distinct by essence. And because both natures are conjoined and distinct in one person, a relation follows from this: just as if God is man, it is necessary that man be God, and if man is God, it is necessary that God be man. And in this passage, Saracens and also Jews can recognize their errors, who do not believe in the incarnation; because they suppose that Christians believe that God so assumed human nature that He Himself did not remain God: just as the matter of bread, which a man eats, which when it is transubstantiated into the species of flesh, leaves the form of bread and its matter, and stands clothed in the form of flesh, and is the matter of that form, in which the relation of the form and matter of bread is lost. And they say the same, that Christians believe that in the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ the divine nature died, and that God did not remain God, and man died, and did not remain man. But inasmuch as Christians believe in the aforesaid relation, God died inasmuch as He was man, and in His own proper being remained inasmuch as He was God, and He was dead according to human nature, and man remained God, inasmuch as God remained man. Therefore, Christians do wrong who do not tell Saracens the relation of the incarnation, and the manner in which they believe in it: because if wise Saracens knew the manner of the incarnation, and had knowledge of the relation, they would suppose the incarnation to be possible, which they now suppose to be impossible, because they have no knowledge of it, and with the possibility supposed with the conditions that a man could give them, and concerning the incarnation according to the process of this book, many Saracens would convert to the Christian faith. Since it is so that there are many wise Saracens who do not believe in Muhammad, because according to the life he led, they have experience that he was not a Prophet, nor a virtuous man, nor a true one.

**On the Actions and Passions of Jesus Christ.**

In the Lord Jesus Christ, the divine nature is active, and the human nature is passive, inasmuch as the divine nature assumed the human, and sustains it in itself, and also in itself became man from human nature. Which human nature indeed has actions and passions, which are of its conditions: just as the action and passion of a natural body, and its actions according to the natures of trees, also its passion which it had on the cross, and its action which it similarly had on the cross then, when it conquered original sin. Saracens say that Christians believe that God had passion in human nature through hunger, thirst, heat, and cold, and on the cross through death. Therefore, wise Saracens do not want to believe that God is man. And because of this, Christians do wrong, because they do not show wise Saracens their belief, in which they deny and would deny those passions, inasmuch as

insofar as the divine nature, and they affirm and would affirm those passions according to human nature: just as water which has a passion through the heat of fire in pepper, and does not have a passion through coldness in a gourd.

On the Habits of Jesus Christ.

Divine nature, receiving human nature, assumed the conditions of man; therefore, it assumed habits in such a way that it remembers as a man under the habit of memory, and understands as a man under the habit of intellect, and loves as a man under the habit of will, and so concerning the habits of other trees, which are of the human condition. And in this step it is recognized that the habits of the Lord Jesus Christ are great, and so are their acts: because God, who comprehends all creatures under the habit of man, wills to comprehend all of them by remembering, understanding, and loving. And in this step it is recognized that great is the love which the Lord Jesus Christ has for his people, and great was the passion which he endured on the cross: whence, just as a logician acquires the habit of logic through knowledge, so the Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, has all things in memory in this, that the Godhead, under the habit of created memory, wills to remember all things which it remembers, insofar as it is man, and insofar as it is God. And thus the Lord Jesus reaches and comprehends all creatures, insofar as he is God, and insofar as he is a creature.

On the Assituation of Jesus Christ.

Divine nature is assituated in human nature: just as the iron of a knife [is situated] in the figure of that which is not of its essence:

[Right Column]

but is an accidental figure assituated in the form and matter of the knife. Therefore, the Godhead is assituated in humanity, insofar as it is clothed by it, yet in such a way that the divine nature is not assituated according to its conditions in any figure: because infinite essence, according to its nature, cannot have a circular, quadrangular, or triangular figure, since it is necessary that every figure be finite, and be sustained in a corporal substance, which is clothed and terminated by that figure. And because Saracens are ignorant of the mode of incarnation by reason of the assituation which they believe, that Christians believe in incarnation supposing incarnation to be impossible, saying that if God were incarnate, it would be necessary for divine infinity to have a finite figure, by which it would be entirely clothed, and in which it would be terminated circularly, quadrangularly, and triangularly. And thus it implies a contradiction in the incarnation, namely, that God is infinite and not infinite. And because of this, Christians do wrong, who do not show the Saracens the mode of incarnation, which they believe in the incarnation, and in its assituation, by telling them that the Godhead, which is God the Son, is assituated in humanity, not insofar as it is infinite: but insofar as God the Son is a terminated and finite man, and assituated under a certain figure, by which he is thus clothed: just as an apple [is clothed] with color, and taste with flavor, when a man eats an apple, yet the substance of the apple is not of the essence of the color, nor the taste of the flavor, nor the iron of the figure of the knife: because if the iron were of the essence of the figure of the knife, a nail could not be made from that very iron.
