Concerning the Time of the Tree of Jesus Christ.

IN the Lord Jesus Christ, eternity
and time participate: because in
this, that the Son of God is eternity, and
in time was made man, eternity
and time participate, yet not
that eternity is in time, for
if it were in time, it would not be what
it is, since it is so, that eternity is a
being without beginning and without any mo-
tion. Secondly, insofar as God is
man, eternity is in time: just as
God who is man is in man. And just as
water which is hot is hot by the heat of fire, and
not by its own nature: for if
water heated in a pot were hot by
its own nature, it would be hot without fire
existing in the pot. And the Saracens
are ignorant of this second mode, according
to which eternity participates with time in the Lord
Jesus Christ, nor is there anyone to show
it to them. Hence they say that
if God were incarnate, His eternity
was perverted into temporality:
just as if cold water were to abandon its natural
coldness, and take on the habit
of heat.

Concerning the Place of the Tree of Jesus Christ.

THE Lord Jesus Christ, insofar
as He is God, is in every place,
and insofar as He is man, He is in the empyrean
heaven: as was said above in the apos-

is man, God is in one place through
man, and not in another place where that
man is not, and insofar as that man
is God, He is in every place through God,
and this is according to the relation which
we have spoken of in this tree, which I desire
that the Saracens should know: for if
they knew it, they would by no means say
that Christians believe that the Godhead
departed from heaven, and that it was not in another

when He was incarnate. Nor would they
say, nor believe, that Christians
believe that the humanity of Christ
is in every place, insofar as the man

just as it is easy to know the
relation which we have spoken of. And therefore Christians
do wrong, because they do not show
the Saracens the relation, which they could

*De Bonitate, magnitudine &*
*Incarnatione.*

Goodness is the reason for the good to do good. And if goodness and magnitude are one and the same in number, goodness is the reason for the good to do great good. In God, goodness and magnitude are one and the same in number: therefore, goodness is the reason for God to produce a great creature, which is good. And therefore, the incarnation of the Son of God is signified, which produces a good and great creature, inasmuch as goodness is the great reason for that production. And if the question arises, whether God is incarnated in multiple men, it must be answered, as will be stated below in the question tree.

*De Bonitate, æternitate & In-*
*carnatione.*

Goodness is the reason for the eternal good, with which it is one and the same in number, that it should produce an eternal good. And eternity is the reason for goodness, that one producing remains, while another is produced. And thus the blessed Trinity of God is signified, and also the incarnation of the Son of God. The Holy Trinity is signified, as we will say in the flowers of the divine tree. The Incarnation is signified, inasmuch as goodness is the reason for the eternal, that it should produce a creature so eternalized and made good, that this creature is eternal, which is so conditioned by the conditions of the eternal itself, just as the eternal itself is conditioned by the conditions of the creature. And in this passage, it is necessary to have knowledge of relation, about which it was said above in this tree.

*De Bonitate, potestate &*
*Incarnatione.*

Goodness is the reason for the powerful, with whom it is one and the same in number, that it should produce a possible good. And the same is true of the goodness of fire, which is the reason for the power of fire, that it should produce a good that is possible, heated, and elemental, although goodness is not one and the same in number with the power of fire. Nevertheless, fire, under the principle of goodness, uses its power, and produces that which reason demands, namely natural instinct and appetite, to the extent that it produces an elemental and possible good, such as pepper and other elemental substances. Hence, if fire produces under the principle of goodness, although in it goodness and power are not one and the same in number, how much more is divine goodness the reason for divine power, with which it is one and the same in number, that it should produce a good that is great, powerful, possible, created, eternalized, and deified, in which the Son of God is made man.

*De Bonitate, sapientia &*
*Incarnatione.*

The goodness of God is the reason for His wisdom, with which it is one and the same in number, that it should understand a created, great, durable, and possible good, which wisdom understands, so that its reason and the reason of goodness, magnitude, eternity, and power may have concordance. Therefore, the blessed Incarnation is signified, without which the reason of wisdom does not correspond to the reason of goodness, magnitude, eternity, and power, and this would be evil.

*On Goodness, Will &*
*Incarnation.*

God's Goodness and His will are
one and the same in number, and goodness is
the reason for the will, that it may love the created
product insofar as it can be a reason for good, that it may produce a great
good, and as great as that can produce and wisdom can understand.
Therefore, the incarnation is signified, so that the will responds to the reason
of goodness in loving that great and good production, and as great as
wisdom can understand it.

*On Goodness, Virtue &*
*Incarnation.*

With virtue, goodness is the reason for virtuous
good, that it may produce a created virtuous good,
and it is a reason for it with the magnitude of power,
wisdom, and will. And if virtuous good did not produce
a created and virtuous good product according to those reasons
which goodness gives to it, it would do evil, and it would be vicious.
Therefore, the incarnation is signified to be true.

*On Goodness, Truth &*
*Incarnation.*

Goodness is the reason for true good with

in such a great reason of truth, as
goodness is the reason for truth. Since it is so,
that divine truth has such great concordance,
as goodness with magnitude, duration, power,
wisdom, will, and truth. Therefore, the incarnation is signified in re-

*On Goodness, Glory & Incarnation.*

Glory belongs to goodness, that it itself is
the reason for glorious good, that it may produce a glorious good,
and it is good for glory in producing it. And in this step,
the production of glorious good is signified: as a cause which has pleasure
in producing a good glorious effect, according as magnitude,
duration, power, wisdom, will, truth, and virtue require,
by two reasons, which are from glory and goodness.

*On Goodness, Difference &*
*Incarnation.*

Between the creator and the creature there is
a difference, and that difference is good. And just as difference requires that
it be good, so it requires that it be durable,
great, and powerful, and of great wisdom,
will, glory, truth, and virtue. Therefore, the incarnation
is signified in that reason, so that it may be the response
of the reasons of which it has been spoken.

*On Goodness, Concordance &*
*Incarnation.*

Between God and the creature there is con-
cordance, which is good, and just as
concordance requires that it be good, so it requires that it be great,
durable, and powerful, and so concerning wisdom,
will, virtue, glory, truth, and difference.
For if these themselves did not have such a great place in concordance as
goodness, the same would follow: malice and
smallness against greatness, and so con-

concerning others. Therefore, the Incarnation is signified through the responses of equal reasons in concordance.

**Of Goodness, Contrariety &**
**Incarnation.**

NO contrariety can contradict the reasons of divine goodness, since it is so that goodness itself is the reason for good, that it produces created good, for which there is reason, with great concordance of magnitude, duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, and difference. Therefore, contrariety cannot contradict the reason of the Incarnation; therefore, it is necessary that the reason of the Incarnation remain within the reason of goodness, in which reason its demonstrability is signified.

**Of Goodness, Principle &**
**Incarnation.**

GOODNESS is the reason for good, which initiates good, and since it is a reason for it with magnitude, it is a reason for good that it may initiate great good. And the same concerning duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, difference, and concordance. Therefore, the Incarnation is signified to be initiated, according as goodness is the reason with other reasons for a good principle.

**Of Goodness, Means &**
**Incarnation.**

THE Good One who is creator is the means for active reasons, so that he may produce created passive reasons, whose production is good, the producer existing as producing, by reason of magnitude, a product as great as it is good; and the same is true for duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, difference, principle, and concordance. But this could not be, unless God were incarnated, however, with the help of a greater end of reason between goodness and the producer, and the created product.

**Of Goodness, End & Incarnation.**

GOODNESS is the reason for good, that it produces created good by reason of an end, which end, indeed, is good, and as great as it is good. And the same concerning duration, power, wisdom, and will, virtue, glory, and truth, difference, means, principle, and concordance. Therefore, the Incarnation is signified in the great reason of goodness and end.

**Of Goodness, Greaterness &**
**Incarnation.**

GOODNESS has greater concordance with magnitude than with smallness: therefore, goodness is the reason for good, that it produces created good in greater created goodness. And duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, and truth, glory, difference, end, means, and principle have the same concordance. By reason of which concordance the Incarnation is signified.

**Of Goodness, Equality &**
**Incarnation.**

GOODNESS is equally the reason for good, that it produces created good in conjunction with the magnitude of duration, power, wisdom, and will, virtue, truth, glory, difference, concordance, principle, means, end, and greaterness: therefore, it is necessary that what is produced be: great, and equal to good, and durable.

& equal to the good, & powerful, equal to that good product, equal, great, durable, powerful, & so on for others. And this in the greatest equality that can exist between uncreated reasons and created reasons. But this could not be, if God were not incarnated.

*On Goodness, Minority & Incarnation.*

Divine goodness is a greater reason with a greater degree of good, that it may produce a created good, than with a lesser degree. And this is because greatness has a greater concordance with a greater degree of goodness than with a lesser degree, and with a greater degree of greatness than with a lesser degree, since it is so that smallness and minority have concordance. And the same applies to the greater degree of duration, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, difference, and concordance, principle, middle, end, and equality. Therefore, the incarnation is signified and proven by a greater concordance. And if anyone makes the argument that the world is eternal according to the consequence of proof, let the answer be that the greater duration of the creature consists through Deification. And that the world is not eternal, has been proven above in the apostolic tree.

*On Greatness, Duration & Incarnation.*

The greatness of duration is that divine and human nature remain what they are, and each with its own conditions, and that together one suppositum, one Jesus Christ, is made. Therefore, the incarnation is, so that greatness may be a reason for duration, and duration for greatness, according to the relation of creator and creature.

[Right column]

*On Greatness, Power & Incarnation.*

Power is a reason for greatness, that it can be and have great works, and greatness is a reason for power, that it can be great through existing things and agents. And these reasons which are convertible, are better signified in the relation of conversion and creation, if there is incarnation. And if there is no incarnation, a lesser signification of conversion is signified, and one reason is lacking; others in conversion and relation, which is impossible, by which impossibility the probability of the incarnation consists.

*On Greatness, Wisdom & Incarnation.*

Greatness is a reason for wisdom, that it may know a great creation, so great that it cannot know a greater: for if it could know a greater, power would have a greater concordance with wisdom than greatness, which greatness would indeed have concordance with smallness of knowing, and with the greatness of power, which concordance is impossible. Therefore, greatness is a reason for divine wisdom, that it may know a creature greater than what it can [otherwise] know, by reason of which greater creature, which ought to be known, it is necessary that incarnation occurs, by reason of which there may be a greater creature, for if there were no incarnation, wisdom would in vain know the possibility of a greater creature.

*On Greatness, Will & Incarnation.*

Divine greatness is a reason for divine will, that it may [will] a great creature

**Arbor christianalis. 311**

[Left Column]

...creature it loves, and so great that it cannot love a greater one: for if it could love a greater one, and did not love it, greatness would not be a reason for the will, that it would love a greater creature, and it would be a reason for its smallness, which reason, indeed, is not lovable by will, nor possible by power. Therefore, the incarnation exists, by reason of which the will loves so great a creature, that it cannot love a greater one.

**On Greatness, Virtue & Incarnation.**

Greatness is a reason for virtue, that it may be great, and virtue for greatness, that it may be virtuous. Therefore, greatness is a virtue between God and creature, if every creature exists, so that there may be an incarnation. And if there is no incarnation, greatness is not a reason for virtue, that it may be a great reason for the creature's virtue. Therefore, the incarnation exists, so that there may be a response between virtue and greatness, and between creator and creature.

**On Greatness, Truth & Incarnation.**

If there is an incarnation, a great truth of the creator in the creature follows, and of the creature in the creator, and so great that it cannot be greater. And if there is no incarnation, the greatness of truth is in privation, and greatness and truth are lacking to the greatness and truth of creation, which is impossible, by reason of which impossibility the incarnation is proven, since it is so, that there is a great truth, that the creator is creature, and creator without contradiction, and according to the relationship which we have spoken of in the leaves of this tree.

[Right Column]

**On Greatness, Glory & Incarnation.**

If there is an incarnation, there is great glory for the creature: for it is great glory for the creature, that it may be united with the creator in the unity of person, who is creator and creature, and great glory is for the saints, who are creatures, and who are of the natures of that so great creature united with the creator. And if there is no incarnation, the greatness of glory is in privation, and the smallness of glory is in being, and it follows that greatness and glory have concordance with privation, and smallness and glory with being, which concordance is impossible, by reason of which impossibility the incarnation is proven.

**On Greatness, Difference, & Incarnation.**

Between creator and creature there is a difference, and if there is an incarnation, there is a great difference between God and creature: for it is a great difference, that two natures are different, and that one person exists, and also that that difference may be greater in goodness, duration, power, wisdom, and will, glory, virtue, and truth, concordance, beginning, middle, end, and greatness, than any other difference which may exist between God and creature. And if there is no incarnation, the possibility of a great difference is in privation, which is impossible, because divine greatness must not be lacking to the greater and nobler difference which can exist between creator and creature.

**On Greatness, Concordance & Incarnation.**

If there is an incarnation, there is great concordance between creator and creature,

**On Magnitude, Equality, and Incarnation.**

IF there is incarnation, the magnitude of equality is between created goodness and created magnitude, and so concerning other forms, from which is human nature, which God assumed. And that magnitude of equality is magnified in a great equality, which is between divine goodness and divine magnitude, and so concerning eternity and other divine dignities. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that there may be a magnification of created equality in a created act through the uncreated Son subject to the equality of divine goodness of magnitude, etc. And if there is no incarnation, there is a magnitude rebellious to its likeness of equality, which is impossible.

**On Magnitude, Lesser Part, and Incarnation.**

Lesser part, according to comparison with greater part, is properly non-being, and smallness, according to comparison with magnitude, similarly; therefore, divine magnitude, which is infinite and eternal, has greater concordance with the greater part of created goodness and created magnitude, and the same is true of created duration and other things, than with the lesser part of those. Therefore, there is incarnation so that a greater concordance may follow, without which incarnation a lesser concordance would follow against the magnitude of goodness, etc.

**On Eternity, Power, and Incarnation.**

Power can do more concerning a creature in eternity than outside eternity: therefore, God can do more in Himself concerning a creature than outside Himself, since it is so that He Himself is eternity. Therefore, God can take human nature, which He assumed, so that He may use His power more in the creature, and the creature in Himself.

**On Eternity, Wisdom, and Incarnation.**

God eternally understands that He can do more concerning a creature in Himself than outside Himself: therefore, it is necessary that what His wisdom understands concerning His power, and concerning His eternity, and concerning His creature, He completes, for if not, His wisdom would in vain understand a greater power concerning the creature in Himself than He has outside Himself. Therefore, there is incarnation, in which is perfected that which His wisdom understands more concerning His power, and the creature in His eternity than outside His eternity.

...in unity than in the form of man, or of another creature; and because divine power is the principle of creation, insofar as it is a principle, it relates to a greater created effect, so that it relates to its greater likeness: therefore, it relates to a created effect united with divine eternity, but this could not be, if God were not incarnate.

*Of Eternity, the Means, and Incarnation.*

Just as a creature is more durable in eternity than outside eternity, so it is more lovable in eternity than outside eternity. Therefore, greater durability and greater lovability are the means by which it is necessary that the Creator and creature be joined in divine eternity to such an extent that both are one person, so that greater durability and lovability of the creature may follow. Therefore, there is the incarnation, without which there would be a greater disposition of durability and lovability in the creature than of durativeness and lovableness in the Creator.

*Of Eternity, the End, and Incarnation.*

The end of the creature is eternity, which it has better attained, if there is incarnation. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that it may have better attained the end. And if there is no incarnation, the end of the creature is not attained in a greater act than eternity can have in the creature: but in a lesser one, which is against the greater act of the divine will, which loves the greater end of the creature, to which greater love the act of eternity is deficient, which is impossible.

*Of Eternity, Greatness, and Incarnation.*

Eternity can better show its likeness with greatness than with smallness, since it is so that eternity is greater than the creature. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that the creature may be in a greatness, beyond which it cannot be greater. And if there is no incarnation, eternity shows its likeness with the smallness of the creature against its own greatness, which is impossible: through which impossibility there is the demonstrability of the incarnation.

*Of Eternity, Equality, and Incarnation.*

A creature is as much lovable by divine will in the magnitude of goodness, as it is eternalizable by eternity in the magnitude of goodness. And this is because eternity and divine will relate equally to the creature: therefore, there is incarnation, through which the creature is eternalized, inasmuch as it is united with eternity in the unity of person.

*Of Eternity, Smallness, and Incarnation.*

The creature is produced from nothing, and because smallness is properly non-being in comparison to greatness (which is far from non-being), it is necessary that there be incarnation, so that eternity may distance the creature from smallness, and place it in a greater greatness, in which it can be placed, which greater greatness indeed stands through the incarnation, without which eternity could not so strongly distance any creature from smallness, nor consequently from non-being.

316 Christian Tree.

*On Power, Wisdom, & Incarnation.*

The Power of God can do as much in creation by enabling, as divine wisdom by knowing: since it is so that divine wisdom can have its knowledge through power, and because wisdom knows more about the power of the creator in creation, if there is an incarnation, than if there is not: it is necessary that power extends itself as much to enabling the creature as wisdom extends itself to knowing. Therefore, there is an incarnation, so that power and wisdom may equally extend themselves to their acts.

*On Power, Will, & Incarnation.*

The divine will can love the incarnation since no inconvenience follows from it. And since the will can love it, power can enable it. And if it could not enable it, the will could extend itself more in the creature's lovability than power in its possibility. And thus it would follow that divine power would relate more to the creature through will than through itself, which is impossible. Therefore, there is an incarnation, so that power can relate as much to enabling the creature as will to loving the creature. And if the will could love the incarnation, and did not love it, power could relate more to enabling the creature than will to loving it, which is impossible. And in this passage, some will argue and say that the power of God can do more concerning creation which the will does not love. And to this it can be answered that power cannot enable those things if the will itself hates them; nor can it be idle in those things if the will itself loves them; nor for this reason is power coerced by will, since they are one and the same in number, nor does will love anything without a magnitude of goodness. And through this passage, objections are answered which some might raise according to the consequence of our proofs, namely that the will does not love multiple incarnations: because the unity of person could not exist if there were multiple incarnations of the divine nature and human natures, nor does the divine will love that power could multiply the grades of creatures against order and proportion, in which it is necessary that they be ordered under an end, which is superior, which is the trunk of this tree. Just as God could not establish in order that goodness would have a nobler end in the species of a horse than of a human, nor color than substance. And this answer suffices for the objections that could be made against the consequences of our proofs or conclusions; nevertheless, we intend to speak more broadly on this matter in the question tree.

*On Power, Virtue & Incarnation.*

The Power of God can do as much concerning the sensitive faculty as concerning the intellective faculty: but since the intellective is nobler than the sensitive, it cannot communicate itself as much through the sensitive as through the intellective, because through the sensitive it cannot be perceived by the senses, since it is so that He is not a corporeal substance, and He can be understood through the intellective faculty, since it is so that He is a spiritual intelligible substance. Power.

--- Page 331 ---
Arbor chriſtianalis. 317

Therefore, divine power relates more according to uncreated virtue to make possible the intellectual virtue than the sensual one, and this according to the natural course. But the power of God ascends above the natural course, willing that there be incarnation, so that it communicates itself as much to the human sensitive (faculty) as to the human intellectual (faculty) in deifying either of those powers according to the mode of incarnation, the sensitive (faculty) being joined with the deity as much as the intellectual (faculty), so that the power of God can extend itself as much in giving virtue through the deity to the sensitive (faculty) as to the intellectual (faculty). And the same for the elementary, vegetative, and imaginative (faculties).

**On Power, Glory & Incarnation.**

The power of God can give greater glory to a creature through incarnation than without incarnation, since it is so that greater glory than a creature can have or give to another creature can be through incarnation, which must be so that power may respond to the greater glorifiability of the created, and the glorifying capacity of the uncreated, without which response, uncreated power could not have rest in glorifying the creature: for if it had rest, it would have it with less glorifying against more, which is impossible.

**On Power, Truth & Incarnation.**

Divine power can effect more concerning created truth in divine truth than concerning created truth in another created truth. And this is because uncreated truth can receive more of making possible and verifying than created truth: and because uncreated truth relates so nobly and fruitfully to created truth, just as divine power verifies concerning created truth in itself, and concerning itself in that (created truth), as much as power can make possible. But this could not be, unless incarnation were (to exist), without which power could verify more concerning uncreated truth in created truth, and concerning created truth in uncreated truth through truly incarnating, than uncreated truth could make possible concerning uncreated power in created power, and concerning created power in uncreated power through making possible to incarnate, which is impossible, and through this impossibility the probability of incarnation consists.

**On Power, Difference & Incarnation.**

That power which can differentiate more, can reconcile more, and the greater differentiating and reconciling that can exist between God and creature, is, if there be incarnation: because there is a great difference, that there are two natures, one infinite and the other finite, and that from them one person is made, and there is great concordance from them in the unity of person. Therefore, incarnation exists so that power may extend itself in the greater difference and concordance that can exist between God and creature.

**On Power, Concordance & Incarnation.**

In the concordance of infinite and finite nature which agree in the unity of person, there is greater positivity, possibility, and capacity to make possible, than in the concordance of infinite and finite nature which do not agree in the unity of person, nor in the concordance of finite and infinite nature.

Therefore, the Incarnation exists so that a greater concord, which can exist through the Incarnation, may be subject to greater possificability and possificativity, and to greater actualization, which can exist between God and creature. For if the Incarnation does not exist, divine power falls short in respect to the greater possificability, possificativity, and actualization which we have mentioned. And consequently, it falls short in respect to greater concordativity, concordability, and the act of concord, about which it has been said. And to it is lacking the magnitude of goodness, virtue, wisdom, and will, which is impossible, by which impossibility the reasonableness of the Incarnation is established.

*Concerning Power, Principle, and the*
*Incarnation.*

Divine power can more greatly originate from the creature a magnitude of goodness in itself, than outside itself. Therefore, the Incarnation exists so that it (the creature) may be subject to a greater principle for the creature in the magnitude of goodness. And if the Incarnation does not exist...

good, great, eternal, etc., and equally God through His dignities. Therefore, it is necessary that divine power equally respond to the greater created good, knowable and lovable through divine wisdom and will. Therefore, there is incarnation, in which an equal response is made by divine power to effect, knowability, and lovability, which attain a greater created good through incarnation.

*On Power, Minority &
Incarnation.*

Lesser created power is in a plant than in an animal, and in a horse than in a human: therefore, the power of God can do more in a horse than in a plant, and in a human than in a horse: and this is by reason of passive powers, which, inasmuch as they are greater in possibility, can be in a greater passion under divine power to effect. Therefore, according to this, incarnation is signified, so that there may be a greater created passive possibility, further removed from a lesser state into a greater active state, which could not exist without incarnation.

*On Wisdom, Will &
Incarnation.*

All that is known through the wisdom of God is loved by His will in the knowability and knowableness of wisdom, not, however, according to the conditions of evil objects through sin: just as God, who knows sin, which is not loved by His will. And since good is against sin, it is necessary that the will love every good that wisdom knows: for if it did not love all that good, it could love sin against goodness, knowability and know-

[Column 2]

-ableness of wisdom: therefore, the will loves every good that wisdom knows, and it loves it according to the possibility of good lovability. And at this point stands the answer to a general objection, which can be made against the consequence that we give concerning incarnation in the conclusion in several places of this treatise. We also say that the will loves all good objects that wisdom knows: and thus it loves a horse known by wisdom, in which horse there is little goodness. And because it has goodness in itself, it is lovable. Therefore, how much more does the will love a lovable created object, because it is united with divine will and goodness, since it is so that it pertains to the divine will to love a great good better than a lesser one. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that this statement may be true: if the divine will loves the small goodness that is in a horse, how much more does it love the great goodness in incarnation. And if there is no incarnation, this statement is true: 'if the divine will loves a great good, it follows that it loves a small good,' which statement is false: for if it were true, it would have a greater proportion in loving a small good than a great one: just as a king, who has a greater proportion with power in giving a horse than a city.

*On Wisdom, Virtue &
Incarnation.*

All that the wisdom of God knows, it knows virtuously, and if it knows a small virtue, it follows that it knows a great one, since it is so that it pertains to it to know a great virtue better than a small one, just as was said concerning the will. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that wisdom may know a greater virtue which can

Arbor christianalis. 323

*On Will, Difference &*
*Incarnation.*

Between the glory of God and of the creature there is a difference, and that difference is lovable in goodness and not in malice, therefore it is more lovable in greatness than in smallness: since it is so that great goodness is more lovable than small. Therefore, there is incarnation by reason of which the goodness of the difference, about which it has been said, is more lovable in greatness than in smallness, without which incarnation would be to the contrary.

*On Will, Concordance,*
*& Incarnation.*

If the divine will did not love a greater concordance of God and creature, the lovable concordance would be in a lesser degree of the end, in which it would find rest, which is impossible, and contrary to the greater goodness of concordance. Therefore, there is incarnation, by reason of which a greater end of concordance is loved.

*On Will, Principle &*
*Incarnation.*

The divine will loves created principiability more in greater principiativity than in lesser, and this is because principiativity is the cause of principiability. Therefore, there is incarnation so that uncreated loving power follows the order of lovableness, which exists between cause and effect in a greater magnitude of goodness through incarnation than without incarnation.

*On Will, Medium & Incarnation.*

Between great loving power and lovableness there is a greater medium than in smallness. Therefore, a greater love is a greater medium through greater loving power and lovableness than through lesser. Therefore, there is incarnation, by reason of which a greater love is a greater medium, between greater uncreated loving power and greater created lovableness.

*On Will, End & Incarnation.*

The divine will loves the end of the creature, for if it did not love it, it would not have created it for any end, or it would have created it against its end, which is impossible. Therefore, the divine will loves the end of the creature, which end it loves with the magnitude of its goodness: therefore it is necessary that in the loved end there be great goodness. Therefore, the end of the creature is loved in a greater degree of created goodness, since it is so that greatness has a greater concordance with greater goodness than with lesser. Therefore, there is incarnation according to the consequence of that which has been said.

*On Will, Greaterness &*
*Incarnation.*

A greater will can love more than a lesser, and a greater will is more lovable than a lesser: therefore, incarnation is proven according to the consequence of this process, since it is so that if there is incarnation, one created will is in greater created lovableness than any other created will. And in this step is signified the answer, which can be made according to truth against a very general objection, which is made against incarnation according to the method of our proof process. And this step is very useful and subtle to understand:

*On Virtue, Equality, and*
*the Incarnation.*

Divine wisdom and will relate virtuously to greater creability. Wisdom relates to greater creability, which can be understood as that which ought to exist from a Deified creature: because wisdom cannot understand a greater creature in magnitude of goodness and virtue: And just as wisdom relates to greater creability through the incarnation, so too does the will, since it is such that it relates as virtuously to the object as wisdom. Therefore, there is an incarnation, since greater creability is loved by the divine will: for if it were not, the divine will would not have rest in the created object through greater creability as wisdom does, and wisdom would be virtuous in its apprehension and will vicious, which is impossible and contrary to the equality in which they relate in receiving the greaterness of creation.

Lesser virtue is not as principiated by the divine principle as greater virtue. And this is because to the virtue of God pertains better a greater principiability of virtue than a lesser one. *On Truth, Glory, and the Incarnation.*

Truth and glory are against falsehood and punishment, and to the extent that truth and glory are against punishment and falsehood, so too are they in a magnitude of goodness. Therefore, there is an incarnation, so that men can be more contrary with glory and truth to punishment and falsehood, and be in a magnitude of goodness: because if there is an incarnation, it is in such a great magnitude of goodness that no creature can be in a greater magnitude of goodness. And through that magnitude of goodness, men can better be against punishment and falsehood with glory and truth, than they would be if there were not the magnitude of goodness which is through the incarnation. To which magnitude of goodness God would be contrary with punishment and falsehood, if the incarnation did not exist.

*On Truth, Difference, and*
*the Incarnation.*

It is a truth that there is a difference between God and creature, and inasmuch as that difference exists, it is in truth, and truth in it: and so that that existence of difference in truth and of truth in difference may be in greater knowability and lovability, it is necessary for God to be incarnate, without which incarnation the existence of the aforesaid difference would not be in such great knowability and lovability, and God would be contrary to the magnitude of goodness. *De Veritate, minoritate, & Incarnatione.*

The closer truth is to minority, the further it is from the majority of magnitude and goodness. Conversely, the closer it is to the majority of magnitude and goodness, the further it is from minority. Therefore, the incarnation exists so that created truth may be in its majority of magnitude and goodness, far from the minority of magnitude and goodness. And God would fail truth, since He would not place it in a greater magnitude of goodness, which defect is impossible.

*De Gloria, differentia, & incarnatione.*

So that glory may be far from contrariety, it has within itself the difference of the glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorifying, which subjects are in concordance with themselves, with which concordance glory can be against contrariety, since it is so that concordance and glory are contrary to contrariety. Therefore, glory is against contrariety with difference, with which it is more contrary to contrariety, according as difference is in greater concordance. Therefore, the incarnation exists so that there may be a greater concordance of the uncreated glorifier and the created glorifiable in the act of glorifying, and that through greater concordance, glory may be with difference in greater concordance against contrariety.

*De Gloria, concordantia, & incarnatione.*

Glory is contrary to punishment, and concordance to contrariety. Therefore, glory and concordance have concordance against contrariety and punishment. And contrariety and punishment have concordance against glory and concordance, and thus there are two concordances and two contrarieties. And the more glory and concordance are in a greater magnitude of goodness, the more they are contrary to punishment and contrariety. Therefore, the incarnation exists so that glory and concordance may be more contrary to contrariety and punishment, overcome by glory and concordance with a greater magnitude of goodness, with which they conquer, if there is incarnation. And if there is no incarnation, they do not have that with which they can conquer the greater magnitude of the evil of punishment and contrariety.

*De Gloria, principio, & incarnatione.*

The derived principle in glory and its nature joined with the nature of glory is derived in a greater magnitude of goodness, if the nature of glory is uncreated. Therefore, the incarnation exists so that the created derived principle may be derived in a greater magnitude of goodness. And if there is no incarnation, God, who is glory, fails the greater principability, He Himself existing through glory with greater principiativity, which defect is impossible, by which impossibility the incarnation is proven.

*On Difference, Concordance, &*
*Incarnation.*

IT is the magnitude of power that different natures in a hypostasis concord without contrariety, provided that the hypostasis itself is from them. Therefore, there is incarnation: through which divine and human nature in one hypostasis concord to such an extent that the natural course does not resist the union, which it has with divine nature above its own nature, nor does the excellence of divine nature resist itself in the union which it makes with human nature, which is lowest in nobility, and this is by reason of the great concordance which divine power has in the magnitude of concord. Which magnitude of concordance it could not have, so great, without incarnation.

*On Difference, Principle, &*
*Incarnation.*

BETWEEN one principle and another there is a difference, just as the Father who is one active principle, and the Son who is another passive principle, and the Holy Spirit who is similarly a passive principle from both. And all these three principles are one common principle, which is the principle, creator, and creatable creature, and to create is from both if there is incarnation, because in incarnation there is creating from the essence of the creator and the creature, just as to substantiate, which is from the essence of the form and matter of a substance. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that divine power may be great in creating and originating, in which without incarnation it could not be so great.

*On Difference, Medium, &*
*Incarnation.*

BETWEEN God and creature there is a difference, and to create is in the middle, nevertheless to create is not of the essence of the creator, but is of the creatable: just as the figures which a seal makes in wax, which are of the essence of the wax, but not of the essence of the seal. Therefore, to create is not a great medium between God and creature according to comparison, as if it were of the essence of the creator and the creature: just as to generate, which is of the essence of the generating and the generable. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that there may be a great medium in the difference between creator and creature, which indeed is great in magnitude of power, inasmuch as it is one trunk from divine and human nature through creating and incarnating.

***On Concordance, Principle, & Incarnation.***

Between the principle and that which can be principled there is agreement, for indeed, to agree is in the magnitude of the lover and the beloved, according to which the originating (principle) is great, and that which can be principled, similarly in originating and in loving. Whence, since there is concordance between the creator and the creatable, the originating and that which can be principled, the lover and the beloved: it is necessary that there be incarnation, so that magnitude can extend itself into a great agreement of the concordant and the concordable, the originating and that which can be principled, and the lover and the beloved. Magnitude could not have this extension without incarnation.

***On Concordance, Means, & Incarnation.***

In concordance, the concordant, the concordable, and to agree behave in such a way, just as in love, the lover, the beloved, and to love (behave). Therefore, concordance is the means between the concordant and the concordable, and inasmuch as the concordant and the concordable relate to great loving, the concordant is great in loving and in love. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that the agreement of God and creature may be in great loving, and in such a great way that it cannot be in a greater (way), so that magnitude may not fall short of the greater degree of concordance and love, and of agreeing and loving.

***On Concordance, End, & Incarnation.***

The end of the concordant, and the concordable, and of agreeing. And the end of agreeing is the agreed-upon (state), for indeed, this agreed-upon (state) is in the magnitude of love and of loving, according to the magnitude of love which the concordant and the concordable have in agreeing and loving. Therefore, there is incarnation, in which the hypostasis is agreed upon through agreement with the magnitude of loving, through the concordant, creating, and loving (one), the concordable, creatable, and lovable (one). And such an agreed-upon (state) requires a greater end, which can exist between God and creature through agreeing to love, and to complete.

***On Concordance, Greater Degree, & Incarnation.***

The divine will loves the concordance of God and creature in that greater degree in which power can make it concordant. And it does this so that wisdom in concordance may know how to love as greatly as to understand. Whence, since wisdom knows that a greater concordance can exist through incarnating, it is necessary that the will love a greater concordance, which it could not love, if it were to dislike incarnating.

***On Concordance, Equality, & Incarnation.***

The more concordance has equal essential concretes in love, the greater equality it has between agreeing and loving. Therefore, there is incarnation, so that there can be a great concordance between agreeing and loving, and so great that the magnitude of the love of concordance may not fall short of the greater magnitude of equality, which can exist between agreeing and loving according to the comparison of both creator and creature.

Less loving in greater concordance could not exist, nor even less agreeing in greater love, without incarnation. And so that a created being may love less in greater uncreated concordance, and a created being may agree less in greater uncreated love, it is necessary that there be incarnation, so that a created being may love more in greater created and uncreated concordance, and a created being may agree more in greater love, and in uncreated concordance.

On Principle, Medium, & Incarnation.

No created principle can come to an end without a medium: for if it could come to an end without a medium, the created principle would be the same as its end, and thus God would not be its end, which is impossible. And in this passage is recognized what the nature of sin is in humans, who love themselves more than God. Hence, since a created principle relates to its end through a medium, according to how great the end is, it relates to a great medium, and according to how great the medium is, it relates to a great end. Therefore, incarnation exists so that a created principle can relate through a greater medium to a greater end: but this could not be, if incarnation did not exist, without which incarnation a greater end would be lacking to a greater principle, and to the medium according to its nature, which is impossible.

On Principle, End & Incarnation.

From a greater end follows a greater principle, and from a greater principle a greater end. Therefore, incarnation exists so that this conjunction can be, namely, that if there is incarnation, through it there is created greatness in the beginning of the world and in the end: for above incarnation there cannot be creation in a greater principle and in the end, for if it were, it could be sustained and magnified in a greater nature than in the divine, which is impossible.

On Principle, Greatness &
Incarnation.

A greater principle that God can initiate in creating, He can initiate in incarnating, namely, in initiating a creature in Himself, and in Himself sustaining and uniting it. Therefore, incarnation exists so that God through it can satisfy a greater initiation, which He could not satisfy without incarnating.

On Principle, Equality &
Incarnation.

Without incarnation, God could not equalize in magnitude of goodness the created principle and the created end: since it is so that naturally in creatures the end is nobler than the principle: just as dwelling, which is a nobler end than initiating a room, and living than eating. Therefore, incarnation exists, so that in it, and through it, the created principle and the created end can have equality in magnitude of goodness, which they had in human nature, which God assumed. Which equality is indeed the end and principle of all other created equalities. And in this passage is recognized the manner according to which God, through incarnation, naturally exalted all creatures through the equality of end and principle.

**On the principle of minority &**
**Incarnation.**

Since the world was created from nothing, and in nothing there is nothing, it was created from the greatest minority from which it could be created. Therefore, its real principle was produced and created from the greatest minority. Therefore, Incarnation exists, so that the real principle produced from the greatest minority may be produced to a greater greatness. And this could not be, if God were not incarnate: because through Incarnation, the created principle is produced to a greater greatness of the end. And if there were no Incarnation, the world would have been produced from the greatest minority to an end sustained in a lesser greatness.

**On the Intermediate End & Incarnation.**

Between a greater means and a greater end, there must be a proportion in the magnitude of virtue: the world is created for some end to which the means must be proportioned, so that through that principle the world may have rest in the end. Therefore, it is necessary that Incarnation exists, because through it a proportioned means is between the end of the world and the principle, inasmuch as it suffices for the useful created good, that one of its parts be conjoined with the divine good, and it suffices for the useful created magnitude, that one of its parts be conjoined with the divine magnitude. And the same for universal created duration, that one of its parts be conjoined with eternity, and so for other primary forms. But this could not be, if there were no Incarnation, without which uncreated virtue would be lacking to created virtue, which defect is impossible.

**On the Means, greatness &**

The means being placed in a greater virtue, the principle and the end are placed in a greater virtue. **On the Means, equality &**
**Incarnation.**

Therefore, Incarnation exists, through which the created means is equal with the created principle, and the created end, these being equal in Incarnation. Which indeed minority of the means, and of the principle ascends to the equality of the end.

*On the End, Equality & Incarnation.*

*On the End, Lesser State &*
*Incarnation.*

The end of a horse is lesser than that of a knight, because the end of a horse is military service, and the end of a knight is justice and peace, as signified in the Imperial Tree. It is therefore signified that the entire created universe is for a lesser end, and that some of its parts are for a greater end: because if the entire created universe were for a greater end than any of its parts, each of its parts would have its end within itself, in which it would rest, and would have no appetite outside itself, and would be like a horse, which would not be for a knight, nor a knight for justice, nor iron for a knife, and this is impossible. Therefore, one part of the created universe is the end of the whole universe, and so that the entire good created universe may relate to that end. And the same for its parts. Therefore, incarnation is, without which no part of the universe could be the end of the entire created universe: because, being lesser than the created universe, it would not be worthy of such great greatness, just as a part is lesser than its whole.

...other primary forms, which all creatures, according to the natural course, ascended to greater virtue through incarnation. And if there is no incarnation, there is common utility and virtue in privation. Therefore, incarnation exists so that the creator may not fail the greater community, virtue, and utility of goodness, magnitude, and other primary forms.

*Concerning Greaterness, Lesser-ness & Incarnation.*

Creator and greaterness have concordance, and creature and lesser-ness. Therefore God is greater than creature, and between creator and creature there cannot be equality, whence when God created the world according to his nature, he first had himself to create it in a greater magnitude of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, and will, glory, virtue, and truth, end, means, beginning, equality, difference, and concordance, than in a lesser one: for if he had related himself to the lesser-ness of forms before the greater-ness, he would have related himself to creation against his nature, which is impossible. This world is created by reason of greater greaterness, magnitude, goodness, and the rest, to which greater greaterness it could not have been created if God had not been incarnated.

*Concerning Equality, Lesser-ness & Incarnation.*

Lesser equality is in the egg than in the hen, because the hen is the end of the egg, and is in a greater magnitude of goodness and virtue than the egg: but if the egg were the end of the hen, the ends would be reversed, so that the egg would be for the hen and the hen for the egg, and both ends would be in a circle, and equal in lesser-ness, and the end would not have a subject in which it would exist with greaterness through the magnitude of goodness and virtue, which is impossible and against the natural course. Therefore the hen is in a nobler end than the egg. And because the hen is originated from the egg, it is necessary that there be some other end greater in magnitude of goodness and virtue than the hen, and so successively from degree to degree, and from end to end, and from lesser-ness to greater-ness up to one supreme created end which is the end of all ends of the creator. Which end indeed could not exist without incarnation, because without incarnation they could not have such great goodness of magnitude and virtue, which would suffice to be the end of all created things. Therefore, incarnation exists, without which in all created things there would be a circle equal in lesser-ness and without the greaterness of an end, like the circle of the egg and the hen, as has been said.

*Concerning the Fruit of the Tree of Jesus Christ.*

We consider the fruit of this tree in four ways, the first is through recreation, the second is through exaltation, the third through manifestation, the fourth through deification. Recreation is, as has been proven in the apostolic tree. Therefore, the recreation of the entire human race is the fruit, from which all blessed saved ones live. And that fruit is sustained in divine and human nature, in which the saved gather the fruit of life, without which all those were dead who had deviated from the end for which they had been created, to which they returned because of the fruit,

[Left column]

ways, namely according to dignities,
according to substance, according to
divine persons, according to generation and
spiration, and according to the negation
of accidents, according to the proof
of divine productions, and according to
completion without any defect.

[Right column]

consider the dignities of God as the roots of the
tree. And by substance, we consider the
trunk, namely the divine essence and
nature. And we consider the personal
properties in the likeness of branches.
And we consider generation and spi-
ration in the likeness of boughs.

On the Dignities of God.

WE call the Dignities of God His essential goodness, greatness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth, glory, and the distinction of persons, and their concordance, beginning, middle, end, and equality. [Left Column]

when the divine substance is touched by its reasons, it responds to those reasons: however, we do not say that the reasons are parts, that is, that they respond according to their reality and numerality in the touch, so to speak, in the interior production or in the exterior influence which it makes to creatures: for if the substance is touched under the reason of goodness, insofar as it is good, it responds to goodness and produces good, so that goodness may have in it its fount and fruitfulness, and abundance. And when it is touched by greatness, the substance responds as great, and produces great, so that greatness may have its fount and fruitfulness in that touch: and so for others. Therefore, in that substance, the one who responds is the Father producing the Son: and because He is touched by goodness, He produces Him from goodness: and because He is touched by greatness, He produces Him from greatness, and from His own goodness and greatness. Therefore the Son is produced good and great, and is good from goodness, and great from greatness. And because He is produced from all goodness and from all greatness, there remains with the Father one and the same goodness, and one and the same greatness, and the same is true for eternity and others. When the divine substance is touched by good people, who do good works for the love of our Lord, divine goodness touches the substance: which substance, which is God, responds through its goodness to created goodness by infusing the grace of goodness. And the same when it is touched by greatness, insofar as people do great and many good things for our Lord, greatness touches the divine substance, and the substance responds by infusing to its servants

[Right Column]

great and many good things. And the same for eternity and the rest. And when evil people touch the substance by doing evil, justice touches the substance, and the substance in turn touches evil people with vengeance, inflicting upon them the evil of punishment. And if the evils are great, justice multiplies the punishments. And in this passage it is understood how God responds to the just and to sinners, according as He is touched by superior and inferior reasons. The divine substance is insensible: because it is not of corporeal things, and it is unimaginable, because it has no circular, quadrangular, or triangular figure, nor does it have any condition by which it can be sensed substantially or accidentally: since it is infinite and eternal: nor is the substance composed of parts, nor of any other thing. For an eternal and infinite being, and one that has no accident in itself, cannot be composite, and especially since it is pure simplicity, and in pure simplification, one simple person, who is the Father, produces from His whole simplicity another person, who is the Son; and the same holds for the Holy Spirit. Therefore no substance that is simple, and in which there is simplifying, eternizing, and infinitizing, can be composite, since simplicity and composition are contrary.

About the Divine Persons of the Divine Tree.

**B**RANCHES of the divine tree are personal properties: namely, paternity, filiation, and passive spiration, and they are in the substance according to the nature of dignities, and the substance is sustained in them, according to

--- Page 358 ---
344 [tab] The Divine Tree.

[Column 1]

according as the essence is sustained in its essential concretes. And from these branches, so to speak, we propose to treat in this manner, namely, in applying dignities to each personal property according to its conditions and the nature of each person, and also to show the threefold number of persons. And this we do for well explaining this tree, although we have spoken quite sufficiently about the Trinity in the apostolic tree.

*On Divine Paternity.*

God is good, and inasmuch as his goodness is the reason for him to do good, we call [it] good: to do good, to produce good. God is disposed to doing good. And because his greatness is the reason for him to do great [things], we call [it] great: to do, to produce great [things]. And this manner of speaking we maintain throughout this whole discussion. God, who is great, is disposed to producing great [things], and thus the substance responds equally to two reasons in producing great good. That great good he cannot produce from another, but from himself: for

--- Page 359 ---
**The Divine Tree.** [Page number] **345**

[Left Column]
reasons require. And because between the producer and the produced, which are at the summit of reasons, there must be greater proximity, and participation, concord, nature, and love: it is necessary that it be by generation, because another production which would not be by generation, could not suffice for the requirements of reasons. Therefore, paternity is proven, by which we understand the first branch of this tree. God is good: and His goodness is to Him a reason, that He should make good, and if God did not respond to reason, reason would be idle, and He Himself would be idle, and power would fail the response, and greatness to goodness, and end, truth, and glory, power, wisdom, and will would fail goodness and the common substratum, and if He made the response only in a created subject and not in the uncreated, He makes the response externally and not internally, and infinity and eternity would fail the reasons, and conversely, which would be evil, and against goodness, and against all reasons, which is impossible. Therefore the response is within the uncreated substance, and it is through the production of the producer and the produced. In the substance of millet, which is in a very small quantity of greatness, of goodness, goodness is a reason to the natural agent, that it should produce good from that substance, and greatness similarly is a reason to the natural agent, that from that substance it should produce great good. And if the substance is in the earth, and has conditions which are suitable for the requirements, production and response follow, and it makes multiplication, which is good and great: inasmuch as from a grain of millet a tree is produced, which has the conditions which we spoke of concerning a vegetative tree. Hence, since it is more proper for God to produce great good, because He Himself is greater good,

[Right Column]
than to produce lesser good: and for millet it is more proper to produce lesser good than greater, because in it there is little good: nevertheless it produces greater good than it is itself, inasmuch as it actually produces a tree with many branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruit: how much more God, who is great, infinitely good: inasmuch as as Father, He produces a Son equal to Himself, according as reasons require.

*On Divine Filiation.*

Filiation is the second branch of this tree: and it is second, because reasons have precedence according to nature to the producer, than to the producible according to the order of production: nevertheless we do not say, that in that anteriority there is time, nor motion, nor greater nobility of one person than another: and this filial property is thus under reasons by way of passion: just as the paternal property is by way of action, namely, goodness is a reason to the good, that it should produce good: and thus reason relates in two ways to the common substratum, because in one way it relates to it by action, and in another way by passion: so to speak. Therefore the common substratum responds in two ways by reason of goodness: because in one way it relates as an agent, and in another as a patient: and inasmuch as it relates as an agent, it relates as a bonifier: and inasmuch as it relates as a patient, it relates as bonifiable. And because greatness is in that reason, it makes the bonifier to be great: and it makes the bonifiable to be great. Therefore the bonifier, because it is touched by greatness: produces from itself, and from its goodness, good-

346 Divine Tree.

[Column 1]
benefited: because if he did not produce himself from himself, he would not be greatly benefited, nor would he have substance in which he would have great action. And in this production, eternity is the reason, inasmuch as it makes the benefactor and the benefitable endure, similarly also in this, distinction is the reason, so that the benefactor may be eternally distinct from the benefitable, and the benefitable from him, to such an extent that one is not the other: and this eternally, so that eternity may make the distinction endure. Also, power is the reason that the benefactor can be distinct from the benefitable, and the benefitable from the benefactor, and that the benefactor can eternally produce the benefitable, the benefited: and to this concur wisdom, will, etc., according to what has been said about magnitude, eternity, power, therefore filiation is a personal property through all reasons: which relate to it passively, just as to the paternal property actively. And in this step it is recognized that every dignity in one way is a reason through action, and in another through passion. However, we do not say that the reasons relate to passion materially: since it is so, that they themselves are simple forms, and not multiple, but one is another in number, according to what has been said in the process of dignities. And just as goodness is one twofold reason, inasmuch as it relates in two ways to the supposit, as has been said: so one and the same form relates in two ways to the common supposit: so that it is forming and formable: like light from light, and God from God, with the duality of form sustained in the persons, and the unity of form in the common supposit, therefore form is from form and not from matter, nor from material passion. The Son is benefited

[Column 2]
and benefitable: he is benefited, so that he does not remain in potency, and that he is complete in pure act: and he remains benefitable, so that the dignities may be reasons in eternity for the eternally producing and producible, namely the Father and the Son. And the Father, although the Son is producible, adds nothing to the Son, after the Son is eternally produced, and produced from eternity and infinity, and from all other forms. Nor does the Father add any thing in Himself, because in infinite and eternal substance there is no addition, nor does He cleave, nor diminish, nor divide any thing from Himself, although He produces the Son from Himself. And these such conditions of the Father and the Son require reasons, each from the other, and from the nature of the essence, which is the common substance, which responds to that requirement, according as it is touched by the reasons. And in this step is recognized the manner, according to which idleness cannot exist in divine reasons.

On the Spirable Divine Property.

**I**N creation there is to create, from the creating and the creatable: formally from the creating, and materially from the creatable. Formally from the creating: inasmuch as it produces the creature from nothing, materially: inasmuch as it produces to create from the creatable. However, the creature does not produce to create: for it would be creating, but it is a passive potency, from which to create can be produced, with the potency subject to the act of creating at that time when it is produced by the creator. And some creatures have this order in working artificially: as in the rational tree, in which the artificial agent produces to operate from the operable: just as a smith who, inasmuch as he produces a nail from iron, produces to operate from the operable, which indeed to operate

--- Page 361 ---
**Divine Tree. 347**

[Left Column]
Rarity is not of the essence of the operator, but in creatures according to the natural course it is not so: just as in a plant in which to generate is of the essence of the generating and the generable, the generator producing from itself, and the generable generating then, when an apple or a horse is generated: and so concerning other substances produced naturally. And this order is a mirror, in which the superior natural order is represented: of which it has been spoken in its own branch, and the second of this tree. Therefore, according to what has been said: in this process we wish to inquire into the nature and mode of the third branch according to this mode. Divine goodness is the reason for the good, which is God, in a threefold way, that He acts good: namely, that He produces good. First, inasmuch as it is a reason for Him that He is an agent: and in this way the agent is the Father: second, inasmuch as it is a reason for the Father that He produces the bonificable (that which can be made good), who is the Son: third, inasmuch as it is a reason for the Father and the Son that they produce "bonificare" (to make good), which is the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we do not say "bonificare" that which is the Father and the Son in generating, but "bonificare" which is the Holy Spirit. And from this matter we will speak more amply in the branches of this tree. Goodness therefore relates threefold to the good, which corresponds to reason threefold: inasmuch as in this response there is a singular number, and a dual number, and a ternary number. Singular: inasmuch as one is the Father, another is the Son, another is the Holy Spirit. Dual: inasmuch as one is the Father, and another is the Son, and the Father and the Son are one "bonificare" of both: just as one is the generating of both. Ternary: inasmuch as the Father relates to the Son, and the Son to the Father under the reason of making good equally, because goodness is an equal reason for both: and because the Son does not

[Right Column]
make good the Father, the Father and the Son relate equally to another "bonificare" (making good), which is to spirate, in which they respond to goodness by spirating the Holy Spirit, who is the third person: as has been said: and we also wish to declare better according to this mode, which is the third person. When a smith makes a nail, he moves the hammer before the nail. Therefore, he relates to working before the nail is worked: it follows then that the working of the instrument is of the worker and the workable. But in divine persons it is not so, because if the Father related to spirating before, or to spirate before the Son, spirating would be an instrument: just as the working of an instrument is in smithing, and the "bonificare" of spirating itself would be an instrument, and it would not be of the essence of the Son: just as the working of the smith, which is not of the essence of the nail. Therefore, the Father relates to the Son, and the Son to the Father, and according to this respect of both, and an equal respect under the reason of goodness, both relate to spirating in spirating the Holy Spirit, who is the third person, inasmuch as it is consonant with the antecedent, which is the respect of the Father and the Son, and equally in the response to goodness under the reason of "bonificare" or "bonificandi" (making good). And in this passage can be understood the error in which the Greeks are, who do not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, but only from the Father. According to the example we gave of goodness in inquiring into the third person, it can be said of magnitude, eternity, power, and the rest, because all dignities are reasons communicating threefold: just as magnitude, which is a reason in the magnificent (magnifying), and in the magnificable (that which can be magnified), and in "magnificare" (to magnify), and this same through the magnificent, and through the magnificable, and through "magnificare", and this same concerning the magnificent

*On Generation & Spiritation.*

Generation and spiration are branches of this tree, because these branches are signified according to the branches of the rational and angelic tree, in which we propose to maintain the method we held in the branches: namely, just as we placed the subjacency and sub-entry of the acts of the dignities under the branches, so we propose to submit those same acts under generating, and spirating, and understanding, and loving, namely under generating through understanding, and under spirating through loving, or through love.

*On Generation.*

Divine wisdom requires its fruitfulness and fount-like nature from the wise one, who is God: and it touches Him in a threefold manner, according to that which is the intellective, intelligible, and understanding reason. And the wise one, who is touched by reason, responds as understanding, intelligible, and understanding: and then understands Himself. And because He understands Himself, He is understanding; and because He understands Himself, He is intelligible; for if He were not intelligible, He could not understand Himself. Therefore, He understands Himself, and has understanding within Himself: without which there could be no intellect, nor understanding, nor intelligible. Therefore, He makes a response to wisdom according to His own property and the nature of that [wisdom], and of the respondent touched by it. To the response which the wise one makes to the reason of wisdom, all dignities equally concur with their acts, which in that touch require their fruitfulness, fount-like nature, and nature: just as goodness, which requires that that understanding be good: so that in it there may be to make good, and magnitude requires that it be great: so that in it there may be

[Column 2]

to magnify: and eternity requires that it be eternal, so that in it there may be to eternalize, and so concerning the other acts, and because to understand and to make good are in the response the one making good, and the one capable of being made good, from which is to make good, and because in the response there is to magnify, there are in it the one magnifying and the one capable of being magnified, from which is to magnify. And because in the response there is to eternalize, there are in it the one eternalizing and the one capable of being eternalized, from which is to eternalize, etc. In understanding there are the one making good, the one capable of being made good, and to make good. The one making good is understanding, and does not make itself good, because it is already good; nevertheless, the understanding one, who is making good, understands itself. And at this point, distinction is present, and generation and production begin to be: nevertheless, we do not say that it begins in time, but in the nature of distinction and response, to such an extent that the one making good and the understanding one are one generative, bonificative, and intellective property. And the distinction is, in that the intellective one, through the bonificative property, does not make itself good: but understands itself. And in that it must remain one supposit with the bonificative one, the bonificative one makes itself good in another, and thus the Word is conceived, which is the Son, and the fruitfulness of goodness remains, and the fruitfulness of wisdom, and to make good and to understand are in the branch which we call generation or the generation. God understands Himself with magnitude: but does not magnify Himself: because He is already great: and so that to magnify may be as great as to understand, to magnify passes into another through understanding, and so that it may be equal to understanding itself. And at this point, distinction is present, so that to magnify may be as great as to understand. And for the existence of distinction and equality, there is generation and pro-

God understands Himself, and it is necessary that He understand the concordance between the understood, the intelligible, and understanding: because if concordance were lacking, He would have nothing by which He would be removed from contrariety: just as by goodness by which He is removed from malice, and by greatness from smallness: and so for others: therefore it is necessary that concordance exist between the intelligent, the intelligible, and understanding. God understands Himself, and cannot understand Himself without the intelligent, the intelligible, and understanding. And thus understanding can be close to ignorance, insofar as it is not of the nature of a principle: which proximity is impossible. And because God is the principle, as has been proven: He does not originate Himself, inasmuch as He is the originator, and because originating must be equal to understanding itself, it is necessary that originating pass from the originator to the originable, and remain between both: and this cannot be done without the help of distinction, which exists between the principle, the originator, and the originable, which must exist between the intelligent and the intelligible.
