That in God there is no habit.

**I**N God there is memory, intellect, and will, and we say that He has memory, inasmuch as He represents to His intellect how much He can do concerning goodness, greatness, and eternity: as His will wills, and His intellect understands. Therefore, that representation which is made in eternity by memory to the intellect is not according to an accidental habit: because accidental habits do not represent in eternity but in time. Therefore, God's memory cannot be an accidental habit, nor is it properly said to be a habit, but a pure act, since its representation is in eternity. And the same is true of the divine intellect and of His will, which receive their objects in eternity. Therefore, the divine intellect, and likewise His memory and will, do not attain extrinsic things which belong to the created universe in past, present, or future time, since they attain them in eternity: but because some created things are in one time, and others in another, the divine will wills that Martin be before Peter his son. And the same is true of contingencies, which are according to the natures of creatures and their dispositions, and contingencies are not in divine wisdom, will, and memory: because those (divine attributes) attain to eternity, and according to the freedom of the divine will, power, etc., and according to the natures, properties, and orders of created subjects existing under contingencies.

That in God there is no assituation.

**P**he Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the same is true of the Holy Spirit, without accidental assituation: because in them there is no circular, triangular, or quadrangular figure, nor length, breadth, or depth, since it is so that the divine substance is spiritual and infinite. Therefore, position, as it is understood in creatures, is by no means understood in God, but according to how He is in creatures, and creatures are in Him, the situation of the divine persons is signified to the human intellect, so that it may be able to have knowledge of them: just as in the will of Martin, who loves his Son, in which understanding is situated in lovingness and lovability: so also, and much better, is the Holy Spirit between the Father and the Son, and the Son is in the Father, inasmuch as He is from the Father, and inasmuch as they are one essence, one is in the other: just as goodness, which is situated in its essential benefactive, capable of being benefited, and act of benefiting, in which it does not yield the figure of breadth, length, and depth, so is the divine essence in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit: yet so that it does not yield divisibility of itself, but in one way it is in the Father, and in another in the Son, and in another in the Holy Spirit: it is in the Father, as Father; in the Son, as Son; in the Holy Spirit, as Holy Spirit.

God is eternity, and an infinite and unmoving substance: because nothing infinite can be moved, nor can things mobile or moved by their nature exist, since they are as great as substance. And we call natures the conditions of substance, and its real principles, and their acts. Therefore, time cannot exist in God: but because God cannot use mobile creatures without time, He acts concerning them with time: just as a smith who works with iron with the heat of fire and with shears, and with a hammer: and just as a smith who makes a nail outside his hands, so God, outside His eternity, originated the world in time, and moves creatures from one place to another, and from one state to another, so that time does not enter into eternity. Therefore, when God created the world, He did not originate any novelty in Himself: namely, novelty stood originated outside eternity, that novelty being sustained in time by reason of a principle without which principle the beginning of the creature could not be originated in time, nor could the creature have that in which it could be produced.

**That there is no place in God.**

Place cannot exist in God, since it is so that He Himself is an infinite substance, which cannot be terminated in place: because if it were terminated in place, it would not be infinite. And it is necessary that it be infinite, so that its amiability may suffice for its great capacity for being loved: to which it could not suffice, if it were finite. It is also necessary that it suffice for infinite generability and spirability, so that the acts of dignities may be infinite. Therefore, God is not terminated in place, indeed He is outside place. He is also in place: because if He were not essentially in place, behold—

[Right Column]

—namely, in the place of a stone and of the sea, and so concerning other substances up to the eighth sphere, His essence would be terminated: therefore, God is essentially in every place, and presentially, powerfully, and wisely, and so concerning His other conditions. And because He Himself is outside place and inside place without any quantity, place is situated and comprehended in Him. Therefore, a certain sinner, when he had sinned mortally, asked where he should go, or in what place he could flee from the justice of God, of which he had great fear: because if he went to the east, God is there; if to the west, similarly; and the same for the south and the north, for hell and heaven. Therefore, that wise man said that he should go to the mercy of God with hope, contrition, confession, and satisfaction, in which mercy, indeed, there is no wrath of God.

**Concerning Flowers, namely, Divine Productions.**

**T**hrough flowers we consider divine productions, which we have proven, and now wish to prove, so that we may better declare the manner according to which the Most High Trinity can be proven with the first forms, and divine productions by reason of the acts of forms, which acts are indeed necessary, and from which acts they cannot cease, so that they exist in completing and producing. And in this process, we propose to make sections concerning the forms of this book, with which we will prove the divine productions, which are through generation and spiration.

On Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, & Will.

Divine will loves the greatness of goodness and eternity: it would not be able to love the greatness of goodness, if in goodness it did not love the good-maker, the good-receivable, and the act of making good, which are of its essence: nor would it be able to love the greatness of eternity, if it did not love in eternity the eternalizer, the eternalizable, and the act of eternalizing, which are of its essence: it would also not love the greatness of eternity, if it did not love the distinction between the good-maker, the good-receivable, and the act of making good, through the nature of understanding and loving, so that eternity could make one to be the good-maker, another the good-receivable, and another the act of making good. And that it makes all three to be and to endure as one essence of goodness, one nature of deity, and one common substance: which is goodness

great, and that in its magnitude eternity and goodness can have rest.

*On Goodness, Magnitude, Eternity & Difference.*

Without distinction of the Benefactor, the Benefitable, and the act of Benefiting, eternity could not be great in goodness: because without distinction it would be idle in itself: and thus it would be small, and it would be a smallness of goodness, since it is so: that without any distinction no operation can exist. Therefore, there is distinction in goodness: namely, between the Benefactor, the Benefitable, and the act of Benefiting, so that eternity can exist in them: because it is a great magnitude of eternity that it causes one to be the Benefactor, another the Benefitable made good, by eternalizing in goodness: and that the made good and the Benefitable remain eternally one produced, and producible, eternalized and eternalizable.

*On Goodness, Magnitude, Eternity, & Concordance.*

In goodness, eternity cannot be great without concordance, since it is so that the magnitude of eternity exists: if in goodness it eternally harmonizes the Benefactor and the Benefitable in the act of Benefiting and Producing: for indeed, to produce could not exist without concordance: nor can it exist in privation, inasmuch as great eternity can exist in goodness, in which it cannot be great without concordance.

*On Goodness, Magnitude, Eternity, & Contrariety.*

Goodness and eternity are far from contrariety with concordance:

[Right Column]

so that the remoteness may be great: which is great, because concordance and contrariety are contrary to each other: and because goodness, magnitude, and eternity are concordance in God, goodness and eternity are far from contrariety with the concordance of the Harmonizer, the Harmonizable, and the act of Harmonizing: for without these three they could not be removed from contrariety with concordance: for without them concordance would not have a subject in which it could be sustained. Therefore, goodness and eternity are removed from contrariety with the Harmonizer, the Harmonizable, and the act of Harmonizing: which are of the essence of goodness and eternity: so that they may be more remote from contrariety, namely goodness from malice, and eternity from time, and magnitude from smallness. Therefore, there is production in God: since it is so, that in the Harmonizer, the Harmonizable, and the act of Harmonizing, there cannot be a sustained privation of production, along with that production in eternity.

*On Goodness, Magnitude, Eternity, & Principle.*

If the Originator did not Originate the Originatable from eternity, and in eternity, it could not be great in goodness, and so that it can be great in goodness, it Originates the Originated from eternity, and in eternity. And the same would follow if it did not Originate the Originated from goodness, without which it could not be great in aeviternity. Therefore, the originating Principle, not the Originated, Originates the Originatable Originated from its own eternity and proper goodness. It also Originates it from the unoriginated Principle, so that it may be eternally Originatable and Originated. Magnitude is produced, in which they are by way of production. Therefore a certain inventor said: that inasmuch as a man is noble, and inclines himself to doing evil, his defect is greater than that of another man who is not so noble. Therefore, the goodness of God would be in great defect, and in a greater smallness of magnitude, than any other goodness: if the principle of bonifying, bonifiable, and to bonify eternally and infinitely were idle. Therefore, in divine goodness there is production from bonifying, bonifiable, and to bonify eternally and infinitely: without which it would be in a greater smallness of magnitude than any other goodness.

*Concerning Power, Wisdom, &*
*Will.*

Wisdom knows power and will: therefore power and will are knowable. Will loves power and wisdom, therefore power and wisdom are lovable. And because in God power is so fruitful, and so foundational as wisdom and will, wisdom and will are capable of being made possible through power: just as power is knowable through wisdom, and lovable through will. Therefore wisdom and will are capable of being made possible. They are not capable of being made possible in such a way that they are produced from potentiality into act, since they are eternal: but they are capable of making possible, inasmuch as from them power can produce the possible beloved and understood, which it must be able to produce: and that it produces, so that it is not idle in them, nor concerning them. Therefore there is production in divine things.

*Concerning Power, Wisdom, Will,*
*& Virtue.*

Through power, wisdom can know virtue, and through power, will

[Column 2]

can love it itself, and power cannot produce virtue, because it is already eternal: but virtue can exist through power, and since it can exist through power, it is necessary that power can produce the virtuous from virtue, so that it can do as much in virtue, and from virtue, through acting as through existing, and that the act which it has from virtue in producing, can equalize its making possible in virtue with the understanding of wisdom, and with the loving of will, which objectify that virtue through power, as has been said: which equality power could not have: if it did not produce the virtuous from virtue.

*Concerning Power, Wisdom, Will,*
*& Truth.*

Since wisdom can know truth through power, and will can love it through power, it is necessary that power through itself can make possible truth, and that what it can do concerning truth, be knowable through wisdom, and lovable through will. Therefore it is necessary that power produce from truth the verifiable verified: so that truth may be objectifiable in acting through power to the same extent as through wisdom and will, without which there would be no production: for truth would be knowable through wisdom, and lovable through will: and without production, power would have no action in truth through itself: but wisdom could know it through itself, and will could love it through itself. Therefore there is production, so that making possible, knowing, and loving can equalize themselves in truth.

*Concerning Power, Wisdom, Will*
*& Glory.*

Wisdom has action in glory with understanding: and will has action

*On Power, Wisdom, Will,*
*and Truth.*

Since wisdom can know truth through power, and will can love it through power, it is necessary that power through itself can actualize truth, and that what it can do concerning truth, be knowable by wisdom, and lovable by will. Therefore, it is necessary that power produce a verifiable verified thing from truth: so that truth may be objectifiable in action through power: as through wisdom and will, without which production it would not be: because truth would be knowable by wisdom, and lovable by will: and without production, power would have no action in truth through itself: but wisdom could know it through itself, and will could love it through itself. Therefore, there is production, so that to actualize, to know, and to love can equalize themselves in truth.

*and Glory.*

to originate the knowable, and the lovable by will, and the self-possible; through such an originating, it can be further removed from ignorance, hatefulness, and impossibility. And because it is necessary that there be that by which it is further removed, it is necessary that there be an originating in producing from a principle that which is originated and that which is originable.

*On Power, Wisdom, Will, and the Medium.*

IN wisdom, there can be understanding in the medium between the intellectual and the intelligible; and in will, there can be loving in the medium between the loving and the lovable. Therefore, it is necessary that in power there can be enabling, in the medium between the enabler and the enablable; for if power could relate more to another through another than through itself, namely, that it could relate to the medium in wisdom and will, inasmuch as understanding and loving can exist through power, and power in itself could not relate to the medium, namely, to enabling, which is in the medium between the enabler and the enablable: and because it is impossible that power can be more fruitful and more foundational in another than in itself, it is necessary that in itself it possesses enabling simply and properly, which it could not possess without the production of the producible, the enabling, and the enablable.

*On Power, Wisdom, Will, and the End.*

JUST as the end of wisdom is understanding and to understand, and the end of will is the beloved and to love: it is necessary that the end of power be the enabled and to enable,

[Column 2]

for if power could attain its end in another, and not in itself, it would attain its end through understanding and the intellect in wisdom, and through loving and the beloved in will, inasmuch as the intellectual can have understanding and the intellect through power, and the loving can have loving and the beloved, and power in itself would be nothing, since it would not have potentiality and actualization in itself, which it must have in itself simply by itself, so that it can have its end in itself and rest in it. Therefore, it has the actualized and to enable, and consequently to produce, which must exist of necessity in every substance in which there is enabling and the actualized.

*On Power, Wisdom, Will, and Superiority.*

THAT power which can (act) concerning wisdom and concerning will, is greater than power which can (act) neither concerning wisdom nor concerning will: therefore, it is necessary that there be production in divine things, so that divine power may have that with which it can be greater than all other power. Therefore, it can (act) concerning wisdom and will, inasmuch as the enabler can produce the intelligible from wisdom, and the lovable from will.

*On Power, Wisdom, Will, and Equality.*

IN God, power, wisdom, and will are removed with equality from inequality, since it is so that equality and inequality are contrary. Therefore, in God are equality, power, wisdom, and will, with the equality of understanding, and loving, and enabling, without which they could not have equality; therefore, in God there is enabling.

**On Power, Wisdom, Will,**
**and Inferiority.**

Inferiority is a being near non-being,
to which, namely, non-being is wisdom
near by ignorance, and will
by hating the good, and power by
idleness: therefore, power, and wis-
dom, and will must be removed from in-
feriority, by enabling, understanding, and
loving, so that in the remoteness of inferiority
they may be removed from non-being. And if in the power
of God to enable were not simply,
He would not have that by which He would be removed
from inferiority, nor from non-being by
Himself, from which inferiority, and non-being
He would be removed by another: namely, by
understanding and by loving the good. He would be
therefore by Himself near inferiority,
and non-being: which is impossible, He is
therefore far from inferiority, and from non-being
with enabling. Therefore, in God there is pro-
duction, without which in Him to enable to be
would not be valid, since it is so, that to enable
and to produce are related to each other.

**On Virtue, Truth, and Glory.**

Virtue and vice are contrary, and
truth and falsity, in the same way
glory, and punishment, and they are more contrary
in existing and acting, than in existing
only: namely, that
in virtue there is to make virtuous, and in truth
to make true, and in glory to be glorious, and in
vice to sin, and in falsity to falsify,
and in punishment to torment. And because it is necessary
that God be more contrary
by virtue to vice than any other
being, and by truth to falsity, and by
glory to punishment: it is necessary that in His
virtue there is to make virtuous, and in His truth
to make true, and in His glory to be glorious:
but this could not be without pro-
ducing, which is by making virtuous, veri-
fying, and glorifying.

**On Virtue, Truth, Glory, and**
**Difference.**

God is glory, and is glorious, and
is virtue and virtuous: therefore it is necessary
that He be truth and true, so that truth
may exist in God fundamentally, just as
virtue and glory: for if it were not so, there would follow
a difference between virtue,
glory, and truth: and glory would be
true by accident, and virtue similarly:
which would be vice against virtue, and
punishment against glory, and falsity against
truth, therefore God is truth and
true: just as He is virtue and virtuous, glo-
ry and glorious. True could not
exist without the production of such great vir-
tuous and glorious things, that truth would make
one to be producing, verifying,
making virtuous, and glorifying, and
another capable of being glorified, capable of being made true, and
capable of being made virtuous: who indeed, being capable of being glorified,
capable of being made true, and capable of being made virtuous, is
produced from the glorifier, the verifier,
and the maker of virtue.

**and Concordance.**

and glory could not have con-

they are one and the same in number, they cannot have con-
cordance, since it is so,
that concordance cannot exist without
several things. And if they do not have a real, natural,
and proper, and essential concordance, their con-

...which privation would be a vice against virtue, glory, and truth, and is a punishment against glory, and against truth, and virtue, and consequently is a real, natural, proper, and essential falsehood against truth, virtue, and glory. And since this is impossible: according to which there is privation neither in glory nor in virtue nor in truth, from which would follow vice, falsehood, and punishment: it is therefore necessary that virtue, truth, and glory have concordance, which they cannot have without the production of the concordant, the concordable, and to concord in making virtuous, verifying, and glorifying.

*On Virtue, truth, glory, &*
*contrariety.*

God would not have complete glory, if by any means He were near punishment, nor would He have complete virtue, if by any means He were near vice: nor would He have complete truth, if by any means He were near falsehood. It is therefore necessary that in God there be a real, proper, natural, and essential production, so that in making virtuous He may be far from vice, and in verifying from falsehood, and in glorifying from punishment. This remoteness the virtuous one has, producing from virtue that which is made virtuous, and the true one from truth that which is verified, and the glorious one from glory that which is glorified.

*On Virtue, truth, glory, &*
*principle.*

By glory God is glorious, and by virtue, virtuous, and by truth, *verosus*, which *verosus* is indeed not a word in use, nevertheless it is necessary that we thus

[Column 2]

speak, so that we may be able to say what we understand about divine truth: and the same applies to *principiosus*, so that we may use words with which we can better declare the nature of God and His properties. And because God is a principle, it is necessary that He be *principiosus* through principle, just as He is virtuous through virtue, and *verosus* through truth, and glorious through glory. He could not be *principiosus*, virtuous, glorious without a proper and essential originating, originable, and to originate, which could not exist without producing the originable from the originating, in making virtuous, verifying, and glorifying.

*On Virtue, truth, glory, &*
*medium.*

Without a medium, there cannot be to glorify, to make virtuous, nor to verify, for if they were, they would not be what they are: since it is so, that to glorify is the medium of the glorifier and the glorifiable, and to make virtuous, of the virtuifier and the virtuifiable, and to verify, of the verifier and the verifiable: just as to generate is the medium of the generator and the generable, and to love of the lover and the lovable. There is therefore a medium in glory, and in virtue and truth similarly, and consequently in producing, which is the medium of the producer and the producible, without which producing could not exist in the nature of the medium, nor could to glorify, to make virtuous, and to verify exist from the nature of the medium.

*On Virtue, truth, glory, & end.*

Truth would be virtuous, if it could not suffice for the end, for which it would not suffice if it were not in verifying and concerning verifying: just as glory which would not suffice for the end, if it were not in glorifying and concerning glo-

--- Page 386 ---
372 The Divine Tree.

glorifying. The truth of glory could not suffice without the verifier and the verifiable, namely, the verifier producing from itself that which is verified: because after truth has in itself really, properly, naturally, and essentially the verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying, the end cannot have any defect through truth. Therefore, there is production, which is the rest of completion.

On Virtue, Truth, Glory, and Greatness.

IN glory, there is greater truth, if in it there is the production of the glorious and the act of glorifying, without which it would be necessary that truth in glory be in a lesser state, which lesser state would indeed be a vice against virtue, and a penalty against glory. Therefore, it is necessary that in glory there be the glorifier, the glorious, and the act of glorifying, properly and naturally, so that truth may be greater in glory and not lesser: we call it greater, inasmuch as truth cannot be greater, nor lesser. And this passage is subtle to understand. Therefore, truth in glory is greater, and not lesser: so that it may be in it virtuously and not viciously: it could not be in it virtuously, if it were in it in a lesser state, and not in a greater greatness, in which it is in verifying, producing, glorifying from itself the truly glorious, with true glorifying.

On Virtue, Truth, Glory, and Equality.

IF in glory there is no equality of the glorifier, the glorious, and the act of glorifying, truth would not have that in which it would be sustained in glory: because in glory it could not be sustained in equality, because such sustenance would be vicious, inasmuch as in it there would be a lesser state: since it is so, that in all inequality there must be a lesser state. Therefore, truth in glory is sustained by the equality of the true glorifier, verifier, and the truly glorious, verifiable, and the true act of glorifying and verifying. This sustenance could not exist without natural and essential production.

On Virtue, Truth, Glory, and Lesser State.

IF in the glory of God there is no production of the glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorifying, truth in glory cannot verify anything: because it cannot verify that one is glorious, and another glorifiable. Therefore, truth in glory is without verifying, and consequently glory in truth without glorifying: and in these there is idleness, so to speak, which is vicious against the virtuous, and almost non-existence through a lesser state: which lesser state must exist in all glory and truth, in which there is idleness of glory and truth. And because idleness, a lesser state, and vice cannot exist in the virtue, truth, and glory of God, it is necessary that in God there be production through glorifying, the glorifier, and the glorifiable, and through verifying, the verifier, and the verifiable.

On Difference, Concordance, and Contrariety.

IN every being in which there is no distinction, concordance, nor contrariety, there must be idleness: since it is so, that operation cannot exist without distinction, nor without concordance or contrariety. And because idleness is not opposed to contrariety, it is necessary that in God there be concordance against contrariety, along with the act of concord. Therefore, it is necessary that in God there be concordance

...greaterness concordance could not exist without distinguishing the agreeing, the agreeable, and to agree, without being contrary, diminishing, and depriving. Indeed, which distinguishing could not exist without producing, the producer, and the producible.

*On Difference, concordance, contrariety, & equality.*

No equality can exist without distinction: since it is so that equality cannot exist without multiple things: and the same for concordance and contrariety. And concordance can exist in equality and in inequality, and it can be more remote from contrariety in equality than in inequality: it is necessary that in the nature of God there be equality of the agreeing, the agreeable, and to agree, in which it is necessary that there be concordance of equality, the equalizable, and to equalize: so that divine nature may be equally remote from contrariety, with equality and concordance, from which contrariety it could not be remote without the production of the naturalizer, the naturalizable, and to naturalize, the distinguisher, the distinguishable, and to distinguish: without which there could not be the agreeing, the agreeable, and to agree, the equalizing, the equalizable, and to equalize.

*On Difference, concordance, contrariety, & minority.*

That concordance which is of accidental forms is in minority: and that which is of substantial forms is in greaterness. Therefore, distinction is more remote from contrariety in substantial concordance than in accidental. And the same is true of concordance, which is more remote from contrariety in substantial distinction than in accidental. Therefore, it is necessary that in God there be production: so that His form may have that with which it is remote from contrariety and from minority: from which it could not be remote without the substantial, to distinguish, and to agree.

*On Principle, middle, & end.*

God is the first principle, and the first end, and it is necessary that He be the first principle, with the act of beginning, which is in the middle of the beginner and the beginnable: because without the act of beginning, which is in the middle of the beginner and the beginnable, properly, essentially, and naturally, the end of the principle could not exist in the principle, nor could one and the same essence remain with it, and God would be the principle, in beginning the creature, which would be the end of the beginning, and the first principle would not have the act of beginning from itself: therefore, it would be a beginner by accident, and by another, and not by itself, which is impossible. God is principle and end simply in Himself, and through Himself, since in Him can exist the act of beginning, in the middle of the beginner and the beginnable. Therefore, in God there is production, without which there could not be the act of beginning, in the middle of the beginner and the beginnable.

*On Principle, middle, end, & greaterness.*

If in God there were not the production of the beginner, the beginnable, and to begin: of the perfecter, the perfectible, and to perfect: the act of beginning, and to perfect, could not be in greaterness, in which it is necessary that they be, so that the act of beginning, and to perfect, may not participate with minority, with which they would participate, if there were not a proper, real, essential, and natural production of the beginner, the beginnable, and to begin, of the perfecter

**The Divine Tree.** 375

[Column 1]

of being, of the perfectible, and of perfecting.

*Concerning the Principle, the middle, the end, &*
*equality.*

A Principle, in which the initiator, the originated, and the act of initiating are equally present, is full of perfection, from which the initiator perfects itself, by equally producing from itself the originated, from which, namely the initiator and the originated, the act of initiating equally proceeds, existing in the midst of the initiator and the originated: therefore, it is necessary that in God there be production, without which there could not be the perfection of the principle in the equality of the initiator, the originated, and the act of initiating.

*Concerning the Principle, the middle, the end, &*
*lesser-ness.*

That principle is lesser, in which the originated is not of the essence of the initiator, and this is because the act of initiating is not of the essence of both, nor can it be in the midst of both. And because that principle is in a state of lesser-ness, it cannot exist by itself in perfection, nor have rest in its own nature. And because God is the principle, and in Himself has His perfection, it is necessary that in Him there be production properly and naturally of the initiator, the originated, and the act of initiating: which remain and are in perfection.

*Concerning Greater-ness, equality, &*
*lesser-ness.*

The greater the equality, the more remote it is from lesser-ness, and the lesser it is, the more remote it is from greater-ness. Therefore, it is necessary that in God equality be in the greatest greater-ness, which can exist between the one making equal, the one being made equal, and the act of making equal: so that in that greatest greater-ness it may be more remote from the greatest lesser-ness of the one making equal, the one being made equal, and the act of making equal.

Concerning the Exemplary Tree.

[Decorative Initial A]HE Exemplary Tree contains a recapitulation of the aforementioned trees through examples and proverbs. And similarly, it is divided into seven parts.
The Roots are examples of the roots of the preceding trees.
The Trunk is examples of the trunks of the preceding trees.
The Branches are examples of the branches, etc.
The Boughs are examples of the boughs, etc.
The Leaves are examples of the leaves, etc.
The Flowers are examples of the flowers, etc.
The Fruits are examples of the fruits, etc.

[A large, very faded illustration of a tree. At the base of the tree, several human figures are visible. Within the branches of the tree, there are banners containing text, most of which is illegible due to the fading of the ink. One banner on the right appears to contain the word "Arbor".]

Bbb          Concerning the Tree

--- Page 392 ---
378 Exemplary Tree.

[Woodcut illustration of a tree with blank scrolls and fruits. At the base of the tree are two figures; the one on the left is labeled "Monachus." and the one on the right is labeled "Raymund."]

Concerning the Exemplary Tree.

This tree is divided into seven parts, namely into roots, trunk, branches, boughs, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Indeed, each of these parts is divided into fourteen parts. Just as the first part, which is about the roots of the elemental tree, vegetal, sensual, imaginal, human, moral, imperial, apostolical, celestial, angelic, aeviternal, maternal, Christian, and divine. And the same is true for the second part and the others. And each of the aforesaid seven parts is divided into fourteen parts, so that we may be able to give examples of the natures and modes of trees, according to what their roots, trunks, branches, etc., are, and so that we may have ample material for giving examples, since it is so that in the fourteen aforesaid trees all things are explained or implied.

--- Page 393 ---
**Arbor exemplificalis. 379**

...implied. And through the examples which we will give, doctrine can be had for knowing natural and supernatural secrets. Doctrine can also be had for preaching, and for having moralities, solace, and the friendship of peoples. Also, a universal capacity can be had for understanding many things, and those things which are pleasing to hear. The examples which we will give, we divide into two parts, namely into narratives and proverbs investigated according to the natures of trees. And we propose to follow this process in this tree, and because the matter is great, we cannot proceed according to its magnitude: since we are very occupied with other things, also because people avoid prolixity, and therefore we will speak briefly about this tree. Nevertheless, according to what we will say, we will give doctrine for finding new proverbs and narratives, and how the human intellect can be extended beyond the excessive material of this tree.

*About the Roots of the Exemplary Tree.*

[Large decorative initial V] Just as fire desires, because its heat in water is good, so that its goodness may have great virtue. Therefore water asked air, that it would remember her in her infirmity. And then the Monk asked Raymund, that he would explain that proverb to him. Raymund responded to the Monk saying, that air lay sick from two infirmities. One infirmity it had on account of love, the other indeed on account of sorrow. It had an infirmity on account of love, because it was discontented with the earth, which had action over fire, which it itself loved very much, and it desired that it would be Lord of the earth, which was its enemy. Air had an infirmity on account of sorrow, because it itself felt the dryness, which fire placed in it, which dryness indeed tormented its humidity. Therefore water said to air, that it should remember her in her infirmity, which she was suffering: because fire placed its contrary in it, on account of which air ought to hate fire. And water said this, so that air would be contrary to fire, and would have agreement with her. But air responded to water saying, that it preferred to be sick, and to be a good and loyal friend of that fire, which gave its likeness to it, than to be healthy and to commit any deception or offense against its friend: because no infirmity is so great, as the infirmity which is through betrayal and ingratitude, which makes a man forget the benefits which he received from his Lord. Therefore air said, that it wished to be subject and subordinate to fire its Lord, so that it might have action in water, in which it might show its dominion with greatness of goodness and virtue: because great virtue is the heat of fire, and a great good, that it be Lord of its friend through concord of love, and of its enemy through contrariety. 2. Water wept, and said to air, that it did not know the falsity, which fire was doing to earth, but air asked water, what that falsity was; water responded saying, that fire and earth were making a partnership, and promised each other, that whatever they gained, they would divide and share among themselves, whence it happened, that earth gained iron, but fire gained gold. And when they came to the division and partition of iron and gold, earth said to fire, that it should divide. But earth said this, so that fire would give it gold, because it gives its dryness to it, and also because he who liberally

And meanwhile, while Fire was thus considering, Air wondered that Fire did not respond to the prayers it (Air) made to it (Fire): and said to Fire, that it (Air) knew well that it (Fire) did not love it (Air) very much, since it (Fire) did not quickly respond to the prayers it (Air) had made to it (Fire) in such a way that it (Air) would be obliged to give thanks. But Fire said to Air, that it (Air) did not know how wisdom responded to will. "And how was this?" said Air. "It is told," said Fire, "that Will had a great desire that it might find a certain man whom it had greatly loved: and asked Wisdom to show it the ways by which it might find that man whom it desired to find: so that it might be able to honor and serve him." But Wisdom responded to Will, saying, that it (Will) was making a just request to it (Wisdom), and that it (Wisdom) would gladly show it (Will) the ways by which it might find its beloved and friend: which indeed it (Wisdom) would not show it (Will), if it (Wisdom) knew that Will wished to kill that man, or do him any harm or damage: since it is so, that that man whom Will sought, has done many pleasing things for me (Wisdom).
6. Fire asked Air: "Do you love me as much as water?" Air responded, and said to Fire, that it (Fire) was not asking a just question: and that it (Fire) knew little about the nature of love. Fire said to Air, "And what is the nature of love?" But Air was silent, nor did it (Air) wish to give any answer to Fire: wherefore Fire wondered, because Air did not respond to it (Fire): and it (Fire) asked it (Air) so many times to respond to it (Fire), until Air recounted these words to Fire. It is told, that Will found Wisdom, while it (Wisdom) was going to a certain city, in which was Memory, to which Will was coming,

[Column 2]
desiring to frequently remember its friend. And because Wisdom was leading Anger, which is an enemy of Will, with it (Wisdom), Will did not receive Wisdom well, although it (Wisdom) had shown it (Will) the ways by which it (Will) could find Memory. And when Will had come to Memory, which remembered its friend, they made a great feast, and had great comfort with each other: so much so that Wisdom stood ill-content against Will, which did not make such a great feast and comfort for it (Wisdom) at their meeting as it (Will) did for Memory. And so Wisdom reproached Will before Memory, saying to it (Will), that it (Will) had shown it (Wisdom) little gratitude for the pleasing things and honors which it (Wisdom) had done for it (Will). Will excused itself, saying, that it felt greater pleasure in giving its own likeness, without suffering, than in assuming the likeness of another with effort.
7. Water was going through a certain large grove, in which it (Water) found stone and iron, from which fire comes forth, which it (Water) blasphemed, and to which it (Water) spoke many reproaches: because they (stone and iron) had been the occasion of its (Water's) weakness, when in a pot or shell they (stone and iron) heated it (Water), and took away from it (Water) its (Water's) coldness, which it (Water) greatly loved. But stone and iron responded to water, saying, that Fire had been faulty in giving them (stone and iron) its (Fire's) power. But Water was amazed by those words, and said to them (stone and iron), that it seemed impossible to it (Water) that anything could be faulty in giving power: wherefore it (Water) asked that they (stone and iron) tell it (Water) the manner, according to which Fire was effective, in that it (Fire) gave them (stone and iron) its (Fire's) power. "It is told," said stone and iron, "that a certain herb stood in a certain meadow, which had the power to cure lepers of their infirmity: that herb was shown to a certain leper, from which..."

against the earth, when however air had made a concord between fire and water against the earth, the earth did not want to give its dryness to fire, nor receive the coldness of water, as it had been accustomed to. Therefore, fire and water were against air with the earth, which they placed in the middle of both. And then air did not want to receive heat from fire, nor give its humidity to water, until fire and water had a concord with it against the earth, which did not want to give dryness to fire, nor receive coldness from water. And so fire and water were always in labor when they wanted to have concord, wherefore they greatly wondered, since they were unable to have concord either through earth or through air. And then they asked Saturn if he knew the reason or root, because of which they could not have concord. Saturn said these words, that there was a certain hermit, who was of holy life and conversation, who said to the Angel who guarded him, that he greatly wondered what it could be, that when he himself contemplated God, he had no temptation to commit sin, and immediately when he ceased to contemplate God and to pray, by his own evil will he fell into temptations, and thoughts, and vanities. His Angel truly said to him, that it was no wonder if man is tempted, and thinks vain thoughts, since between God and himself there is no medium that makes them be in concord, namely that man is removed from all nature of sin, vanity, and the contrariety between God and man. And this, said Saturn, air does not have, when you others want to have concord in it against the earth, because you are not removed from the contrariety in which you are, although you wish to have concord in the air. Fire and earth made one daughter in pepper, who was called 'majority', and air and water in the same pepper made another daughter, who was called 'minority'. Both daughters were wives of pepper, which from them generated one son, who killed his Father. And then the tailor cursed the scissors and the needle. But the Monk told Raymond to explain that example to him. Raymond answered him saying. It is narrated that the needle of a certain tailor generated for him one daughter, who was called 'riches', and his scissors generated one daughter, who was called 'honor'. The tailor truly took those two daughters as wives, from whom that tailor generated one son, who at his death did not want to give a small cloth, with which he could have been covered, and they buried him completely naked in spite of riches and honor. Therefore that tailor cursed the scissors and the needle, with which he had gathered riches and had given honor to his son. But the scissors and the needle excused themselves from that curse, saying that they were without fault, because he had placed himself in a lesser share of riches and honor, and his son in a greater share. Therefore it was necessary that his son and he at his death should have had contrariety. Raymond, said the Monk, and what was his son called? Raymond answered saying, that the tailor's son was called 'privation', privation, namely, the end of honor and riches. 26. In pepper, fire is in the majority, and water in the minority. "It is told," said air and earth, "that there was a man who was very rich, and had a wife to whom he said these words: 'I want you to be my lady, and that concerning me and my riches you do your will. Fire in pepper invited air and earth to help it against water, which was equally contrary to it by coldness and heaviness in general, which equality it indeed sought to destroy by destroying the equal proportion which they have in pepper; because, with the equality of both qualities in pepper destroyed, it wanted to destroy water: just as envy, which by destroying the special equality of being loved and lovability, wanted to destroy the charity of two brothers. "And how was this?" said air and earth. "It is told," said fire, "that there was a certain merchant who was very rich, and had two sons, to whom in his life he gave wives, and at the time of his death he ordained in his will that both should equally possess and succeed to the goods which he had left, to such an extent that while they themselves lived, they should not divide those goods. And that merchant did this, so that they might have equal charity towards each other." And then envy considered, how that charity—

[Right Column]
—it could destroy: which said to the firstborn son, that it was not fitting that he should be equal with his brother neither in riches nor in honor, after God made him to be born first; therefore he ought to negotiate with the court that those goods should be divided, and that he should have the greater part of the riches; who responded to envy saying, that he did not know that intention which his father had in the making of his will. "And what intention did your father have," (said envy) "in the making of his will?" who said to it, "Our father killed a certain man of this city, who had one son, who has as much in riches as we others have, and he wanted that we should not divide the goods which he left, so that we might have charity towards each other; and if he had left to me a greater part, and to my brother a smaller part, charity among us would not be in equality, and the enemy could first kill my brother if he were in lesser power, and me after him. And you, envy, from now on do not speak such words to me." 18. It is told, that fire was going on a pilgrimage, and water similarly, who met each other on the way. But fire said to water these words: "In this land there are many knights who are my friends, and who would do for me whatever I wished, to whom I have done many favors and courtesies"; while fire was speaking thus, water knew, according to the words which it said, that it had fear of it. Therefore it knew that it had less virtue and power than it: because if it had had less virtue and power than fire, in that land in which they found themselves, it would have had fear before fire, which it did not have, after fire said those words.

*Of the Proverbs of the Imaginal Trunk.*

Flesh complained about imagination,
which heated it and made it
grow, when it imagined lust.
And imagination complained about
memory, which, when it recalled
lust, made the flesh stir: but
memory complained about will,
which did not make it forget
lust. The goat saw a wolf, which it had
never seen before, and had fear of it.
And a certain man saw his wife combing

jealousy. Betrayal touched imagina-

gallows. Eyes saw a certain beautiful
Lady, who wore beautiful garments:
but imagination imagined her chemise.
A certain man wanted to buy a horse,

A certain man asked the king
to do justice concerning a certain
city: but the king imagined injustice.
Fear makes one imagine death,
and audacity honor. Modesty
makes one imagine a fault, and legality
completion. The good reputation
of the hermit makes him imagine hypocrisy.
Imagination imagines at
night that which it does not find by day.

*Of the Proverbs of the Celestial*
*Trunk.*

FROM many corruptible forms
follows an incorruptible body.
From forms which are in the first motion,
follows the prime mover. The first mo-
tion does not give the nature of ceasing. The forms
of heaven are primary by light, just as
they are primary by motion. So do
the forms of heaven relate to the first circle, as
they relate to the first motion. So do
the forms of heaven relate to the greater mo-

cle. From greater roundness follows
greater mobility. From forms naturally
round follows a round body. Simple
circular motion does not pass through the middle. No

*Of the proverbs of the aeonian tree trunk.*

IN aeon there is no end at the end. The head of eternity is in time: and its tail is in aeon. Aeon has no middle. In aeon motion is not extended. In aeon number is not multiplied. From aeon no being can exit. Aeon is a mirror of eternity. No creature can be greater than aeon. Aeon will last as long as eternity. Eternity and aeon have contracted a partnership.

*Of the proverbs of the maternal trunk.*

SINCE our Lady is equal to piety: let no one despair of her. If anyone is full of conscience and weeping, let our Lady be followed with piety and love. Our Lady has such virtue: that she can cleanse a sinner from sins. Whoever calls upon our Lady: she will respond with forgiveness. Whoever calls upon our Lady, no demon can harm him. Our Lady desires that everyone touch her with penitence. Our Lady never fails the person who has repented well of his sins. Whoever wishes to be loved by our Lady: let him make her son honored. Our Lady has maternal love for any penitent sinner who has contrition. From our Lady he has sufficiency, who praises her son: and procures that he be praised and loved throughout the world.

*Of the proverbs of the Christian tree trunk.*

HUMAN nature touches divine nature with the piety of its people. Divine nature truly recalls its creature with piety. Human love touches divine love with the piety which it has for its people. Divine love, however, recalls the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, which he endured on the cross to honor divine nature. Human nature in the presence of our Lord asked divine nature for its people. Human nature loves its people, and divine nature loves human nature. No creature is so good in itself: as in God. God can do more concerning a creature in Himself, than outside Himself. God can love a creature more through incarnation than through creation. God can participate more with a creature through incarnation than through understanding. Without incarnation, a greater concordance of divine and human nature cannot exist. A greater unity of creature was made in the unity of divine nature.

DIVINE goodness said that it willed good from itself, and desired that good to exist; will also loved this, and power thus perfected it. Divine goodness said that it willed to be in good, and willed to be that good; wisdom also thus knew this, and power thus perfected it. Goodness said that it willed to be through

Goodness said that it wanted to make good, that God might be: and power said that it could give to Him: and will said that it wanted to love that: and wisdom said that it could know Him, and eternity said that it could eternalize Him. *Of the Branches of the Exemplary Tree.*
*And first, of the example of the elemental branch.*

FIRE, air, water, and earth, in difference, concordance, and contrariety, met each other. Therefore the principle of difference said that it happened to it as to a certain Lady concerning her husband: but the principle said to difference, how was this? It is told, said the principle, that a certain Lady had a husband, whom she loved very much by reason of marriage, and because of the children they had. That Lady was discreet and well-behaved: but her husband was very extravagant and prodigal, who squandered his goods. Therefore that Lady could not be without hating and loving, nor did she find an end in which she could rest: because she could not perfectly love her husband, on account of the defects she had seen in her husband, nor could she hate him entirely, because for the sake of the marriage and her children she loved him. Therefore you, difference, said the principle, cannot have rest in concordance, nor in contrariety, since it is anger that each element meets another in concordance and in contrariety from which contrariety they cannot withdraw, nor do I find a means by which I can come to an end without labor. And when I am at the end, it happens to me as it happened to a certain Lady. And how was this? said difference. It is told, said the principle, that a certain knight with his wife and son was captured by Saracens, and the King of the Saracens told the Lady that she might go free with her husband or with her son, and because the Lady did not know whom she could choose, she did not know whether to go or to stay: for charity and sorrow held her hindered and perplexed, to such an extent that she did not know how to use the liberty which the King had granted her, and so she stood and wept, nor did her will move itself to go, nor did it rest. And then difference recognized that through the meeting which the elements make, great labor must be endured in them.

The Imaginative Branch of the Example.

It is narrated that a certain ewe had two lambs. One day it happened, while she stood in a certain meadow with both her sons, that a wolf took one of her sons, and killed him before her, and ate him. The ewe did not flee from the wolf, but rather begged him not to kill her son, but to return him to her. She wept and cried out very strongly from the pain she had, when she saw her son being eaten, who cried out to his mother to help him. While the wolf was thus eating the lamb, a certain crow and a dove were in a nearby tree, who had heard the words the ewe had spoken to the wolf, and had seen the lamb being killed and eaten. But after that wolf had departed, a certain man came, who took the other lamb, and killed it before its mother ewe, and ate it with other men. And then, with bent knees, she raised her eyes to heaven, praising and blessing God, who had given her fruit to serve man, who was created to serve God. And then she was cheerful, and gave to oblivion the anger she had felt for her son, whom the wolf had killed and eaten before her. Then indeed the dove said to the crow, that she greatly wondered about the ewe, who had no discretion in begging the wolf, who was her enemy, nor had any imagination of the enmity that existed between wolves and sheep, nor was she angry about the lamb that men ate.

The crow replied, who spoke these words: It is narrated that a certain shepherd had a son, and a lion took his son. And while it was killing and eating him, the shepherd's son cried out to his father to help him. But the shepherd, who had discretion, went to the lion, and took his son from it, although he had brought no weapons. He did not stop at the imagination of the fear he ought to have had of the lion, nor even at discretion: because he did not come armed against it, but stood by the love he had for his son. Therefore, the ewe likewise had no fear of the wolf: because the love she had for her son made her forget fear, nor did it allow her to imagine danger, nor even the enmity that exists between wolves and sheep; rather, it made her have hope in her enemy, inasmuch as she begged the wolf to restore her son to her, and not to do her harm. And then the dove recognized that charity is a great thing, which destroyed discretion in the shepherd, and imagination in the ewe. And then she said to the crow, that he should certify to her why the ewe had no anger towards the man who had eaten her son.

It is narrated, said the crow, that a certain knight had a large greyhound, whom he loved very much, with whom he went to catch deer. It happened one day, that the knight with his horse and greyhound went hunting in a certain large forest very distant from his castle. It happened that when he was in that forest, a certain knight came, who was his enemy, who came armed, and killed the knight, and led away the horse. But the greyhound remained for that whole day near its master, and on the morrow a certain wolf came, who wanted to eat the dead knight, but the greyhound defended him, and fought with the wolf, so much so that the wolf had to flee. But the greyhound re-

About the Example of the Corporeal Human Branch.

**I**t is narrated that a certain lion held a parliament or made a council, and asked of his people if he had need of anything in his kingdom, or if he had any beast in his kingdom that was disobedient to him. And the stag responded and said that there was no peace in his kingdom, because man and horse were making war with other beasts, which man killed with arrows. The lion, however, sought counsel from the fox, which is a very discreet beast, which said these words to the lion, "Lord, man is a beast that uses skill,

[Right Column]

with which he conquers and kills beasts, because he rides on a horse that runs strongly, and carries a bow and arrows, with which he kills beasts. Therefore, it would be good that you have peace with man, because man uses discretion, and knows how to ride, and to shoot with a crossbow, which kills beasts from afar, and is stronger than you: for when strength fails him, he helps himself with skill. Therefore, it would be good that you send messengers to him, who would negotiate peace between you and him. And such men who would be from his court and your friends, who would speak well of you to him, and make known to you his status, so that the beasts could truly defend themselves when he wanted to do them harm. The lion, however, considered good what the fox had told him, and the fox said that it would gladly go among other messengers, but the dog said to the lion that it would not be good for the fox to be a messenger, because it ate chickens, which live and stay with man, and also presumptuously boasted about being a messenger. The lion indeed recognized that he was speaking the truth, and chose the dog to be the messenger: but the wolf said to the lion that the man killed the beasts that the dog sought, and that he (the wolf) wanted to go to man so that he could eat bread. And the wolf said this so that the dog would not go to guard the sheep. The lion indeed consented to the wolf's counsel, and asked the dog if it would be good for the wolf to go to carry out the embassy. The dog indeed consented that the wolf could go to man, so that man might kill him, because he (the wolf) kills and eats sheep. And because the wolf had a great desire to eat sheep, he went on the embassy, not considering the danger due to the enmity that exists between him and man. Then indeed.

**Of the Example of the Spiritual Human Branch.**

It is narrated that memory, intellect, and will desired to ascend to heaven to see God, but then there was resistance among them, because each wished to go first, so that it might first see the goodness of God and His greatness. Memory indeed argued that it ought to go first, because it first received objects, while intellect and will received them afterwards, and when intellect and will relinquished their objects, memory preserved them; therefore, it argued that it ought to go first. Intellect, however, argued that it ought to go first, because it showed objects to the will, and made light for itself in memory, with which the will found those objects. Will, however, arguing for itself, said that it ought to go first, because it had greater power than intellect or memory, inasmuch as it could love that which the intellect could understand, nor could memory recall when men wished to recall, or understand some things which have already been recalled and understood in past time, and in the present time it cannot recall or understand what the will wishes to love. While all three thus stood, a certain nightingale came to that tree, under whose shade the three Ladies stood, and when it understood the resistance in which they were, it said to them,

[Right Column]

that they did not know what a certain gentile had said to a certain Christian, and to a certain Jew and Saracen in a book which Raymond made about the gentile and the three wise men. "And what was that?" (said the Ladies). The nightingale, responding, said that a certain Christian and a certain Jew and Saracen disputed before a certain gentile, who asked them not to dispute by means of authorities which are recalled, supposed, and loved, nor understood according to the nature of the intellect, inasmuch as they are believed. But that they should dispute according to the nature of argument and demonstration. Then indeed the intellect went first, which made light for memory and will to see if the positions they had made were true or false. Then indeed those three Ladies ordered that intelligence should precede. Nevertheless, there was resistance between will and memory as to which of them should precede after the intellect. But the nightingale judged that the will should go first, and memory went last. And therefore it spoke these words: It is narrated that future time and past time came to lodge in the inn, which belonged to a certain good man, who was called motion, and they brought one donkey, which carried provisions. That good man said that he would not open the gate of the inn until it had been agreed whether the head of the donkey or its tail should enter first, and then they easily agreed that the head of the donkey ought to enter first according to the nature of its motion. And then the donkey entered, head first, and he asked which of them should enter first, to which they said that it had already been determined by the entrance of the donkey; then indeed future time entered first, and afterwards past time. Memory therefore knew, which has a greater cause—

by the truth, and that if she did not answer him, he would kill her. But she said that she would tell him the truth, provided that he would not kill her if she told him the truth. And then the knight asked his wife, in which beauty she was whiter and cleaner, either in her face, or in her intention, on account of which she applied colors: she replied to him that the beauty was whiter and clearer in her face, and that in her intention it was the opposite: because she had foul thoughts, from which she clothed her intention, by reason of which she adorned and painted her face; then indeed that knight asked his wife, whether beauty was more beautiful in the face or in the will, but she replied to him, that as much as the soul is better than the body, so much more beautiful is beauty in the will than in the face. Then indeed the knight clothed his wife in a vile cloth, because her intention was foul.

And then the baron who was luxurious, and others who were in the parliament, recognized that the king had clothed the baron in vile cloth, because his soul was foul, nevertheless, the sage was not content with that, to whom the king spoke these words.

It is narrated that a certain worm, which is called a vermicule, which is generated in the hands, complained to God, because God had made it such a small creature, and had made man so great and so honored. And then God placed it in man, in which He honored it, inasmuch as He placed it in his society, and that this worm would eat him, and so that man would not be proud on account of his honor, and that the worm would forget its smallness and vileness in the society in which it was with man, and honored in him. Then when the King said this example to the sa-

[Column 2]
-ge said to the king, that he did not know what the boy said to the dove. "And how was this?" said the king. "It is narrated (said the sage) that two apes had placed wood upon a lamp: which they believed to be fire: because they were cold, they wanted to light a fire and warm themselves. But the dove often said to the apes that the lamp was not fire, and that it was clear that the apes, who used to be men, had such a foul figure in the likeness of men. But the boy said to the dove that she ought not to chastise a crooked and obstinate man: because from this she could suffer harm, because a crooked and obstinate person does not allow himself to be chastised, and causes harm to those who chastise him. But the dove did not want to believe the boy in the counsel he gave her, and believed that the apes would not have heard her from a tree in which she stood. And then she descended to the ground to them, and said to them that the lamp, which is called a glow-worm, was not fire. Then indeed the apes took the dove, and killed and ate her. But the boy said that in the dove he had lost his words, nevertheless in himself he had experience of those things which he had foretold to the dove."

**On the example of the apostolic branch.**

**I**t is narrated that honor and wisdom went on a pilgrimage, and when they were lodged in an inn, wisdom prepared a meal, and set the table and placed black bread upon white cloths. The cloths considered it a disgrace to them: because black bread lay upon them. But the bread replied to them that they would not be white or whole if it had been white, and then.

But the Astronomer inquired further, and found that he could not pass the year. While that King stood in sadness and sorrow, it happened that another King sent him a girl, who had been nourished with poison, and ate nothing but poison. The Astronomer, however, said that he could not believe that that girl had lived with poison: because his knowledge could not support it, and especially because she was born under the dominion of Aries, which is of a humid and warm complexion, which is contrary to the complexion of poison, which is dry and cold. The messengers, however, who had brought that maiden, in the presence of the King and the Astronomer, gave her poison to eat and drink, so that that maiden had no ill effect from what she ate or drank. And then the King had little pleasure, and thought that the art of Astronomy did not always give a true judgment. Nevertheless, because of the great fear of death that he had, the maiden's experience did not cast out the fear of death from his heart: because he dwelled on it too much. And so, with the King being in sadness and fear, a certain wise knight, who was a great friend of the King, came to see the King, and asked him what was wrong: The King, however, secretly told him that he was to die that year, according to what that Astronomer, who stood before him, was saying. And then the knight realized that the Astronomer had plotted the King's death with some man of that city: because the Astronomer himself was saying that the King was to die that year, so that the King might die from fear. Then indeed the knight said to the Astronomer, if he knew how long he himself was to live, who responded, saying to the knight, that his life was only 10 years. And one day the knight said to the Astronomer, if he truly knew what he was saying: who said to the knight that a long time had passed since he had been certain about the term of his death. And then the knight, with a sword he carried, cut off the head of that Astronomer, so that the King might be cheerful, and so that he might know that that Astronomer had lied, and also his science. Then indeed the disciple of that Astronomer cursed his master, who said that he would never again have confidence in the art of Astronomy.

Concerning the Example of a branch of the Angelic Tree.

It is told that a certain avaricious man, who was very rich, wondered at this, that he could not be satisfied with riches: because the more his riches grew, the more he desired to have the goods of his neighbors. It happened one day, however, when he was riding near his castle, he found three poor men on the road, who were eating from one large loaf of bread and one small dish of meat, and each of them invited the other to eat: who then considered that among the poor there was charity in great things and in small, and that in himself there was cruelty and avarice, because from his own goods, which were great, he did not invite the poor, and he had envy for those small goods which they had. And then he cursed his riches, and desired to be poor, so that he asked those three poor men to admit him into their company, so that his will might be satisfied, and that he might be allowed to sleep: because in great goods and small, it so strongly labored him-

--- Page 416 ---
402 Exemplary Tree.

...he could have no rest. It is told, the poor men said, that Saint Michael and Saint Gabriel met God in a garden: with whom they had solace, and the more one loved God, the more the other loved Him. But while they stood thus, Lucifer came, who said that he wanted to be in their company, but on such a condition, that he himself wanted to have all of God, and the others would have nothing, who then recognized that he was not a good angel, because he wanted to have everything on such a condition that he would not suffice for all others who wished to have Him. Therefore they said to Lucifer that he was a bad angel, inasmuch as he wanted to have the whole general good, which is necessary for many particular goods. And then the avaricious man knew that those poor men did not want to have his company: because they feared that he would eat all the bread and meat, of which he would not invite them.

Of the Example of the branch of the eternal tree.

Lucifer cursed his intellect. And how was this, Raymond? said the Monk. It is told, Raymond said, that Lucifer sent his intellect to God, so that it might bring him hope from God. And when his intellect was before God, it saw the truth, which it read in a book, and it said that Lucifer did not have the will to love hope, and because he did not love it, it said that he would never have it. Therefore the intellect returned to Lucifer without hope. And then Lucifer cursed the intellect, because it did not bring the hope of God's mercy.
But the intellect excused itself, which spoke these words. It is told that there was a very just king, and one who understood the wills of men, in whose land there was a certain knight who greatly hated that king, and with one of his sons plotted the death of that king, and asked the king that it would please him that his son be of his court, and serve him at his table, and he said this so that his son might poison the king, who said to his son that after the king's death he would arrange for him to be king. And because of the great desire that son had to be king, he consented to his father's will, nor did he regard the danger that could befall him: indeed, that danger made him forget his father's counsel, and also the desire he had to be king, nor did the father care about his son's danger because of the ill will he had against the king: then indeed the king, who knew everything, said that contrary wills made one daughter, who was called Despair; that daughter the king gave to the knight's son as a wife, who begat offspring from her. But the king said to the knight, whether he believed that from his son's wife hope or despair would be born. And then the knight knew that the king understood the wills of men. He also knew his own death, and had no hope in the king: because so great was his ill will which he had towards the king, that he could not convert it to loving the king, and he preferred to die hating the king, and in despair of life and indulgence, than to love the king and have hope in his mercy. And so he was angry in death, like a certain man who cursed his being in his life. Raymond, said the Monk, how was it—

was this?" "It is narrated," said Raymond, "that there was a certain sinful man, who greatly loved the vanities of this world, on account of which he had committed many disgraces and dishonest acts against God. It happened, however, that God wished to show great mercy to that man, and gave him grace, so that he recognized his sin. And for a long time he strove to procure God's honor according to his ability. It happened that that man was sick for a long time with a grave illness, and so that God might punish him in this life, He permitted that a demon would place him in despair of God's mercy, by recalling his great sins and God's justice more than His mercy. Therefore he was losing the great love he used to have, and because he believed he would die daily due to the great illness he had, he held the pains of hell in his imagination, in which he believed he would stand eternally, and he affirmed his damnation more certainly than a man who holds bread in his hand and believes that he must eat that bread: nevertheless he had some hope in Our Lady, because of a book which he had previously made for her love, in which book he greatly commended and praised her. That man imagined the pains of hell so much, that when he had been cured, it seemed to him that he had been there, and many conditions and secrets of hell had been revealed to him in his illness. While he thus remained desperate in his illness, it happened one day that a cat took a rat or a mouse before him, which it killed and ate before him, and that man, because of the great sadness and fear in which he was and which he had concerning infernal and eternal pains, desired to be that rat which the cat was eat-

[Column 2]

ing, saying of himself, that his existence was cursed, because it awaited so many and such lasting infernal pains."

*Of the Example of the Branch of the Maternal Tree.*

"The wise man blessed the dignities of God." "Raymond," said the Monk, "and how was that?" "It is narrated," said Raymond, "that goodness, greatness, eternity, and the other divine dignities asked the Son of God, that He, who through them was so good, so great, eternal, powerful, wise, loving, virtuous, true, and glorious, would, for the love of them, make a son among creatures so good as His goodness requires or required, and so great as greatness requires, and so concerning the others. And the Son of God responded to the dignities that had asked Him, and said that He could not make that son so good and so great as He wished without a mother who would be as good and as great as would be fitting for that son. And then the aforesaid dignities asked the Son of God to make such a mother, and that He would, namely, place His will, His likeness, in that mother, for the more He would place, the more content they would be. They also said that each of them wished to be the mother of that mother's son, which mother they would make from their own likenesses. And then the blessed Son of God brought about and ordained the conception of Our Lady, the glorious Virgin, and her nativity in great magnitude of goodness, of greatness. And so concerning the other created likenesses, therefore the world said to God that it was satisfied. Ray-"

-mond, said the Monk, and how
is this? It is narrated, said Raymond, that
when God created the world, the world
asked Him, for what purpose He
created it? God answered it, saying
to the world, that He created it, so that from it
He might make one son, who would be brother
of the Son of God, and that from the world He might make one wo-
man, who would be the mother of the Son
of God Himself. Then indeed the world laughed and was joyful,
which said, that it was a great honor
for it, that from it there should be one part, which
should be God, and another part, which should be His mother.
And then it said, that it had no fear,
nor has, nor will have of
despair. Raymond, said the Monk,
and why did the world say this?
It is narrated, said Raymond, that
in England there was a certain Lady, who
had long loved Our Lady,
but her husband had killed a knight,
and that husband was dying,
who left one son; that
son remained with his mother, who asked
his mother that she would let him go on a pilgrimage
to a certain city, in which there was an altar
of Our Lady, who performed many miracles there.
And the Lady, because of
the fear she had for her son, did not permit
him to go on the pilgrimage:
because she feared that the relatives
of the knight, whom her husband had killed,
would kill her son on the way. The son
indeed said to his mother, what was it
that she loved more? And she
answered him, that there was nothing that
she loved as much as Our Lady.
Then indeed her son rebuked her,
saying that she did not love Our Lady
more than him, since she was unwilling
that he should go to do honor to Our Lady,
and to see her miracles:
nor did she have hope in Our Lady,
that she would defend him from the hands of his
enemies. And then
that Lady permitted her son to go
on the pilgrimage, and commended him
to his holy mother Mary, saying
that she who is the mother of God and the Lord
would guard and save her son on the way,
since she commended him to her.
It happened, however, that when her son
was a day's journey away from that city
in which he was born, that his enemies
seized him on the way, and cut off his hands
and also pulled out his eyes. And he,
as he could, went to the church, who said
to Our Lady that his mother was failing in her hope.
Finally it came to the knowledge of his mother
that he was destroyed, who said that she
did not believe anything of this, who
went to the Church, and found her son
healed, so that he had no harm.
And she said that she knew well
that Our Lady was such a good mother,
who would by no means wish her daughter's hope to fail.

Concerning the Example of a branch of the
Christian tree.

At sunrise the hermit blessed God.
How was that, Raymond,
said the Monk. It is narrated, said Raymond,
that a certain hermit lived on a certain high
mountain, where he contemplated and praised God. That
hermit was a simple man, who was ignorant of letters.
It happened that a certain Jew came to dispute with him,
who said to the hermit that he should show him the way
by which the divine and human nature could be one person
of Jesus Christ, without the conversion of both
natures: because if he could show him the way, he would make himself
Christian.
