[Column 1]
he wanted to become a Christian. Then indeed the hermit responded to him and said that he himself was a simple man, and that he was ignorant of letters, nor did that question which he asked him pertain to him, but to men who had more letters (were more learned): nevertheless he would ask God that night that He would reveal to him the manner, according to which divine and human nature could be one person of the Lord Jesus Christ: who asked the Jew that he should return to him on the morrow, because he would tell him about that question what seemed right to him, and also according to what God would reveal to him: because in Him he had hope concerning this, and would have. And then the Jew departed from the hermit. The hermit, however, asked God that He would reveal to him the manner of the incarnation, which he could not understand by any reason, indeed, he began to doubt in faith: and he said that since he could not understand the manner, he wanted to simply believe, nevertheless, because of the doubt he had about faith, he so multiplied the doubt of faith in his consideration, that he remained all that night in very great suffering and temptation, so much so that he could not sleep, and he believed that the faith of Christians was not true, and then he cried out to God, why He did not help him in temptation, and because God Himself did not acknowledge the many labors and afflictions which he endured for His love. While the hermit thus stood in sadness, the sun, very shining and bright, rose, and then he blessed God, who created such a beautiful creature. And because he blessed God in his tribulation, that blessing caused humility, wisdom, and piety to descend from heaven: which showed him the manner of the incarnation: who blessed and praised God, who remembered him in his labors and great dangers.

[Column 2]
And when the Jew came to him, he spoke these words. It is narrated that wisdom, will, and power met each other in a certain garden, which had been planted with many good, great, and virtuous trees, finally it was agreed among these three that in that garden they would perform one beautiful work. In that garden there was one small tree, therefore Will asked Wisdom if she knew in Power such great virtue, that it could give nature from that small tree to all other trees of the garden, so that they would be great, so much so that all would be clothed with the nature of that small tree. Wisdom responded to Will and said that she knew that Power had the virtue of clothing all those trees from that small tree according to the nature of great trees, and not according to the nature of the small one. And then Will asked Power that it would be so great in those trees, which are goodness, greatness, eternity, and other divine dignities: just as the knowing of Wisdom, and the willing of Will, which desired that clothing. Therefore the manner of the incarnation was in the equality of power, wisdom, and will, which they had in those great trees, and in the small tree. And then the Jew understood the manner of the incarnation, who praised and blessed God, and desired to be a Christian, and to promote the honor of God according to his ability at all times.

*Of the Proverbs of the branch of the*
*vegetal tree.*

[Large initial N] It is narrated that in an apple were
found generation, corruption, privation,
and renewal. Corruption descended
from the top, and generation ascended,
which in the middle found privation and
renewal, which spoke of this from the
wheel of fortune. It is narrated, said
privation, that there was a certain very
beautiful lady, who painted her face,
and adorned her clothes, and on her
head wore a crown of precious stones.
One day however it happened that that
lady looked in a mirror, and saw herself
very beautiful and well adorned, who
asked of her beauty where it would stand
when she was dead; beauty however
responded that it would receive lodging
in worms, who would eat her eyes and
her face. And then the lady said these
words. O God who has beau-

[Column 2]

-ty in the power of the producer and
the produced, you are the beauty of our
salvation. To love is beautiful in doing
good, and to do good is beautiful in
loving, and to exist thus is beautiful in
enduring. Goodness which exists is
worth more than beauty which tends to
corruption. Goodness is more beautiful
in virtuous thought than in colors or in
vicious adornment. Beauty which kills
the soul has no real nature. Foolish is
he who delights in any beauty which is
in the body, which quickly stinks and
corrupts. That beauty is worth nothing
which remains in a bad dwelling. Beauty
which lives forever and does not die is
worth more than all corporal treasure,
which is loved by men in this world.
Beauty which is of a friend and a beloved
does not die, if it is inherent in goodness.
Goodness is more beautiful in humility
than a crown on the head. After the
Lady had said these words, she broke the
mirror, and said that she would never
look in it: because it had the nature to
make many beautiful Ladies recall pride
and luxury more often. Then indeed that
Lady made a mirror out of goodness, in
which she very often looked at herself,
and when it happened that she saw herself
good in the mirror, she praised and
blessed God, and when she saw herself
vicious in the mirror, she confessed, and
wept for her sins, and repented of them.

On the Proverbs of the Imaginative Branch.

It is narrated that sight and taste
met each other in the imagination.
But taste said to sight that it
saw a house that was beautiful in a bad way.
"And how was this, Raymond?" said the Monk.
"It is narrated," said Raymond, "that there was
a certain merchant, who was very rich, and when he came
to death he said to his son that
if he wished to build houses, he should not
make beautiful gates, so that the beauty
of the gate might neither reveal his riches
nor display them." That merchant died,
and his son did not understand him,
and in the houses in which he lived there
was an ugly gate, which houses were
indeed beautiful inside. That son imagined
one beautiful and large gate, which
would be in the houses in which he
lived, and when he had made that gate,
he saw that it was not proportionate
to the houses, which were very small,
and then he tore down those houses,
and made them larger and more beautiful,
which were proportionate to that gate
in beauty and in size, which cost him
half of all his goods, and diverted him
from the art of merchandising: and he
imagined that the lord of such beautiful
houses ought to be a knight, and keep
a horse and a falcon and a large retinue,
so that the rooms would not be empty,
and thus he made great expenses.
It happened, however, that one day the King
passed through that street where those houses
were, and because of the beauty of the gate
he wanted to enter the houses, and when
he was inside the houses, the beauty of the
houses and their multitude made him imagine
treasure: for he thought that that merchant

the merchant had many florins. And then he
said to the merchant, that he asked him

It is narrated that there was a certain

had war with that prince.
But the prince, because of the great
avarice he had, and because of the
old imagination he had in gathering
a great treasure, could not imagine
the damage that the King inflicted,
or that he could inflict, nor did he keep
soldiers who would defend the city
in which the Prince was. Then indeed
the king came, who occupied the city
and the prince, and took his
treasure. To whom the prince said
that with that treasure he could restore
the city. And he (the king) had the gold melted
and placed in the prince's mouth, to whom he
said that he should drink the gold since he
loved it so much. And then the prince
died, and while he was dying, the eyes
said to the taste that it had poorly seen avari-

wished to go. But the prayer answered
it, that it wished to ascend to heaven,

**Exemplary Tree. 411**

...it did not have the duty of consulting anyone: since it was common to any of the gates: and while it excused itself, a certain Lady who was called Grace, said these words. It is narrated, that one man labored for a long time in pursuing the honor of God: which he could not bring to an end. It happened however one day, that he was thinking, and greatly wondering, why God did not help him to perfect that business, which he was pursuing for His love: nevertheless he considered, that perhaps he had some vice in himself, by reason of which God did not give him the virtue, that he might bring that business to an end. And while he was thus thinking, and seeking that vice in himself, he slept: and in dreams it seemed to him, that a certain Lady was before him clothed in diverse garments: whose colors were white and black. That man asked the Lady, what those colors of her garments signified? The Lady responded, and said, that the white color signified the will of those men, who love the honor of God so much, that they care nothing for their own honor: indeed they wish, that all honor be God's. Also the white color signified the will of those, who have no fear concerning their honor, nor have shame in pursuing the honor of God. And she said, that the black color signified the will of those men, who honor God, so that they themselves may be honored: and they have fear of shame, so that they may not receive dishonor. Then however that man awoke, and entered the Church through the gate of majority to see this deed: who said, that from then on he would not desire his own honor, nor have fear from shame, nor from dishonor, nor would he hesitate to undergo death in pursuing the honor of God. And then the saint gave him white garments, and asked me and the majority, that we should be friends in all good things, and that we should guard him from evils and less good things. Therefore that man brought to an end and to completion that holy business, in which he had labored for a long time, so that God might have honor in this world. And when power, object, and act had heard these words, they entered through the gate of majority, and asked the saint, saying these words. Holy Lord, said Love-Power: if it pleased you, I would wish to love you according to the greater majority of my power, my wisdom, and my will, since you are lovable with the majority of possibility, intelligibility, and lovability, so that between you and me, loving may be clothed in a majority extended in magnitude of goodness, duration, power, wisdom, will, glory, virtue, and truth. And then the saint gave to all three that, which they asked from him. And he said to Grace and to Majority, that he should associate them, and that they should not pass through the gates of minority.

**Concerning the Example of the branches of the Imperial tree.**

It is narrated, that a certain King on that day on which he received the crown, asked his council, what were the conditions which a King ought to have in reigning? And his council responded to him, and said, that among other conditions which a King ought to have, there are seven principal conditions, namely justice, wisdom, charity, power, fear, honor, and liberty. Then indeed the King in the presence of his people asked if they would consent and concede-
Fff 2

--- Page 426 ---
412 [tab] Exemplary Tree.

[Left Column]

grant that the King ought to have those
conditions. And all together supplicated the King,
that he himself should have those seven con-
ditions: because without them no King could
rule his kingdom. And then the King responded and
said, that he would wish to have those conditions,
and he asked his people, that they
should be enemies of any man who
would advise him anything that would be
against those conditions. The people, however,
granted this, and an instrument (agreement)
was made between the King and his people
concerning that grant. Therefore the King
accepted those conditions from the hundred names
of God, and he had them written at
the gates of his palace, so that if anyone wished
to ask him anything against those conditions,
they would have fear of him and his people.
And in this way the King
had liberty in reigning, and in
being good and a friend to his people.
And when anyone asked him anything against those con-
ditions, he made them read those conditions
which were written on the palace gates, and he made
them repent of the requests they made,
or he made them die a bad death.
Those conditions are these, which follow.

On Justice.

O God! who art true justice, when
I recall my crimes, I fear You in
my conscience. God is just by
His power to His will and wisdom,
which have whatever they desire to
have. So much does God give from the act of making good,
and to the goodness that has been made good: just as He gives from
the act of loving, and to the beloved will. If God
were idle in Himself, He would not be just
nor glorious. God is just in
judging, and He is just in sparing, and
He is just in equating justice and His mercy.

[Right Column]

mercy. If God were not
incarnated in man, He would not have great
generosity in created being. Justice
brings humility, mercy,
and piety, and makes man loving
through will. He who wishes to judge
himself, more quickly obtains mercy
from God. It is more valuable for man
to recall what is just, to love what is just,
and to think, than to possess gold or honors.
I offer myself to the Justice of God,
and I commend myself, that He may do
or act concerning me according to His will in
judging, and from it I ask for pardon
for my sins by repenting. Mercy
and good will have made a great partnership
from justice and piety.

On Wisdom.

O God! who art wisdom, and knowledge, I
would wish to love You, and to hold You as beloved,
according to what my will can fulfill.
God is His pure intellect: therefore
He understands all that is. Because God
in His goodness understands magnitude: therefore in
it He knows bonificability (the capacity to be made good), which is good, and great intelligibility.
God understands that by Himself He is intellect, and
He understands that intellect is personified, so that
in it His understanding can extend itself. In
understanding there cannot be intention, if
there is no distinction between the understander
and the understood, so that the end of understanding
may be with perfection. If nothing
followed from understanding, the goodness of the understander
and the understood would not exist, and good would be
placed in ignorance. Understanding through
distinction must exist so that in
it there can be agreement, by which
it is removed from contradiction. That
man who is deified has a greater
intelligibility of good than anything
else.

understood that an Angel, by its nature, did not pass through a medium, but passed through a medium according to the nature of the place, which place imagination indeed imagined. But Will responded and said that it likewise ascended above the sensitive and imaginative faculties, and also above itself; above the sensitive, just as a man who feels hunger, and I will that he fast; above the imaginative: just as a man who imagines carnal delights, and I make the imagination imagine the contrary. I also ascend above myself, inasmuch as I love God more than myself, and I labor more for His honor than for my own. But Intellect responded and said that it ascended above itself to God, inasmuch as it mortifies itself by believing about God that which it does not understand, so that it might honor God, and that to that same degree, as much as Will itself was capable.

*On the Example of the Branches of the Celestial Tree.*

**I**t is narrated that Saturn and Jupiter asked the Sun to tell God that they ask Him to place a medium between them, because contrary temperaments cannot have peace. But the Sun responded to them that they did not know what God responded to the hermit. "And how did He respond?" said Saturn and Jupiter. "It is narrated," said the Sun, "that a certain hermit was standing on a certain mountain, who had many temptations, and daily asked God that He would take those temptations away from him, because they vexed him too much." But God responded to him that those temptations were good for him, because when he was tempted by lust, he re-

[Right Column]

called and loved chastity; and when he was tempted to eat, he loved fasting; and when he was tempted to sleep, he recalled and loved prayer; and when he was tempted by pride, he recalled his vileness, and many sins which he had committed, and the vile place from which he was born, and the vile dwelling in which he ought to stand after death, where worms would eat him: therefore the temptations which that hermit had, excited and moved him to do good, and that he should not be idle, and that he should always do the contrary of those temptations. Therefore that hermit was a just man, and daily acquired great merits through the good works which he did, and because he overcame many evil temptations.

*On the Example of the Branches of the Angelic Tree.*

**I**t is narrated that in a certain cathedral church there was a certain Bishop, who was an unlearned man, who did not know how to preach well, nor to reprehend his canons for the evils which they did, because he did not know their sins nor their defects. But the canons desired that that Bishop had died, and that they might have a wise Bishop, who would know how to preach well, and to know their good qualities. But it happened that that Bishop died, and they had a discreet Bishop, who preached well, and knew the sins and other defects which they committed, and reprehended them to such an extent that he kept them in daily labor. And it happened one day that the canons asked counsel from a certain old canon, a certain

--- Page 430 ---
416 Exemplary Tree.

[Column 1]
what they should do about that Bishop, because they were not able to bear the labors he imposed on them. That canon replied, saying: that they should do what a good Angel does. And what does a good Angel do? said the canons. The canon replied; a good Angel mixes his branches together, and mixes them in harmony: therefore if you mix the desire you had when the other Bishop was alive, with what you know about this Bishop, and if the mixture is in harmony, you would have peace with him: because he is good, and he would recognize you as good, and would love you as good; but that he is good and discerning, and you are bad, and you want him to be wise, you are the cause of your own trouble.

Of the Example of the branches of the eternal tree.

It is narrated that a certain prelate had committed a mortal sin very shameful to confess, and a certain prince was in the sin of lust. It happened, however, that both, namely the prince and the prelate, were speaking about confession: and the prelate asked the prince if he confessed. The prince replied that he desired a true confession, which he could not have: because when it came into his will that he should confess, he considered that he would not abandon that sin for the sake of confession, therefore he was unwilling to confess: because he said that confession was worth nothing without contrition and satisfaction. The prelate, however, said to the Prince that he should not cease to confess on account of this: because although that confession, as far as salvation was concerned, would not suffice for him, nevertheless it would be worth something to him as far as the body and as far as

[Column 2]
as far as the soul: because the body would have suffering, and the soul shame: and he used confession, and also recalled infernal punishments, from which his confessor instilled fear in him, therefore his confession was an occasion for good. It happened that the Prince believed the prelate based on the advice he had given him: and because of the practice of confession that the Prince made: he began to have contrition, and to imagine eternal punishments: to such an extent that one day he proposed to overcome himself in making a true confession, after he had so often falsely confessed: then he confessed with the intention that he would not return to the sin of lust: and after confession he felt himself strengthened in the way of chastity: and then he praised and blessed the mercy of God, who remembered him. And it happened that at another time the Prelate asked the Prince if he had confessed. And the Prince told the Prelate what had happened to him through his advice. And then the Prelate had great pleasure: because the Prince believed him. And it happened

**Concerning the Example of Sensual Relation.**

**I**t is narrated that Relation of power
& object & act sought great good-
ness in the eyes, nor could it find it:
because eyes do not see at night, & they see
many evils. And because it desired to find
great goodness, & did not find it in the eyes:
it sought it in the ears, in which it did not
find it: because ears do not hear at night,
while men sleep: & sometimes they hear
evil words. Then it went to seek great
goodness in the nose, in which it did not
find it: because the nose senses foul odors,
& through it foul odors pass in, & go out.
Relation went to the taste, which believed
it would find great goodness, in which it
did not find it: because it itself is wearied
in eating. Afterwards it went to the touch,
in which it believed it would find great
goodness, in which it did not find it:
because it feels pain, heat, & coldness:
which cause evil to all. It also went to
speech, so that it might find great goodness
in it, which it did not find in it: because
it often lies, & the lies, which it made,
were evil. Relation wondered greatly:
because it could not find great goodness
in the body: & it came to a beautiful
inn in which it sought it, & it did not
find it: because the Lord of that inn
had died that day: & it sought great
goodness in the riches of that man, nor
did it find it: because the lord of the inn
had lost them. Again it went to seek great
goodness among the friends of that dead
man, among whom it did not find it:
because they had forgotten that man,

[Right Column]

who had loved them much, & through
him they had received many good things.
While Relation thus went seeking great
goodness from one place to another, it found
a man who fled honor, from whom it asked
where it might find great goodness: who
answered it, that he himself did not know
where he might find it, since he himself did
not find it in the honor of this world, which
is loved by so many men. "And how was
that?" said Relation. Relation said this: "I
have often desired that I might find great
goodness, & that I might be with it, &
participate: & I thought that in those things
I might find it, which men desire to have,
& for which they labor more, which is the
honor of this world. And when I came to
honor, & believed to find in it great goodness
& utility, in it I found great labor, which
men give to those who love & have the
honor of this world, & that so great labor
does not permit me to sleep, nor even to
rest, nor to have any good: indeed the honor
of this world has so strongly burdened me
with faults & sins, that I can scarcely bear
them, & it has placed me in such great
enmity of men, that wherever I go, I go
in danger of death: because I wanted to be
honored more than them: therefore I flee
from honor, nor do I want to have anything
of it, & so let it be for whoever wants it:
because in it is not that good, which is
believed to be there." And then Relation did
not seek great goodness in this world. And
it sought it in another life in spiritual
substances, & in God, in whom it completely
found it, & with whom it stayed & remained.

# The Exemplary Tree. 421.

**On the Example of the Action and Suffering of the Imaginary Tree.**

It is narrated that a certain sinful man, who had long remained in mortal sin, went hunting and quickly caught a hare. He then imagined the suffering that hare endured in death, for he heard that the hare cried out loudly, and the hunting dog broke its bones so that the hare could not defend itself. Through that imagination of the hare's suffering, he imagined the suffering that sinners experience in hell, and the actions that demons take against them in doing evil.

And then the desire came to him to depart from that mortal sin in which he had long remained. But when he wished to receive money, he imagined that God's mercy was great, and he proposed that he would confess at the point of death and thus depart from that sin. And so he remained in sin. Nevertheless, his conscience gnawed at him daily because of the imagination he had of the hare. And because his conscience gave him great trouble, he wanted to abandon sin. But when he wanted to go to confession, he recalled God's great mercy and remained as obstinate as he used to be. Therefore, that man decided that he would choose one path entirely, for he could not endure the torment in which he stood. He proposed that he would either not imagine the pains of hell that sinners endure, or that he would have no hope in God's mercy.

He then went to a discreet religious man, from whom he sought counsel, and to whom he narrated the trouble in which he stood. To him, the wise man said that he should ascend a very high tower and stand well up on the wall on one foot. That sinful man ascended the tower and wanted to do what the wise man advised him. But because of his imagination, as he imagined the danger of death, he did not dare to do what the wise man advised him. And then the wise man said these words to him: "Which was the greater danger, to fall from the tower to the ground, or to fall from this life to hell?" And then the sinner so strongly intensified his imagination in picturing the pains of hell that, because of the fear he had of the sufferings of hell, he confessed, hoped for God's mercy, and departed from the sin in which he was. He made satisfaction and lived a holy life through the grace of God.

**On the Example of the Disposition of the Human Tree.**

It is narrated that Beauty and Goodness came to a certain Lady, so that they might remain with her. And Beauty remained in her body, and Goodness in her soul. And through these two qualities, with which that Lady was endowed, she had great fame in the city, for they often spoke of her beauty and goodness. That Lady had a husband who was ugly and ill-mannered. Therefore, the Lady's Beauty complained to Goodness about the husband's ugliness, because it was not pleasing to her to be associated with her opposite. Whereupon the Lady's Goodness said to Beauty that she did not know the reproaches that the flame and oil made in the lamp. "And how was this?" said Beauty. "It is narrated," said Goodness, "that in a certain room there was a lamp which burned every night, and the flame illuminated that room, in which were depicted a man and a demon. That man was clothed...

Ggg 3

--- Page 436 ---
**422 Exemplary Tree.**

in white garments, and had a very beautiful figure: and the demon was dressed in black garments, and was made of a very ugly figure. And then the flame had great pleasure in showing those two figures: because through the ugly figure of the demon, and the black garments, people praised the beauty of the man's figure, and the beauty of his garments. While the flame boasted of the good work it was doing, the oil complained about the flame, which consumed it: and said that it did not want to suffer, so that the flame might have delight. But the flame said to the oil, that it could not participate in the good work it was doing without labor and suffering. Then indeed beauty was content with the good example that goodness narrated.

**Of the Example of the Situation of the Moral Tree.**

It is narrated that on a certain feast day a certain Prince sat on his throne: and he was dressed in gold and silk: and on his head he had a crown of gold and precious stones, and in his hand he held a golden staff: and before that King stood many people who said that the King sat very nobly on his throne, and that his situation well signified the nobility of the King: nevertheless, in his soul he was badly situated: for no one loved him, indeed people desired his death, because of the evil works he did, because he was a very vicious man, and very ill-mannered, and an enemy of virtues. And while the King thus sat, his body said to his soul. O my dear soul, rejoice in my honor. The soul responded, and said to the eyes of that

***

**[Right Column]**

body, that they should rejoice in that honor of the body: and that the ears should weep because of the dishonor that the King had in the words of the people, who spoke much evil of the King, who in those words stood more dishonored than honored on his throne. Therefore the eyes laughed and the ears wept. And the soul thought that that body could not live long.

**Of the Example of the Time of the Imperial Tree.**

It is narrated that a certain Prince had one daughter, whom he loved very much: for he had no other son or daughter but her, nor did he believe he would have any. But the King said to his daughter that he wanted to give her a husband, and after his death he wanted her husband to be King. But the maiden said to her father that she did not want to have a husband: for she always desired to remain a virgin in glory, in the presence of our Lady, to whom she wished to be assimilated in some way, so that our Lady might love her more because of that assimilation. But the father rebuked his daughter: and said that he wanted a King to remain in his Kingdom from his lineage, who would be the son of his daughter: and so successively from one King to another, until the end of the world. And then the maiden asked her father to tell her the truth about a petition she wanted to make to him. And the King said, yes. Then the maiden said to her father: if he believed that there were more bad Kings than good? And the King said, that in his time, there were more bad than good, even in past times, in which according to report there were more bad Kings than good. Also I ask, said the maiden, if you believe

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Concerning the Example of the habit of the*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Christian Tree.*

It is narrated that necessity and contingency met each other in difference, which clothed them with its own cloth, and called them ideas. And they asked of difference, that since they were different, why it clothed them with one and the same cloth. And difference responded, and said, that they were different in creatures, and not in the creator: because in the creator both are one idea, and by reason of unity it clothed them with one and the same cloth, by reason of which it called them ideas. And because the habits were diverse in form, the cloth was diversified in figures in diverse sustained creatures. And then the Monk said to Raymond that he should explain that example to him: because it was so subtle that he could not understand it. Raymond responded to him, that that example was written, and that he should read it so many times until he understood it, since it is so, that the habit of knowledge is aided by multiple repetitions: nevertheless, if he did not understand that which he had read three times, that he should read in the divine tree in the chapter on habit: because in that passage

that was signified which he had foretold about the idea. And Raymond advised the Monk that he should maintain this order in other places of this book, in which some things are understood by means of others.

*Concerning the Example of the position of the divine tree.*

It is narrated that a certain man considered God, how God was, and stood before the world was: because he said that God does not have a body: and he said, that he did not stand circularly, quadrangularly, nor triangularly. And because he could not imagine according to the three bodily positions, he supposed that God was nothing: because if he were something, he would stand under one of the aforesaid positions. And when he supposed that God was nothing, he had very great sorrow in his soul, and said that he had lost all the fasts he had made, and all the Lord's prayers which he had made for the love of God: because he supposed that there was no other life than this one in which we are. And then he no longer wished to fast, nor to say the Lord's prayer. And he proposed that he would go to a certain city to take a wife, and that he would have the bodily delights that he could have. While however the hermit was descending from the mountain to go to the city, he found a dove, which was standing in a tree, which asked the hermit where he was going. The hermit indeed narrated to it what had happened to him. And then the dove said these words to the hermit. It is narrated that a certain Christian and a certain Saracen disputed, and spoke to each other about God. The Christian indeed asked the Saracen, where was the will of God, before the world was created? The Saracen-

its nature is cold, and no
bad messenger procures peace well.
Fire descends with humility, and
ascends with pride. If there were no

because it wore white clothes. Pepper does not grow in all lands. The horse rebuked the king, who spoke ill of barley. Wine strengthens the heart with warmth, and destroys the brain with dryness. Wine is stronger in the cask than in the cup, and is closer to its end in the cup than in the cask. The beetle does evil, which is born with a black color from white flour.

*On the Proverbs of the Flowers of the*
*Sensual Tree.*

The eyes said to the intellect, that it should understand God in His infinitude: and the intellect said to the eyes, that they should look at the sun at midday. The mule asked its mother, the mare, not to say that it was the son of a donkey, but she replied to him that he signified this in his own form, wherefore she could not conceal it. The mule found a horse and a donkey, and greeted the horse, but refused to greet the donkey. A certain man saw a place in which he had fear, and he remembered his enemies. The soul remembered its sin, and the eyes wept, and the mouth performed fasts. When a man cut flesh with a knife, he felt softness: and when he cut bones, he felt hardness. Man feels bitterness in a sweet apple, so that the intellect might understand weakness, and that the will might love health. No water feels heat, nor is any visibility seen. The eyes desire to see visibility, and they see color, which is not of the essence of visibility. No man is visible.

*On the Proverbs of the Flowers of the*
*Imaginal Tree.*

No imagination is seen. The rational soul sleeps when it moves the sensitive [soul] without imagination. The imaginative faculty can imagine in one moment the whole circuit of a town, but not the whole circuit of the firmament. In this life it is better to imagine death than life. Bad is the imagination that imagines beauty without goodness. A prince ought to imagine the gallows before the crown. Imagination has greater concordance with the intellect than with the will. Without the multiplication of species, imagination could not extend itself in magnitude. Every imagination is an instrument of the imaginer and of the imaginable. Because of too much imagining, memory is weak.

*On the Proverbs of the Flowers of the Human*
*Corporal Tree.*

The life of man consists in the concordance of his parts. A sinful man cannot have right in anything that pertains to God. That man belongs to the devil, who loves himself more than God. He who loves God more than himself, procures more honor for Him. It is more useful for man to think well than to feel good. Scarcely is there any man who does that for which he was created. All men who have a good reputation are not good. Good reputation in a bad man is the habit of hypocrisy. That man is worth less than a donkey, who wishes to be strong more through the body than through the soul. That man who more often imagines whence he came, knows the ways of day and night.

Of the Proverbs of the flowers of the spiritual human tree.

Will asked intellect to tell its beloved that it loved him more than itself. Therefore, intellect wished to understand God more than itself, and memory to recall Him more than itself. If will had loved its beloved very much, it would not have consigned him to oblivion. In one hand of the beloved, intellect saw a sword, and in the other a flower; therefore, it told will to have fear and to send hope to mercy. Will loved its beloved so much that it did not have enough time to love itself. Memory recalled the beloved, and intellect understood him, and will desired that he should be honored by all men. Will sent hope to the beloved, that he might have memory and pity for sinners. Will was weakened by too much loving: and to recall and understand itself more greatly with the goodness of its beloved

In no man is humility so beautiful as in a Prince.

*About the proverbs of the flowers of the apostolic tree: and about the articles of divinity.*

Since it is so, that this which is, is because God is: if God were not, no other being would be. If there were many gods, infinity would be nothing. It is impossible that there be two infinite Fathers. Because of the touch of divine reasons, the Son God is born from God the Father. From the meeting of the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit. If the world could be eternal, there could be possibility without positivity. The recreation of the world has doubled the servitude of men. Every man is created to know the great glory of God. No being can divert the world from the end for which it was created. God can do more in Himself than in another.

*About the Proverbs of the flowers of the apostolic tree, and about the articles of humanity.*

More noble and better is the conception of Jesus Christ than the recreation of the world. Because it is better for God to produce great good than small: He could be born better from a Virgin than to create the world. Through the death of Jesus Christ lives the great love of men. Jesus Christ descended into hell, so that he might make holy men ascend to the heavens. The resurrection of Jesus Christ is the mirror of the universal resurrection. The end of Christ's humanity is in the highest. The greatness of judging is in the truth of feeling and understanding. He who hates Jesus Christ, hates the end of all things. No name is more virtuous than the name of Jesus Christ. No testimonies are truer than the articles of faith.

*About the Proverbs of the flowers of the celestial tree.*

The elementary is the flower of the lion, the sun, and Sunday. To vegetate is the flower of Sagittarius, Jupiter, and Thursday. To feel is the flower of Capricorn, Saturn, and Saturday. To imagine is the flower of Cancer, the Moon, and Monday. Aries, Taurus, and Gemini mock men who say that they know all their natures. The Sun and Venus rebuked Mercury, who makes men muse in quicksilver, which is born in the earth. Who is he who could know how many times Aries, Taurus, Gemini met each other with Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury? Silver in the purse is worth more than in Mercury. He is a heretic who has greater fear of Gemini and Cancer than of God. The power, wisdom, and will of God have greater friendship with each other than Capricorn, Mars, and Saturday.

*About the proverbs of the flowers of the angelic tree.*

Greater is the glory of Saint Gabriel than his entirety, or his parts. When man sins, he brings reproach upon his good angel. A good angel advises him to understand, and a bad angel with imagination, A good angel

Concerning the Fruit of the illustrative tree.

[Large decorative initial N in a square frame] IT IS TOLD, that in the King's ring gold and emerald contended with each other: because gold said, that the elements existed more for its sake, than for the emerald: because it (gold) served the emerald more, but the emerald said, that it (emerald) served the king more & gold served merchants, & gold said to the emerald that it (emerald) did not know that which iron said to wood. "And how was this?" said the emerald. "It is told," said gold, "that a certain king was winning a war, a dispute was between the king's shield and sword: because the shield said, that it protected the king who was not wounded, because it sustained the blows of spears and swords, which wanted to kill the king,

**Column 2**

who would have been dead if it (the shield) had not been there. The sword indeed said, that it conquered the war inasmuch as it killed & wounded those, who wanted to kill the king. And then the emerald said to the gold, that it had given an example against itself: because although it (gold) is beautiful in the king's shield, it would not be good in a sword which wounds & kills soldiers, whom it could not kill, if it were made of gold. Also it is given to soldiers, that soldiers have swords of iron, with which they guard the king, & defend. And that they kill those, who wish to kill kings, & thus the sword has two offices: one namely that it defends the king, & another that it kills his enemies. But the shield has only one office. And then gold was ashamed, since it had given an example against itself: because it well knew, that the emerald guarded the king from poison, & made the king's heart joyful.

Concerning the Example of the fruit of the vegetal tree.

[Decorative initial] IT IS TOLD, that in an apple there was a dispute between the elemental power & the vegetative power: because the elemental power said, that the apple was its fruit, inasmuch as it was a body because of the elements, & the qualities which it had, it had through the elements. The vegetative power indeed alleged & said to the elemental power, that it had not heard the judgment which a certain judge gave between the beginning & the end. "And how was that?" said the elemental power. "It is told," said the vegetative power, "that flour, & water, & an oven made one bread, which a certain man wanted to eat, so that he could live. Water indeed, flour & oven said, that they did not want that man to eat the bread. The man however said,"

*Concerning the Example of the fruit of the*
*sensual tree.*

[Large initial N]
It is narrated that a certain miller was feeding a pig, to which he gave to eat from the grain that he stole: one day it happened that the miller was giving grain to the pig, and a donkey wanted to eat some of that grain with it. The miller, however, struck it with a stick, so that it would not eat of the grain. The pig wondered greatly, because the miller did not want the donkey to eat of the grain, and asked the donkey, why its Master struck it? And it told him that its Master was evil & a thief, because it carried the grain, & he did it wrong, because he did not give it to eat. And the pig said to the donkey, that in this it appeared that its Master loved it more than the donkey, & that it was more honored, because it did not labor in carrying grain nor in anything else, & its Master gave it to eat of the grain according to his will, & did not want to give to the donkey, which labored in carrying the grain. The donkey, however, said to the pig, that it poorly saw the friendship of its Master & its honor, because its Master castrated it, so that it would not make offspring, & that it would not labor, so that it would become fat, & when it ate much grain, & was fat, he would strike it with an axe, & put it in salt, & eat it in dishes. This greatly displeased the pig, what the donkey had told it, & it said, that it ate the grain poorly for its own purpose, because for this reason it ate so that it might die, also because it ate stolen grain, concerning which it had a conscience because of the fear of death: therefore it said that it would go to do penance in a certain vineyard in which there were many bunches of grapes. And it said that it would never eat stolen grain, nor be with its Master, who had done it great disgrace & evil: because he castrated it, because it did not seem to itself that it was of the race of beasts.

And then it went to the vineyard & wanted to eat the grapes, which told it that they were the fruits of the Lord of the vineyard, & not of itself, which thought least of the vineyard, of which man thought, therefore it was committing a sin. Then indeed the pig said that it did not want to have a conscience except because of the fear of death, & it ate of the grapes according to its will, meanwhile, while the pig was eating the grapes, a raven said to it that it was the fruit of the Lord of the vineyard after it ate its grapes, who would kill it when it became very fat. Then indeed the pig had a conscience about the grapes which it ate, & it left the vineyard, & fled to a large forest, where it said that it wished to eat so that it would not die. And it preferred to be lean & live long, rather than be fat & die quickly.

It is narrated that honor and salvation
of peoples contended with each other in the apostolic tree,
because each said that it was the fruit
of that apostolic tree. Honor, however,
argued and said that it itself
was the fruit, because the Pope was more
honored, a man than another. Salvation

**Concerning the Example of the Fruit of the Angelic Tree.**

It is narrated that a certain hermit saw an Angel and a demon, who were resisting each other: because the Angel said that to do good was the fruit of existing, and the demon said that to exist was the fruit of doing evil. But the Angel argued and said that to do good was the fruit of existence: because goodness is greater in the memory, understanding, and love of an Angel who contemplates God, than in the essence of the Angel. But the demon said that natural goodness is evil because of evil memory, understanding, and love. Therefore the hermit said that they did not know what a certain Greek used to say to a Latin and a Saracen: because if they had known, they would not have resisted in that in which they were resisting. And what is this? said the Angel and the demon. It is narrated, said the hermit, that a certain Latin and a Saracen met each other in a certain vineyard, in which there were many bunches of grapes. And while they were eating from the bunches of grapes, the Latin said to the Saracen that wine is made from grapes: and the Saracen answered him that wine was not made from them, but Nabit was made from them: which is said in Arabic like wine. Of the Example of the fruit of the maternal tree.

It is narrated that a certain Monk was accustomed to praising Our Lady, to whom he would say that she was the mother of recreation, so that her son might recover the fruit of the world, which he had lost because of original sin. Therefore, he would say to Our Lady that she was obligated to ask her son for sinners: because if there were no sinners, she would not have been the Mother of God. For a long time the Monk persisted in such a prayer, until one night it happened, when the Monks had said matins and had left the Church, that Monk came to the altar, who, as was his custom, asked Our Lady, and he saw her sitting upon the altar, who, weeping, spoke these words. Those who say that sin is the occasion of my honor, inflict great disgrace upon me: for sin cannot be the occasion of any good, for if it were, it would not be the occasion of evil, and those speak great honor to me, who say that I am the Mother of God, because God willed to be man, and I am obligated to such men to ask my son, after I have been greatly praised and honored by them. And those who say that I would not be the Mother of God if there were no sin, say that the fruit of motherhood is not my son Jesus Christ, but sin. Therefore, they do not know that which the intellect said to the will. And what was that? said the Monk to Our Lady. It is narrated, said Our

[Right Column]

Lady, that the intellect said that it wanted to understand the Trinity of God, the incarnation, and the articles [of faith], and the will said that it did not want the intellect to understand, so that it might believe the Trinity of God, the incarnation, and the articles of the Christian Faith, so that it might have great merit from its belief, and through great merit, great glory, which it would not have if it understood the articles of faith. The intellect, however, responded and said to the will that according to what it was saying, it would follow that the less it understood the articles, the greater glory it would have. And thus in grace, which is contrary to understanding itself, there would be an occasion by which it would have great glory, for which reason it did not want to believe the will. And it said that just as the will wanted to have great glory through great loving, so it [the intellect] wanted to have glory through great understanding. It also reproached the will, and said that it was created more to understand God greatly than to have great glory: just as the will was created more to love God greatly than for its own sake. It also said that although it might understand the Trinity of God, it would not therefore follow that it would lose the habit of faith: for in the beginning it believed the Trinity, and in the end it proposed that when it forgot it, it would deposit it into the habit of faith, which it retained, and in which it found it when it wanted to understand it, therefore it said that faith was conjoined to its understanding, and that it gathered the blessed fruit of the Trinity in understanding then, when it understood it, and in faith then when it believed it, because it could not understand it. And then the Monk, by the words which Our Lady had said to him, said to Our Lady

Concerning the Example of the fruit of the Christian tree.

It is narrated that the will sent the intellect to a certain garden, in which there were many beautiful and good trees, among which there was one larger and more beautiful, which produced more beautiful and better fruit. And it (the will) said to the intellect, that it should bring her some of the fruits of those trees: because she herself wanted to eat of them. The intellect, however, went to that garden: and because it was lazy, and had greater weariness in climbing large trees than small ones, it brought of the fruits of the small trees to the will, which (the will) did not find great flavor in them, because from small fruit great flavor does not follow, which (the will) said to the intellect, that it should return to the garden, and that it should bring her better and more flavorful fruits, because those small fruits could not satisfy her. And then the intellect had to return to the garden, and had to climb the larger trees, from which it had great weariness, and brought of the fruits to the will, from which the will could not satisfy itself, because its appetite was greater than the flavor of those fruits. Therefore it (the will) said to the intellect that it should return to the garden, because it had not brought her of the fruits of those trees which are more flavorful and larger, because if it had brought them to her, she would have been satisfied. Then indeed the intellect said to the will, that she was an envious

Lady, who does not lament the labor of her servants: nor can a man satisfy her will, nor did she have thanks for anyone for the service he rendered her: because he brought her silver, gold, and precious stones, apples, figs, cherries, horses and falcons, castles, cities and honors, beautiful women, sons and beautiful garments, nor did she hold herself content with the fruits he brought her. The will, however, said to the intellect if any tree remained in that garden which would bear greater and better fruit than any of those from whose fruits he had brought her. The intellect, however, responded to her, that a certain tree was there, which he had not climbed, which produced greater and better fruit than any of the others, but he did not want to climb it, because it was too great a weariness for those who wanted to climb it. Then the will said to the intellect that it would happen to him as it happened to a certain avaricious rich man: "And how was that?" said the intellect. "It is narrated," said the will, "that in a certain city there was a certain rich man who was very avaricious, whom the King of that city asked to lend him a thousand talents. He, however, excused himself, saying that he could not lend them. The King, however, on the contrary, said that he could lend them to him; but that rich man said to the King that he could not lend him those talents, because his will was unwilling, nor could he compel his will, which was of God." Then the King said that he should choose from three what he would prefer; which (the King) said to him, because he held himself disgraced, because he so basely denied him: to lend a thousand talents: one was, that he should eat.

--- Page 455 ---
**Arbor exemplificalis. 441**

[Left Column]

...eat fifty raw onions in one hour of the day, or receive a hundred blows or lashes in one day, or lend a thousand talents on that day. That avaricious man considered that it would be better for him to eat fifty onions than to receive a hundred blows or lashes, or to lend a thousand talents. And then he began to eat onions, and when he had eaten twenty, he could eat no more, and he threw them all out of his mouth, and for that whole day he was near death. But on the morrow, the King asked him if he wished to lend him a thousand talents, or receive a hundred blows or lashes: he said that he wished to receive a hundred blows or lashes, and when he had received thirty blows or lashes, he could suffer no more, and then he said that he would lend him a thousand talents.

And so you, Intellect, said the Will, have had weariness and labor in climbing through all the trees, which you would not have had at all if you had first brought me fruit from the largest and best tree, which fruit you shall bring me immediately, and know that I am not content with you, inasmuch as you have dishonored me, because you brought me food of little flavor, and you did not bring me from those which have great flavor.

And then the Intellect went to the great tree, on which he ascended with great weariness, and from the lower branches he gathered justice and prudence, and the other cardinal virtues, and from the uppermost branches faith, hope, and charity, and from another branch, which was higher still, he gathered Jesus Christ, and all the fruits, and carried them with him to the Will, who first ate of the virtues, so that in loving Jesus Christ she might find a greater savor. And the more she ate of Jesus Christ by loving Him, the more she felt satisfied, and

[Right Column]

she found a greater savor in eating, therefore she did not wish to cease eating, and she said to the Intellect, that he should forget his labor, and rejoice in the pleasures which his Lady felt in eating.

*Of the Example of the Fruit of the*
*Divine Tree.*

It is narrated that a certain Philosopher, who was a master in Theology, had the custom that when he was weary of study, he would ride on his palfrey, and go for a walk through the gardens and meadows that were near that city. It happened one day, however, that he was riding through a meadow, going to see a beautiful spring that was under a beautiful tree, which was laden with beautiful fruits. While he was riding through the meadow, he found an ox lying down, ruminating the grass it had eaten. And when he was at the spring, and under the tree, he considered that the spring signified knowledge, which thus flowed from the intellect into the will, just as water flowed from the spring into the meadow, and afterwards he considered that he was similar to that ox which ruminated grass: because he always desired to know, and was never content with what he knew. And when he saw the fruits on the tree, he considered what fruit followed in him from what he knew, since he was not content with it, and desired to know more. And when someone disputed with him, he was proud because of what he knew, and he spoke reproach to people, and often alleged errors against truth and doctrine, so that people might not know that his intellect was defeated

The Question Tree.

**T**HIS TREE is divided
into seven parts, namely
into roots, trunk,
branches, boughs,
leaves, flowers, & fruits.
In the roots we will seek questions,
which will be made concerning the roots of other
trees. In the trunk we will seek questions,
which pertain to the nature of the trunks
of other trees, & so on in order.
And we propose to maintain this process,
so that we may give instruction for solving
foreign questions, which could arise
according to the natures of other
trees. Which instruction we will give
in the solutions of four thousand
questions, which we propose to place in this tree,
because according to how we solve those,
men who know this science are enabled
to solve other foreign questions.

therefore.
Kkk 2

--- Page 458 ---
444 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Questions of the roots.

[Left Column]
It has been said that this book is a tree of general knowledge for all sciences: because it is constituted of general principles, whose investigation is general and artificial. And the same applies to the conclusion of this tree, which is the practice of the other preceding trees. We will provide solutions to questions in the shortest way we can. And this is because we avoid prolixity, and naturally, in a shorter solution to a question, there is more investigation and art; because the abbreviation of words is more general than their prolixity, and concerning this, we have given instruction in the inventive art, and in the general table, and in the tree of philosophy. The process which we propose to follow in solving questions consists of three methods. One method is insofar as we transmit the answer to certain places of the preceding trees, in which a person can attend to the solution according to the nature of those places, and the nature of the question and its terms. For example, if a question is made about the goodness of fire, the answer consists in the roots of the elemental tree, in such a way that the affirmation of the question is drawn from that text, according to how it signifies better by one part than by another, the text always remaining in its own condition, and similarly the definitions of the roots. And it is the same similarly, if a question is made about the goodness of pepper. The art wills that a person inquire for the solution in the roots of the vegetal tree, and so in order according to the nature of those roots, and the natures of the questions which agree with the roots. And this same thing that we say about the roots, we say about the trunks, and about the other parts of the trees. The same method is to solve questions by conditional maxims

[Right Column]
according to the natures of the trees, that maxim agreeing with the conclusion of the question, affirming or denying. And if a maxim is obscure to some, we advise that they recur to the natures of other trees, and to their places, with which the maxim has concordance: as if someone wished to draw a conclusion from this maxim: "Every principle is nobler by existing and doing good works, than by merely existing:" this maxim is general to everything that has been said in other trees about principle, and what has been said about the greater magnitude of goodness, duration, power, etc. And some of its particulars are in the roots of the elemental tree, and some in the trunk, and some in the branches, and the same in order for the other parts of the tree, and for the other parts which are of other trees. And for each question, we propose to make one maxim according to this second investigation, which, as in a maxim, is composed after the question. The third method of solution is composed of the first and second methods, according to which we sometimes propose to solve some questions, by transmitting them to the places of other trees, and by giving one maxim to the question. And note, that when the solutions of two or more questions are referred to one and the same place or chapter, then after the first question, the place of the extended solution will be assigned, but for the second and third, etc., it will only be said "therein".

more than the whiteness of water. Why is the sun
more shining at midday than in the
morning? Solution. From green wood comes
more smoke than from dry. Why is the
water of springs colder in summer
than in winter? Solution. Winter draws the
friends of the sun out of the house. Is
the sun heavy? Solution. No
circular motion moves downwards.
Is the sun hot? Solution. If the sun
were hot, it would be necessary that Venus
and Mars be corruptible, and that
fire would burn everything.

*Concerning the Questions of the roots of the
angelic tree.*

Is there an angel? Solution. The
more simple a substance is,
the more active it can be. Does an
angel, when it wishes to act, consider reason
before nature? Solution.
No angel is as creatable
as God is lovable. And go to
the roots of the angelic tree. Does an
angel have extension? Solution.
The magnitude of an angel is as impossible
to imagine as its goodness,
duration, power, truth, virtue,
will, and wisdom. Is an angel
corruptible? Solution. No simple
circle (so to speak) is divisible. Is an
angel of a natural kind? Solution.
Go to the roots of virtue. Is the natural
goodness of an angel substantial? Solution
in the same place. Is an angel audible?
Solution. Between God and creature is
a noteworthy Idea. Is an angel
of contraries? Solution. No angel
by nature is under a genus. How
is the obstinacy of an evil angel?
Solution. Go to the roots of virtue.
In the same place. From what is an angel? Solution.

[Right Column]

*Concerning the Questions of the roots of the
eternal tree.*

Is the glory of an angel multiplied
because of the good it does for
humans? Solution. God would do an injustice
to an evil angel if He gave it as much
punishment for one sin as
for many. Does an angel do
good for humans so that it may acquire
greater glory? Solution. The will of God
fulfills the wills of all good
angels. Does a demon make
humans sin so that it may have more
punishment? Solution. The entire will of a
demon is full of evil. Since a demon
sinned in time, why does it have
eternal punishment? Solution. Go
to the roots of the eternal tree. Is the
entire natural goodness of a demon
empty and idle? Solution. Without an end, no
substance is full. And go to the
roots of virtue. Is the punishment of a
demon as great as its fault? So-
lution. Every fault is against infinite
goodness, against which there is no
(sufficient) punishment. Does a demon sin more
against reasons than against na-
ture? Solution. If God did not exist, and
a good angel existed, a good angel would
love its nature more than its
reasons. Is there as great power
in an evil angel as in a good angel?
Solution. No demon is
free. Does a demon by itself have
any power in a human?
Solution. No human lives on
stones. And go to the roots of virtue.
Is contrariety the principle of an
evil angel? Solution. Natural
contrariety and fault are not one and the
same in number.

Concerning the Questions of the roots of the maternal tree.

Whether Our Lady has any occasion to contradict a sinner who has great hope in her? Solution. Go to the roots of the maternal tree. Why does Our Lady not ask her son about justice, but asks him about mercy, since it is so that in her son justice and mercy are equal? Solution in the same place. Whether Our Lady appeals to her son with justice when sinners seek mercy? Solution. Our Lady would do an injustice to a sinner who has hope in her and who seeks mercy, if she did not ask her son because of his love. Whether the rational principles of Our Lady are mothers of sinful men? Solution. Between the rational principles and the nature of Our Lady there is great harmony. Whether any mother can be greater in magnitude of goodness than she who is mother

[Column 1]

it is not a condition that it is locally
in all places of the world where
God is man. Whether human goodness
is a reason for divine goodness to do good
to men, and to remit their
sins? Solution. Through the union
which is of body and soul, in every
man, when the body of man has
heat and thirst, imagination imagines
shadows and cold springs, and the soul
desires them, and moves the body towards
them. Whether Jesus Christ, when he
was in this world, could sin?
Solution. It is impossible, while the soul
is in the body, for the body to be
dead. And go to the roots of virtue.
Whether divine goodness was wounded
on the cross? Solution. Just as Jesus
Christ is man in divinity, and is man
by his nature, divine goodness was
wounded on the cross, inasmuch as God-
man was wounded, which according to
its nature was not wounded. Whether
the elements in the Lord Jesus Christ
are contrary? Solution. Just as
Jesus Christ is man in Divinity, and
is man by his nature, so the ele-
ments in the body of Jesus Christ are in
concordance, and are contrary according
to their nature, whose contrariety is
overcome, and reduced to concordance.

*Of the Questions of the dignities of God*
*of the divine tree.*

Whether God exists? Solution. Go to
the flowers of the apostolic tree. Whether
production is in God? Solution. If in
God there were no production, all his
reasons would be idle in infinite
extensiveness, and in infinite duration. And
go to the dignities, and to the flowers of the
divine tree. Whether the dignities of God are
real reasons? Solution. If the dignities

[Column 2]

of God were not real reasons, the
divine nature would be idle in itself. And go to
the dignities of virtue. Since the dignities
of God are one and the same, how
can there be many? Solution in the same place.
Whether divine goodness is a greater reason to
produce a greater good than a lesser?
Solution. Magnitude and greaterness have
concordance, and smallness and lesser-ness.
Why are the reasons of God? Solution. Go
to the dignities of virtue. Whether in God
any reason is greater than another? Solution. No
lesser-ness is infinite. And go to the
dignities of virtue. Whether God can be
idle in himself? Solution. No divine
reason can be deprived. Whether
God can acquire goodness? So-
lution. Infinite goodness cannot be
multiplied, nevertheless he can acquire
created goodness through participated incarna-
tion. Whether divine reasons are
creative? Solution. Just as, and much
better, man feels by reason of seeing,
hearing, and so of other senses, God is
creator through his reasons: and just as
man feels by the nature of his
senses, God is creating by the nature
of his reasons.

this question is signified by a similitude.
Why do gluttonous men not want to
share meat at the table? Solution
in the same place, to the second paragraph. A
hermit asked God, after he loved
him so much, why he gave him so many
tribulations? And why so strong-

go to the trunk, as above. Are
moralities natural habits?
Solution. Good moral habits are na-
tural in man's end by disposition, & are
artificial in the beginning & middle through
deliberation & choice. Can one morality
be from contraries? Solution. It is im-
possible that virtue & vice should
relate to one end. Is morality
sensible? Solution. If morality
were sensible, it would have to be
natural. Can equal moralities exist
in man? Solution. Because of the like-
ness of equality that is in the moral trunk,
moralities are disposed to be
equal: but because in the trunk there are like-
nesses of greater & lesser,
there is no equality of moralities in po-
tential. Is one morality from
another? Solution. From greater mora-
lities, lesser ones are derived. Does
one good morality occupy another good
morality? Solution. In simple touch, not
all reasons of habits are received. Is morality
imaginable? Solution. No imagination
reaches above itself.

*On Questions of the trunk of the*
*vicious moral tree.*

From what is the disposition of vices?
Solution. Vicious morality is
from a disposed privation. How does vice
begin? Solution. When a virtuous person
begins to be idle, vicious morality begins.
From what does vice live? So-
lution. From the privation of the species of oil, the flame
of fire lives in the lamp. How is
sin multiplied? Solution.
Go to the vicious trunk of the
moral tree. How can sin be deprived?
Solution. The agent who moves

[Right Column]

form & matter to the end for
which it exists, has no fault in that
movement. Is the vicious trunk from
natural parts? Solution. Just as a
stone which an ass carries naturally has an
appetite to descend to the earth: so the
world, if God did not sustain it, would
tend & return to nothing. Does sin
have any power? Solution. Vicious
custom & the privation of virtue is the
power of sin. Is there a choice of good
& evil in the vicious trunk? Solution.
It is impossible that a virtuous trunk
& a vicious trunk should be in one
man at the same time. Is the vicious
trunk from full parts? Solution.
No part is full which is
against the end. Since vice is deprived from vir-
tue, why is it sustained in a real
& natural object? Solution. From
the disposition of the privation of virtue, &
the power of virtue, man feels himself free
to choose good or evil.

*On Questions of the trunk of the*
*Imperial tree.*

Why does a good Prince have greater
merit than another man?
Solution. That man who has more
good is more removed from evil than
another man. Should a Prince pardon
his kinsman for offenses more quickly
than another? Solution. It is difficult
for a Prince's relative to be humble.
Does intellect pertain more to
justice than will? Solution.
No intellect can run as quickly
as the will. Why does a Prince
make his firstborn son his heir?
Solution. He who is first to the
beginning is nearer to the end according
to the natural course. Where does the
Prince keep his treasure? Solution.
                                              Treasu-

--- Page 473 ---
Quæstiones radicum. 459

[Column 1]

The Prince's treasure is in his sword, and in the will of the people. Why does the Prince have fear? Solution. No man has so many enemies as the Prince. Why does the Prince love honor more than money? Solution. The dominion over many wills is nobler and stronger than that of much money. Why ought the Prince to be more humble than another man? Solution. Humility, which descends to great and to lesser things, and finds equals in the middle, is in that man who is more subject. Why does greater legality pertain to the Prince than to another man? Solution. In no man is there such a bad precedent as in the Prince. Why does the Prince have a wife? Solution. Because of the love which the Prince has for his son, he loves his kingdom.

*Concerning Questions of the Trunk of the Apostolic Tree.*

Why ought the Apostolic [Pope] to be the Lord of the Prince? Solution. Go to the trunk of the apostolic tree. Why ought the Apostolic [Pope] to have greater concord with the Prince than with another man? Solution. Fear guards the vineyard. Why does the Prince kiss the foot of the Pope? Solution. In a lamp, oil is above water, because it has concord with the flame. Why does the Apostolic [Pope] have such a great chair? Solution. That man who is higher sees further. Why does the Apostolic [Pope] have white garments? Solution. The Apostolic [Pope] remits the sins of men, and water makes white cloths. Why does the Apostolic [Pope] not have a wife? Solution. If the Apostolic [Pope] had a wife, he himself would look to the earth. Why is there an empire? Solution. One

[Column 2]

Apostolic [Pope] and one Emperor could acquire the whole world. Why are there not more Apostolics [Popes]? Solution. One God is in heaven, and the image of His unity is one on earth. Why is vice greater in a prelate than in another man? Solution. That man who is higher can be seen better than another man. Why does the Pope need greater counsel than another man? Solution. The more universal the person's role, the more he needs general counsel.

*Concerning Questions of the Trunk of the Celestial Tree.*

Whether the firmament has a soul, and if it has a soul, what kind is it? Solution. Go to the trunk of the celestial tree. Of what is the firmament? Solution there. Whether mobility is of the nature of the firmament? Solution. Every round part desires motion. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether the light of the sun descends here below? Solution there. Why is there less water in rivers in summer than in winter? Solution. Water is sown in winter and collected in summer. And fasting men have more blood than non-fasting men. Why is there more water in rivers in winter than in autumn? Solution. A barrel full of wine yields more wine than a barrel that is half-full. Since the firmament is simply a circular figure, why does it influence the lower things with a quadrangular and triangular figure? Solution. Go to the trunk of virtue. Why is there more coldness in the dawn than in the middle of the night? Solution. Fire asked the sun to help it draw its heat from water. And go to the trunk of virtue. How the sun plan-

--- Page 474 ---
460 Questions of roots.

[Column 1]

how much does it multiply? Solution. Just as the visual faculty multiplies the visibility of the species through continuous and discrete quantity, so the sun multiplies the generability of the plant through continuous and discrete quantity. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether the sun influences its power upwards, namely to Mars, to Jupiter, and to Saturn, and to Leo? Solution. Only the center is the end of the circle, so that all corporeal things exist for the sake of humans.

*Concerning the Questions of the Trunk of the*
*Angelic Tree.*

Whether in an angel essence and substance are one and the same? Solution. In that an accident cannot exist by its own essence, and is sustained by substance, a difference follows between substance and essence. Since an angel is not a body, nor of the nature of a body, it is asked whether its parts can be in each other, some mixed in others? Solution. According to the nature of will, the lover and the beloved are in loving. And go to the trunk of the angelic tree. Whether an angel has a figure? Solution. If corporeal substances could be perceived by form, their figures would be superfluous in nature. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether an angel is from form and matter? Solution. If no capacity for good existed from the essence of the good-maker, no goodness would be great, nor anything to make good. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether an angel has any corporeal condition? Solution. If an angel had any corporeal condition, there would be an emptiness of magnitude in the difference that is between corporeal and spiritual substance. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether

[Column 2]

an angel can understand corporeal substances without imagining and sensing? Solution. So strongly is each part of the angel mixed in another, and joined in the trunk of the angel, and so strongly do all parts help each other, that for receiving corporeal objects it does not need to imagine nor to sense. Whether an angel who is in the East can understand those things which humans do in the West? Solution. Yes, and much better, an angel extends its intellect to great and to small objects without increase and extension of its parts, just like imagination. And go to the trunk of virtue. Whether several angels can be in one place? Solution. Just as in the trunk of an angel its parts can be, some in others without occupying space, so angels can be in each other in one place. Since angels understand from afar what humans do, why do they descend from heaven and are on earth with humans? Solution. In the presence of the angel, the soul of man receives benefit, [the angel] who guards him. Whether if a needle were to prick the substance of an angel, it would leave a point in it which would have a circumference? Solution. No corporeal punctuality can be sustained in loving.

*Concerning the Questions of the Trunk of the*
*Aeviternal Tree.*

Whether in the other life merit can grow or diminish? Solution. Go to the trunk of the aeviternal tree. Whether God can pardon Mohammed, who is in hell? Solution there. Whether in the merit which is gathered at the end, the beginning and the middle remain? Solution. In this life merit is sustained in the beginning, and in the middle, and in death, and in the end. Whether in the Lord Jesus Christ divine and human nature passed into a third number? Solution there. Why was the Son of God not incarnated in multiple men? Solution. It is impossible that the Son of God could be one person with multiple men. Why did the Son of God not assume angelic nature? Solution. It is impossible that the Son of God in the nature of an angel could participate with all creatures. Whether the human nature of Jesus Christ can recede from the divine nature? Solution. Just as human nature did not choose its deification, so it cannot choose separation from the deity. What name is greater? Solution. He who names Christ speaks of all things.

**On Questions of the Trunk of the Divine Tree.**

Whether in God essence and substance are one and the same? Solution. Go to the trunk of the divine tree. Whether in God essence and being are one and the same in number? Solution. Being and non-being are contraries, and if in essence there were no being, it would not be removed from non-being by itself: and in this step it is recognized that in creatures there is a difference between essence and being, so that essence is near non-being, from which it is produced into being: because if it and being were one and the same, it would be removed from non-being by itself, and would be eternal, nor could it be in privation: and because being cannot exist without essence due to the dependence that essence has on non-being, being has an inclination to non-being, from which it is produced by creation. And this step is a general principle for knowing many particular truths. Whether the substance of God, which is from its reasons, passes into a third number? Solution. Go to the trunk of virtue. How does the substance of God respond then, when it is touched? Solution there. Whether the goodness of God is generative? Solution there. Whether the substance of God is composite? Solution there. Whether God can annihilate himself? Solution there. It is impossible that eternity can be deprived. Whether God can annihilate the world? Solution. Against the divine will, divine power has no possibility. Whether God can create a contradiction? Solution. In God there is no negation. Whether God can create sin? Solution. Go to the trunk as above, and look at the divine substance, how it responds then, when it is touched, so to speak.

**On Questions of the Trunk of the Exemplary Tree.**
**And first, concerning the elemental.**

Why is it said that all excess is evil? Solution. Go to the first paragraph of the trunk of the exemplary and elemental tree, in which the answer is indicated. How does envy begin? Solution there, at the second paragraph. Whether fire is worth more than water in all things? Solution there, at the third paragraph. What are the first principles of praise and infamy? Solution there, at the fourth paragraph. How does sadness begin? Solution there, at the fifth paragraph. Which is worth more, beauty or utility? Solution there, at the sixth paragraph. How are prayers heard?

Why is the sin of lust closer to the soul than to the body?
Solution. Go to the first paragraph of the proverbs of the trunk of the human tree. Why does a man who blames another excuse himself when he blames? Solution there, to the second paragraph.
