*Concerning the Questions of the branches.*
*And first, of the elemental tree.*

QVESTION: Why are there four elements, and not more, nor fewer? Solution. Go to the branches of the elemental tree. Why are there three figures from the four elements, and not more, nor fewer, namely the circular, triangular, and quadrangular figure? Solution there. Whether the dryness of fire is a proper quality of fire or an appropriated one? And this same concerning the heat of air, and the humidity of water, and the coldness of earth? Solution. If fire were hot and dry by its nature, and air humid and hot, and water cold and humid, and earth dry and cold, no element would have an appetite for being in another: just as air, which would not have an appetite for receiving the heat of fire, after it itself were hot by itself: it would also not have an appetite in the generation and corruption of elemental substances, and there could be

[Right Column]

more elements than four, which is impossible according to the natural course, and according to what has been proven in the branches of the elemental tree. Whether the figures of plants are natural, and concerning general figures? Solution. Go to the branches, as above. The fullness of substance, from what is it? Solution. The complement of elemental substance is from the roots and branches of the elemental tree. And go to the same branches. How do the elements fill the elemental substance? Solution. The circle, quadrangle, and triangle are natural instruments, with which the elements fill elemental substances from themselves. And go to the branches of virtue. Why cannot elemental substance be empty? Solution. In the mixture of the circle, triangle, and quadrangle, which are natural, elemental, and corporeal figures, there cannot be a vacuum. Why does one candle that ignites another not diminish anything from its flame? Solution. The trunk lives from its roots, and from the trunk branches are derived, and some are mixed with others, and composite elements emerge from simple ones, and pass through the candle which ignites another candle. Since the four elements are from the same roots and from one trunk, why are they different? Solution. Go to the branches, as above. Why is the sphere of fire more superior than the spheres of the other elements? Solution there.

**On the Questions of the Branches of the Sensual Tree.**

Whether utterance is a sense? Solution.
Since from utterance a greater operation follows
than from another sense, and in man
with memory, wisdom, and will it has a greater
concordance than any of the other senses,
its end would be in the minority of magni-
tude, goodness, virtue, and truth,
and it would have less of entity than
any of the other senses, which is im-
possible: And go to the branches of the sensual tree.
Why are the particular senses six, and not
more, nor fewer? Solution. The six
rectitudes of the body have a greater concordance
with the six senses, than they would not have
if there were more than six, or fewer:
from which greater concordance it is necessary
that a nobler end follows. And
go to the branches of virtue. Whether
the six particular senses are substantial
or accidental powers? Solution.
If the particular senses were not substantial
parts, no part of the substance would be

*On Questions of Prudence.*

Why is Prudence? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. The Hermit asked Prudence whether it simply had greater concordance with the intellect than with the will? Solution. There is one nature, and in the difference of reasons there are diverse modes. And go to the chapter on prudence. Whether a wise man in judgment considers understanding before loving. Solution there. Whether prudence considers art before nature? Solution. No man could take a wild lion by force. The Hermit asked the Jurist why prudence used memory more than intellect? Solution. All good customs have not yet come into the world. Whether prudence has greater concordance with the eyes than with the ears? Solution. Experience is from the eyes, and positions are from the ears. The Hermit asked Prudence whether it first had a good opinion, rather than a bad one? Solution. Prudence responded and said that it itself was not its sister charity, which is deceived by many men. The Hermit asked Prudence at what time it had greater power at the table? Solution. Few are those men who, while hungry and eating, have memory of temperance. The Hermit asked Prudence whether it was stronger in greater necessities? Solution. Prudence responded and said that in that (matter) all men were not equal. The Her-

mit asked Prudence if it was permitted for it to lie? Solution. Prudence responded and said that a certain girl lived on poison.

*On Questions of Fortitude.*

What is Fortitude? Solution. Go to the question of fortitude, which is in the branches of the moral tree. How is Fortitude? Solution there. Of what is Fortitude more? Solution there. Why is Fortitude? Solution. Fortitude exists so that men can have deliberation for using their reasons. The Hermit asked Fortitude whether it was greater through love than through fear? Solution. In every virtue, love is before human reasons, and fear behind, since it is so that fear is a consequence of love. The Hermit asked Fortitude whom it loved more, either the intellect or the will? Solution. Fortitude responded that the intellect showed it happiness and danger, and the will advised it to accept happiness and not to have fear of danger. The Hermit asked Fortitude with whom it won war? Solution. Go to the question of virtue. The Hermit asked Fortitude where it stood? Solution. Fortitude responded that it was in all those who loved it. The Hermit asked Fortitude how it grew? Solution. Fortitude responded and said that it had such a nature as contrariety, which the more it is touched, the more it grows. The Hermit asked Fortitude on what it lived? Solution. 478 Questions of the branches.

*On the Questions of the branch of Hope*
*of the moral tree.*

**W**hat is Hope? Solution. Go to the branches concerning hope in the branches of the moral tree. Why is Hope? Solution there. The Hermit asked of Hope whether it had deceived any man? Solution. Hope replied that if it had deceived any man, it would have greatly erred against Our Lady, who greatly loved it and often recalled it to her Son: but its figure deceives many men against its form. And go to the branches of virtue. It was asked of Hope whether it was in those men who love themselves more than God? Solution. Hope replied that it was the sister of mercy and justice. It was asked of Hope how it conquered the justice of God? Solution. Hope replied that in this, that the sinner judged himself and loved the justice of God, it brought forth the mercy of God, with which God spares sinners. It was asked of Hope how it grew? Solution. Go to the branches of virtue. The Hermit asked of Hope whether it had fear? Solution. Hope replied that always when a wise man trusted in his wisdom, and a King in his power, and a healthy man in his health, it had fear. The Hermit asked of Hope why it was greater in sick men than in healthy, and in poor men than in rich? Solution. Hope replied that in their necessities men recall their friends. The Hermit asked of Hope whether the mercy of God was greater than sin? Solution. Hope replied and said to the hermit that he should ask that question of Our Lady, who had all that she wanted concerning the mercy of God, then when she speaks to him of those who trust in her. The Hermit asked of Hope whether it was sad? Solution. Hope replied and said to the hermit that Despair, its enemy, never made any man cheerful.

*On the Questions of the branch of Charity*
*of the moral tree.*

**T**he Hermit asked a prelate whether he knew what Charity was? Solution. Go to the question of charity in the branches of the moral tree. It was asked of Charity, why it was? Solution there. Charity, said the hermit, of what are you full? Solution there. The Hermit asked of Charity why it was more willingly in poor men than in rich? Solution. Charity replied and said that because of money and possessions it was for the most part despised. It was asked of Charity, whose are rich men? Solution. Charity replied and said that rich men ought to be the stewards of poor men. Charity, said the hermit, who invited you? Solution. Charity replied and said that it ate at the table of justice and hope. Charity, why do you not have fear? Solution. Charity replied and said that it did not have fear because it loved its creator more than itself. Charity, why do you prefer to be in the will than in the intellect? Solution. Charity replied that in this life the will was prior to the beloved, than the intellect to the understood. Charity, in what time are you more honored? Solution. Charity replied that in that time it was greatly honored,

who through her were so honored, and so rich? Solution. Justice wept, and said to Faith that she was not making a great question, nevertheless she wanted to write that question which she was making in her book, so that she could recall it on the day of judgment.
It was asked of Faith and Justice, whether they were friends? Solution. Go to the question of Justice and Faith in the branches of the moral tree.
"Faith," said Justice, "and why do you weep?" Solution. "Justice," said Faith, "and why do you not help me?"
"Faith," said Justice, "do you have money?" Solution. Faith answered Justice, asking why she did not pose that question to the will of men, who love themselves so much.

On the Questions of Justice and Hope.

Justice asked Hope, whether she was ever tired in her? Solution. Hope replied that there was always concord between the two of them. And go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. The Hermit asked Justice and Hope, from what do they live? Solution. Justice and Hope replied that they lived from concord. The Hermit asked Justice, whether she could be overcome? Solution. Justice replied that she could not be overcome in those people who have hope in her. The Hermit asked Justice, "Since she punishes sinners for sin, why do they have hope in her?" Solution. Justice replied that no sinner had hope in her who did not grieve for his sins, against which grief she could do no injury to Hope.

On the Questions of Justice and Charity.

The Hermit asked Charity, "Whether if she were in all men, Justice would be idle?" Solution. Charity replied that if she were in all men, Justice would be busy in rewarding all men through love. "Justice," said Charity, "why do you weep?" Solution. Justice replied that she wept because she judged more men to damnation than to salvation, and then Charity wept for a long time with Justice, and said that they had come to the punishment of evil men.

The hermit asked prudence and charity whether they had greater concordance in equality than in greatness and in smallness? Solution. Prudence and charity replied and said that God was equally intelligible and lovable with the magnitude of goodness and truth. The hermit asked prudence and charity whether they had a great friendship? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the branches of the moral tree.

*On Questions of Fortitude and*
*Temperance.*

THE hermit asked temperance, with whom she conquered her enemy, gluttony? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the branches of the moral tree. The hermit asked fortitude, who rewarded her for her labor? Solution, in the same place. The hermit found virtue, and asked her, from what she lived? Solution. Virtue replied that she lived from fortitude in temperance, and from temperance in fortitude. And go to the branches of virtue. The hermit asked temperance, at what hour of the day she was greatest? Solution. Temperance replied that she was greatest at that hour of the day in which she had such great concordance with fortitude that she conquered gluttony, so that she felt no passion.

*On Questions of Fortitude and*
*Faith.*

THE hermit asked faith, with whom she compelled the intellect? Solu-

[Column 2]

tion. The power of supposition, which chooses affirmation or negation without doubt, binds its legs to the intellect. And go to the aforesaid rubric in the branches of the moral tree. How does the intellect receive the habit of faith, which God bestows upon it? Solution. Just as the will receives the habit of charity by loving God more than itself, so the intellect receives the habit of faith by obeying another and not itself. And go to the branches of virtue. The hermit asked faith, how she grew? Solution. Faith replied that she grew so much stronger, the more fortitude with truth compelled the intellect. The hermit asked fortitude, whether she was as great by demonstration as by credulity? Solution. Fortitude replied that she was greater at the end than at the beginning, since it is so that the beginning is for the sake of the end.

*On Questions of Fortitude and*
*Hope.*

THE hermit asked fortitude, how she used hope? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. It was asked of the sinner, whether fortitude in him was greater when he judged himself, or when he hoped for the mercy of God? Solution. The sinner replied that when he judged himself worthy of great punishment, he felt passion because of the great fear he had of God's great justice: which he greatly loved, by reason of which fear he wept, and when he hoped in God, and transmitted his hope to the mercy of God, he felt no sorrow nor passion, and filled his heart with cheerfulness and boldness. The hermit asked fortitude:

--- Page 497 ---
...tude asked, whether it had ever been defeated? Solution. Fortitude responded that it was always defeated when hope departed from it. The hermit asked fortitude whether it could compel hope? Solution. Fortitude responded that it could not compel hope: because God gave it freely. And it went and came freely.

*On Questions of Fortitude and Charity.*

The hermit asked charity, why God gave so many passions to his friends in this world? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. Charity, said the hermit, why does God command man to love his enemy? Solution. Charity responded that God wills that man should love his enemy, so that it may have great fortitude. The hermit asked charity whether it had greater fortitude in loving its friend than in loving its enemy? Solution. Charity responded that it loved its friend with harmony without passion, and it loved its enemy with contrariety and passion, therefore to love it went heavily with one foot and lightly with the other. Charity, said the hermit, why does a poor man have greater merit if he gives alms of one denarius than a rich man of one talent? Solution. He obtains greater merit who does good with all his power.
***

*On Questions of Temperance and Faith.*

The hermit asked faith and temperance whether fortitude had invited them? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. The hermit asked faith, of what was its fast? Solution. Faith responded that its fast was spiritually from supposition without doubt, which is the prison of the intellect: just as fasting is corporally from temperance in eating savory and delicate foods. The hermit asked faith whether it was greater in credulity than temperance in abstinence? Solution. No corporal virtue can be equal in magnitude of goodness with a spiritual virtue. The hermit found temperance, from which he asked, where it was going? Solution. Temperance responded that it was going to mortify satiety and taste beyond the nature of appetite: just as faith was going to mortify the inquiry of the intellect beyond demonstration.

*On Questions of Temperance and Hope.*

The hermit asked temperance, how it fostered friendship between justice and hope? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. How is hope the cause of temperance? Solution there. The hermit asked temperance, of what was the cloth of its tunic? Solution. Temperance responded that the cloth of its tunic was from justice and hope. # Questions of the Branches. 485

asked, whether it was so great because it loved virtue, as when it hated vice? Solution. Hope replied, that it would refer that question to the will, which is greater in the magnitude of goodness by loving than by hating. The Hermit asked Charity, whether it was so great in loving God's justice, as in loving His mercy? Solution. Charity replied, that it loved God's justice according to its nature, and loved His mercy, because hope advised it.

*Concerning Questions of Holiness.*

What is Holiness? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. The Hermit asked the prelate, what is the more common virtue? Solution, there. Holiness lay sick, and a certain old woman asked it, in what place it felt greater pain? Solution. Holiness replied, that in that place, through which it was greater, it was more strongly wounded. It was asked of Holiness, in how many people it was? Solution. Holiness replied, that its contrary was in so many people, that it did not know how to count them.

*Concerning Questions of Patience.*

What is Patience? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. Why is Patience? Solution. If patience were not, fortitude could not acquire merit with greatness. And go to the question of virtue, How is Patience stronger than fortitude? Solution. Because patience has greater concordance with humility than

[Right Column]

fortitude, and has more friends than fortitude. It was asked of patience, with whom was the battle won? Solution. Patience replied, that it overcame proud men, and angry men, mockers, and adversities with humility and hope.

*Concerning Questions of Abstinence.*

What is Abstinence? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. How does Abstinence begin? Solution, there. What does Abstinence acquire? Solution. Abstinence acquires prudence, temperance, humility, and hope. How does Abstinence die? Solution. The will went to war, and did not take prudence with it, whence abstinence died in battle.

*Concerning Questions of Humility.*

What is Humility? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. How does Humility raise men to the greatness of goodness? Solution, there. Why does Humility desire to be in so many people? Solution. No proud man desires to have an equal. A certain ass asked Humility, in what subject was its greater greatness? Solution. Humility replied, that the ass was doing wrong, who forgot Jesus Christ, who took on its likeness.

*Concerning Questions of Piety.*

What is Piety? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. Why does a living man abhor to touch a man
PPP 3

--- Page 500 ---
**486 Questions of the branches.**

[Left Column]

...dead, and does not abhor touching a dead animal? Solution there. The hermit asked God whether He would have such great pity for sinful men if He had not been incarnated, crucified, and died, as He does if He is incarnated, and as a man crucified and died. Solution there. Why is a woman naturally more pious, and has greater fear than a man? Solution there.

*Of Questions of Chastity.*

What is Chastity? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. Why is Chastity? Solution there. Why is a chaste woman more commended for her chastity than a man who is chaste? Solution. A certain small man conquered a certain great man in battle, for which he received great praise. Why does a father have greater pleasure that his daughter be chaste than his son? Solution. Naturally, women have greater modesty than men, and from the modesty of the beloved, the friend derives modesty.

*Of Questions of Generosity.*

What is Generosity? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. The hermit asked God whether He could create generosity in greater greatness without incarnation? Solution there. Why does a generous man have greater pleasure in giving than in receiving? Solution. Naturally, he who gives is further from avarice and nearer to charity than he who receives. Why is an old man naturally not as generous as

[Right Column]

...a young man? Solution. Naturally, the sanguine temperament and generosity have a concordance, and the melancholic temperament and avarice: and the sun gives greater virtue to a flower of a humid and warm temperament when ascending than to a flower of a dry and cold temperament when descending.

*Of Questions of Legality.*

What is Legality? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric in the branches of the moral tree. Why is man naturally more lawful through love than through fear? Solution. Because in God there is love and not fear, every will is nobler for loving than for hating. With whom does Legality go? Solution there. Where is Legality? Solution there.

*Of Questions of Constancy.*

What is Constancy? Solution. Go to the aforementioned question in the branches of the moral tree. Why is Constancy? Solution. If a horse did not flee, its tether would not exist. And go to the question of virtue. The hermit asked the King whether he was more constant in his purpose through hope than through fortitude? Solution. The King replied that he could not transmit his fortitude to God, to whom he transmitted his hope. The hermit asked constancy whether it was as close to belief as to understanding? Solution. Constancy replied that it was close to doubt through belief, and far through understanding. Therefore, it had a conscience when it acted against what it understood.

more diligent in nourishing her
son when he is small, than when
he is grown? Solution. While a boy is
small, he requires natural nourishment,
and when he is grown, moral nourishment, which
his father ought to give him. A hermit asked a
merchant, why he was more diligent
in acquiring money, than
virtues? Solution. The merchant
replied and said, that his Father was
more diligent in acquiring money,
than his Prelate in acquiring
virtues. Why is a knight more
diligent in acquiring honor and praise,
than in procuring the health
of his body? Solution. Those things
which are more similar to God, are naturally
more desirable.

488 Questions of the Branches.

*On Questions of Contrition.*

What is contrition? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. From what is contrition? Solution. Contrition arises from the likeness of conscience, mercy, justice, and hope. Why is contrition? Solution, there (i.e., in the same place). The Hermit asked contrition, why it wept, and why it confessed? Solution. Contrition answered and said that it wept because it repented of the deeds which it had perpetrated against its Lord, and it confessed so that it might seek counsel on how it could recover grace from its Lord.

*On Questions of Shame.*

What is shame? Solution. Go to the aforesaid question in the branches of the moral tree. Since a woman naturally has greater shame than a man, why ought a man, when he sins, to have greater shame than a woman? Solution. According to morality, shame in a woman restrains the lesser part against wrongdoing, and in a man, the greater part. And go to the question of virtue. The Hermit asked a chaste Lady, why she abhorred lust more on account of shame than on account of fear? Solution. The chaste Lady answered and said that no appropriate quality has such great concordance with fortitude as its own quality. The Hermit asked a beautiful, wanton Lady, whether she loved shame as much as a chaste Lady who is ugly? Solution. The beautiful Lady answered, saying that she lost shame in this, that she lost chastity, and she says that the chaste Lady ought not to have shame about her ugliness, since she could not be beautiful; rather, she (the chaste Lady) ought to have shame so that she might be chaste.

*On Questions of Obedience.*

What is obedience? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the branches of the moral tree. The Hermit asked about the King's obedience, whether it was as great as the obedience of his people? Solution. That obedience which is through human goodness is nobler than that which is through servitude. The Hermit asked obedience, whether it had as great a passion when directed towards the Lord as when directed towards subjects? Solution. He who obeys many has greater passion than he who obeys one. A certain King wept because he was not the son of a peasant man and woman, and obedience asked him why he wept? Solution. The King answered and said that he wept because he did not have as much liberty in conscience as the son of a peasant, whom conscience permitted to sleep. According to the process which we have held in making questions from principal virtues mixed with each other, we wish to make questions from consequent virtues, mixing certain virtues with others. But because we avoid prolixity, we are unwilling to make more than one question from one virtue with another. And if you, reader, wish to multiply questions under any rubric, you will be able to multiply them if you go to the aforesaid rubrics, as for example, if you wish to multiply questions about sanctity and patience, go to the four questions and their solutions which we spoke of concerning sanctity, and go to the other four ques-

--- Page 503 ---
Questions of the branches. 489

questions and solutions, which we discussed concerning patience, and from the meaning of those which you will receive from them: if you know how to understand them, you can multiply questions at will, and find one solution with another, and this is a general rule in this whole science, by reason of which the intellect has great material for making more questions, and for inquiring into and finding natural and moral secrets.

*Concerning Questions of Holiness, and*
*of virtues applied to it.*

**H**Ermit asked of holiness, whether it was as general a virtue through action as through passion? Solution. In a certain sermon in which a certain Preacher praised God to many men, his speech had more general holiness in the praise which he gave of God, than any man in hearing that praise. Abstinence, said the hermit, are you as general a virtue as holiness? Solution. Abstinence replied saying that holiness alone is a general virtue. Humility, said the hermit, in which virtue are you greater? Solution. Humility replied and said that it ought to be greater in that person who is more common. Since holiness is such a common virtue, and virtue in man is more common than in woman, why does piety make women weep sooner than men? Solution. One commonality is that which is moral, and the other is that which is natural. The Hermit asked of chastity, whether it was more holy in man than in woman? Solution. Chastity replied and said that it was more holy in woman through modesty, and in man through fortitude. The Hermit asked of holiness, whether it had greater fear of avarice than of lust? Solution. Holiness replied and said that men did not have such great conscience through the sanguine temperament as through the melancholic temperament. The Hermit asked of holiness, whether it had as many friends through the modesty of legality as of chastity? Solution. Holiness replied and said that legality is a more common virtue than chastity. Holiness, said the hermit, do you have as great constancy through loving as through understanding? Solution. Holiness replied and said that it has greater fear of that act which comes and goes more quickly, than of that which goes slowly. The Hermit asked of diligence, whether it was more holy through charity than through prudence? Diligence replied and said that it was holy through prudence in the head, and through charity in the tail. The Hermit asked of gentleness, whether it was as holy through patience as through humility? Solution. Gentleness replied and said that it was more holy through patience in fortitude, and through charity in humility. Holiness, said the hermit, do you have as great a conscience through love as through fear? Solution. Holiness replied and said to the hermit that he would find the answer in the meaning of his questions in its aforementioned rubric, and in the questions which we discussed concerning conscience. Fear, said the hermit, are you as holy through charity as through justice? Solution. Fear replied and

he knew a certain place where partridges were sold, and a certain tavern where good wine was sold. "Patience," said the hermit, "do you have fear?" Solution. Patience responded and said that she had fear whenever charity and justice were idle. "Patience," said the hermit, "are you as great in the contrition of a Prelate as in the contrition of a Prince?" Solution. No contrition can be as great through corporal things as through spiritual things. "Patience," said the hermit, "why do you have greater fear from shame in temperance than in truth?" Solution. She responded that the shame she had in temperance was greater in temperance than that which she had in truth: because people rebuke drunken men more strongly than lying men. The hermit asked Patience whether she was as obedient to a Prince as to a Prelate? Solution. Patience responded and said that one ought not to ask a question about that which a man has by experience.

**Concerning Questions of abstinence, & of applied virtues.**

Humility asked Abstinence whether it was further from pride in a holy Prelate than in a holy religious person? Solution. He who has a greater reputation for goodness is closer to hypocrisy. "Piety," said the hermit, "why do you have greater abstinence in weeping for men than in weeping for women?" Solution. All greater abstinence can be with greater fortitude than with lesser. "Chastity," said the hermit, "why do women have greater abstinence against lust than men, since men have greater fortitude

[Right Column]
than women?" Solution. Greater is abstinence in a woman through shame and through fear, and in a man through fortitude and through love. "Why does a prodigal man have greater abstinence in lying than an avaricious man?" Solution. Abstinence and generosity are further from avarice and falsehood in an avaricious man than in a prodigal man: therefore falsehood is closer to an avaricious man than to a prodigal man. "Why does a lawful man have greater abstinence from committing treason than from committing lust?" Solution. Treason is a more general vice than lust. The hermit asked Abstinence whether it was touched more by constancy than by fear? Solution. No fear is as general a virtue as constancy. Diligence wished to be idle, and Abstinence said to Prudence and Charity, who had spoken ill of her? Solution. Prudence and Charity said to Abstinence that they knew that in the idleness of diligence, she was their enemy. Sweetness asked Gluttony why she cast out abstinence from temperance? Solution. Gluttony responded and said that she did not cast out abstinence from temperance: but she (abstinence) had gone out from her (temperance), because charity, patience, and humility, O sweetness, do not wish to remain in you. The hermit asked Abstinence, with whom did she consult? Solution. Abstinence responded and said that she consulted conscience, when men wished to commit deception or another fault. "Abstinence," said the hermit, "do you have fear?" Solution. Abstinence responded and said that if fear were not, she would be nothing. "Abstinence," said the hermit, "why are you?" Solution. whether it had shame? Solution.
Humility responded that it did not have shame when it descended, but when it ascended: and then the hermit knew through this, from Humility, why hypocritical men have no shame. Humility, said the hermit, are you free? Solution.
Humility responded that Pride, which is its contrary, is subject to disobedience.

*Concerning the Questions of Piety, and the virtues applied to it.*

Piety, said the hermit, why are you greater in a chaste woman than in a luxurious one? Solution.
Piety responded that a chaste woman is in an order in which she can be greater than outside of order. The hermit asked Liberality, why do generous men weep more quickly than avaricious men? Solution.
Liberality responded that generous men have Piety, which is the mother of tears, and avaricious men have Cruelty, which derides poor men. The hermit asked Legality, who derided Piety? Solution.
Legality responded that a false man weeps as he sighs, so that he may appear lawful. Since there is not so much constancy in a woman as in a man: why is she moved more quickly to Piety than a man? Solution.
A lesser virtue is moved sooner than a greater, nevertheless the greater has a greater movement. The hermit asked the Diligence of the Prince, whether he had Piety concerning the Saracens, who go to hell? Solution.
The Diligence of the Prince responded that he would put that question to the Diligence of the Prelate. Piety and Sweetness were weeping, and the hermit asked them, why were they weeping? Solution.
Piety

[Right Column]

and Sweetness responded that they were weeping because they were not as beloved in the crowns of princes as gold and precious stones. Conscience, said the hermit, why do you have the nature of sadness? Solution.
Conscience responded that it had the nature of sadness, so that Piety might weep for its sins. Piety, said the hermit, do you have fear? Solution.
Piety responded that it was a sign that Fear carried on its banner. Contrition, said the hermit, how are you known? Solution.
Contrition responded that it was known by the tears of Piety, and was unknown by the tears of false men who weep so that they may deceive lawful men. Piety, said the hermit, do you have shame? Solution.
Piety responded that it wept because it had Piety concerning the prince, who has shame in asking God, and in speaking with humble men, because they will have great punishment on account of that shame. The hermit asked Piety, whether it had freedom when it wept and sighed? Solution.
Piety responded that the more it wept and sighed, the more it felt itself free, therefore it knew that its freedom lay in weeping and sighing on account of the sins of men disobedient to the virtues.

*Concerning the Questions of Chastity, and the virtues applied.*

The hermit asked Liberality, whether it was as great in a chaste Lady as in a luxurious Lady? Solution.
Liberality responded that its figure was great in a prodigal man, and its form in a generous man. The hermit asked Chastity, whether there was virtue in a treacherous man? Solution.

Questions of branches. 495

Answer. Conscience excused itself, because avarice did not want this. Generosity, said the hermit, why does avarice not have fear of the judge? Answer. Generosity replied, that avarice had more money, with which it made the judge silent. Contrition, said the hermit, why are you greater in a generous man than in an avaricious man? Answer. Contrition replied, that an avaricious man is a greater enemy of restitution than any other man. The hermit asked Generosity, whether it had shame, because avarice had more friends than it itself had? Answer. Generosity replied, that it not only had shame, but rather was sad and often wept. The hermit asked Obedience, whether it was as great in generosity as in avarice. Answer. Obedience replied, that it was greater in generosity, according to will, and in avarice according to the body.

*On Questions of Legality, and applied virtues.*

Constancy, said the hermit, why do you have greater friendship with legality than with falsehood? Answer. Constancy replied, that a legal man builds his chamber on a rock, and a false man on sand. Legality, said Diligence, why do you weep? Answer. Legality replied, that it was a friend of falsehood, it knew this. Why do legal men speak eloquently, and walk humbly on the way? Answer. False men speak quickly, so that they do not have time for deliberation to speak the truth, and walk proudly, so that man may have fear of them. Why do legal men not excuse themselves so strongly, when a man reproaches them for falsehood, as false men excuse themselves? Answer. Legality does not have such great fear as falsehood, because it trusts in truth, conscience knows this. The hermit asked Legality, of what did it have greater fear? Answer. Legality replied, that it had greater fear of false testimony than of any other thing. The hermit asked Legality, whether it had contrition when it confessed? Answer. Legality replied, that it was contrary to the confession of a false man, who confesses with falsehood. The hermit asked Legality, why was there a red color on the face of a legal man, who is unjustly reproached? Answer. Legality replied and said, that it so moved the blood to a red color in the face with shame, when it had been unjustly reproached, just as falsehood with fear (moves) a yellow color, when it is reproached according to truth. The hermit asked Legality, whether it had ever been obedient to sin? Answer. No falsehood is obedient to virtue.

*On Questions of Constancy, and applied virtues.*

Constancy, said the hermit, do you have diligence? Answer. Constancy replied, that that question would be made in Jerusalem, which knew this. The hermit asked Constancy, whether it had sweetness? Answer. Constancy replied to the hermit, asking him whether he was asking about that sweetness which was in the time of the Apostles, or about that which is in the time in which we are. The hermit asked Constancy, whether it was the foundation of conscience? Answer. It replied, that he who toriens

# Questions of the Branches. 497

science, who is your confessor? Sol. Conscience replied that contrition heard its confession: because it wanted to know how it made threats to men who do evil, and how it advised men to do good. The hermit asked Conscience if it had shame? Solution. Conscience replied that it often had shame at the clearing of the table, when men were full of wine, who believed me to have it, because they had failed against temperance, which shame indeed I would have wished to have at the beginning of the meal. Conscience, said the hermit, why are you always sad? Solution. Conscience replied that it was always sad, because it was always a handmaiden.

*On Questions of Fear, and Applied Virtues.*

**H**ermit asked Contrition whether it had greater agreement with fear than with love? Solution. Contrition replied that love moved it with fear. Since shame is a good virtue, why do men have it with fear? Solution. Just as men do not laugh when doing good: so naturally they do not have shame when doing good. Since obedience is such a good virtue, how do men fear it so much? Solution. Naturally, intellect and will desire freedom.

*On Questions of Contrition, and Applied Virtues.*

**S**hame, said the hermit, why are you? Solution. Shame replied that it was, so that it might have contrition for the hypocrisy it had, because he existed alone, and ate raw herbs, and lay upon a post. The hermit asked Obedience whether it had as great contrition in a Prelate as in a Canon? Solution. Obedience replied to the hermit that it did not make a great question, because the answer was not suitable for it.

[Column 2]

*On Questions of Shame and Obedience.*

**H**ermit asked Obedience whether it had shame? Solution. Obedience replied that it would put that question to the sensitive faculty, to which more men were obedient, than to the intellective.

*On Questions of the Branches of the Vicious Moral Tree, and firstly concerning Gluttony.*

**W**hat is Gluttony? Solution: Go to the vicious branches of the moral tree and to the rubric on gluttony. Why is Gluttony? Solution. Gluttony is, because abstinence, fortitude, and prudence do not help temperance against the will, which has greater agreement with the vegetative appetite than with the digestive. From what is Gluttony? Solution. Gluttony is from the private end of temperance and from the idleness of justice, prudence, and fortitude. How is Gluttony? Solution. Gluttony is with imagination which imagines the delight of eating and drinking in sensitive taste, moving itself with the natural vegetative instinct to too great

498 Questions of the branches.

**On the Questions of avarice.**

Avarice, what is it? Solution. Go
to the vicious branches of the moral
tree in the rubric concerning avarice. Generosity
asked of avarice, whether it was a creature?
Solution. Avarice replied that it itself
was not a creature, but was a likeness
against hope, which makes the purposes of money
idle, and also the purposes of vegetative
substances. Generosity asked of the avaricious
man, with what did he produce avarice? Solution.
The avaricious man replied that he produced
avarice with a likeness of goodness
against the purpose of goodness, with that purpose owed
to men who have need
of the goods which he gathers, concerning which
his will produces neither justice,
nor prudence, fortitude, charity,
nor hope. Avarice, said
generosity, why are you contrary to me? So-
lution. Avarice replied that it was
contrary to her, because justice, prudence,
fortitude, charity, and hope were not
her friends.

**On the Questions of lust.**

Lust, what is it? Solution. Go
to the vicious branches of the moral
tree in the rubric concerning lust. Lust,
from what is it? Solution. It is from elemental,
vegetative, sensual, and imaginative instinct
and appetite, and from inordinate rational appetite
against the order of carnal coupling.
Lust, why is it? Solution.
Lust is because of an excessive abundance
of eating and drinking: that abundance
directed or ordered towards carnal
delights, desired by the will,
and understood by the intellect,
and recalled by memory, and imagined
by imagination, not compelled
by justice, nor reproved by pru-
dence, nor overcome by fortitude,
nor bound by abstinence, nor
placed in the order of matrimony. Chastity
asked of lust, why it had
greater concordance with the will
than with memory and with the intellect?
Solution. Lust replied that the
will is a power which receives
its object more quickly than memory and
intellect, concerning which it has fear
in the beginning, lest they consult justice,
prudence, and fortitude, which often
reprove the will, because it loves vices.

**On the Questions of pride.**

Pride, what is it? Solution. Go
to the vicious branches of the moral
tree. Pride, from what is it? Solution.
Pride is from the privation of humility,
and is from an inordinate appetite, which
desires great things in goodness with a
magnitude not due in superiority to him
who desires; and who forgets his own superiority
over his neighbor, and who recalls the
inferiority of that one, and who forgets his
own inferiority. Pride, why
is it? Solution. Pride is, because hu-
mility is not. Humility asked of
pride, why it had greater
concordance with the intellect, than
with memory nor will? Solution.
Pride replied that the intellect
properly relates to understanding, just as
fire to heating and to shining, but
the will is more variable, and the same
applies to memory for desiring things
due and undue, compared to the intellect
for understanding things true and untrue:
therefore, the proud man who does not consider
his own defects, and considers the defects
of others, has greater concordance
with the intellect than with other
powers.

**Concerning the Questions of Acedia.**

**A**cedia, what is it? Solution. Go
to the vicious branches of the moral
tree. Acedia, from what is it? Solution. Acedia is from idle ends, and from a sad
appetite, because ends are not idle.
Acedia, why is it? Solution. Acedia is,
because diligence for moral ends is not
present. Diligence asked of acedia,
why it had greater concordance with
the intellect, than with memory or will? Solution. Acedia responded,
that the intellect is that faculty which
has greater labor in finding its object,
than any other faculty: because it first
seeks species with which it attains
secrets and truths of things, and in
seeking those species it has great labor,
since it is so that the secrets and
truths of things are very strongly hidden,
and under many false similarities,
and from those species which the
intellect receives and collects for revealing
secrets and truths, the will receives
and collects light for loving its object
by loving or hating, and those species
which the intellect receives and finds,
it hands over or recommits to memory,
and in it (memory) it makes old ones,
and seeks other new ones, and thus it
forms the habit of knowledge with which
it clothes itself, and from which memory
and will have practice, which do not
have such great labor in receiving

Questions of the branches. 501

Gluttony and Superbia answered, that they themselves were weeping because he himself did not eat meat, nor drank wine, nor wore beautiful clothes. [They are found] in rich people, who have more money, and love special good more against the public, than poor people.

De Quæstionibus gulæ & accidiæ.
Questions of Gluttony & Sloth.

How do Gluttony & Sloth have concordance? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the vicious branches of the moral tree. The hermit asked Gluttony, whether it was as bad a vice as Sloth? Solution. Gluttony answered, that it itself is not as common a vice as Sloth. The hermit asked Sloth and Gluttony, what sign they made on their shield? Solution. Gluttony and Sloth answered, that they made the sign of sadness and laziness when people ate too much, and when healthy people have gained temperance, good morals, money, and a good reputation. Gluttony & Sloth, said the hermit, what is your end? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric.

De Quæstionibus gulæ & inuidiæ.
Questions of Gluttony & Envy.

How do Gluttony & Envy have concordance? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the vicious branches of the moral tree. Gluttony, said the hermit, are you as bad a vice as Envy? Solution. Gluttony answered, that an envious person can have envy hungry and full, and it [Envy] is more contrary to charity than it [Gluttony]. Gluttony & Envy, said the hermit, why are you friends? Solution. Gluttony and Envy answered, that they were friends because they had fear of their enemies. The hermit asked Gluttony & Envy, when he lost them, where he would find them sooner? Solution. Gluttony and Envy answered, that they were willingly in rich people, who have more money, and love special good more against the public, than poor people.

De Quæstionibus gulæ & iræ.
Questions of Gluttony & Wrath.

How do Gluttony & Wrath have concordance? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric in the vicious branches of the moral tree. Gluttony, said the hermit, are you as bad a vice as Wrath? Solution. Gluttony answered, that it itself killed the human body slowly, and Wrath suddenly and quickly. The hermit asked Gluttony & Wrath, whether they had fear? Solution. Gluttony answered and said, that it itself had fear of temperance: and Wrath said, that it itself had fear of patience. Gluttony & Wrath, do you sell yourselves for money? Solution. Gluttony and Wrath answered, and said, that they were not sold for money, but gave themselves willingly to all who wanted them.

De Quæstionibus auaritiæ & luxuriæ.
Questions of Avarice & Lust.

How do Avarice & Lust have concordance? Solution. Go to the vicious branches of the moral tree in the aforesaid rubric. Lust, said the hermit, are you as bad a vice as Avarice? Solution. Lust answered and said, that it itself was not so strongly against nature as Avarice, nor was it so public a vice. The hermit asked a lustful old woman, why she did not have as great pleasure from the lust of her daughter-in-law, as from the lust of her daughter? Solution. The old woman answered and said, that she loved money more on account of her daughter than on account of her daughter-in-law, and she loved her own likeness of lust more in that woman whom she loved more. Lustful old woman, said the hermit, why do you reprehend your son—

Rrr 3.

And then the hermit said that they could quickly be found. The hermit asked avarice and envy whether they were of noble lineage? Solution. Avarice and envy responded that their lineage was very ancient, and they were especially in the tops of trees.

*Of Questions of Lust, &*
*Envy.*

How do Lust and Envy have
agreement? Solution. Go
to the aforementioned rubric in the
vicious branches of the moral tree. The hermit
asked Lust whether it was as bad
a vice as Envy? Solution. Lust re-
sponded that she herself was a worse
vice in touching, and Envy in see-
ing. Why is a woman better dis-
posed to be lustful than en-
vious, and a man to be envious
than to be lustful? Solution.
It does not become any woman to have
riches as well as a man, and every
coerced will desires to be free.
Why are women more blamed
for Lust than men for Envy?
Solution. The judgment of women is not
as great as the judgment of men.

*Of Questions of Lust,*
*& Wrath.*

How do Lust and Wrath have
agreement? Solution. Go to
the aforementioned rubric in the vicious
branches of the moral tree. The hermit asked
Lust and Wrath which of them
was more evil? Solution. Lust responded
that she herself sometimes had fear.

[Column 2]

And Wrath said that she never
had fear. Someone wanted to give
a young woman in marriage
to a certain old man: who asked
her whether it pleased her? Solution.
The maiden responded that if he
wanted to have her as a wife, and
they were to quarrel with each other, there would
be no one to make peace between them.
Why is a lustful man not
angry against his own sin, and
is angry against his lustful
wife? Solution. Every
rooster is lord in his own dunghill.

*Of Questions of Pride, &*
*Sloth.*

How do Pride and Sloth have
agreement? Solution. Go
to the aforementioned rubric in the
vicious branches of the moral tree. Pride,
said the hermit, are you as bad a vice
as Sloth? Solution. Pride said
that she herself was more contrary to God
than Sloth: because she wanted
to be without equal. The hermit asked
Pride and Sloth whether they were
contrary? Solution. They responded
that they were contrary, inasmuch
as among men each wanted to be
greater than the other. Pride asked Sloth
where she stood? Solution. Sloth said
that many knew her home.

*On Questions of consequent vices. And first, on injustice.*

What is injustice? Solution. Go to the first paragraph on consequent vices in the vicious branches of the moral tree. From what is injustice? Solution. Injustice is from the privation of justice. Why is injustice? Solution. Injustice is, because justice is not. The hermit asked injustice, with which sense it has greater concordance? Solution. Injustice responded that it had greater concordance with speech and with hearing, because these are two senses through which the habit of justice exists in Jurists.

*On Questions of indiscretion.*

What is indiscretion? Solution. Go to the second paragraph. From what is indiscretion? Solution. Indiscretion is from the privation of prudence. Why is indiscretion? Solution. Indiscretion is, because prudence is not. Indiscretion, said the hermit, against which power of the soul are you stronger? Solution. Indiscre-tion responded that it was more contrary to the intellect, than to memory and will, because intellect and prudence have a great friendship.

*of heart.*

What is weakness of heart? Solution. Go to the third paragraph. Why is weakness of heart? Solution. Weakness of heart is, because fragile and fox-like men forget hope and shame, and more often consider those things which are dangerous. Why are sanguine men more audacious than phlegmatic men? Solution. Fire pours out blood, and water restricts it. Why are men after eating more audacious than fasting men? Solution. In men after eating, vital spirits perform their functions: and in fasting men they have performed them: therefore the virtue of the heart is more extended, through all

# Questions of Sections. 507

[Ignorance] replied that it did not have fear of fortitude while prudence slept.

### On Questions of Infidelity.

What is infidelity? Solution. Go to the fifth paragraph. From what does infidelity arise? Solution. Infidelity arises from errors which the human intellect supposes to be true against the articles of the Catholic Faith. Why is there infidelity? Solution. Infidelity exists because of the absence of good pastors, who do not well guard their sheep: and it exists materially, so that holy Christian men may have material for doing great good in destroying errors, and in sustaining passions for praising and preaching the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. How can infidelity be destroyed? Solution. Infidelity can be destroyed with the diligence of good pastors, according to the method which Raymond placed in his petition, which he presented to the Lord Pope and his college.

### On Questions of Despair.

What is despair? Solution. Go to the sixth paragraph. Why is there despair? Solution. God permits despair to exist, so that it may be material for men, that they may have great hope in Our Lady. How does despair exist? Solution. Despair exists insofar as sinful men recall the great justice of God, and forget His great mercy. Why are desperate men sad? Solution. Desperate men are sad, because despair induces fear and permits evil, and no good.

### On Questions of Cruelty.

What is cruelty? Solution. Go to the seventh paragraph. The hermit asked cruelty, why it preferred to stay among rich men rather than among poor men? Solution. Cruelty replied that rich men love envy and avarice more than poor men. Cruelty, said the hermit, will you ask forgiveness from God in the presence of the poor? Solution. Cruelty replied that it dared not speak falsely in the presence of witnesses. Cruelty, with what do you conquer charity? Solution. Cruelty replied that it conquered charity with the laziness of love, and with despair, avarice, and pride.

### On Questions of Treachery.

What is treachery? Solution. Go to the eighth aforesaid paragraph. How can treachery be destroyed? Solution there. Legality, said the hermit, with what vice is treachery more contrary to you? Solution. Legality replied that treachery was contrary to it with lust in young men, and with avarice in old men. The hermit asked treachery, with what sense was it more contrary to legality. Solution. Treachery replied that no sense is as common for procuring falsehood as speech.

### On Questions of Homicide.

What is homicide? Solution. Go to the ninth paragraph. Homicide, said life, how could you be destroyed? Solution there. Homicide,

the hermit said, "From which sense do you (Life) have greater fear?" Answer. "Through no other sense do so many men die as through taste." Then indeed the hermit knew that through no sense do so many men live as through taste and temperance. Life, said the hermit, "With which power of the soul is homicide most contrary to you?" Answer. Life responded that no spiritual power listens so little to reason as the will.

*Of Questions of Robbery.*

What is Robbery? Answer. Go to the tenth paragraph. Robbery, said the hermit, "Who is your greatest friend?" Answer, there. Robbery, from whom have you stolen more? Answer. Robbery responded that more has been stolen from God than from anyone else. Robbery, what things have you stolen more from God? Answer. Robbery responded that more has been stolen from God concerning truth and honor than concerning any other thing: because more men are in error than in truth, and more men labor to acquire their own honor than to honor God. And then the hermit said to Robbery that it was a very evil vice.

*Of Questions of Lying.*

What is Lying? Answer. Go to the eleventh paragraph. Lying, said the hermit, "What are your greatest enemies?" Answer, there. Lying, in which sense are you greater? Answer. Lying responded that no sense lied against nature, except speech only, and then the hermit knew that speech, when

[Right Column]

it spoke the truth, was more a friend of God than any other servant. The hermit asked the will whether it had as great a fault in lying as the intellect? Answer. The will responded that he should ask this from truth, which is the object of the intellect.

*Of Questions of Cursing.*

What is Cursing? Answer. Go to the twelfth paragraph. Cursing, "What are your greatest enemies?" Answer, there. Cursing, about whom do you speak more evil? Answer. Cursing responded that it spoke more evil about him who is worth more: then indeed the hermit knew that it wanted to say this about Christ, about whom bad Christians speak evil while they play dice: and unbelievers, who are more numerous than Christians, who speak much evil about the Lord Jesus Christ, about whom the will speaks evil, which does not love him as much as itself. Cursing, why are you greater than blessing? Answer. Cursing responded that it was greater than blessing, because it had more agents, and because when wolves eat sheep, the shepherds flee.

*Of Questions of Impatience*

What is Impatience? Answer. Go to the thirteenth paragraph. Impatience, from whom do you have fear? Answer, there. Impatience, how are you overcome? Answer, there. Impatience, why do you have such great audacity, and are so proud? Answer. Impatience said that while anger is its friend, it has no fear of being overcome.

Quæstiones of the branches. 509

On the Questions of Inconstancy.

What is Inconstancy? Solution. Go to the fourteenth paragraph.
Inconstancy, who are called your greatest enemies? Solution, in the same place.
Inconstancy, which sense has greater agreement with you? Solution. Inconstancy said that speech was that sense which is less stable.
Inconstancy, why do you have greater agreement with the will than with the intellect? Solution. Inconstancy said that the will easily turned itself from one purpose to another without deliberation: but the intellect, when it wanted to speak, before it spoke, considered for a long time with deliberation, in that which it wanted to say, because of which they wished evil upon themselves.

On the Questions of Impurity.

What is Impurity? Solution. Go to the fifteenth paragraph.
Impurity, why are you so great? Solution. It responded that it was so great because it was more contrary than any other vice to the common habit of virtue.
Impurity, why is it greater spiritually than corporally? Solution. No purity is as great sensually as intellectually.
Impurity, of which water do you have greater fear? Solution. Impurity said that it had greater fear of the water which eyes emit by weeping through contrition, than of the water with which beautiful Ladies wash their face.

On the Questions of Falsehood.

What is Falsehood? Solution. Go to the sixteenth paragraph.
Falsehood, of what do you have greater fear? Solution. Falsehood responded that it had greater fear of the death of hypocrisy and simony than of the death of any other vice.
Falsehood, are you as strong as truth? Solution, in the same place.
Since you, Falsehood, are not as strong as truth, why do you stand in more people than truth? Solution. Falsehood said that it would ask this of the shepherds who poorly guard the sheep.

On the Questions of Sloth.

What is Sloth? Solution. Go to the seventeenth paragraph.
Why is Usury? Solution, in the same place.
Sloth, where are you going? Solution. Sloth said that it was going to dwell in fat people, who have good beds, and who eat delicate foods.
Sloth, why are you more in rich people than in poor people? Solution. Because of the lack of meat, the wolf eats grapes.

*On Questions of Indiscretion, &*
*Mixed Vices.*

Indiscretion, from what is your strength? Solution. Indiscretion responded that its strength was from the fragility that a soldier has in war against courage. Intemperance, where is your dwelling? Solution. It responded that it dwelt in the indiscretion that gluttonous men have in eating and drinking. Indiscretion, why are you so great? Solution. Indiscretion responded that it grew every time that wolves eat sheep. Indiscretion, why are you despairing? Solution. Indiscretion responded that it was despairing because prudence did not speak to sinful men about the great mercy of God. Indiscretion, why are you so cruel? Solution. Indiscretion responded that its credulity grew while prudence forgot charity. Indiscretion, did you ever commit treachery? Solution. Indiscretion responded that it always committed treachery when men omit to confess their sins because of shame. Indiscretion, did you ever kill any man? Solution. Indiscretion responded that hell knew this, into which so many men go because of ignorance and foolishness. Indiscretion, did you ever commit robbery? Solution. Indiscretion said that it often stole money from the poor, so that they might have hunger, and gave it to the rich, so that they might have vain glo-

Solution. Indiscretion responded that it spoke ill of good Ladies, so that luxury might have great fame in the world. Indiscretion, why are you impatient? Solution. Indiscretion said that it was impatient because prudence slept, and wrath watched. Indiscretion, you who do not understand, how do you have knowledge of inconstancy? Solution. Indiscretion said that in its ignorance, constancy had knowledge of inconstancy. Indiscretion, from what is your impurity? Solution. Indiscretion said that its impurity was from culpably remembering, loving, being ignorant, seeing, hearing, speaking, tasting, and touching. Indiscretion, you who are a deprivation of prudence, how do you have knowledge of falsehood? Solution. Intemperance, what is your custom? Solution.
Intemperance answered that she placed men in the hope of temperance at the beginning of the month, and in the middle of the month she cast temperance from the table. Intemperance, are you a doctor? Solution. Intemperance said that she was a doctor who, with cruelty, killed the poor against charity, and by herself, the rich, who are her friends. Intemperance, why do you commit betrayal against those who trust in you? Solution. Intemperance said that she had the duty of betraying her friends. Intemperance, with what do you kill men? Solution. Intemperance said that she killed men with many delicate foods, and by eating for many hours of the day. Intemperance, how did you steal temperance from the Monk, who had her in the refectory? Solution. Intemperance said that she had stolen temperance from the Monk whom the Abbot had invited to the infirmary. Intemperance, what method do you have in lying? Solution. Intemperance answered that she had a method of lying, in that she promised health and cheerfulness in eating many delicate foods, by reason of which she gave sadness and infirmity to those who ate too much of them. Intemperance, why do you speak ill of temperance, who is such a good virtue? Solution. Intemperance said that it is no wonder if one contrary speaks ill of another contrary. Intemperance, why are men who have eaten too much impatient? Solution. Intemperance said that they are impatient because natural instinct feels the beginning of the infirmity which she had procured at the table.
Intemperance, what do you do with good strong wine? Solution. Intemperance said that she knew how to do many works, among which inconstancy was one of them. Intemperance, why do men spit so often? Solution. Intemperance said that men spit so often because she made them eat and drink too much. Intemperance, have you ever committed falsehood? Solution. She said, and answered that she often committed falsehoods against a certain hermit who ate nothing but bread and water through hypocrisy, by which he was weakened. Intemperance, why are men lazy in August? Solution. She answered that men are lazy in August because they are full of figs and must. Intemperance, at what time are you taught? Solution. Intemperance said that she was taught at the clearing of the table when men were sated with food and drink. Intemperance, have you ever been obedient to temperance? Solution. Intemperance said that she had often been obedient to temperance, who made men eat little at supper, so that she might make them eat too much at dinner.

*On Questions of infidelity & mixed vices.*

Infidelity, why do you not have hope? Solution. Infidelity answered that she could not have it because faith and hope agree with each other. Infidelity, can your friends have charity against cruelty when they give alms to the poor? Solution. Infidelity said that her followers who give alms have the appearance of charity and not the essence: for if they had the essence, they would agree—

...they would have agreement with faith, which is contrary to itself. Infidelity, how do you commit betrayal? Solution. The cat makes a likeness, becoming a rabbit, when it flattens its ears and hides its tail, so that it may catch rabbits, and the fox pretends to be a hen, so that the chicks may come to it. Infidelity, how do you commit murder? Solution. It replied that it committed murder with ignorance and falsehood, and the idleness of pastors. Infidelity, with whom do you commit robbery? Solution. Infidelity said that it stole the souls of men with ignorance and the disparagement of the Christian faith. Infidelity, why do you live by lies in so many people? Solution. Infidelity said that it lived by lies in many people: because few people know and want to speak the truth. Infidelity, are you angry: because Christians speak ill of you? Solution. Infidelity said that it did not care about this, that Christians spoke ill of it: because it was praised by more people than it was blasphemed. Infidelity, do you have impatience? Solution. It replied that it ought not to have impatience after it possessed the city of Jerusalem, but impatience belonged to the Roman faith. Infidelity, are you strongly built? Solution. Infidelity said that its edifice was fortified with iron, wood, and ignorance: therefore it had no fear that it would be conquered. Infidelity, do you have impurity? Solution. Infidelity said that Saracens do not hold napkins at the table, and when they eat, they wash their fingers, and are more luxurious than other men. Infidelity, could your falsehood be destroyed? Solution. Infidelity said that the possibility of its destruction is written by Raymund

[Column 2]
in his book. Infidelity, do you have laziness? Solution. Infidelity said that if there is one Christian, there are a hundred who are not Christians: therefore it had laziness: because it did not destroy Christians, nevertheless it had diligence in the land of Syria, Turkey, and Barbary, which used to belong to Christians. Infidelity, do you have any courtesy? Solution. Infidelity said that it was courteous in the Synagogue of the Jews, whom it makes to observe well the Sabbath day. Infidelity, do you have more obedient people? Solution. Infidelity said that it would seek this from the south and the east, which are full of its people.

Despair, do you have greater cruelty than hope has charity? Solution. Despair replied that that question should be put to the purses of the poor and to wolves, who eat sheep. Despair, why do you commit betrayal? Solution. Despair said that it commits betrayal because legality has agreement with hope. Despair, with whom do you kill the souls of men? Solution. Despair said that it kills the souls of men, inasmuch as at the point of death it promised them discretion, confession, contrition, and satisfaction: because at that point imagination more strongly imagines cold springs than the sins of men and the mercy of God. 516 Questions of branches.

On Questions of Treachery, and mixed vices.

Treachery, where were you begun? Solution.
She answered that she had her beginning then, when Cain killed his brother Abel through envy and through avarice, therefore because she was of such a kind, she was of the lineage of death. Treachery, could a man steal you? Solution.
She said that it was not necessary for a man to steal her, since she would give herself to any man who wished to have her. Treachery, of which sense are you more a friend? Solution. She answered that she loved flattery more than any other sense, because it spoke many lies, and with it she procured the deception which she causes for men. Treachery, why do you speak ill of goodness and charity? Solution. She said that for this reason she spoke ill of charity and goodness, because they are sisters of legality. Treachery, why are you impatient? Solution. She answered that she was impatient because pride is her brother

# Questions of the branches. 517

**On the Questions of Robbery, and**
**mixed vices.**

Robbery, why do you not have
shame in lying? Answer. It answered,
that it could not perform its office without lying.
Robbery, with whom do you steal goodness?
Answer. It said, that it stole goodness,
with slander, simony, and hypocrisy.
Robbery, why are you impatient?
Answer. It said, that it was
impatient, because it did not remember the gallows.
Robbery, do you have weakness? Answer.
It said, that the King's justice made
it tremble. Robbery, why do you go
by night? Answer. It said,
that it went by night so that people would not see
its shameful garments. Robbery,
why are you illegal? Answer.
It said, that it was illegal, because with
legality it could not deceive people.
Robbery, why are you? Answer. It said,
that it existed, because it had laziness in
digging the vineyard, and in going to
market. Robbery, were you ever
obedient? Answer. It said, that
it was often obedient, much to its own
dislike, to the gallows. Robbery, are you
educated? Answer. It said, that it would put that ques-
tion to simony, which had stolen the episcopate,
and that similarly it would put
that question to hypocrisy,
which had stolen sanctity.

**On the Questions of Lying, Slander,**
**and the vices mixed with them.**

Lying and Slander, why did you
form a partnership? Answer. They
said, that they formed a partnership, so that
they might destroy goodness and truth,
which are friends. Why are lying
men more impatient than others?
Answer. A lying man always excuses
himself when he is reproved. Lying,
of what is your foundation?
Answer. It said, that its foundation
was of pride, envy, anger, avarice,
and hypocrisy. The hermit asked from the mouth,
whether it was as shameful to lie,
as the shirt of a leper by leprosy?
Answer. The mouth answered, that it would put
that question to hypocrisy, which
is more shameful than the shirt of a leper.
Lying, how do you make falsehood? Answer.
It answered, that simony and hypocrisy
knew this. Lying, do you have
diligence? Answer. It said, that through
the whole world it had sown its seed.
Lying, are you well educated?
Answer. It answered, that it had learned
rhetoric, so that it could deceive people.
Lying, were you obedient? Answer. Lying said,
that it would put that question to the Tar-
tars, and to the Jews, and to the Saracens, and
to the money of Christians, and to the habit of
hypocrisy.

**On the Questions of Slander, and**
**mixed vices.**

Slander, why do you speak ill
of humble people when they have
patience? Answer. It said,
that it was of the lineage of pride, anger,
and cruelty. Slander, why do you not
speak ill of inconstancy, which is
a bad vice? Answer. Slander said,
that it did not wish to dishonor its
sister, of whom holy men speak ill.
Slander, why do you speak ill of clerics?
Answer. Slander said, that it spoke ill
of clerics, because vices resided worse
in them than in other people.
Slander, why do you not speak ill
of simony and hypocrisy? Answer.

Slander said that it did not speak evil
except with falsehood. Slander, are you
lazy? Answer. It said that about no one
has so much evil been spoken as about
the Trinity of God and His incarnation. Slander,
why do you speak discourteously?
Answer. It said that pride, anger, and
envy advised it. Slander,
do you have more friends? Answer. It said
that the greater part of men, poor
and rich, obeyed it.

On Questions of impatience, and
mixed vices.

Impatience and Inconstancy, why are
you friends? Answer. They answered
that they were friends because they had
more friends. Impatience, why
are you ugly? Answer. It said that it
was beautiful to anger and to pride,
which greatly love it. Impatience,
why are hypocritical men so strongly
your friends? Answer. It
said that it loved hypocritical men,
because they deceive lawful men,
who are holy men. Impatience,
why do you have more friends than
patience? Answer. Impatience said
that it was more diligent with anger
than patience with abstinence. Impatience,
why are you badly taught? Answer.
Impatience answered that
it was badly taught because with gluttony
and with pride, anger, and avarice it had formed
a partnership. Impatience, why are you disobedient
to abstinence? Answer. It said
that it was disobedient to abstinence,
because it was a relative of patience.

On Questions of inconstancy, and
mixed vices.

Inconstancy, why are you ugly? Answer.
It said that it was ugly because
constancy was a kind of holiness.
Inconstancy, why are you false? Answer.
It said that it was false, because if
it could not deceive lawful men
by one method, it deceived them by another
method. Inconstancy, are you
lazy? Answer. It said that it was
so diligent that men could not
find it in truth. Inconstancy,
why are you taught at one time,
and badly taught at another? Answer.
It said that it was badly taught,
so that it could speak reproaches. Inconstancy,
to whom are you most disobedient? Answer.
It said that indiscretion, lust, pride,
gluttony, and avarice knew this.

On Questions of uncleanness, and
mixed vices.

Uncleanness, are you as great in hypocrisy
as in secular matters? Answer.
It said that falsehood knew this. Uncleanness,
do you have laziness? Answer.
It said that it would ask this of lust,
which it procured in many men.
Uncleanness, why do you speak while
you eat, and hold your mouth full? Answer.
It said that it and discourtesy formed
a partnership. Uncleanness, do you have
fear? Answer. It answered, and
said that it would put that question
to holiness and obedience, which
were weeping.

On Questions of falsehood, and
mixed vices.

Falsehood, do you have laziness? Answer.
It said that it would put that question
to Judges and Lawyers, who prolong
lawsuits for peasants. Falsehood, how
are you known? Answer. It said that
its banner was from discourtesy and from hypocrisy.
Falsehood, to whom are you most disobe-

**On Questions of Counsel.**

The hermit asked the Prince, "Of what persons should your counsel consist?" Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric.

The hermit asked the king's sword, "Why are you not straight?" Solution. The sword said that it was crooked because the King did not have good counsel.

The hermit asked, "Should the King's counsel consist of many persons?" Solution. The more persons there are in the King's counsel, the greater is the confusion of counsel and its secrets are fewer.

The hermit asked the King, "Of which men do you have greater fear?" Solution. The King said that no men could do him as much evil as those of his own counsel, nor deceive him as much.

Then the hermit told the King that he should not have negligent, indiscreet, cruel, proud, injurious men in his counsel, and that he should especially avoid an avaricious man more than any other man, because an avaricious man does everything for money.

**On Questions of Procurators.**

The hermit asked the King, "In what should your procurators be clothed?" Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric.

The hermit asked the King, "Do you have good procurators?" Solution. The King said that his people knew this.

The hermit asked the King, "Is there simony in your procuration?" Solution. The King said that he should ask this of avarice.

"King," said the hermit, "where are legality and your riches?" Solution. The King said that legality and his riches are in those men...

**Questions concerning the branches. 525**

...[he] is the common hypostasis,
who produces the Son from all and with all
his reasons, and through all his
reasons. How is the Son from passion? Solution. The Father, inasmuch as he considers his activity, considers possibility from his activity. And go to the rubric of virtue. How is the Son from the Father, and not from another? Solution. The Father, in considering his possitivity, and from his own goodness, infinity, eternity, and other things, considers possibility. How is the Son possible and posited? Solution. In God, possitivity, which is the Father, and possibility, which is the Son, relate to each other. And because God is pure act, eternal, infinite, and complete, the Son is posited; and therefore in the Son, posited and possible are one and the same, and can be all acts of reasons eternally and infinitely. How are the Father and Son distinct? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue. How are the Father and Son one essence, one substance, one nature, one goodness, one magnitude, one eternity, etc.? Solution. If infiniting and infinible, eternizing and eternable, possifying and possifiable, could be different essences, substances, and natures, and different goodnesses, then contradiction could be a real being, which contradiction is impossible. The hermit asked the Son whether he was from matter, or if he was matter? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue. How is the Son the Son? Solution therein. The hermit asked the Son whether he was augmentable? Solution therein.

Concerning the Questions of the Holy Spirit.

How is the Holy Spirit passive spirability without matter? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. The Holy

[Column 2]

Spirit, how is he the third person? Solution therein. How is the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son? Solution therein. Since the Father and the Son are distinct persons, how are they one spirativity? Solution. The Father and the Son are distinct by their proper properties, and are one spirativity through a common spirativity. Since the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, how is he one spirability, one person and not many? Solution. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, inasmuch as he is from a common spirativity, and is one person, and one spirability, inasmuch as he is from one spirativity, and not from many. How is the Holy Spirit equal to the Father and the Son? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue. How are the Father and the Son equal in the Holy Spirit? Solution. In this, that the Father and the Son equally love each other, and are one spirativity and not many, they are equal in the Holy Spirit. How are the Father and the Holy Spirit equal in the Son? Solution. The Father generates the Son from his whole self, and the Son spirates the Holy Spirit from his whole self. How are the Son and the Holy Spirit equal in the Father? Solution. The Son spirates the Holy Spirit from his whole self, and is wholly begotten by the whole Father, and the Father spirates the Holy Spirit from his whole self, who is wholly spirated from the whole Father. Since the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, how is he wholly from the Father, and wholly from the Son? Solution. In this, that the Father and the Son are distinct persons, the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son: and inasmuch as the Father and the Son are one spirativity, and not many, the Holy Spirit is one spirability, and not many: and the Holy Spirit is wholly from the Father, and is wholly from the Son.
