662 Question: Of a hundred forms.

Does work begin within a substance or outside? Solution. A natural form begins earlier in its own proper subject than in a subject appropriated to it, but concerning artificial forms, it is the contrary.

[Concerning Questions of Reflux.

XLIX.

What is Reflux? Solution. Reflux is the return of influence through concordance or contrariety. And go to the aforementioned rubric. Why is there reflux in natural substances? Solution. From influence and reflux follow the acts of natural powers. Does a power flow back its virtue to an object, or does an object flow back to a power? Solution. Air flows back its dryness to fire, because it is against humidity, and fire flows back that dryness to the air with its heat so that it may mortify the humidity. What does matter flow back to form? Solution. Form produces from matter possibilities into actualities, and matter flows back the action, which comes through disposition into a given state of being acted upon.

Concerning Questions of Influence.

XLVIII.

What is Influence? Solution. Influence is a gift or a coercion through the communication of a thing or things, from which follows a plenitude in which parts experience activity or rest. Is influence a general form? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Is influence a cause of corruption? Solution. Let this be sought from water, whose virtue fire corrupts, because it imparts its heat to it. How many species of natural influence are there? Solution. In natural and corporeal substances there are two species of influence, one is that which agrees with quality and with its own proper subject, thus the heat of fire infused into hot water, with its proper subject, which is fire, which moves its own proper heat into water against coldness and against the subject of that. The second species is influence, which comes from similarities, one similarity influencing its similarity into another, although it does not place its essence in that, nor its proper subject, just as the Sun, which influences its virtue into fire, and a seal [influences] its similarities into letters of wax: and imagination, which receives a similarity instilled by heat and taste.

Concerning Questions of Production.

L.

What is Production in natural substances? Solution. Production is that form which is the reason for producing into actuality forms which are in potentiality, so that possible beings may be actualized. From what is to produce? Solution. To produce formally the acts of production is materially from form and matter through action and passion. And go to the aforementioned rubric. With what does one form produce another form? Solution. In natural productions, fire with its heat produces dryness in the air. And in artificial productions, a mechanic produces forms with the instruments of his trade. Productions

--- Page 677 ---
**Question of a hundred forms. 663**

Productions which are above the natural course, how are they made? Solution. The idea of the eternal, placed in potential, is produced in a created subject through creation above the natural course, which idea indeed is produced in act by a natural agent and by divine reasons above the natural course. And in this it is recognized that the idea retains the nature of production above the natural course and of the natural course, and therefore insofar as it retains the nature above the natural course, it is an idea, and insofar as it retains the nature of the natural course, it is a creature.

*On Questions of Origin.*

L I.

What is origin in natural substances? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Of what is origin? Solution. Origin is formally of itself, and its act is to originate, which originates from form and matter, from which arise the acts of primary forms from which common form and matter are constituted. In what does origin arise? Solution. Origin is born in species and in its own individuated substance. Why is origin? Solution. Origin is so that there may be new substances in which species may be sustained, and the acts of primary forms.

*On Questions of Exit.*

L II.

What is natural exit? Solution. Exit is that by which one form exits from another, and by which an act exits from potential and object. And go to the aforementioned rubric. From what does exit exit, and in what does it exit? Solution. Heat

[Right Column]

exits from fire, and humidity from air, and coldness from water, and dryness exits from earth, and qualities exit in a constituted composite from their own subjects, which in it exit with new forms, and from old ones they exit through generation and corruption. Is exit a general form? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue. Since to exit an influx is from things, how can it be a general form? Solution. To exit insofar as it is an act exits from things, and insofar as exit is a form in the abstract, it is a general form, of which to exit is its act formally, and insofar as to exit exits from other forms, it is materially their act. And in this passage there is much of philosophy.

*On Questions of Separability.*

L III.

What is separability? Solution. Separability is that form by reason of which many things can be from one. And go to the aforementioned rubric. Of what is separability? Solution. Separability is from parts moved in a new real number. Why is separability? Solution. Separability is in two ways: in one way by reason of form, just as a smith who separates one iron into many nails; in another way it is by reason of end, just as a smith who separates a nail from a mass of iron, so that it may be a nail, and that he may have money. With which of the primary forms does separability have greater concordance? Solution. If inseparability were nothing, difference and separability would be the same in number.

**664 Questions of a hundred forms.**

*On Questions of Inseparability.*

LIV.

What is Inseparability? Solution.
Inseparability is that form by reason
of which different beings are not separated
from one another. And go to the
aforementioned rubric. Why is Inseparability?
Solution. Inseparability exists so that natural
qualities are not divided from their proper
subjects, or separated, when they exist as
appropriated to other foreign subjects,
just as the heat of fire, which is appropriated
to air. If inseparability did not exist, what
would follow? Solution. With inseparability
removed from natural subjects, every
appropriated quality would abandon its
proper subject, and the natural course
would be destroyed, nor would any composite
exist from the elements. From what is
Inseparability? Solution. Inseparability is
from parts joined and mixed, some in others,
under such a condition, that one cannot
exist without the other: just as goodness
which cannot exist without power, nor
matter without form.

*On Questions of Possibility.*

LV.

What is Possibility? Solution. Possibility
is that form by reason of which
matter is disposed, that from it posited
essences can exist. And go to the
aforementioned rubric. From what is
Possibility? Solution. Possibility is from
passive power subject to the action of
active power. How is Possibility a general
form? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue.
Why is Possibility? Solution. Possibility
exists essentially through itself: just as Martin
who by his essence is a man, and possibility
exists by reason of an end: because
without it no act could exist.

*On Questions of Impossibility.*

LVI.

What is Impossibility? Solution. Impossibility
is that form, against
which its contrary has no power. And go
to the aforementioned rubric. Is Impossibility
from power? Solution. If impossibility
were from power, the possible and the impossible
could be numerically the same. If impossibility
is not from power, from what is it? Solution.
Thus, impossibility is from the privation
of power: just as vice is from the
privation of virtue. Is Impossibility a
creature? Solution. Impossibility is a
creature in which created power is terminated
and comprehended, without which
impossibility every created power would
be infinite.

*On Questions of Similitude.*

LVII.

What is Similitude? Solution. Similitude
is a general form, by reason
of which similitudes are given in its genus.
And go to the aforementioned rubric.
From what is Similitude? Solution.
Similitude is from passive impressions
and active ones differing by essence,
and preserved in the same species. Why
is Similitude? Solution: If similitude
did not exist, no being could participate
with another, nor signify anything about
itself. Is Similitude a real or intentional
being? Solution: it is a real being by nature,
and an intentional being by artifice.

If one and the same form were transmuted from one matter into another matter, that form would be pure passion, and in this step it is recognized that one and the same form remaining in its species, accepts one matter and dismisses another, and in this step there is much of Philosophy.

*Concerning Questions of light.*

LXII.

What is light? Solution. Light is an instrument of difference, which with light signifies its act to particular senses. From what is light? Solution. Light is formally from itself, inasmuch as it is the color of celestial bodies and fire, and finally is an instrument of difference. Why is light? Solution. Light is thus by color, just as man is man by humanity, and white by whiteness. And go to the aforementioned rubric. Is there light in Hell? Solution. In Hell there is light, so that difference may have an instrument with which it can show ugly figures to the eyes, who in this life through sin desired to see beautiful figures, and that light is the cause of darkness to eyes which will not have the appetite for seeing ugly figures.

*Concerning Questions of shadow.*

LXIII.

What is shadow? Solution. Shadow is a confused color of water and earth in the absence of light. And go to the aforementioned rubric. From what is shadow? Solution. Shadow is from the privation

[Right Column]

of light and of thick vapors, which through the air are not purified, which cannot show its color in them. If shadow were not, what would follow? Solution. If shadow were not the absence of light, nothing would be. Is there shadow above the Moon? Solution. If there were shadow above the Moon, the Sun would not give its likeness to Venus, nor Venus to Mercury, nor Mercury to the Moon, nor would fire receive the influence of the Sun.

*Concerning Questions of line.*

LXIV.

What is a line? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Is a line a general form? Solution. If a line were not a general form, the primary forms would not have concretes, in which they would be sustained. From what is a line? Solution. A line is from itself in its priority, and is from punctual parts, which are above it, from which it is composed, and is the matter of parts which are in the inferiors, which are of its species. Is a line in a spherical body? Solution. In every body in which there is length, breadth, and depth, there must be a line.

*Concerning Questions of punctuality.*

LXV.

What is punctuality? Solution. Punctuality is that form, by reason of which a point is indivisible. From what is punctuality? Solution. Punctuality is from simple indivisible points. Since a line is from points, and points are indivisible, how is a line divisible? Solution. Every line which is from points is compo-

[Column 1]

composite, and every composite is divisible. Since a point is indivisible, how can one point be in another? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric.

*Concerning Questions of Surface.*

LXVI.

What is a surface? Solution. A surface is that form with which a body is naturally endowed with color. From what is a surface? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Why is a surface? Solution. A surface exists so that a body can be bounded, and that it may be visible and palpable. Is there a surface in an indivisible point? Sol. Just as any indivisible point is a part of a divisible body, so an indivisible surface, sustained in an indivisible point, is a part of a divisible surface.

*Concerning Questions of Figure.*

LXVII.

What is a figure? Solution. A figure is the likeness of a form extended in color, which is extended on a surface. From what is a figure? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Is the figure of a nail a created thing? Solution. If the figure of a nail were not a created thing, the visibility and imaginability of the nail would not be created things. Where is the figure of a nail before the nail exists? Solution. Particular figures are potentially in the universal figure, before they are their own proper subjects.

*Concerning Questions of Rectitude.*

LXVIII.

[Column 2]

What is rectitude? Solution. Rectitude is that form by reason of which lines are straight. From what is rectitude? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Why are there six rectitudes, and not more nor fewer? Solution. Without six rectitudes, there would be no center nor surface in any body, and the same if there were more than six rectitudes. Does the firmament have six rectitudes? Solution. Because the firmament is the supreme body, beyond which there is no natural body, it does not have rectitudes above itself, and because it contains within itself a general, confused, and spherical body which extends from Saturn to the center of the Earth, there are six rectitudes in that body.

*Concerning Questions of Masculinity.*

LXIX.

What is masculinity? Solution. Masculinity is that essence by which there are many males. From what is masculinity? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Why is masculinity? Solution. If masculinity were not in natural substances, generation would not exist. Is the masculinity of Aries a quality proper to itself, or an appropriated one? Solution. Just as heat is an appropriated quality for Aries, because it is an instrument for heating, so masculinity is appropriated for Aries, because it is an instrument for moving the virtue of masculinity in males.

does a flower impress its scent into
the air? Solution. Just as the matter of
bread which a man eats is an impression
through transmutation into vegetative
and sensitive matter, so the scent of the flower
is impressed into the air through transmutation.

*On Questions of Grafting.*

LXXV.

What is grafting? Solution. Go to the
aforementioned rubric. Why
is grafting? Solution there. Why can
the grafting of a pear be done on an apple tree, and not
on a fig tree? Solution. According as
species of plants are related and
concordant in nature, some can be
grafted onto others. Can fire be
grafted into water? Solution. If fire could
be grafted into water, in that grafting
fire and water would have greater
concordance than contrariety.
And in this passage it is understood why
the grafting of a pear cannot be done on a fig
tree.

*On Questions of Perfection.*

LXXVI.

What is perfection? Solution. Go to the
aforementioned rubric. Why is perfection?
Solution. Perfection is through form and through
matter in natural things, and therefore
it is through form alone, and perfection
is that the ends of things are sustained
in it. From what is perfection? Solution.
Perfection is from form and matter, and it is
from their end. Is fire simply that which it
is by itself? Solution.
Go to the aforementioned rubric.

*On Questions of Individuality.*

LXXVII.

What is individuality? Solution. Individuality
is the general form which
is the reason and cause for specific
individuals. Why is individuality? Solution.
Individuality is so that from one, many could
exist. From what is individuality?
Solution. Thus is the individuality of Martin and his
son, of the apple tree, of the horse, of the crane from general individuality,
just as is the color of Martin and
his son, of the apple tree, of the horse, and of the crane from general
color. And go to the aforementioned
rubric. Why are unity and plurality
equally causes of individuality?
Solution. The plurality of the Father and the Son
and the unity which they have in breathing forth the Holy
Spirit are the reasons by which
in creatures plurality and unity are
equally causes of individuality. And in
this passage there is much of Theology
and Philosophy.

*On Questions of Attraction.*

LXXVIII.

What is attraction? Solution. Attraction
is that by which one
radical humor attracts to itself from another
radical humor the nutritive
humor. How is attraction?
Solution. Go to the aforementioned
rubric. By what does a magnet attract
iron to itself? Solution. Just as the visual
faculty attracts to itself the visibility of
color, so the great earthiness of the magnet
attracts to itself the earthiness of
iron. By what does seed attract to itself
the multiplication of its species? Solution.
Go to the rubric of virtue.

670 Questions of a hundred forms.

*Concerning Questions of Necessity.*

LXXIX.

What is necessity? Solution. Necessity is
that form, by reason of which from the
impossible follows its possible contrary: just
as if it is impossible that the whole be less
than its part, it is necessary that the whole
be greater than its part. How many species
of necessity are there? Solution. Go to the
aforesaid rubric. Of the two species
of necessity, which is more necessary?
Solution. That substance which exists instantaneously
according to the natural course
is more necessary than that which exists
by succession, and the same applies to the sub-
stance which is above the natural course,
such as God being the end of all beings.
If necessity did not exist, what would follow?
Solution. If necessity were nothing,
everything that exists would exist by contin-
gency, and God would be nothing, and everything that
is impossible would be possible, and vice
versa. And in this passage it is signified
that God exists by necessity, and that
He is one in the Trinity of persons.

*Concerning Questions of Contingency.*

LXXX.

What is contingency? Solution.
Contingency is that by which
certain ends deviate from others by their
contraries. And go to the aforesaid
rubric. From what does contingency arise?
Solution. Contingency arises from contrary
ends, some of which impede their
necessities for others. Why does contin-
gency exist? Solution. Contingency
exists because a principle cannot have

[Column 2]

its own proper or natural means,
by which it can pass to its necessary end.
If contingency were nothing,
what would follow? Solution. If
contingency were nothing, no man
would have liberty, and the ass would always bray
out of necessity, nor would the goat have
fear of the wolf, and frost would always
burn the almonds.

*Concerning Questions of Perfection.*

LXXXI.

What is perfection? Solution. Perfec-
tion is that instant in which succession
finds rest. From what does perfection
arise? Solution. Just as the possible is that
which does not participate in the impos-
sible, so perfection is that which
does not participate in defect. With what
is perfection? Solution. Perfection
is with the acts of natural forms
and with their moral similitudes.
Why does perfection exist? Solution.
Perfection exists so that there may be rest in existing and
acting. And go to the aforesaid rubric.

*Concerning Questions of Imperfection.*

LXXXII.

What is imperfection? Solution. Im-
perfection arises from the privation of
perfection, and thus it is its contrary, just as
evil is the contrary of good, and heat of cold,
and blackness of whiteness. Is imperfection
a creature? Solution. Imperfection is
a creature in natural works. And
go to the aforesaid rubric. And it is not a crea-
ture in moral works. And go
to the vicious moral tree. Is imper-
fection a general form? Solution. If
imperfection were not a general form,
the succession of perfection would be nothing.

**Questions of a hundred forms. 673**

*On Questions of sleep.*

XC.

**W**hat is sleep? Answer. Sleep is that form, by reason of which those who have labored have an appetite for rest. From what does sleeping come? Answer. Sleeping is from a preparation, which prepares and disposes matter so that there may be acts of natural forms. And go to the aforementioned rubric. Why could no man live without sleeping? Answer. If a horse that runs did not rest afterwards, it could not run another time. Why do men who are inebriated have a greater appetite for sleeping than others? Answer. Because wine is very vaporous, it suddenly causes vapors from the belly to ascend to the brain, which close off the imaginative species that it receives from the senses, which have no similarities with which to satisfy the powers of the rational soul.

*On Questions of waking.*

XCI.

**W**hat is waking? Answer. Waking is the succession of fantastic species moved from the senses through the imaginative faculty up to the powers of the rational soul. From what does waking come? Answer. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Why do some men wake more than others? Answer. No man sleeps as much as a phlegmatic person: nor does any man wake as much as he who loves much. Does a man who dreams participate more with waking than with sleeping? Answer. In men who dream, the imaginative faculty is more awake than any other power.

*On Questions of dreaming.*

XCII.

**W**hat is dreaming? Answer. Go to the aforementioned rubric. From where does dreaming come, and how many are its species? Answer, in the same place. Why does man dream more than irrational animals? Answer, in the same place. Why does a melancholic man naturally dream more than another man? Answer. No memory retains as many species as that which is of the complexion of earth, and this is because it has a more durable foundation.

*On Questions of joy.*

XCIII.

**W**hat is joy? Answer. Joy is that form which represents the desired end. Where does joy naturally begin? Answer. Go to the aforementioned rubric. Does an orchard have joy, and fire that heats water? Answer, in the same place. Does a child have joy through sensing before through loving? Answer. In children, the imagination first receives delight through the senses, before the will or intellect through imagination, and this is because an infant at the beginning does not employ ancient moral principles.

*On Questions of sadness.*

XCIV.

**W**hat is sadness? Answer. Sadness is that figure which represents the loss of the desired end. Where does sadness naturally begin? Answer.

674 Question of a hundred forms.

Go to the aforesaid rubric. What is moral sadness about? Solution. Moral sadness is from the aforesaid definition. Why is a melancholic man naturally sadder than another man? Solution. No element is so remote from Saturn as earth: nor is any planet so near Saturn as Jupiter. And go to the aforesaid rubric.

*About Questions of Health.*

XCV.
What is health? Solution. Health is the proportion of conjoined parts in an elemental substance with greater concordance than contrariety. Where does health naturally begin? Solution. Go to the aforesaid rubric. What is the difference between natural health and moral health? Solution. Natural health is through form, and moral health through end, by reason of which natural health physicians are concerned. Why are men healthier in winter than in summer? Solution. **Question of the hundred forms. 675**

Solution. Substance is by itself formally and finally, so that substantial and accidental forms may have a subject in which they can exist, and from which they can act.

*On Questions of Essence.*

XCIX.

What is Essence? Solution. Essence is that form by reason of which being is sustained in a substantial or accidental concrete [thing], which being is indeed interchangeable with that concrete [thing] through existing and acting, and the act of essence remains sustained with it, and with the essence having one and the same nature, and in this passage there is much of Philosophy. How is Essence above substance? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric. What are the proper and principal parts of essence? Solution. The rational soul and the body joined with it are properly parts of humanity, and the simple 'bonifying', 'bonifiable', and 'to bonify' are parts of goodness. Of what is Essence? Solution. One essence is general and common, which is from several essences, just as humanity which is from the goodness of magnitude and other human forms: there are other special essences, which are under that general essence, and are of it, such as the essence of the rational soul and the essence of the human body.

*On Questions of Being.*

C.

What is Being? Solution. Being is a genus which is above everything that is of substantial and accidental nature. How is Being a general form? Solution. Go to the aforemen-

[Right Column]

tioned rubric. He who considers being, considers accident before substance. Solution. Accidental figures are windows of substantial being. How is Being investigable and discussable? Solution. Go to the rubric as above.

*On Questions of the Application &
Practice of the Hundred Forms,
which are at the end of the
Sensual Tree.*

In this passage we will give doctrine for making questions about the sensual tree through the hundred forms, and for solving those questions. And according to the method which we will hold concerning the hundred forms in the sensual tree, it can be held in other trees. By what nature is the sensitive power one, and is it of several things? Solution. Go to the aforementioned rubric, first paragraph. It is asked whether Peter, son of Martin, could be he who he is, and that Martin had never existed, and that Peter had been the son of William? Solution. According to the nature of numerical unity, Peter could not be he who he is, if Martin did not exist, with Peter being the son of William, because if it could be, the whole plurality of elementation, vegetation, and sensuality could thus agree with one as with another. Is the common sense simple or composite? Solution. It is simple according to the nature of the unity of the sensual tree, it is composite according to the sensual tree being from several causes, namely from the elementative, vegetative, and sensitive. And go to the rubric of virtue to the second paragraph. Is sight a simple or composite power? Solution. It is necessary that every particular be from that nature from which its universal is, for if it were not, it would not be a part of it.

Insofar as the sensitive faculty is about difference, it has its own nature of sensing diverse objects differently through species, and insofar as members and instruments are about difference, it is the appropriate nature of the sensitive faculty of members and instruments, that through it it may attain objects differently. And in this passage, there is much of Philosophy. How are nourishment and impression forms of sensation? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue to the thirtieth paragraph. Are insertion and self-subsistence parts of sensation? Solution there to the thirty-fourth paragraph. Can the sensitive faculty be by itself what it is? Solution. No form that is inserted in another can be by itself without the influence of that in which it is inserted. Are individuality and attraction parts of sensation? Solution. Go to the rubric of virtue to the thirty-fifth paragraph. In sensation, is there attraction from passion to action, and from action to passion? Solution. If air were to attract the heat of fire to itself, in that attraction the air would be the active form, and the fire the passive, and the fire would not give its heat to the air. In all passive forms of the common sense there is a distinction: because certain forms are internal, which with active forms are of the essence of sensation, and forms which are external are instruments, which are not of its essence nor of its species. In utterance, is there an act which is of the essence of utterance? Solution. Just as hearing is by touching, and that touch is in the species of hearing, although it is not of the essence of hearing, so utterance is by touch, although that touch is not of the species of utterance. Introductorium magnæ artis generalis

Insobriety.                                Hatred of neighbor.
Incontinence.                              Quarrelling.
Disobedience.                              Contradiction of mind.
Acting badly in heart.                     Anxious unrest.

B   Goodness is an entity by reason of which the good acts good: and thus good is being, and evil is non-being.
C   Magnitude is an entity by reason of which goodness or duration are the master of the encompassing extremity of being.
D   Eternity or duration is an entity by reason of which goodness, magnitude, etc. endure.
E   Power is an entity by reason of which goodness, magnitude, etc. can exist and act.
F   Wisdom is an entity by reason of which the wise one understands.
G   Will is an entity by reason of which goodness, magnitude, etc. are subject to the will.
H   Virtue is the origin of union, goodness, magnitude, in one good, great, etc.
I   Truth is that which is true concerning goodness, magnitude, etc.
K   Glory is the very delight in which goodness, magnitude, etc. rest.
    Difference is a property by reason of which goodness, power, etc. are clear and unconfused concepts.

  Sensual is said to be that being which feels, or can be felt by the senses, namely by seeing,
hearing: likewise as a stone & a tree, & any thing.
  Intellectual is that being which is spiritual by nature, such as God, Angel, rational
soul, etc.
  Cause is a principle by whose operation follows the caused, which is its effect.
  Effect is said to be that caused which has been brought into being by the operation of the cause.
  Efficient cause is that agent which effects or produces an effect: such as God who created the
world, etc.
  Material cause is that from which a thing is secondarily: such as the body in man, iron
in a knife.

--- Page 702 ---
Introductorium magnæ artis generalis

The formal cause is that through which a thing principally exists, and through it is preserved in its being, just as the rational soul in man, and the vegetative [soul] in a tree, etc.
The final cause is that for the sake of which a thing principally comes to be or is made, just as God who is the final cause of every creature, and the dwelling of a house, etc.
Substance is that which exists through itself and in itself: just as God, an Angel, man, etc.
Accident is that which does not exist through itself, nor in itself: just as whiteness, health, virtue, vice, knowledge, and there are nine kinds of accidents, namely of quantity, and of quality, etc.
Quantity is an accident through which beings are quantified, finite, and terminated, etc.
Quality is an accident through which beings are qualified or determined, just as grammatical quality.
Relation is that accident through which one being necessarily refers to another: as the relation of a master to a disciple, of a Father to a Son.
Action is the operation of an agent upon a patient, as a Lord upon a vassal, a hammer upon a nail.
Passion is the operation of a patient under an agent, as that which is heated under that which heats.
Habit is an accident by which a subject is invested, as whiteness in a white thing, knowledge in one who knows.
Position is the proper and ordered position of parts in a whole, and vice versa, as a roof on walls, and a beam in a house.
Time is an accident in which all beings begin, as the time of the world.
Place is an accident through which beings are placed and some are contained in others, as the place which any corporeal substance has.
The medium of conjunction is that which joins diverse things into one, just as a nail [joins] two posts.
The medium of measurement is that by which equals are measured, as by a point of a circle, other parts of the circle, etc.
The medium of extremities is that which exists between extremes: as a wall between a roof and a foundation.
The end of perfection is said to be that in which a thing is perfected, or that for the sake of which a thing was finally made: just as God who is the perfection of man, and man of his parts.
The end of termination is said to be the limit of a thing: as the limit of a kingdom, of a field, etc.
The end of privation is said to be the non-being in which a thing ends, or the non-being in which its being ends naturally, morally, civilly, artificially, as death, sin, disruption, etc.

Concerning the Nine General Subjects.

The nine aforesaid general subjects ought to be treated with four conditions, namely with definition, difference, concordance, and superiority. With definition, namely, that each subject may have its own proper definition with which it may be known and differ from any other. With difference, namely, that the difference which is between one subject and another, be preserved. With superiority, namely, according as one subject is higher and nobler, let higher and nobler principles, and definitions of rules and their species, be attributed to it than to any other, by following and preserving the definition of difference in concordance and superiority, as has been said.
In irrational sensible beings

--- Page 703 ---
**Raymund Lull.**

...in irrational, sensible beings, instinct is placed in the stead of wisdom, appetite in the stead of will, and delight for glory, recollection in the stead of memory.

**Of the first subject, which is God**

**G**od is that being in whom goodness, greatness, eternity, etc., His dignities are one and the same in number, and God is that being who has in Himself all completeness, and needs nothing outside Himself. God is goodness, greatness, eternity, etc., His dignities without contrariety, superiority, and inferiority.
Man can treat of God through ten general questions, asking or investigating, whether God, what God, concerning what God, etc., following the four aforementioned conditions, affirming all perfection in God, and denying or removing every defect.

**Of Angels.**

**A**n Angel is a created intellectual substance, more similar to God in nature and simplicity than any other creature: in an angel there is essential and natural goodness, greatness, duration, etc., contrariety excepted. And it can be treated through ten questions, asking whether an Angel. What an Angel, etc., following the four conditions already stated.

**Of Heaven.**

**H**eaven is that body which has a more extended greatness than any other body.
Heaven has essential goodness, greatness, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without contrariety. And it can be treated through ten questions, asking whether heaven, etc., following the four aforementioned conditions.

**Of Man.**

**M**an is a sensible and intellectual substance, or is an animal that humanizes, or to which it properly belongs to humanize. Man has natural, essential goodness and greatness, etc., in two ways, namely sensible and intellectual, because he is composed of a rational soul and a body.
And the rational soul is the intellectual form informing the very body of man, giving it human being and preserving it in the human species. And he essentially has three powers, namely memory, intellect, and will, with which he does whatever he does.
And the body of man is constituted from the elementary, vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative [principles], moved to its operations by the aforementioned form. And it can be treated through ten questions, investigating concerning man by 'whether', 'what', 'concerning what', etc., following the conditions already stated.

**Of the Imaginative [Faculty].**

**T**he imaginative [faculty] is a power, or part of the animal, by which the animal itself imagines those things which have been presented to it by the bodily senses: and it has essential and natural goodness, greatness, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without essential contrariety. And it has three co-essential powers, namely the instinctive, the appetitive, and the recollective. And it can be known by asking concerning it through 'whether', 'what', 'concerning what', etc., following

--- Page 704 ---
Introductorium to the Great General Art

**About the Sensitive.**

The Sensitive is a power with which an animal perceives sensible things, namely visible things, audible things, etc. And it has essential and natural goodness, greatness, etc. And it can be known by inquiring about it through 'whether', 'what', 'about what', etc. And it has six particular senses, namely sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell, and savor, in which it is diversified: and similarly, its essential principles and its particular ones ought to be treated with the four conditions.

**About the Vegetative.**

The Vegetative is a power through which transmutation naturally occurs from one substance into another, such as from rain into a plant, and from food into flesh, etc. And it has essential and natural goodness, greatness, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without essential contrariety. It also has four powers with which it naturally operates, namely the appetitive, through which it desires to attract to the subject; through the retentive, it retains; through the digestive, it digests what is retained; through the expulsive, it expels that which is not suitable for the subject. And it can be treated concerning itself with ten questions, namely 'whether', 'what', etc., following the aforesaid four conditions.

**About the Elementative.**

The Elementative is a natural being, or a power in the elements, through which elements enter into composition, and exist so that they may act in those elements which are composed of them. The elements are four, namely fire, air, water, earth. Fire is hot and dry, light and luminous. Air is humid, hot, light, diaphanous. Water is ponderous, cold, humid, white. Earth is dry and cold, ponderous, and black. The Elementative has goodness, greatness, etc., with contrariety by reason of the elements which are contrary through their proper and appropriate qualities. It can be investigated by ten general questions, namely 'whether', 'what', 'about what', and so concerning any elementative thing, of which each has its own proper essential and natural goodness, greatness, etc. And it can be treated with ten general questions following the aforesaid four conditions.

**About the Instrumentative.**

The Instrumentative is a power, or a habit, through which non-natural works are made, such as artificial things and the like: and it contains three species, namely moralities, liberal arts, and other sciences, and mechanical arts. In the Instrumentative there is goodness, greatness, etc., in its own way in general, and each of its species has goodness, greatness, etc., differing from another according as they are different among themselves. The General Artist treats of the Instrumentative generally and specially with ten questions, and the same applies to its species, because they are contained in it and under it, and also concerning anything contained under anything, always regulating the aforesaid four general conditions, which are definition, difference, concordance, and superiority.

**Introduction to the Great General Art**

[Left Column]
...sole essence which is its very own goodness, magnitude, etc.
Pure simplicity in creatures: something is called simple in which there is one by its number, or by respect to another, such as an Angel, soul, fire, simple.
Composition is an aggregation of multiple essences in something composed of many, such as man who is composed of body and rational soul: and like an elementate from four elements, and created substance from matter and form.
Form is an essential principle, by which action primarily consists.
Matter is an essential principle, to which passivity properly belongs, and by reason of it, composite substance is passive.
Body is a substance having length, breadth and depth: such as a stone, tree, etc.
There are six directions of bodies, namely up, down, front, back, right, left.
A point is the smallest part of a body.
A line is a certain length drawn out, composed of multiple continuous points, whose extremities are two points.
A sphere is a proper place which every element seeks, such as fire upwards, earth downwards. A celestial sphere is called a circle in which the signs and planets are situated.
Reason is the light of the intellect for knowing the realities of things.
Vacuum is that object in which no entity is considered. Plenum is the converse.
Universal is that being which contains many particulars within itself. Particular is the opposite.
Property is a being with which an agent acts specifically: such as an animal, a plant.

[Right Column]
Transformation is an act naturally occurring in the transformed thing, the old form being stripped away, and a new form being put on.
Alteration is a change from one quality to another, the substance remaining the same: such as wine into vinegar, health into sickness, virtue into vice.
Generation is a natural operation, by which that which is in potency naturally exists in act, causing a new form.
An angle is a part of a figure in which the ends of the lines meet acutely or directly.
Figure is an accident constituted from the position of lines, and the disposition of the surface or colors.
There are three general figures: namely triangular, quadrangular, and circular.
A triangular figure is one which has three acute angles, contained by three lines.
A quadrangular figure is one having four right or oblique angles, contained by four lines.
A circle is a figure, contained by a single circular line.
A surface is the upper extremity of a body, in which its color appears.
Instinct is a principle by which natural beings are regulated to their natural operations according to their species and nature: such as fire, and an animal, and it is a likeness of the intellect.
Appetite is a principle by which natural beings desire that which is proper to them, namely their nature, such as fire to ascend, man to drink, to eat, and it is a likeness of the will.
Motion is a principle by which moving beings move movable things to some fire, and it is twofold, namely natural and artificial or violent motion. There are six natural ones: namely generation, corruption,

...ruption, augmentation, diminution, alte-
ration, and change of place.
   Corruption is a natural operation, by
which that which is in actuality is in privation,
corrupting the old form, namely that by
which the corrupted thing was in its actual
being.
   Privation is a middle between genera-
tion and corruption, by which being passes
with non-being: these three general principles
are in three things by which the course of
nature is sustained in generable and
corruptible things, namely in elements,
plants, and animals.
   Infinity is a being without end and
measure. And it is threefold, namely in magni-
tude, duration, and number. Infinity
of magnitude is immensity. Infinity
of duration is eternity. Infinity
of number is with respect to the one numbering,
which does not reach the limit of number,
although the numbered thing itself may have a finite
number.
   Comprehension is a likeness of finitude
and apprehension: just as by tasting, he
who tastes apprehends the salty sea.
   Capacity is a form, by which the ca-
pable can comprehend and attain
comprehensible beings through itself.
   Existence is the essence of a being that
exists. Agency is the being of acting, but to
act is the act of an existing thing, just as to make
hot is for the hot thing: to do good is for the good thing.
   Potency is that which with its act
relates to an object: just as sight with
seeing, hearing with hearing, and there are in
man ten natural powers: namely
hearing, sight, taste, touch, smell,
speech, imagination, memory, intellect,
and will, to which consequently
correspond ten modes of objects. In
another way, potency is taken for a being
that is not yet, but can be, as knowledge
in the intellect, fruit in a tree.

[Column 2]

   An object is that being which is ap-
prehended by a power: just as flavor
by taste.
   Act is the work of a power, with which
the object is taken up by the power: as
seeing for sight: similarly, act is twofold,
first when a being is in being, second
for its acting.
   Immobility is the property of an
immobile being which has no desire
to move itself: just as God who is an
immobile being, since He is an eternal
and infinite being, having His perfec-
tion eternally and infinitely in Himself.
   Succession is a change from one
to another through motion.
   Attraction is an act of power, which
desires to attract something according to its
nature and the property of the attractor
and the attracted: as a magnet (attracts) iron,
theriac (attracts) poison.
   Reception follows attraction rela-
tively.
   Signification is the revelation of secrets,
demonstrated with a sign.
   Novelty is a being, by which a subject
is habituated with new habits, or a new
quantity.
   Monstrosity is a deviation of the motion
of nature from beginning to end, through
superabundance or great deficiency,
as six fingers, or only four,
and thence it is called a monster.
   Color is a quality perceived by figure,
and there are four general colors,
namely luminosity, diaphaneity, whiteness,
blackness.
   Shadow is a quality deprived of light
or illumination, and it is a quality of air
darkened by opposition to the earth.
   Necessity is that being which cannot
be otherwise. A necessary thing is that which
can in no way be avoided.
   A contingent thing is that which comes
without necessity, and it is twofold, namely
simple and ne...

[Column 1]

& necessary. Simple contingent is that which is in no way necessary, like being a craftsman. Necessary contingent is the future necessity of one of two contradictories, such as Peter being saved or damned.
Fortune is an accident encountered without the intention of the fortunate one.
Occasion is a thing which has an intention towards those things which can happen, such as a man putting wood into a fire so that it may be burned is the occasion of burning: a doctor of health.
Definition is a certain and express manifestation of a thing and its properties.
Question is an unknown request, through which the powers of the soul are extended so that they may rest in their actions, and it occurs in ten ways in the interrogative, namely by whether, what, concerning what, why, how much, of what kind, when, where, how, with whom.
Obstinacy is an excessive action of memory and will concerning an object, through which the intellect stands firm by the affirmation of the false against the true negation: as concerning vice and love.
Opinion is a supposition or belief about something with doubt.
Supposition is a certain confusion established concerning the possibility of affirmation and its contrary negation, so that truth may be found by investigating.
Demonstration is a manifestation of the unknown by the known, or of the less known by the more known. And it occurs in three ways, namely by what (or by cause), by why (or by effect), and by equivalence. First: just as the Sun is, therefore day is; second: day is, therefore the Sun is; third: just as divine goodness is infinite and eternal, therefore divine power is man, because God's goodness and man's are equal.
Or demonstration is a necessary or consequent apprehension of some particular position or privation pro-

[Column 2]

ceeding from a necessary or convenient position, or from an impossible privation of definitions and properties of universal principles and distinctions, and rules of the general art.
Preaching is an art, with which the preacher informs the people to have good morals and to avoid bad ones.
Transcendent point is an instrument of the human intellect with which it reaches its object according to the natures of the lower powers, and reaches the supreme object above its own nature.
Or transcendent point is the height or difficulty of the reality of the object, implying a contradiction in potency, because that very potency by its own nature cannot fully reach it.
Idea in God is a being or object eternally producing things in time through divine wisdom, and this Idea in God is God Himself.
Idea in time is a likeness of the eternal Idea, and such an Idea or likeness in a creature is created.
Predestination in divine wisdom is an act which understands men eternally elected with justice for salvation, and this predestination in God is the Idea which is God. Predestination is an act of divine wisdom which understands those to be reprobated with justice for damnation, and in God it is the Idea which is God.
Liberty is an intellectual property given to a rational creature, so that it may freely love good and avoid evil. Free will is that in the rational soul by which it freely moves itself to good or evil by loving or hating, by accepting or rejecting. And it is twofold, namely speculative when it will or will not do what is deliberated, and practical when the choice has been made.

to pronounce, and to write fittingly and correctly.
   Medicine is the science teaching how to preserve health, or to restore what has been lost, according to the possibility of nature in a sentient body.
   Morality is a habit outside of nature by which someone is disposed to do good or evil through virtues or vices.

   Politics is the art with which citizens manage the public welfare of the city,
   Preaching is the art with which a preacher informs the people to have good morals and to avoid bad ones.

*The proper principles of each science according to its proper subject follow.*

*And first concerning Theology.*

God is the subject in Theology, and is called the subject because all things that Theology itself treats are directed to giving knowledge of God. The end of Theology is to know God and to love, honor, praise, and serve Him, and with Theology itself to use virtues against vices to attain perpetual blessedness. The principles of Theology are divine essence, life, dignities, acts, form, relation, ordination, action, articles, precepts, exposition, first intention, second intention.

**[Right Column]**

*Concerning Philosophy.*

The delight of knowing is the subject in Philosophy; the end is to know the first cause and secrets. The effects of the principles are the first cause, motion, intelligence, orb, universal form, prime matter, nature, elements, simples, appetite, potency, habit, act, mixture, digestion, composition, alteration.

*Concerning the division of Philosophy.*

Philosophy is divided into three parts, because it is natural, another moral, another sermocinal: natural is the science ha

the science considering speech, of which there are three

### Of Law.

Justice is the subject in law, the end [is] that
among peoples there be peace & concord, & that
God be served with purity & honesty.
The principles are to love God, to live
honestly, to render to each what is his own.
To love God is a principle for
using virtues & avoiding vices:
to render to each what is his own is a principle
for satisfying God Himself regarding oneself,
oneself regarding oneself, one's neighbor
regarding oneself.
Or the principles of law are these: form,
matter, general law, common, spe-
cial, natural, positive, canon,
civil, customary, Rhetorical,
practical, military, comparative,
ancient, new.

### Of Medicine.

Health is the subject in medicine:
the end [is] that the sentient body may be able to
have its operations, which are suitable for it:
the principles are three, namely natural things,
non-natural things, [and things] contrary to nature.
Natural things are seven, namely ali-
ments, complexions, humors, members,
faculty, operations, kinds & four
things annexed to the aforesaid are, age, color,
figure, difference between male & fe-
male. Non-natural things are ten,
namely food, air, drink, sound, wakefulness,
exercise, action, repletion, inanition,
accidents of the soul. Things contrary to nature
are three, namely disease, cause, acci-
dent.

### Of Geometry.

Immovable continuous quantity is
the subject in Geometry, the end [is]
to know the lengths, widths,
& depths of corporeal things:
the principles are ten, namely point,
line, angle, figure, quantity,
center, capacity, length, width,
depth.

### Of Astronomy.

Movable continuous quantity, or
celestial influence, is the subject
in Astronomy: the end [is] to know the virtues
& motions which the heavens effectively have in
lower things: the principles are the
signs [and] planets. The Signs are twelve:
Aries, Taurus, Gemini,
Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio,
Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius,
Pisces. The Planets are seven: namely
Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sol (Sun), Ve-
nus, Mercury, Luna (Moon).

### Of Arithmetic.

Absolute number is the subject
in Arithmetic: the end [is] by numbering
to sum many units, & to retain them more
easily by number. The principles are
parity, imparity (evenness, oddness): numbers are three, namely
articulate number, digit, composite number. The spe-
cies (kinds) of number are ten: numeration,
addition, subtraction, mediation (halving), duplica-
tion, multiplication, division: progression,
extraction of roots, squares, &
extraction of cubic roots.

### Of Music.

The concordance of voices or melo-
dy is the subject in music, the end

TTtt 2

--- Page 714 ---
Introductorium magnæ artis generalis

the harmony or melody of voices is the subject in music; its purpose is, by harmonizing different voices, to produce delight in song. The principles are ten, namely: pitch, infinity, mediocrity, length, brevity, fullness, lightness, subtlety, proportion, and the accent of vowels and consonants.

### De Grammatica.

The correctness and rectitude of speaking is the subject in Grammar: its purpose is to speak, pronounce, and write correctly and properly. The principles are the letter, syllable, sentence, word or the eight parts of speech, or the agreement of the substantive and adjective, of the subject, appositive, relative and antecedent, and the modes of signifying.

### De Logica.

Arguments, or the signification of argumentative reasoning, is the subject in Logic: for its purpose, by arguing, is that truth and falsehood may be found, and one distinguished from the other. The principles are, term, proposition.

### De Rhetorica.

The order and beauty of words is the subject in Rhetoric: its purpose, through ordered and beautiful words, is to move the will of the listener to some desired end. The principles are, form, matter, end: the parts are five, namely, invention, disposition, elocution, memory, and delivery.

Since general science has principles and questions and general rules for all arts and sciences, and for every particular contained within them, and the unity of art or science is revealed in the general art by following its process: just as the particular in its universal, inquiring into goodness, magnitude, etc., and inquiring about it through 'whether', 'what', 'about what', etc., and therefore the general art itself is a mirror for the human intellect in which the truths of all knowable things shine forth and appear. The purpose of speculative science is truth, that of practical science, action.

[Circular library stamp with a palm branch: BIBLIOTHEQUE DE L'ARSENAL]

THE END.
